item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on meeting Fedor Emelianenko | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"保温杯里的冠军哲学"——被忽略的最强隐喻

大多数人听这段访谈会记住"Fedor击败巨人"的画面，但真正的信号藏在那个保温杯里。2004年，一个正在统治世界的Pride重量级冠军，跑到达吉斯坦地方赛去打比赛，打完一场，走回后台，倒茶、就着蜂蜜、慢慢喝——然后再上场。

这不是"放松"，这是一种拒绝仪式化紧张的姿态。绝大多数顶级运动员会在场边用音乐、跺脚、拍脸、嘶吼来"进入状态"，把自己的神经系统调到高频；Fedor 反其道而行——他用日常动作稀释比赛的重量，让"打Pride冠军战"和"在家喝茶"处于同一个能量层级。Khabib 15岁的记忆里最强烈的画面不是拳头，而是茶壶，这本身就说明：真正的威慑力来自把非凡场景当作平常事的能力。

二、跨领域连接：Fedor的"幼儿园老师脸"与日本能剧的"面"

Khabib提到俄罗斯圈子里开玩笑说 Fedor "长得像幼儿园老师"，然后他一拳KO巨人。这个对比让我想起日本能剧的"中间面"（中間面）——那种表面上无表情、微微下垂、看起来温和的木刻面具。能剧大师会告诉你：越是"无表情"的面，越能承载复杂情绪。观众必须自己把恐惧、悲伤、愤怒投射上去。

Fedor 的脸就是格斗界的"中间面"。他不给对手任何情绪坐标——你看不到愤怒（可以对抗），看不到恐惧（可以利用），看不到快乐（可以打断）。这种"空"是一种心理战武器：对手在这张空白的脸上读到的一切，都是他自己内心投射出来的怪物。这就是为什么Khabib说"他用冷静征服了很多人的头脑"——不是Fedor做了什么，而是对手在这面空白镜子前吓到了自己。

三、意料之外的观察：Khabib其实在承认自己"不如"Fedor

整段话里最微妙、也最少被注意的一点是——Khabib 主动划了一条线："我认为Fedor在气质上比我更平静。That's my impression."

一个从未败绩、无可挑剔的传奇冠军，在自己的播客里、面对全球观众，主动承认另一个人在某个维度上超越自己。这在顶级运动员中极其罕见。这里藏着一个反常识的真相：真正的强者不需要争"谁最强"，因为他们知道"最强"是个多维空间。

更深一层——Khabib 说"内心沸腾，表面冷静"，然后又说 Fedor "内心可能真的就没有沸腾"。这两种"冷"是完全不同的技术路径： - Khabib 的冷 = 控制（emotional regulation，需要能量） - Fedor 的冷 = 本质（emotional flatness，天生结构）

这就像古典音乐里两种极端：一种是Argerich那样把狂暴压进指尖的爆发力；另一种是Michelangeli那种从骨子里就克制的冰冷。听众常以为它们是同一种"高级"，其实是两种完全相反的神经系统解决同一个问题。Khabib 敏锐地识别出了这个差别，并诚实地承认——自己走的是"控制路径"，而Fedor走的是"结构路径"。

四、最后的钩子

Fedor那句名言"能打败我的只有我自己"被引用了无数次，但Khabib给出了这句话真正的技术解读："主要的比赛是先跟自己比。你先打败自己，然后才真正开始跟对手比。"

这句话可以直接搬进创业、写作、投资——任何一个"表面上你在跟外部竞争，实际上你在跟自己的恐惧、贪婪、走神做搏斗"的领域。Fedor 和 Khabib 不是在描述格斗，他们是在描述所有高压表现的底层物理定律。

📝 转录文本

关于Fedor：不得不问的那个人

Well, I have to ask about Fedor. What can you say about him? He had some legendary fights. He beat Cro Cop, Big Nog, Mark Coleman.

Yeah, and Kevin Randleman. And then, he had those legendary fights with the Japanese fighters who were big stars over there. Man, I loved it. Honestly, he inspired me just by the fact that he was from Russia, and he was a fighter. He was closer to our school of training combat.

2004年，达吉斯坦：Pride冠军来打地方赛

And there was this moment, back in 2004, the Dagestan combat championship. Can you imagine? 2004, the Dagestan combat championship, and Fedor showed up. He showed up. He came to compete in the Dagestan open combat championship while being the reigning Pride champion.

I was 15 years old at the time. I was right there in the venue. My father actually invited him. He was sending out invitations to different schools back then. It was Stary Oskol, where he used to train. Fedor's coaches were sent an invitation. He came with his brother Alexander. They both made it to the finals back then.

I just remember — $5,000, $3,000, $1,000. First, second, third place. At heavyweight, they gave a car. When the two brothers arrived, they beat everyone to get to the finals. They didn't fight each other. One of them took first place, that was Fedor. Alexander took second place.

那个保温杯：15岁少年的近距离观察

I remember back then, when he was warming up, I was standing next to him while he warmed up. It was this building, you know, a venue that fits maybe 1,500 people, and over there was this partition, like a wall, and everyone was warming up behind that wall.

At that time, well, practically very few people even knew who Fedor was, but I knew Fedor. I knew who he was, that he was the Pride champion. At that time, he beat Nogueira, beat Mark Coleman, beat Randleman. This was before his championship fight against Cro Cop.

I would come over and just sit there, watching how he warmed up, what he did. I just remember very well — I don't know, maybe Fedor will see this podcast — he had a thermos.

[laughter]

He had a thermos and he was just drinking tea. And I remember he fought Ibrahim Magomedov. He was also a legendary fighter of ours, a heavyweight who fought in Pride, too. He fought against him. It was either his first or second fight.

热身细节：连鼻子和耳朵都要热身

And he was warming up incredibly well. I remember how he was warming up his nose and his ears. I watched him and it was unusual for me at that time. I never warmed up my nose and ears. I just — I just remember how Fedor was really working on his nose, his ears, his whole face.

And he went, fought, came back. This was in Makhachkala, 2004. It's the same as a UFC champion now coming and fighting at the Dagestan Combat Championship. Can you imagine that? Back then, it was the best heavyweight organization in the world. He comes there and fights.

So, he finished a fight, goes back, and he had this big thermos with him. His team was sitting separately over there.

[sighs]

Uh — he was drinking tea. He just fought, walked back, poured some tea, and drank it. He had something to snack on with it, maybe honey or something. I just don't remember. And I was, "Wow, Fedor is right here." For me, that was just such a, you know, great source of motivation back then. It's really hard to put those emotions into words.

想问Fedor：茶里到底放了什么？

By the way, maybe you could ask him about that on the podcast.

Uh — about the thermos?

No, no. About the tea, what was in it? Thyme, mint? What did he put in there?

Uh, well, I would love to talk to him on this podcast, but I think he rarely does interviews.

I think you can reach him. I can help you.

Well, if you could put in a good word for me.

Yeah, of course. I think it would be interesting for people to hear him.

Absolutely.

冷静的气场：像幼儿园老师，却KO巨人

Yeah. But psychologically, he's kind of like you in a way.

You mean calm?

Yeah.

Yes, that calmness. You see the Pride era, those huge fights, those really tough matchups, and still he always stayed calm.

It's his aura. Yeah. I don't know about others, but for me that was his aura. The fact that he'd come out with such a calm, cool-headed look, and knock out giants, strong fighters at that time, right?

Yeah.

You know, we used to joke about his face that he — uh — kind of looks like a kindergarten teacher, you know? And then he goes out there and knocks out absolute giants.

And he was like that. Both before and after the fight, he never showed much emotion. But I think we're a little different in that regard. I think Fedor by temperament is calmer than I am. That's my impression. But with that cold-blooded calmness of his, I think he got to a lot of people mentally.

内心沸腾与表面冷静：两种不同的"冷"

It's like something's happening inside both of you. Like something's boiling inside. So, when we look at your face —

of course it's boiling. What do you think?

You know what? It's one thing when it's boiling inside and you show it, but there are some who can't hide their feelings.

[gasps]

But, it's a different thing when it's boiling inside and on the surface you stay cold, cold-blooded, calm, and you can handle all these different emotions that hit you at the same time. There are a lot of them, and they all hit differently.

顶级运动员的独特之处：同时处理多种情绪

When you compete, what makes a fighter and athlete at the highest level so unique is that so many different emotions hit you at the same time. Fear, nerves, the fact that people are watching you, the thought that you might perform badly, that you might not show what you've trained for, that you might mess it up, that you might, I don't know, fall.

So much enters your head, and you can put each emotion where it belongs. So, you know, if all of that gets inside your head and turns into chaos, you won't be able to handle it emotionally. But, you stay cold-blooded. And you know that if you don't handle these emotions that are coming at you, if you don't handle this pressure, then it will be difficult for you to compete, because the main competition is against yourself first.

You fight yourself, you beat yourself, and only then do you actually start competing with your opponent. So, I think it happens to everyone, not just him or me. The big difference here is how much you can control it.

Fedor 的名言：能打败我的只有我自己

Fedor himself famously said, "The only person who can defeat me is me. The only person who can beat me is me."

He was talking about that fight with yourself, I'm sure. Because if you lose to yourself, then you'll lose to your opponent very easily.

Mhm.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib and Islam speak different languages - Dagestan has 30+ languages | Khabib Nurmagomedov
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、语言的"不可通约性"：一种被低估的文明基础设施

最令人意外的观察是：Khabib 和 Islam 作为师徒、兄弟、同乡，日常竟然"根本听不懂彼此的母语"。这不是方言差异，而是两套完全独立的语言系统（Avar 与 Kumyk/Lak 语族分属完全不同的语系）。他们能并肩训练二十多年、共同征服 UFC，靠的其实是第三方语言（俄语）作为"中立协议层"。

这颠覆了我们对"团队亲密度"的常识——通常我们认为"共享母语"是信任的前提，但达吉斯坦的案例揭示：当没有人能强迫他人使用自己的母语时，反而催生出一种更平等的沟通契约。这与硅谷早期工程师文化异曲同工——正因为大家母语各异，英语作为"降级过的通用协议"反而促成了更快的协作。

二、跨领域连接：达吉斯坦是"生物多样性"的语言学镜像

30+ 种语言挤在一个略大于苏格兰的地区——这个密度在全球仅有巴布亚新几内亚、亚马逊河上游可比。有趣的是，这三个地方有一个共同的物理特征：地形极度破碎（高加索山脉、热带雨林、山地部落）。

这里藏着一个跨学科的"啊哈时刻"：语言多样性遵循的是生态学中的"岛屿生物地理学"定律。每一个山谷就是一个"进化孤岛"，语言像加拉帕戈斯的雀鸟一样各自演化。Khabib 一句轻描淡写的"我们有 30 多种语言"，实际上在陈述一个地理学、进化生物学、认知科学交汇的深层规律。

更反直觉的是：格斗冠军的密集产出与语言的高度碎片化，可能共享同一个根源。当每个村庄都必须自我防御、每一次跨谷通婚都需要谈判与力量证明时，"身体语言"（摔跤、khash 摔法）就成了唯一超越语言隔阂的通用协议。MMA 冠军之乡的秘密，或许写在语言地图上，而不是训练馆里。

三、隐藏的系统真相：文化"消化力"决定文明韧性

Khabib 提到达吉斯坦"吸收了很多文化和信仰"——伊斯兰是主流，但饮食里同时能看到欧洲、亚洲、高加索的层叠痕迹。这是一个值得放大的系统性观察：

一个地区能在 1500 年里保留 30 多种语言而不被同化，同时又"消化"了无数外来元素——这需要一种极特殊的文化代谢机制：吸收营养但保留骨架。

与之形成鲜明对比的是许多"熔炉型"文明（比如美国的 Melting Pot 隐喻）——它们通过同质化换取效率。而达吉斯坦走的是另一条路：分布式冗余的文明架构。用软件工程的话说，这是"微服务架构"对"单体架构"——每个山谷是一个独立服务，故障不会蔓延，但系统整体依然能对外接口。

这或许解释了一个更深的悖论：为什么在全球化最凶猛的今天，这些"看似落后"的碎片化文化区反而展现出惊人的输出能力（顶级格斗手、独特音乐、独立的道德叙事）。碎片化不是弱点，而是一种反脆弱的战略储备。

📝 转录文本

语言的多样性

We have so many languages — more than 30 different languages — and people just don't understand each other.

Take Islam and me: we have different languages, come from different backgrounds. Islam is Lak and I'm an Avar. When we talk, it's not like it's a dialect — we don't understand each other at all. But since Islam has been with us for nearly 25 years, he actually picked up some Avar over time.

历史的印记

But anyway, the deep history of the region — it all left its mark. It created many different languages and traditions.

Basically, of course, Islam is our primary religion, but Dagestan has actually absorbed a lot of cultures and faiths. Even our food culture, it is incredibly rich: we have European, and Asian, and Caucasian — our own unique cuisine.

独一无二的达吉斯坦

So on the people themselves, the last 1,500 years of history have left a huge mark.

If you're into history and you start reading about Dagestan, I think you'll get completely immersed and be amazed by what a unique place it is.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] How Nuclear Will Unlock Energy Abundance with Valar Atomics Founder Isaiah Taylor
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：核能行业的"模拟陷阱"——一个跨行业的隐蔽病理

Isaiah 说了一句非常锋利的话："大多数核能公司其实是建模仿真公司。" 这不只是对核工业的批评，而是揭示了一种普遍的组织病理——当一个行业因监管或恐惧而无法迭代真实硬件时，它会退化成一个"论文工业"。

有趣的跨领域连接：这与生物医药行业的"临床前动物模型工业"惊人相似。药企养了成千上万只小鼠，产出无数漂亮的机制论文，但真正让新药通过 FDA 的成功率却低于 10%。同样的病理也出现在自动驾驶——多年来 Waymo 之外的公司大都在"模拟里数亿英里"，但真实道路的边角案例才是决定性的。当反馈周期被切断，任何行业都会用"复杂性"替代"真实性"，因为复杂性可以被作者控制，而真实世界不能。

Valor 真正的哲学突破不是核物理，而是重新恢复"tick rate"作为组织的第一性度量——这个词借自游戏引擎，暗示了一件让人意外的事：Isaiah 把核反应堆公司当成了一个实时游戏系统在设计。

洞察二："事故概率" vs "事故后果"——一个被误用了半个世纪的心智模型

传统核能安全的整个哲学是降低事故发生概率（odds）；Valor 的哲学是降低事故后果（consequence）。这两者在数学上是等价的风险控制手段，但在组织行为学上完全不同。

出人意料的观察：追求"低概率"会让组织变慢，追求"低后果"会让组织变快。因为降低概率需要无穷的冗余、审查、模拟、防御性工程，每一层都会滋生官僚化和责任回避；而降低后果只需要在架构层做一次正确的物理选择（TRISO 燃料 + 石墨慢化 + 氦冷却 + 被动散热几何），之后组织可以自由地快速迭代。

这是一个非常深的元规律：你在设计上把"最坏情况"处理好了，你在流程上就可以放开了。 这个原则不仅适用于核能，它解释了： - SpaceX 为什么敢炸火箭（可回收 + 无人驾驶 = 最坏后果被架构消除） - Netflix 为什么敢在生产环境放 Chaos Monkey（微服务架构本身容忍失败） - 加密协议为什么可以开源审计（密码学保证最坏情况的安全边界）

"架构上的悲观主义"是"执行上的乐观主义"的前提。 这几乎是所有能高速迭代的高风险系统的共同秘密。

洞察三：能源是"一切成本的极限"——AI + 机器人正在把这个哲学论点变成会计事实

Isaiah 最后那个"麦克风思想实验"看似漫谈，但藏着一个可能重塑二十一世纪经济学的观察：当 AI 和机器人把"人力"这一输入项转换为"能源"时，能源就变成了所有物品成本的渐近极限。

传统经济学的三大生产要素——土地、劳动、资本——正在被悄悄地归约为一个单一变量：焦耳。土地是能量场的空间承载；劳动是热力学做功；资本是过去凝结的能量。当机器人可以替代几乎所有物理劳动时，边际成本函数会退化成一条纯能源曲线。

跨领域的意外连接：这与信息论中的朗道尔极限（Landauer's limit）在哲学上是同构的——擦除一比特信息的最小能量代价是 kT ln 2。物理学告诉我们，信息、计算、制造，最终都是能量的不同形态。Valor 押注的不是"更便宜的电"，而是"把整个文明的成本函数压缩到一个变量上"——一旦这件事发生，那么"能源便宜 10 倍"意味着 "GDP 便宜 10 倍"，这是一个远超普通商业机会的赌注。

最让人意外的暗示：如果 Isaiah 的世界观成立，那么"AI 竞赛"和"能源竞赛"其实是同一场竞赛，只是从对偶的两端逼近同一个瓶颈。谁先把"能源单位成本"打下一个数量级，谁就先获得了下一个文明台阶的入场券——而这个洞察，恰恰是大多数 AI 公司和大多数能源公司都还没真正内化的。

Uh because if we're going to go explore the stars and we're going to set up, you know, a place for us to live on Mars and explore the universe, we're going to need a lot of stuff and it's going to be it's going to need to be a lot cheaper than it is right now. So that's very exciting to me.

Exciting to me, too. That's a great place to end. Thanks, Isaiah.

Thanks so much for having me.

结语

Find us on Twitter at No Priors Pod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. That way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-briers.com.

item.description:
## 洞察一：核能行业的"模拟陷阱"——一个跨行业的隐蔽病理
Isaiah 说了一句非常锋利的话："大多数核能公司其实是建模仿真公司。" 这不只是对核工业的批评，而是揭示了一种普遍的组织病理——**当一个行业因监管或恐惧而无法迭代真实硬件时，它会退化成一个"论文工业"**。
有趣的跨领域连接：这与生物医药行业的"临床前动物模型工业"惊人相似。药企养了成千上万只小鼠，产出无数漂亮的机制论文，但真正让新药通过 FDA 的成功率却低于 10%。同样的病理也出现在自动驾驶——多年来 Waymo 之外的公司大都在"模拟里数亿英里"，但真实道路的边角案例才是决定性的。**当反馈周期被切断，任何行业都会用"复杂性"替代"真实性"**，因为复杂性可以被作者控制，而真实世界不能。
Valor 真正的哲学突破不是核物理，而是**重新恢复"tick rate"作为组织的第一性度量**——这个词借自游戏引擎，暗示了一件让人意外的事：Isaiah 把核反应堆公司当成了一个实时游戏系统在设计。
## 洞察二："事故概率" vs "事故后果"——一个被误用了半个世纪的心智模型
传统核能安全的整个哲学是**

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on Dana White: He is a cold-blooded businessman | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"冷血"不是缺陷，而是一种基础设施

多数人把 Dana White 的"cold-blooded"理解为性格特质，但 Khabib 在无意间揭示了一个更深的结构性真相：冷血本质上是一种"决策带宽"。当一个组织的领导者能够把"人际关系"从"业务判断"中彻底剥离，他实际上是把自己变成了一台不会因情感噪音而降频的处理器。这不是道德问题，而是信息论问题——情感耦合越多，决策熵越高，长期系统就越难维持一致性。

有意思的是，Khabib 引用了"黑帮电影里家族至上"的比喻，但这里出现了一个反直觉的置换：Dana 的"家族"不是人，而是品牌本身。UFC 这个抽象实体被拟人化为"家人"，而具体的血肉之躯（包括冠军、员工、朋友）反而被降级为"业务变量"。这是一种极其罕见的忠诚对象的抽象化转移——很多创业者做不大，恰恰是因为他们效忠的仍是具体的人。

二、被忽略的悖论：UFC 的"品牌免疫力"来自它敢于让单场比赛失败

Khabib 说了一句几乎所有人都会滑过去、但极其关键的话："即便某场比赛不成功，UFC 还是 UFC。"

这是一个隐藏的反脆弱结构。传统体育联盟（尤其是欧洲足球俱乐部、传统拳击推广公司）的品牌价值高度依赖"每一场都要精彩"，一旦砸了就动摇根基。而 UFC 反其道而行：它把"品牌"从"单一产品质量"中解耦出来，让品牌成为一种"入场券资格"而非"质量承诺"。

这里可以做一个跨领域的连接：这正是苹果 App Store 的逻辑，也是米其林指南的逻辑——策展平台的品牌力，来自"我在场"而不是"这一场很好"。UFC 30 年做到别的体育 100 年才达到的高度，秘诀可能不是"办了多少好比赛"，而是成功地让自己变成了 MMA 世界里的"操作系统"，而所有具体比赛只是运行其上的 App。你可以卸载某个 App，但你不会因此卸载 iOS。

三、真正让人意外的观察：Khabib 在赞美 Dana 的同时，也在为自己的"退出"辩护

这段访谈表面上是"退役传奇谈论老板"，但如果你把它放在 Khabib 自己的人生弧线里——他在职业巅峰急流勇退、拒绝金钱诱惑、回归家庭和信仰——你会发现一个镜像结构：

  • Dana：把"人"抽象为"品牌"，让 UFC 成为家人。
  • Khabib：把"品牌"抽象回"人"，让家人重新超越 UFC。

Khabib 说"我也运营过自己的联盟，我懂那种关系"——这句话看似谦逊补充，其实是在为自己当初 walk away 的选择提供了一个隐晦的合理化：正因为他理解 Dana 那种"必须冷血"的位置，他才更清楚自己不愿意成为那样的人。他对 Dana 的尊敬是真诚的，但也是一种保持距离的尊敬——像一个僧侣在赞美一位战功赫赫的将军。

跨领域连接：这与乔布斯之于 Wozniak、马斯克之于早期 PayPal 团队是同一模式——最出色的"人性化奉献者"往往主动让位给"冷血系统化者"，因为他们意识到：规模化的爱，需要有人愿意暂时放下爱。这是所有伟大组织背后一个几乎无人明说的、令人心碎的分工。

📝 转录文本

Dana White 是谁？——一个罕见的商业天才

Lex： From where you are now, you can see the entire fight business and you know Dana White very well. I'd say he's one of those rare geniuses in sports business. In business, period. I don't think the UFC would exist without Dana White. There are important people there, of course, but he's really at the center of it all. What can you say about him? What qualities, what traits have made him such a successful businessman?

双重视角：既是格斗者，也是联盟运营者

Khabib： First of all, I think if you look at it, I also—kind of, well, not kind of—I understand his position a little. I also ran my own league for a couple of years. I know what the relationship between a promoter—well, a league owner—and the fighters is like, not just as a fighter. Dealing with a league owner. I've been on both sides of it.

冷血的商业哲学：业务与情感的绝对分离

He's very good at separating business from personal relationships. For him, the two never, never overlap. He draws a clear line between them.

In business, he's extremely cold-blooded. He's made decisions, some major decisions, regardless of whether people like them or not. And those decisions, they were best for the league and for the UFC.

He always had that mentality, you know, like in those mafia movies where family comes first, right?

Lex： Mhm.

Khabib： Well, for him, the UFC always came first. That's the only way he was able to push their brand forward.

团队功不可没，但"樱桃"始终是 Dana

Of course, a lot of people contributed to that success. There were a lot of them. You have to give credit to Bruce Buffer, to Joe Rogan, to the commentators who were there. There were a lot of things that made the UFC unique, but the cherry on top was always Dana.

Dana did an incredible job promoting the UFC, and he still does. No matter what, the UFC is always there. You know, no matter how—no matter how unsuccessful a particular event might be, the UFC is still the UFC.

When they go into a new market outside the United States, even if a show doesn't go so well, people will still come back for the next event simply because it's the UFC. Over the last 30-plus years, they've established themselves as the premier MMA league in the world, and they put on the best fights.

So, in that respect, I think a huge part of the credit goes to Dana. The fact that the UFC has come this far is a major achievement.

建立这样的联盟有多难？

Lex： Building a league like that is incredibly difficult.

Khabib： Yeah, a lot of people have money, and a lot of people have tried. Many have come in, but building what the UFC has built is extremely hard.

And what they've achieved now with Paramount—that's something unique. It's a unique achievement. In just 30 years, they've grown to a level that some entire sports needed 100 or 150 years to reach.

归功于一人：Dana White

And you have to give credit where it's due, and that credit goes to one person: Dana White.

So, I think that his genius as a promoter—the way he promotes and pushes fights, and pushes his league as a whole—that is just remarkable. In my opinion, that's something a lot of people could learn from him.

item.title: [YC Root Access] Building And Structuring An AI Native Company
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这场演讲在无意间宣告了"科斯企业理论"的死亡

Ronald Coase 在 1937 年问了一个问题：如果市场这么高效，为什么还需要公司？ 他的答案是——因为"交易成本"（协调、谈判、信息传递）在公司内部比在市场上更低，所以我们把活动圈进公司这个"层级"里。

Michael 讲的整套东西，其实是在说：AI 让内部协调成本趋近于零。当协调不再需要"人作为中转"，公司这个组织形态存在的经济学根基就被抽掉了。他讲"中层管理消失"只是表象；真正在消失的是"公司作为一种降低交易成本的容器"这个概念本身。未来最锋利的组织可能不是"更小的公司"，而是"一个人 + 一个 company brain + 一群被临时召集的边缘人类"——这已经不是公司，是一种新的经济单位，我们暂时还没有名字给它。

二、"夜里修 bug 的第二个 agent"其实是硅基的 REM 睡眠

他描述的那个"头炸了"的时刻——第一层 agent 白天做查询，第二层 agent 夜里扫失败日志、发 PR 修复——这几乎是神经科学里 REM 睡眠记忆巩固机制的一比一复刻。人脑在睡眠中做的事情，就是回放白天的失败案例（海马体重放）、修剪无效突触、把 episodic memory 转写成 semantic memory。梦，本质上是大脑对自身运行时错误的"pull request"。

这里有个反直觉的推论：如果 AI 系统开始拥有"睡眠周期"，那意味着它们迟早会需要"做梦"——即在离线态生成反事实场景来测试策略边界。今天大家焦虑的"agent 幻觉"，可能在架构成熟后被重新解释为一种必要的功能，而不是 bug——就像人不做梦会崩溃一样。你听到的不是一个工程 trick，是碳基智能架构在硅基上的第一次自发涌现。

三、投资人电话录音那一段藏着一个博弈论炸弹

他轻描淡写地说"我不觉得对不起投资人，因为他们肯定也在录"——但这句话背后是信息不对称市场的塌缩。VC 行业的整个 alpha，历史上很大程度来自"我见过 500 个类似 pitch，你只 pitch 过 3 次"这种非对称经验。当创始人也能通过 YC 的 company brain 模拟"a16z 每一位合伙人在第 7 分钟一定会问什么"，pitch 会议就从"信息博弈"变成"表演博弈"——双方都知道对方知道对方知道，剩下的只有戏剧张力。

更隐蔽的一层：这创造了一种共同监控均衡（mutual surveillance equilibrium）。类比冷战期间的"相互确保摧毁"——一旦一方开始录音+AI 分析，另一方不跟进就会系统性吃亏，所以所有人都必须录。结果是"隐私"在 B2B 世界里悄悄死掉，但没有人会为此举办葬礼，因为它是通过纳什均衡而不是通过立法完成的。这可能是未来五年商业世界最重要、也最少被讨论的相变。

四、一个额外的跨领域连接：Roman contubernium 与 Dunbar 数字

他用罗马军团开场，但没讲透一件事——罗马人为什么把最小单位定为 8 人共帐？人类学的答案是：这是能维持完全信任、无需正式协调的最大单位（Dunbar 层级的最底层，5-15 人区间）。有趣的是，当代高效的 AI agent 编排研究（multi-agent orchestration）发现，agent 集群在超过 7-12 个时会出现指数级的协调 overhead——需要引入"层级 agent"来协调 agent。

换句话说：我们正在硅基上重新发现邓巴数字。层级并没有真的死；它只是从人类身上迁移到了 agent 身上。Michael 说"middle management is gone"是对的——针对人类而言。但AI 的 middle management 才刚刚诞生，只是我们还叫它 "orchestrator" 或 "supervisor agent"。历史不会重演，但会用不同的基质押韵。

📝 转录文本

Opening & Caveat

How's your day going so far? — Good. Great.

Um, so I've got about 25 minutes or something. Um, and I'm going to try and talk about building AI native companies. This is based on a talk I gave about a month, maybe six weeks ago. It's on YouTube. Um, I've updated it. I've added some thoughts.

I think the main caveat I want to start with is: no one knows how to do this. And so this is um very theoretical. It's based on hundreds of YC companies that we're working with right now. Um lots and lots of people are trying things, and I think if anyone tells you they've got it all figured out, they are probably lying.

I think internally at YC, we have an amazing software team. We've been pushing the boundaries of I think what LLM can do for a couple of years now. I think we have a bunch of really interesting use cases um which — and I'll give examples of those as we go through — but I don't think we've yet got it fully figured out.

But I expect, um, by the end of 2026, or possibly by the first batch in 2027, it will be possible — I don't know if we'll take the PR risk of it — it will be possible to, from end to end, have an AI fully read all the applications, pick the companies to interview, conduct the interview, select the companies to fund, give them advice throughout the batch on how to run their companies more effectively, introduce them to investors, review their pitch decks, and then debug their pitch meetings.

I think an AI will be able to do all of that end to end probably by the end of this year, if not by the first three months of next year. We've got quite a lot of it working already and we're exposing a lot to our founders. I'll tell you more about that, but that's sort of where this talk has come from.

What Is (Not) an AI-Native Company: The Roman Legion Analogy

So what is an AI native company? Well, the first thing to start with is what is not an AI native company.

This is how the Roman legions were structured. The smallest unit was the contubernium — so eight soldiers who share a tent, equipment, and a mule, and there's a decanus. And then 10 of these things called a contubernia form a century, which is actually 80 men not 100, which is very confusing. But you see this kind of hierarchical um way of organizing humans, right?

The Roman legions used this to project power across North Africa, across um near Asia, up into the UK, up to Hadrian's wall. This was the way that the Roman Empire projected connected power. And they would pass information down and receive reports up, and a human being was responsible for being that conduit the whole way.

And bizarrely, like 2,000 years later, we're still basically running the same kind of thing. And like they look slightly different — this is a Karpathy tweet which I thought is very good — but um like they're all organized slightly differently but the same principle is true, which is that humans are the conduit for information going up and down the rungs, right?

Humans as the Gating Mechanism

And so there's a Jack Dorsey tweet which kicked this whole thing off about 2 months ago. There's an underlying assumption that organizations have to be hierarchically organized with humans as a coordinating mechanism. And I think basically AI breaks that apart. So you don't have to have humans as a coordinating mechanism any longer.

And I basically think most companies have misunderstood — is the wrong word — most companies sort of experienced ChatGPT as a Q&A bot. They put questions in, they get answers out, and then maybe they've sort of moved to longer running perhaps what you might call an agentic system or something. But basically you tell — you ask the agent to go and do something. It goes away until it gets stuck and it comes back to you. And you as a human are like the gating mechanism.

And so while you are asleep, the thing can't work, right? Like if it stops halfway through at 3 in the morning, like it's waiting on input from you, it can't go anymore. You as a human are the gating mechanism.

And so, you know, you can do things like making engineers 20% more productive. You can add co-pilots for lawyers to make their existing workflows go a little better. You can ship more software with AI. But really, all of these things — the men in the suits are coming from me, I don't know what I know — um uh really it's dependent on humans being the coordinating mechanism in all of these places.

Reimagining the Company as AI Loops

And if you think about it not just as like increasing productivity but in terms of new capabilities, that's interesting. Oh, there we go. Um, where basically a single person can do way more work than previously thousands of people. Your entire company becomes queryable, and you're not just shipping more software, but the software you ship is like agent native. These are a lot of buzzwords. I'm going to go into more detail about what I mean.

AI at the moment — a lot of companies like bolting AI onto the side of their company, right? In all the ways we've spoken about. They're cute question-answer bots. They're sort of very um lightweight agents that can call tools effectively like a web search or something like that.

Um but if you think about the company as a series of self-improving AI loops from the ground up, you actually get to a very very different conclusion. Okay, previously AI is like make each person 20% more productive or 30% more productive. What happens if we reimagine the company as a series of AI loops?

What is an AI loop? It's basically like — um so at the top you've got um product telemetry, inbound messages. This is like data from the real world, right? Like billing signals, support tickets, code changes, stuff that gets you information in.

And then you go down to the perhaps a policy layer, which is like: what rules constrain the AI? What things it must ask for approval for? What does it have to log?

Um, you have a tool layer where it can call perhaps internal APIs um, send emails, update the billing — um and you might have APIs for this or MCP or whatever.

And then you have a series of quality gates, which could be a human, and I'd argue probably should not be a human in all but the most extreme cases. But the quality gate can often be a second adversarial LLM. It might be something that's looking at the output saying: are we suffering from prompt injection here? Or, in a case of a bank: are we giving financial advice here, yes or no? And if we are, we can't, you know, like constrain it. Or a really easy example for engineers is like um the quality gate might simply be a second model doing code review.

Um and then a learning mechanism, which is basically you loop back around, right? You deploy the thing, you make the change, and you see how it impacts the real world.

If you can do this entire loop without a human, your product starts improving itself when you're sleeping.

Example 1: YC's Self-Fixing Data Query Agent

Can you scroll down a little bit to the bottom of this, please? Yeah. All the way to the bottom. Thank you very much.

So, um, the first time I saw these things, it like broke my brain a little bit. Um, internally at YC, we got a lot — we got data on 7,000 companies, 20,000 founders, like many hundreds of thousands of applications.

So, a year or two ago, we built an AI agent that — it basically human, it's like English to SQL, right? Like it's a simple data querying agent. You can be like, "What was the split of European versus uh American founders this batch?" And it would go and translate that human query into SQL and run it and come back with the answer. It's like, "Yeah, pretty magical." But that feels like a tool that kind of makes a data analyst 20 or 30% more productive, or actually makes me as a partner 10 or 20% more productive and I don't have to hire a data analyst. It was fine, and it would keep hitting edge cases or like not be able to do certain things and I'd be like, "Oh, that's annoying."

And then we shipped something about two or three months ago, which for me was like the head explosion moment, which was a second agent which uh sort of lives on top of this um data query agent. And the second agent runs overnight and it looks for all the queries that any human has done during the day, and it looks for success and failure.

So the success is like: yeah I copy it, I send the email, I do whatever. The failure is like: ah this didn't work, or it I hit a permission issue or whatever like the database index doesn't work, or it has to it requests some permission it doesn't have.

And then that second AI agent overnight goes and puts in pull requests to fix all of the problems from the day before. And so if you go back as a human on the second day and run the same query as yesterday, it now works.

And so this process of like evaluating what the system is doing and then proposing changes to the system and updating — the makes a whole thing self-improving. And that for me was like a head explosion moment.

Example 2: Self-Improving Products (PostHog) and Auto-Research (Karpathy)

I think if you were here earlier for um James' talk from PostHog, they basically have the same thing for products. Now they take in all your product telemetry and they see where it's breaking and then they put in pull requests, and eventually you'll auto-merge those pull requests. So your entire product surface will become self-improving. It will just dynamically — you'll have a bunch of headline metrics you want to optimize for, you'll have a bunch of product like vision documents which says this is the kind of thing we want to build, this is in scope and out of scope. And the AI will basically look at your product telemetry, come up with ideas, deploy those ideas, test them with humans, and see if it moved the needle or not, and just self-improve.

Karpathy um uh had a great tweet about three weeks ago now on like the auto research thing. Basically applying this to machine learning, just having the AI — I think it was on GPT-2 equivalent or something like that — but coming up with research ideas, testing it, running overnight, and just hill climbing.

All this is is hill climbing. If you have an end measurable outcome that you can just come up with ideas, you can test it. Did we go up the hill or down the hill? If downhill, discard. If up, like keep, and just keep hill climbing. And computer systems are really, really good at this kind of hill climbing work because they never stop. They will just run indefinitely until you reach local maximum. It's kind of cool because they don't have to sleep.

Example 3: Office Hours → Living User Manual

Um, another example from YC: we started recording office hours about 6 months ago. Um and I was given the job of rewriting a section of — we have a user manual internally um which is written over the last 15 years and it's like 500 pages long, and a lot of it was very very good like 5 years ago and then AI happened and like honestly a bunch of the advice is just not relevant anymore. And I had the job of rewriting a bunch of this stuff and I like procrastinated and procrastinated and procrastinated.

And we started recording the office hours 6 months ago and now we have like I don't know 3 or 4 thousand hours of office hours recorded. And someone on the team, Hajj I think it was, had the idea of: what if we just transcribe and then mine all of the advice we actually give in office hours, and then use that to rewrite the user manual?

And so when the advice changes, the AI will see what the humans are saying, extract the insight, and just rewrite the user manual and push it. So it becomes this like living guide of how we actually advising companies.

And then obviously, once you've got it in the user manual, you just make the entire thing queryable to an advice agent, right? Like if a founder asks us a question in Slack — and we get a lot of questions that are pretty similar, honestly, like how should I price my first customer, or my third customer is about to churn what should I do, or this customer has asked for this esoteric feature — and just, like, we've answered versions of this question like 500 times. And so now the AI can give not just Tom's answer, but like: here's how Nicolo would answer it, or here's how [someone] would answer it.

I think you can actually get superhuman advice from this thing, because it's able to recall perfectly and access the intelligence of 16 partners, not just one with fallible memory.

AI Employees: Agents Inside Virtual Machines

And so you can kind of see how these like loops can run in the background and get better and better and better and better. And then I think you give them a virtual machine. So you give your agent a virtual machine with things like tools — so, search the web, crawl your internal company directory, search your slack history, persistent file storage. So it can write — it can come up with a plan and write the plan to disk. So if it fails halfway through, it can resume. And then it can write code and execute the code to solve a problem, and then see how that worked against the plan and adjust and repeat.

And now you've basically got an AI employee. And I — we're at the very very early stages of this with something like OpenCloud or Hermes is basically VMs with an agent living inside on basically on a repeating loop.

When the Loops Start Talking to Each Other: The "Company Brain"

So where we are now, I think YC has a few of these loops internally. I think the next thing that happens — like, occasionally a human has to intervene, right, be like, well the loop's going wrong or whatever, or like let's take some insight from there and put it over there.

I think the thing that happens afterwards is the loops start talking to each other, or the AI employees start communicating with each other to share ideas and replan and assess and whatever. And you end up with this like — I mean, "company brain" is like an overused term now. It got very very popular about six weeks ago, and as of like two weeks ago, I see people in the audience with "company brain" written on a t-shirt now. There he is. [laughter]

Um, but so what is this as an idea? I'm going to steal some of Jack Dorsey's words, but: in a conventional company, intelligence is spread throughout the people and the hierarchy routes it. So in this new model, intelligence lives in the system.

What I mean by that basically is that um lots and lots of companies try and write down standard operating procedures, right? Like the way things should be done. But then when you actually observe people how they actually do the job, they were like, "Oh, well, in this edge case really I should do this other thing." And there's a lot of stuff in people's heads that if it weren't in people's heads and it was actually written down, you'd get a lot of value out of it.

And so this idea of a company brain, I think, is the combination of like basically taking all of the data in your company — and that's things like YC's application data, it's transcripts of every call, of every meeting with every founder, it's the advice we give, um the way we pick companies — and then you record that and make it legible. You make it so that the AI can access all of it, and then you have a bunch of these reinforcing loops that run indefinitely and then are able to talk to each other, and the entire thing becomes a self-improving company.

I think that's basically where we're going: that you just pump tokens in, you get access to all of your data, and the entire thing becomes self-improving.

Humans at the Edge

And people live at the edge, right? So you have this kind of company brain, this data, these self-reinforcing loops, and then the human beings live around the edge, where this intelligence makes contact with reality.

So I think Jack Dorsey said: "People reach into places the model can't yet go. They sense things the model can't perceive. Intuition, opinionated direction, cultural context, trust dynamic, the feeling in a room. Um, they make the calls a model shouldn't make on its own — especially ethical decisions, novel situations, and high stakes moments where the cost of being wrong is existential. A world model — this company brain — that can't touch the real world is just a database."

And so these humans, what he's saying I think is, the humans are in the sales calls, right? They're like visiting the client office to reassure people, to convince the CEO, to pitch the investor. It's all of the emotional uh kind of interpersonal stuff that the humans are there for.

But the humans are no longer necessary to do the information routing, right? Like all of the information is routed automatically to the person who needs it. They don't need to go through layers and layers of management to get approved.

Um, and so that's basically what I think companies are going to be. They're going to be much much smaller. They're going to be centered around a kind of company brain, and the people will interface with the real world and then feed all that information back into the brain.

Practical Tips (1): Burn Tokens, Not Headcount

A reasonable question is: sounds great in theory. How do — like this seems like sci-fi kind of — like will it happen? Who knows? What can we actually do now to make it happen?

Um, and so practically these are the tips we're giving founders right now.

The first is: I'd burn tokens, not headcount. So we're seeing founders get to demo day with a million dollars of revenue, and some getting to Series A um with 10 million of revenue with like a fraction of the people they had before. You can argue about whether it's a thousand-x or whatever, but it's multiple times more, right? Like someone — a polyglot who really knows how to use these tools — is worth many many times the people before, um, and you can just do this.

As a result, it means the headcount of the whole company is going to be less. In particular, it means no middle management. I just don't think you need layers and layers of like directors and VPs anymore.

The key roles for me are: the IC — everyone has to be an individual contributor actually doing the work, coming to meetings with working prototypes not decks. And DRI — like DRI is for me actually the biggest thing a lot of companies are missing, which is like a single person whose head is on the block to make something happen. As soon as you have a committee — I worked at a bank and we had so many committees for everything, and it grinds things to a halt. So having a single person who's directly responsible for the outcome.

I think these are the two most important roles, and I think middle management is gone.

Practical Tips (2): Make Everything Legible

Practically speaking, um, I would try to make — and this is by the way easier when you're starting out — I would make everything in your organization legible. Legible is like a really popular word in Silicon Valley right now. It means you can read it.

  • Make all your data readable to AI. That means recording everything, transcribing literally every meeting.
  • If you can't get access to Slack DMs, I would ban Slack DMs. Make everything in public channels the AI can access.
  • Every action needs to create an artifact. It needs to create a written or recorded version. Otherwise, it basically didn't happen to the AI.
  • Obviously, I think on-demand internal software for all company operations is um absolutely necessary.

Practical Tips (3): Record Your Investor Calls Too

A really cool thing we've just started doing, which I don't think we've spoken about yet — um, and it's inevitable it comes out anyway — so, um, obviously you record all your um sales meetings, right? And you can feed those sales meetings back into an AI to be like: how did I do with my sales meeting?

What if you also recorded all your meetings with investors, and you took those investor calls and you had access to several hundred or thousand companies that all meeting all the same investors every 3 months?

The first thing you can do is tell founders: here's what's going wrong with your pitch. You spent 90% of the time talking, or you really fumbled this question, or you need to be much more concise on your go-to-market. Very very easy to do. And many of our founders are taking 40 or 50 or 60 investor calls. You just pump them in and the AI will — if you're recording them — tell you what's going well and what's going badly.

But we also get data on the other side of that conversation. These founders are meeting the same investors. So investor X will definitely — here's how like we could simulate the investment call, right? We could say: here's exactly how Andreessen Horowitz does every single investment call, whereas Founders Fund will ask you this question, this question. Or this particular partner will always say "what's your wedge?" or "what's your moat if Anthropic comes after this?" — and here's a great way to answer that.

And I'm sure — I don't feel bad about doing this at all because I absolutely know that those investors are also recording this and pumping into their AI. And so anyway, basically if you can record it, if you make it legible, then the AI can start to comprehend and give you superpowers.

Closing

I will finish on this. If you were starting a company today, would you build it like this?

And for — this was a talk to very early stage YC founders. Most of you are even earlier stage, and you're small enough to just build it right from the start.

So anyway, I'll finish there. I think we have — no, we'll just do questions with all of us, I think, rather than me taking questions on my own. Why do we do that?

Thank you. [applause]
