item.description:
## 一、这场演讲在无意间宣告了"科斯企业理论"的死亡
Ronald Coase 在 1937 年问了一个问题：**如果市场这么高效，为什么还需要公司？** 他的答案是——因为"交易成本"（协调、谈判、信息传递）在公司内部比在市场上更低，所以我们把活动圈进公司这个"层级"里。
Michael 讲的整套东西，其实是在说：**AI 让内部协调成本趋近于零**。当协调不再需要"人作为中转"，公司这个组织形态存在的经济学根基就被抽掉了。他讲"中层管理消失"只是表象；真正在消失的是"公司作为一种降低交易成本的容器"这个概念本身。未来最锋利的组织可能不是"更小的公司"，而是"一个人 + 一个 company brain + 一群被临时召集的边缘人类"——这已经不是公司，是**一种新的经济单位**，我们暂时还没有名字给它。
## 二、"夜里修 bug 的第二个 agent"其实是硅基的 REM 睡眠
他描述的那个"头炸了"的时刻——第一层 agent 白天做查询，第二层 agent 夜里扫失败日志、发 PR 修复——**这几乎是神经科学里 REM 睡眠记忆巩固机制的一比一复刻**。人脑在睡眠

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] How Chess.com Became the World’s Biggest Chess Community with CEO Erik Allebest
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Chess.com 是"反 Silicon Valley 剧本"的活体标本

请注意一个几乎所有人都会忽略的时间线：Chess.com 是在 2005 年从破产拍卖里以 5.5 万美金买下域名开始的，直到 2024 年——将近 20 年后——Erik 才第一次感觉"这可能是一门大生意"。这不是慢，这是"违反物理定律"的慢。

在同一时段里，硅谷的正统剧本是：斯坦福 MBA、Sand Hill Road、烧钱买增长、快速上市。Erik 做了每一件相反的事：找了个 San Jose State 的朋友当 CTO，远程办公，没融资，零付费获客，选了一个所有 VC 都告诉他"unnvestable"的市场。

这里藏着一个真正的悖论——当年拒绝投资 Chess.com 的那些 VC 不是判断错了市场，他们是判断对了自己的商业模式。Chess.com 那种"以现金流速度成长"的曲线，对 VC 来说确实无法投资，因为 VC 需要的是 7 年内的指数曲线，而不是 20 年的复利曲线。Erik 意外证明了一件事：当一个市场不适合风险资本时，恰恰是护城河最深的地方，因为没有人愿意烧钱来抢。这是一个"反选择效应"（adverse selection in reverse）。

二、跨领域连接：AI 让国际象棋更繁荣的机制，其实是"Beatles 效应"

Erik 提到一个极其精妙的类比——音乐无限爆炸的时代，人们反而回到 Beatles 和 Led Zeppelin。这个观察比它表面看起来要深刻得多。

把这个逻辑投射到 AI 时代：当 AI 可以在一夜之间生成 10,000 个新棋类游戏、无限的音乐、无限的内容时，人类反而会向"共享的、不可篡改的、无 patch 更新的经典结构"迁移。国际象棋的 64 格、6 种棋子、固定规则——这些"无法被 AI 改写的约束"变成了它最大的竞争优势。

这里的跨领域连接是：这与区块链、宗教经典、宪法、奥运会规则的持久性遵循同一逻辑——在一个"一切皆可生成"的世界里，"承诺不变"本身成为最稀缺的资源。Chess.com 的估值本质上不是在给一个游戏公司估值，而是在给"人类共同记忆的载体"估值。这解释了为什么 Louis Vuitton 会围绕象棋做时装秀——它不是复古，它是在借用"不可被 AI 稀释的符号资本"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Erik 无意中在给"后 AI 时代的人类活动"跑一个 30 年 A/B 测试

这是访谈里最容易被忽略的一层。Deep Blue 在 1997 年击败 Kasparov，比 ChatGPT 早了整整 25 年。也就是说，国际象棋是唯一一个我们已经拥有"机器超人类之后 30 年数据"的人类活动领域。而结果是什么？

  • 参与人数比机器出现前多了几个数量级
  • 顶级棋手的实力比机器出现前更强，而不是更弱
  • 年轻棋手成才速度急剧加快（7 岁挑战 GM 的现象）
  • 观赏性因为 Leela Zero 的"神经网络式激进风格"而提升

这里有一个反直觉的洞察："机器超越人类"从未导致该活动衰亡，反而每次都触发了参与规模的跃迁。这不是巧合。真正的机制是——当机器解除了"追求绝对最优"的心理负担后，人类反而释放了"以人类身份参与"的表达欲。

进一步推演一个大胆预测：未来 20 年，我们会看到"AI 无法威胁的人类活动"（如舞蹈、瑜伽、烹饪）反而衰落，而"AI 已经明确超越的人类活动"（编程比赛、写作比赛、辩论、数学奥赛）会像国际象棋一样爆发式增长。因为只有在"机器已经赢了"的语境下，人类的参与才被重新解读为"纯粹的自我表达"而非"追求胜利"。

四、彩蛋洞察：Gambit（扑克评分系统）是一个更深的社会实验

Erik 提到把国际象棋的 rating 系统移植到扑克。这看起来是产品扩展，但它其实是在用技术手段解耦"金钱"和"技能证明"——这是一个自 20 世纪初以来赌博行业的根本性设计变革。

当你的扑克 rating 比输赢的钱更让你在意（Erik 亲口承认这一点），扑克就从"金融风险游戏"回归为"纯粹的博弈艺术"。这与《游戏化改变世界》里描述的转化路径正好相反——不是把生活游戏化，而是把已经金融化的游戏"去金融化"。如果这个模式成立，它可能会波及股票交易、体育博彩、甚至加密货币——任何"技能和金钱纠缠"的领域都可以被"纯 rating 层"重构。

📝 转录文本

开场：从 COVID 浪潮到"这不是昙花一现"

COVID happened, Queen's Gambit happened, some news cycles happened, and we're like, "Oh, this might just be a flash in the pan," like treadmills and sourdough bread. But then in 2023, we had another crazy wave where all these kids started playing in schools because of short form content and the mittens bot and the cheating scandal and we just spiked again and then when we came down again, we were so much higher and we maintained this baseline.

预告：为扑克设计评分系统

How do you think about like how to design a rating system for poker?

We're bringing the chess playbook, which is like how good are you really? Not just can you buy the most chips or can you use a bot or can you steal the most money, whatever it is, we've all played those games where you're playing for M&M's and someone's just like all in all the time and they just reby more M&M's.

As people get used to like, wait, I actually care about my poker rating, people are going to care about it as much as money because it's a reflection of like the value and their skill as a player. I think this is going to be quite an interesting innovation for poker.

节目介绍

Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today I'm here with Eric Alabest who bought the chess.com domain out of bankruptcy auction in 2005 for 55 grand when almost every investor told him it was an uninvestable niche passion project.

Two decades later, he's built the dominant chess platform with more than 250 million members, 200 million a year in revenue, and a mission to get a billion people to play chess. It's a game that's more popular than ever despite computers outclassing humans at it for the last 30 years.

We talk about what AI means for games, the future of chess.com, how to build a rating system for poker, and the future of human skills.

Welcome, Eric.

Eric, it's great to have you on No Priors. Welcome. Thank you so much for having me.

Chess.com 今天的规模

So, I'd love to just make sure our listeners have a little bit of the backstory of Chess.com and how you built this business, but could you paint a little bit of a picture of just, you know, usage and both the company and the user base and product today first?

Yeah, sure. We are much larger than I ever thought we would be. So, it's kind of wild to say these numbers for me.

  • 约 1000 万日活用户
  • 约 4000 万–5000 万月活用户（北半球夏季稍慢）
  • 超过 2.5 亿注册会员
  • 今年营收将略超 2 亿美元
  • 团队约 650 人

Um, we have more than 250 million registered members and more revenue than I thought we would end up with as a chess company. Um, at a little I think this year we'll do a little over 200 million. Um, which is frankly again surprising.

We have about 650 people on our team who love chess, are passionate about the game, and are working hard to, you know, make our members happy and to grow the game. Um, and to be the best possible place to work. Those are our three kind of the three areas of our mission.

从破产拍卖买下域名开始

Amazing. And you took a I guess somewhat unconventional startup path or founder CEO path to get here. Um, certainly think of you as founder. Um, what, how did you end up owning the business?

Well, we didn't start by owning a business. We just started by owning a domain name that we got from a bankruptcy auction in 2005. Someone else owned the domain name. They were building chess software, but they, you know, couldn't pay their debts and the money they'd raised a little bit of money to try to do that. Um, it ended up with a failed business.

And so, a friend and I bought the chess.com domain name for $56,000. And we were going to build a chess community. We wanted to be like MySpace and build a chess community where people could kind of come and express themselves and learn and share. We bought the domain name and started building.

融资：所有人都说 "uninvestable"

Well, bridge the gap from that to the scale of community you have today. How did you grow? How did you think about fundraising?

Yeah. So, we did think about fundraising. Uh, you know, obviously I was at Stanford Business School at the time. So, you know, Sand Hill Road was right there and I had access to a lot of venture capitalists. They were teachers and were guests in classrooms I was in.

And so I had a lot of meetings and basically most of them said this is uninvestable. You should get a real job. Don't waste your time with this. And so, I wasn't able to raise any money. No one believed in the vision. I asked some classmates if they wanted to like join me on this venture and they're like, "Nah, we're going to go like do something serious."

And so then my friend and I, you know, he was kind of the CTO. I was the product person. Just the two of us started building it together. Didn't raise any money. Eventually I started putting money in. I had money from a couple previous businesses I had sold. Um, borrowed like a little bit of money from my friend's mom and then paid it back later.

But you know, we just really kind of grew at the speed of cash. And after we launched in 2007, right as I graduated from school, and then I think within like 18 months we were starting to charge memberships for like online chess learning and we pretty quickly became profitable and then we just grew, you know, as we had more revenue we would just hire somebody new — whether it was a community manager, a developer, a system admin, you know, eventually designers — and it just kind of grew as we had money for it to grow.

And we never then again considered raising money. It never crossed our minds. We just thought, hey, we're profitable. Let's just keep growing. And we always thought like, oh, when we hit like 50 people, like we're never going to have more than 50 people on our team. And of course, we blew and we're never going to have more than 100 people on our team. And then we just stopped saying that because chess just continued to surprise us as to how big it got.

And it still surprises me. But what's interesting is now I'm like, if 250 million people have said they want to play chess at some point on chess.com, like why don't we have 50 million daily active users? You know, a billion people should be playing chess.

So now our ambitions are pretty big and we see the good that chess does in the world and brings people together and gives them confidence and, you know, teaches them that you never really lose if you learn and it's a great game for learning and spending time. So now our mission is huge and we're like, we're going to be bigger than we are today. So we're quite excited about our mission.

竞争与用户体验优先

How did you think about competition and like the rate of growth you needed to have? Yeah. And how do you think about it today? Because there are — I don't know if you can say the words — but there are platforms like Lichess out there. Amongst the many drivers of people raising a huge amount of capital, some businesses are more capex intensive than others, but even when they're not naturally, the desire to like be the dominant player in a market, the way chess.com is, right, is I think a common driver.

Yeah. And I think that's fair. And I want to give the caveat that the chess industry, as we call it today, didn't exist 20 years ago. It was like some apps and like one, you know, a couple of players. There was Free Internet Chess Server FICS, there was ICC (Internet Chess Club). Those were the two major players. There was Yahoo Chess.

And we came on and we just relentlessly focused on what we wanted as players ourselves. We wanted a product that felt great. We wanted it to be free to play. We wanted to be in the browser. We wanted it to feel great, you know, we wanted it to be a wonderful experience.

So we really just focused on the user experience above all. And over time, that wins out. And so most of the others kind of fell by the wayside. Obviously, Lichess exists today. They're kind of the — I would say the Linux of, you know — they exist for a really important reason. It's great for the community. It's open source. It does what it does and we coexist here, and we drive the growth of the game through what we do and through the investments we're able to make due to the fact that we do generate revenue. Um, and they serve a different part of it.

The interesting thing is chess is like not patentable. There's, you know, thousands if not tens of thousands of chess apps in the app store and chess websites, and at the end of the day really product is going to win out — and community and content — and so it's just really this relentless focus on creating the best possible experience.

I do think there's other markets and businesses where you need to raise money — whether to move at speed. Again, we've built this for 20 years. So others need to move faster or more at speed or there's more investment in certain areas or obviously if there's like hardware or inventory. Those are different types of businesses.

But for a pure software and content business like ours, one where we didn't have — like no major tech company was bearing down on us — we were able to kind of take a little bit of the slower road there. Which was great. It developed a great culture and allowed us to not need outside capital.

什么时候意识到"这是一门大生意"

So you said that part of why you were able to grow in the way you did was there were not a lot of people who believed that the business would be as big as it is or the industry would actually be an industry. At what point was it a progressive thing? At what point did you think like, oh this is actually going to be a big business versus, you know, it's something I'm personally passionate about?

Yeah, I think 2024 was when we thought this would be a big business.

That was not that long ago.

Not that long ago because before COVID and Queen's Gambit, we had like a million daily active users and we were shocked at that.

But then when COVID and Queen's Gambit happened, some news cycles happened, and we're like, "Oh, this might just be a flash in the pan like treadmills and sourdough bread and other things that people did during COVID, and we might just come back down to where we were." But we actually stayed really high after that, a little bit lower than our peak in 2022.

Mhm.

But then in 2023, we had another crazy wave where all these kids started playing in schools because of short form content and the Mittens bot and the cheating scandal and all these other things in 2023, and we just spiked again. And then when we came down again, we were so much higher and we maintained this baseline.

And so kind of in 2024, we're like, "Oh my gosh, this thing is actually sticking around. It's actually growing and compounding over time." I think this is a lot bigger than we thought it was going to be, which was fascinating.

It's also terrifying in some ways because it's always like — if your business is shrinking it's scary because how do you make it grow? If your business is flat it's scary because how do you make it grow? If your business is going up it's scary because like how do you maintain that growth or how do you deal with it?

You know, we had issues with scalability across the product and the tech and all those things. And so it's been pretty white knuckle. I think for the last year, it's actually been more calm than it ever has been just because we've had the team in place and our growth is more predictable. And we finally kind of gotten our hands around organizationally what it means to be a 650-person fully remote company.

So it's been pretty smooth and we're now focused on a lot of experimentation and product improvements and infrastructure and tech and obviously the integration of AI and what that's meaning. So it's been an interesting last 12 months for sure.

Queen's Gambit 与国际象棋的文化崛起

I want to ask about two more businessy topics and then talk about AI in the context of chess and your reflections on that. The first would just be — how do you like the Queen's Gambit and the increasing cultural relevance of chess? Like what's your reflection of that?

Yeah, honestly it's incredible because when I got into chess a little bit late in life — I was 18, still going to college and getting into the game — and I'm like nobody plays chess. No one talks about chess. Like it's almost like a secret hobby. I was kind of like a skater snowboarder who kept chess as like the secret thing I did.

When I was in high school it was like for nerds. No one would talk about it. Like why would you spend time on that? So that's what I grew up with.

And then now to have my own kids where all their friends are playing chess and like chess is cool and the jocks play chess and the nerds play chess and everybody plays chess, and then you've got like Louis Vuitton centers their whole fashion shoot around chess, and it just blows my mind.

I do feel partly just along for that ride. But I also feel that we've been partly responsible for that. That we've kind of revolutionized what it means to be a chess player. Chess can be in your pocket. You can do it any time. The content is funny and relevant and interesting.

And we also just redefined what it meant to be a chess player. Cuz previously it was like you weren't really a chess player until you were 2,000 or above, right? Rated. And if you weren't that you weren't really a chess player. But now everybody — we kind of changed the narrative and we celebrate your mistakes and when you hang your queen and when you — if you're rated 500, that's fine. You're still a chess player. You're still part of the community and you're on your journey.

So it's been honestly one of the great honors of my life to be a part of that and to see that we kind of culturally changed what it means. And you know, when you see pictures of Lewis Hamilton flying in his private jet playing chess on his phone, it just blows my mind. So it's been wild.

Yes. I was the high school nerd that played chess, but my kids now — my eight-year-old plays and teaches chess. And it's like very — I mean they're in a nerdy town but it's common enough that, I don't know, 20% of the kids do after-school chess. Right. Which is a totally wild thing to think about. Soccer. Seriously.

CVC 投资：仍然是一家自举公司

You had a huge announcement recently that's a big change in terms of the CVC investment. Tell us about that — what it means for the business, how you thought about working with a private equity firm after so many years of just being a bootstrapped business.

Yeah. Well, I'll tell you, we're still a bootstrap business because CVC came in, but they, you know, they came in and bought secondary. That was part of the fundraising cycle.

Obviously, General Atlantic was really the first private equity to believe in us — back in 2020 or 2021. They saw our growing business and they had conviction that we were a strong player in an interesting market and they came in.

And we had another investor — it's kind of interesting because if you go back in time, we were just entirely privately held and then someone comes along and it's like "Oh I love chess I want to invest" and we're like "no no no" and they're like "oh we…" and finally we said yes and they bought like a little bit and they're like "I'll hold on to this forever, I just want to be a part of this." And then like 5 years later, "I need to get out of this. I need to sell." Like — you what? You said you were going to be here forever. "Like don't worry. I got another guy."

So then this other investor came in. He's like, "No, but I want to own X%." And we're like reluctantly let him a little bit more in. And he's like, "but I love chess. I'll be here forever." And then 3 years later, he's like, "I got to sell." What? You said you were going to be here.

So then we were at such a scale that we had to find a different scale of investor. And so we did the rounds with all the private equity and really just did not enjoy that process and really didn't enjoy most of the people that I met during that time. Really were focused on I thought the wrong things.

But when I met General Atlantic and Tanzine there, they really believed in our mission and they believed that if we focused on our mission that we would build a wonderful business. And that aligned with what we felt and so they made an investment — bought again secondary, buying shares from existing investors, no infusion of capital.

And then eventually they came to their fundraising cycle times — they've got to return, make returns to partners, and do their thing. And so then we again had to now look for another person to come in. And we found CVC and we were very very happy to be working with CVC. They have such a deep experience in gaming, in sports, in community businesses, and we really just felt like a bond and an alignment that when you take care of your community and your product, you'll build a great business.

So they invested in buying out different shares from different people. The General Atlantic reinvested as well, so they're still with us in this new venture together. And we're as committed as ever to continue to grow the game and to follow our mission. But yeah, we're still — no capital needed to grow this business.

大规模外部投资者如何改变了运营

How does it change? Has it changed the way you run the business to have these increasingly at-scale outside investors?

Yeah, it actually has, but in a wonderful way.

Okay, this is like against the conventional wisdom of like private equity being involved. So say more.

Yeah, that I can recognize that a lot. You kind of hear the tropes about private equity and where they give you money and then just say "work harder" or whatever, "do better." It hasn't been like that at all with General Atlantic or with CVC at all.

Really, it's great knowledge sharing across what they've seen in the industry and what we do. They're in the weeds on the product and the community and they've really been great at pushing us to be our best. Not just saying, "do better," but like "here's some areas, have you looked at this?" And it's just made us stronger.

And then all the operational stuff, all the forecasting and all the operational excellence that we've really brought to bear that we've needed to do to kind of grow up and do this. It's been wonderful and has made us better and stronger. And as our reporting gets better, we learn more about things and we experiment and we learn — all those things really matter, not just for reporting to investors but actually operating the business.

So yeah, I actually have really enjoyed our time with General Atlantic — made us great. I've learned so much as a CEO. You know, being an entrepreneur with two to five other people on your team or 10, that's one thing, but being the CEO of a many-hundreds-of-people company and many-billions-of-valuations, like it changes the landscape of what I do. And I'm just grateful that they've been there to help me learn to grow into these different roles. So we've matured a lot and it's been great.

AI 与国际象棋：30 年的自然实验

Super cool. One of the reasons I was excited to talk to you, besides being excited about chess, was that chess is probably our longest running experiment in what happens to a human activity after the machines become like superhuman at it — because it's been like, what, Deep Blue was 30 years ago, right?

You know, we were just talking about how there are different drivers — it could be cultural orientation of the community, could be tools, it could be moments and content like Queen's Gambit — but the answer is humans definitely care more about chess than they did 30 years ago, right? I think there were a lot of predictions when Deep Blue beat Kasparov that chess was over, right? Like what did people misunderstand about why humans play games, or what do you think happened instead?

Yeah, it's so interesting. Fundamentally, humans want to do human stuff. That's humans competing against other humans. It's humans making things. It's humans solving problems.

And there's certain areas where machines have gotten better than humans at things. But it really, in the case of chess, has pushed humans to be better and to do better in their field.

And it's really interesting because grand masters and world champions were using early versions of computers to kind of help them with ideas that they would then take into the human versus human realm. And then at some point the computers got so much better and there was like Stockfish as this kind of chess engine. And that chess computer actually made chess pretty boring for a little while cuz it was so perfect and all these players tried to play like the best computer. They were grinding out these boring end games and it kind of just got boring.

But then neural nets came along and so that was the next iteration of AI — you know, early in the game of Go with Leela and these neural nets came along and they started training chess on different chess positions and they let this self-reinforcing learning come out and they ended up with Leela Chess Zero, the chess engine. And that started beating Stockfish in ways that were unexpected, and it was actually aggressive and it did unconventional things and really pushed the game forward.

And so what was interesting is that computers at first made chess a little bit more boring, but then made it so much more exciting. And we're seeing more exciting chess than we ever have. And the players have gotten better.

And really computers are now able to help us unlock the game in ways that make our enjoyment of the game better — whether it's the AI kind of coach on game review that reviews your game and helps you learn from it, or playing against the computer, or generating puzzles that are specific for you. So AI has just really helped humans enjoy chess more.

I don't know exactly how that's going to play out. I know that right now AI and mathematics is a big deal. Like is it solving too many problems? But then you've got AI that's unfolding proteins and solving for cancer, but humans are doing the research too. So it's really this kind of hand-in-hand partnership where the best of human creativity, the best of AI, can help move humans further. So I don't know. I'm pretty optimistic about the future, honestly.

工具让人类学得更快

I'm very inspired by the idea that AI can help humans get better at things much faster than they used to, or technology in general. Like if you took a talented 10-year-old today versus 30 years ago, how much faster do you think they could reach ELO 2000 or master or something?

I mean, we're seeing it already. There's just younger and younger players. There's seven-year-olds who are giving a run to Grand Masters, and — I'm going to butcher her name so I'm not even going to say it, but there's a 10-year-old from India, from England. She's crushing everybody. She's incredible.

And to your point, like take the 10-year-old and give them the tools and see where they come out. When my son was younger than 10, he obviously had access to YouTube and different things. And now he's 18 years old, and he is a better video game creator than I ever would have been because he self-learned everything on YouTube and with different AI tools. He doesn't use AI in the creative side, but he uses it for research on how to solve problems.

And so this access to information, this access to superhuman intelligence, really is making people learn faster and better. And so to your point, who knows what's going to be coming next in the next generation for those who are young now, as they learn faster — what will they create?

I think the downside and the scare that everybody has is like, well, when there's a superintelligent AI that knows everything, why would anyone ever write an essay ever again? Why would they ever think? Why would they ever do anything? If you can just have AI say "draw me a picture of XYZ thing," why would a human ever do it?

And I understand that point of view. I have my worries. I think there's research that shows that people who use AI in certain areas do stop thinking and engaging their brain. So we have to set up guardrails. We're going to have to figure out what works and what doesn't. But again, I think it's going to push people further into learning and creating better things.

为什么不是人人都同样强？重复的力量

If everyone has this information access that you describe, why aren't we all equally good at chess, right? What is having access to this due to the skill distribution in your data or in your experience?

I mean like anything, you've got to do the repetitions to put it in your brain. Just because we have access to it on the computer.

Yeah.

So it's really about people putting in a little bit of work. And one thing that I really love is the concept that if you just take any given day in your life and multiply that by a thousand, that's kind of what your life looks like.

So if you do five chess puzzles a day, multiply that by a thousand, you've done 5,000 chess puzzles. You're going to be much better. Right? If you want to do a 100 puzzles a day, multiply that by a thousand, right? Or play 10 chess games a day, or do yoga every day for 10,000 years — it's not 10,000 days, it or a thousand days.

It's not the actual individual one thing that you do on one day, but it's your habits that really compound over time. You can put that into any field, right? Whether you do one sketch a day or you go for one small run every day. And it's the same in any field, right? If you do research into any topic.

And that's one thing that I do think AI is so great at — like you can literally get into whatever AI program you're using and you can start researching something and it can walk you through and help you get exposure to ideas, refine ideas, you can walk through and have these conversations and access to like walking into a professor's office and starting to ask questions, but you get it in your pocket all the time.

And of course there's issues with biases and with like it tells you what you want to hear and it overinflates your ego and there's all these problems with it. But honestly, for people who use it well, you can deep dive into subjects and learn and train at a tremendous pace.

数据集里的启示：没有捷径

You have this incredible data set with chess.com of humans learning — millions of people at every rating making mistakes and improving. What can you tell us about how humans acquire expertise or how to get them up that ramp faster?

Fortunately and unfortunately, it's actually quite an easy answer.

Oh no.

Yeah. It's just repetition of like the small building blocks.

And so it is doing puzzles, it is reviewing your mistakes. It is if you want to play certain openings, just training. And so there's really not shortcuts to the process. There's shortcuts in the tools.

We've tried to make it as easy as possible to do your puzzles and to train on your different elements, and we have a whole set of tools coming later this year which is going to make it even easier. But you have to put in the repetitions into your brain. You have to store that. It's the same as when you train a neural net, right? Like you give it a bunch of data and of course it can train it in parallel where it can do all these different memory channels at once training on these things. Our brains don't work quite that way — but we have to put in the repetitions.

And I think a lot of people these days because of the immediacy of social media and the immediacy of our lives in general kind of forget that practice is — you can't really shortcut practice. You have to put in the time.

反作弊：AI 时代的老问题

I'm gonna ask kind of a funny question. Feel free to not answer. Like how do you guys think about cheating at chess.com? Because you have also dealt with an issue that I think a lot of the world is dealing with now — maybe they will call it cheating or not, but it is: machines can create superhuman output and it can pass off as human performance, right?

It's tough, right? I wish humans didn't have this drive to take advantage of someone else or put themselves above somebody or steal from them. But there's some segment of the population where either for financial gain — where they're using AI tools and technology to steal from people — or even if they're just getting on to online chess and loading up a computer to steal rating points or boost their ego or whatever it is.

It is sad, and it bums me out that humans can't just get in there and be honest and full of integrity at all times.

That said, chess has been dealing with cheating for a very long time — much longer than AI. As we've had these chess computers. And so a lot of people thought it was an existential threat to the game and that it would end the game. But unfortunately, we also have technology to fight the cheating.

And so we spend a lot of time, a lot of money, a lot of resources on anti-cheating basically. And we have a whole set of tools which I'm not going to get into because I don't like to give ideas to people on how we do it, but we track a lot of stuff. We have more data. We have more statistical models, machine learning models, and that really tracks how people play chess. And again, we have access to all this data. We know what it's like when humans play chess. We know what it's like when computers play chess. And we just get better and better all the time.

So it's definitely an incredibly important thing that we think about often — to protect the integrity of the game both at the casual level and at the professional level. And we actually have two different work streams that do that. Like, how do we just detect it in general? And then how, when we have prize money on the line and professional events, how do we deal with that?

So it's something we spend a lot of time on and we feel really great about our role to protect the game and we feel very confident that we're doing a great job. Cheating can't be prevented because you can't put a webcam in every single person's home. But we do do a really good job at catching it and banning people who do that and trying to educate them as well. So definitely something I'm very passionate about.

为什么象棋特别？"Beatles 效应"

Because you are super passionate about it and you know the craft of chess, what do you think makes chess special as a game? Like why should a billion people play chess versus the many other games that are out there?

There's something special about chess, especially in a world where anything is possible these days. I mean, you could give an AI a prompt and you could have 10,000 new board games tomorrow.

We've seen this with the explosion of music, right? Like over the last several decades that there's infinite music. And when there's infinite music, sometimes people go back to like the Beatles and Led Zeppelin because it's like the classics that everyone can kind of rally around and have a shared experience.

And I think that's the same about chess. Like there's no loot boxes, there's no new skins that dropped, there's no changes to the rules, there's no new heroes to learn. It's like the simplest set of rules. It's a full information game and there's no luck involved. And you just can load up a game on your device or get your chessboard out of the drawer and set it up, and you're having the same shared experience forever.

And it has enough complexity that can just blow your mind, but enough simplicity that you can learn it. And so it's just kind of fits that sweet spot between complex and basic and timeless. And so I don't know, evolutionarily it just became the king of games — we can say — because of its many attributes. And I think a lot of people in today's world are looking for things that they can hold on to, in a world of increasing exploding proliferation of everything.

Chess.com 是游戏公司？教育公司？社交网络？

Do you think of chess.com as like a game company or an education company or a social network? Or, you know, you have creators and influencers, like a media company. How do you frame the business besides the mission of "get everyone to play chess"?

Well, we're just definitely a chess company. I'll say that. The easy answer is we all love chess. We love playing it. So we're a chess company, but that does have many facets to it.

We have said we're a gaming company, we're a content company, we're a social network. We are all of those things because chess, the game, encompasses all of those things.

More recently, we have branched out. Not that we're like "oh, we're now a games company," but a lot of us do love a lot of different games. So even though chess is like 99.99% of what we do, we recently launched Gambit at gambit.com, which is our poker site, and you can play Gambit on your phone as well.

But we're doing poker in a different way, too. We're bringing the chess playbook, which is like poker for ratings. How good are you really? Not just can you buy the most chips or can you use a bot or can you steal the most money, whatever it is, but like how good are you really?

And we're going to roll out other games as well. Because we like the playbook of what we've done. So we're cooking up a bunch of other classic games. And we're going to be launching those out there.

We have our take on how we feel like gaming should be done and can be done — in like a pure and wholesome and great learning and educational way. So you'll see us rolling out more games in the future, but it doesn't — it's a small team that's doing it. It doesn't really take away from our mission of chess. But we are branching out.

给创业者的建议：别再听建议

Okay. I have two more questions for you about the future. One for founders who are trying to figure out if they're in the right market, in a niche market, too early or just wrong. What wisdom do you have for folks thinking about those questions? Because you were, when you did this, a lot of people told you it was too small.

I think one of the curses of being a founder today is just how much founder advice there is out there.

Okay.

You know, at the time when I was getting into doing this 20 years ago, the playbook was like: hire a technical founder from Stanford, raise a bunch of money, get an office, go after a big market, spend a bunch of money on customer acquisition. And we literally just did like all the opposite of that. Like I hired my friend from San Jose State. We worked remotely. We didn't raise any money. We didn't pay any money for customer acquisition. We picked a tiny market.

So I don't know. Like I think people should listen to their heart and listen to what they want to do, and they should think of "what do they want to see exist out there in the world," and then they just relentlessly go after that more than what does the market say, what are these different things.

Of course, you've got to listen to your customer, right? And you've got to pivot if it's not working. But like — what's your vision for the world? What is the minimum amount of resources you need to go prove that out? Who are the great people you want to work with? None of the rest of it matters. Just go execute and put something beautiful into the world that's unique and creates value for people, and you'll figure the rest of it out. And stop listening to people just giving you advice on what to do. Just go do it.

关于 AGI / ASI：技术之外，是文化问题

Okay, last question for you. Do you believe in AGI? Do you believe in its — or ASI — and its imminent arrival? And what's one thing you believe about the world if that is true?

I do believe in superhuman intelligence and that it will move at a faster and faster pace. I think it will be a little bit scary if we don't put guardrails around that and rules for how it should engage with humans. Um, I hope we can do that.

I would say I'm more optimistic than pessimistic about the impact of that though. I would hope that it can help us solve some of the biggest problems around climate, biggest problems around even politics and education, and create a more equitable world. I worry that it can have the opposite effect.

I think we're already seeing the economic impact of just big tech and that just too much money is flowing into the hands of too few and we're not doing enough as humans to share what we're creating. So I think this is less a technology problem and more a cultural problem.

And I hope that we can solve that by loving one another, by sharing with one another, by connecting and feeling that we have a greater stewardship and responsibility to this world. I think the technology is somewhat irrelevant to that. Meaning: we've had nuclear technology and we've had guns and we've had an economic system for a long time, and it's really what we do with that as a culture more than what the tool is itself.

So a superhuman intelligence and AGI/ASI can be used for good or for evil. It's going to depend on the people who are in charge. I wish I felt more confidence around the people who are in charge of this world right now — whether that's the super billionaires or politicians. I don't know how we got into a place where the people who should probably not be in charge of the world are in charge of the world, and the people who should be are not. I don't know if we're going to get out of that, but we are where we are. So I'm hopeful we can make some cultural changes and put some things in place to protect us.

I think the interest and growth of chess is actually — it's not a solution to all the world's problems, but it's incredibly optimistic to me because it is so clear that people want to acquire human skills even when the machine can outperform them, and they want to watch — they appreciate exceptional human skill even when the machine could do much better.

Right. Yeah.

Maybe you limit that to gaming though. I think in a world where you believe there is more capability and more abundance, I do think people are going to spend a lot of time playing games. But I think the idea that human skill is no longer relevant in the world of superhuman AI, just as a product of the technology itself, is nonsense.

Right. So there I think we're super aligned. And there's a bunch of complexity around the guardrails and distribution of the fruits of that technology still.

Yeah.

Chess.com 在 AI 上的投入

What are you investing in at chess.com from an AI perspective? Like if it's tools or how the product changes?

Yeah, we use AI extensively as a business, as an organization, all across many different facets.

  • 客服：It powers a bunch of our support team through automations to get people faster answers. But then obviously we have a bunch of great humans who work in our support team who help create those and who help with the human-to-human needs that are there. So we've seen a great symbiosis in the support department.
  • 数据与分析：We use it for data and for analysts and they're able to ask questions and use LLM technology to get in and ask and answer really interesting things.
  • 内部知识系统 GNS：Our CTO Josh sees the future and long ago started building kind of what everyone else is like "wait a minute, we need this," which is we have our own internal system called GNS, which is like an authentication and knowledge layer that goes across our whole organization with all the right permissions and things and stores it.
  • MarTech：We're building our own martech technology so that we can more deeply integrate with our users and our data.
  • 开发流程：And then of course we're also using it in our development and product life cycle. As we build specs, as we do more agentic development where, as I like to say, "have an idea or see a problem, fix a problem." We're just trying to shorten the timeline between when something is either an opportunity or a problem and we push code live to our users, because ultimately that's really what matters.

Software development cycles can get really long by the time you — "oh, let's do an in-depth product scope. Let's get it on the roadmap. Let's build it. Let's build it again. Let's test it. Let's QA." Like all those different handoffs and different pieces make it sometimes very long to get something out to users. And so we're really trying to shorten that down. And we're seeing great success with that. And that's ultimately what we're here to do.

产品：口袋里的 AI 教练

What do you think is the biggest way AI could change the product at chess.com?

Well, we're also using it in our product research and in the output of what users are getting as they, you know, on their chess journey.

So we're working on things like getting all of your aggregated stats into your advanced stats and then comparing those to other users like you or users right above you. What do you need to improve on to get to the next level? We do a lot of that analysis through a lot of different research methodologies, including using LLMs and AI.

We're working on AI technology for — so you can have a chess coach in your pocket. Obviously, it's not a replacement for a human. If you really want to have a sit down with a human, you should go hire a great chess coach near you or online. But if you want a little bit more of a casual experience or an on-demand coach, you have your AI coach in your pocket.

We're working on future products. Also, right now we're prototyping having more of an interactive experience where your AI coach kind of looks at your games over the last week and gives you some feedback and some recommendations, even if you want to have a chat with that coach.

So there's a lot of areas we're exploring right now where AI can be infused into the product in a positive way to help you on your chess journey.

扑克评分：用 rating 重构游戏

I'm gonna ask one more question. I don't know if there's a good answer, but I'm just curious because — my three games are chess, Go, and poker, right? And poker's very different from the other two and I play them very differently, as I think most humans would.

Yeah.

How do you think about how to design a rating system for poker when so much of it is interpersonal and — also, if you play poker for money, it depends on how you think about financial risk?

This is a great question. We're still evolving this as to how we're doing ratings in poker. It does have to do with, again, the rating of the other people at the table and how many chips you win and how many hands you've played. And so we do have a rating algorithm that I'm sure we will adjust over time.

As to how people play versus when there's like playing a $100 game of poker versus a $1,000 game of poker — like things change a lot. Or if you're playing for peanuts or M&M's on the table. We've all played those games where you're playing for M&M's and someone's just like all in all the time and they just re-buy more M&M's. So it does matter.

But I think that as people get used to like, "wait, I actually care about my poker rating and I treat this as something important," I think people are going to care about it as much as money because it's a reflection of the value and their skill as a player. And of course, even in chess, your rating goes up and it goes down and you have your wins and your losses. But we think that people are going to care a lot about their poker rating.

I certainly do. Losing a 100 bucks at a table, it's not my favorite thing, but I don't care that much. But honestly, losing 100 rating points on poker, that just really bothers me. So I think this is going to be quite an interesting innovation for poker.

Yeah, I think it's super exciting. I am excited to start trying to work on my rating here. Because I think it will be a very equalizing thing for people who play poker to say like, "well, is Eric better than I am or does he just have more M&M's and is he a bully?"

That's a very good way of putting it.

Eric, thank you so much for doing this. Super interesting and congratulations on the business that you have passionately built. It's great to talk.

Thank you so much for having me and for this great conversation.

结束语

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. That way, you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.
