## 一、最反直觉的观察：Chess.com 是"反 Silicon Valley 剧本"的活体标本
请注意一个几乎所有人都会忽略的时间线：**Chess.com 是在 2005 年从破产拍卖里以 5.5 万美金买下域名开始的，直到 2024 年——将近 20 年后——Erik 才第一次感觉"这可能是一门大生意"**。这不是慢，这是"违反物理定律"的慢。
在同一时段里，硅谷的正统剧本是：斯坦福 MBA、Sand Hill Road、烧钱买增长、快速上市。Erik 做了**每一件相反的事**：找了个 San Jose State 的朋友当 CTO，远程办公，没融资，零付费获客，选了一个所有 VC 都告诉他"unnvestable"的市场。
这里藏着一个真正的悖论——**当年拒绝投资 Chess.com 的那些 VC 不是判断错了市场，他们是判断对了自己的商业模式**。Chess.com 那种"以现金流速度成长"的曲线，对 VC 来说确实无法投资，因为 VC 需要的是 7 年内的指数曲线，而不是 20 年的复利曲线。Erik 意外证明了一件事：**当一个市场不适合风险资本时，恰恰是护

item.title: [Zhang Xiaojun Podcast] NVIDIA VP Ming-Yu Liu: Cosmos 3, World Models, Kung Fu, What Jensen Taught Me
item.dc:creator: Zhang Xiaojun Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外的观察：Ming-Yu Liu 是"反 Sora 的胜者"

表面上看，Sora 出自他曾经的实习生 Tim Brooks，是他"没能做成"的遗憾。但深入观察你会发现一个反直觉的事实——正是"没做成 Sora"这件事，让他获得了做 Cosmos 的资格。

如果 Ming-Yu 早两年就做出了 Sora，NVIDIA 会把他锁死在"内容创作"这条路上。因为一旦成功，路径依赖会形成——组织会把资源、叙事、KPI 全部围绕内容生成堆叠。而恰恰是 Sora 在 OpenAI 手里"证明了这条路"之后被战略性放弃，让 NVIDIA 看清了两件事：视频生成的技术可行性 + 消费级内容不是 NVIDIA 该打的战场。Ming-Yu 在这个"真空窗口期"写信给黄仁勋，把整条视频生成的组织能量转向 Physical AI。

这是一种系统性反讽：他的"落后"变成了他的"选择权"。在 AI 竞赛里，第二名的隐藏红利是"看清赛道后再下注"。

二、跨领域连接：中国武术、CUDA 与 Cosmos 的同构性

Ming-Yu 从 18 岁开始练八极拳。他说八极拳的本质是"从脚到手的力的传导序列"——必须在瞬间完成全身协调，任何一个环节掉链子，整个力就散了。

对比一下他描述 Cosmos 3 的架构决策：把过去 22 个模型收敛为 1 个，把语言、视频、动作、音频"贯穿一体"。再对比 CUDA：把上层软件、编译器、寄存器、硬件"贯穿一体"。

这三件事在深层结构上是同一个东西——都是关于"如何让一条完整的力/信号链路，在最短路径上无损传导"。武术里叫"整劲"，计算里叫"stack integration"，模型里叫"foundation model"。

这解释了一个隐藏的悖论：为什么一个练武术的人，会成为最能理解基础设施哲学的研究者？因为二者训练的都是同一种直觉——拒绝局部最优，追求整链贯通。Louis Vuitton 减少 SKU 反而销量上升的比喻、"防御处处则处处薄弱"的《孙子兵法》引用——都是这个直觉在不同领域的投影。

三、隐藏的系统真相：NVIDIA 的"不裁员"是一种反脆弱协议

大多数人把"不裁员"理解为温情文化。但如果你换个角度看，会发现这是一个极其精密的博弈设计。

"不裁员"意味着员工敢说真话——尤其是敢说"你的技术方向错了"这种话。在末位淘汰的公司里，说错话等于社会性死亡，所以每个人都会做防御性判断：不押注、不表态、不越界。而 NVIDIA 通过"不裁员 + Top 5 邮件 + Mission is the boss"，把组织变成了一个信息高透明度的耗散结构——微弱信号可以从任何一个角落传到 Jensen 的邮箱。

更反直觉的是：这套设计的代价是"转型慢"。Ming-Yu 明确说了，如果你直接裁掉旧人招新人，转型会更快。NVIDIA 选择了慢——因为它赌的是十年尺度的长期博弈，而不是季度尺度的技术迭代。

这里有一个可能让你震撼的连接：NVIDIA 的"不裁员"和 Cosmos 的"开源"是同一种战略——都是"放弃短期锋利，换取长期生态密度"的选择。Jensen 让 Ming-Yu 做到 Cosmos 97、员工可以留在公司 20 年、CUDA 卖亏本卖了十几年——这家公司在所有维度上都在做同一件事：把时间当作武器。

而这或许就是"marathon company"最深的定义：别人在优化速度，它在优化时间的复利。

📝 转录文本

NVIDIA VP Ming-Yu Liu: Cosmos 3, World Models, Kung Fu, What Jensen Taught Me

This English translation was generated by AI and is for reference only.

开场：一位"不像研究员"的研究员

Hello, everyone. I'm Xiaojun. Today I'm in Shanghai, and my guest is Ming-Yu Liu, NVIDIA's VP of Research. Our conversation takes place one month after Jensen Huang's recent visit to China.

Ming-Yu has always struck me as someone who dresses very plainly, carrying a somewhat worn crossbody bag, with a very humble demeanor. But people inside NVIDIA told me he doesn't seem like a typical researcher. He's more like an engineering leader. Jensen Huang gave him an evaluation: GSD — getting shit done.

Not long ago, Ming-Yu Liu led his team to release NVIDIA's world model, Cosmos 3. So in this interview, we talked about the Cosmos 3 world model, and also about a researcher's 20-year-long quest. And this researcher's identity is quite special: he works inside NVIDIA, a massive infrastructure-type system, which has changed many of his research approaches. Of course, we also somewhat inevitably talked about some inside stories about NVIDIA and Jensen Huang.

Ming-Yu Liu says that to build models, you have to be low ego. Model competition shouldn't be a Squid Game. What follows is my interview with Ming-Yu Liu, NVIDIA's VP of Research.

几个核心引言

  • Jensen (Huang) often talks about how he likes this kind of zero-billion-dollar business. It can be unprofitable, but when this business succeeds, it has to be very influential — it has to be enormous.
  • The prosperity of an economy is measured by how fast money flows from one person's pocket to another's. The prosperity of research should be measured by how fast an idea flows from one person's head to another's.
  • When we finished Cosmos 1, we asked Jensen whether we should keep going, and Jensen said to me, "You just keep going all the way to Cosmos 97."
  • Because he's a very disciplined person. Even when something is very important, he'll tell you to pace — pace your steps. He just wants you not to rush. He's good at fighting marathon battles.
  • Every day he feels the company has only 30 days of cash left, that it will go bankrupt in 30 days.

Now, you happened to have joined NVIDIA exactly 10 years ago. Yes. Have you changed much over these 10 years? How many times has your NVIDIA stock multiplied?

一、进入正题：VP of Research 的角色与团队

Hello, Ming-Yu. Why don't you first say hi to the audience?

Hello, friends online. I'm Ming-Yu Liu.

We just talked about how you've been in the U.S. for 20 years and at NVIDIA for 10 years. Do you still speak Chinese much at the company?

Sometimes I do speak Chinese, but most of the time it's still English, because most of the time many people on the team don't speak Chinese. So communication is mainly in English. But if it's a small group meeting where everyone participating speaks Chinese, then we naturally switch into Chinese mode.

What's your itinerary like on this trip to China? How often do you come to China?

Right now I come to China about two to three times a year, because the main task the company has given me — my personal interest is in Physical AI. Here in China, the development of Physical AI is flourishing. Many companies, many researchers, are making major breakthroughs. We come here to exchange ideas with everyone and to understand how we can help them.

Did you feel anything different this time, compared to before?

This time, what I saw was more and more work on hands — dexterous hands — making breakthroughs in this key technology, and then pursuing the next key capabilities that Physical AI can achieve. Compared to my last visit, I found the pace is very fast — progress is very fast. I learn a lot every time.

This should be your first time doing a Chinese-language podcast. I'd like to help the audience or listeners form an impression. Your current title at NVIDIA is VP of Research. Could you introduce this role, as well as the structure and size of your team?

I'm currently VP of Research, and also VP of the Cosmos Lab. Our team consists of researchers plus engineers. Those reporting directly to me number about eighty to ninety people.

In addition, the company has other teams also working on Cosmos — in English it's called a dotted line. Although they don't report to me directly, I'm the overall PIC (person in charge) of the whole mission — the one who calls the shots, the one who decides the direction. So these people also follow my guidance and work together with this team to push the goals forward. The whole Cosmos effort should have between 200 and 300 people. This is a very significant project within NVIDIA. We invest a lot of resources. We feel this level of staffing is what's needed to produce good results.

二、从 Deep Imagination 到 Cosmos：一个十年的信念

I saw that you previously also led a team called the Deep Imagination Research Group. Did Cosmos evolve from it? What's the relationship between them?

Yes. I joined NVIDIA about ten years ago. When I joined NVIDIA, my goal was — back then, in my job talk, when I was pitching myself to NVIDIA, what I talked about in my job talk — that was ten years ago — what I said was:

One day, the dominant computation for generating video will be deep learning. One day, the dominant computation for generating video will be deep learning. One day, the dominant computation for generating video will be deep learning.

It won't be traditional computer graphics.

In that era — computer special effects, movie special effects — using that kind of graphics, using that kind of graphics, the traditional graphic pipeline to generate beautiful graphics — that was the mainstream. I was one of the early people in the field who believed deep learning was the future trend.

I remember back then, with our chief scientist, Bill Dally, in the presentation at that time — my presentation was all about deep learning. Because it's data driven, it can do many things traditional graphics can't. For example, one day I could take a novel as input, put it into this deep learning system, and it would produce a movie. You could do many of the controls that traditional graphics now requires massive manpower to achieve.

Back then, I — the company was very interested in this, and I was honored to join NVIDIA. After joining, I kept working toward this direction.

GAN 时代的早期工作

In that period, the dominant model was the generative adversarial network (GAN) — yes, the GAN. I was among the early people in the field working on GAN research. I kept doing research in this area. I did several pieces of work I'm very proud of.

One of them is — I was the first to propose that you could do this kind of what we call unsupervised unpaired image translation. In AI learning, a lot of the time you rely on supervision. You need corresponding input and output before you can learn this input-output relationship. Unsupervised means you don't have corresponding input-output pairs. You don't know what this person looks like when they smile. You don't know what a horse would look like turned into a zebra. Back then, we were early to use an information bottleneck to be able to do this — what we call unsupervised image-to-image translation.

Back then, when I joined NVIDIA, NVIDIA was not recognized as an AI company. At that time, deep learning wasn't as hot as it is now. NVIDIA had traditionally done computer architecture, designing GPUs. No one was doing research on the application side. I was essentially among the early people to build this direction at NVIDIA.

I did many things. One work was called GauGAN. In Chinese it seems to be translated as "Ma Liang's Magic Brush." It's like a little paint program: you dab a few colors, each color representing a different semantic meaning. After you paint a bit, it can turn into a beautiful landscape painting. That work made me — it helped NVIDIA build an image of being able to not only make great GPUs, but also make great AI models.

Back then, I also had some colleagues working together on StyleGAN research. It was this group of us who made NVIDIA the first — essentially the first to use this kind of generative network for media generation — we brought it to prominence.

Deep Imagination Research 的诞生

After doing this for a while, the company felt I was ready, and I could start building my own team. The team I founded back then was called Deep Imagination Research, consistent with the goal from my original job talk.

What year was this?

Between 2019 and 2020. At that time I became a research director. But back then, knowing I was going to build a team, together with a few partners I worked with, we started building this Deep Imagination Research.

Then, after Deep Imagination Research, we kept solving related problems. Step by step, we wanted to go from — toward the goal of putting a novel in and producing a movie. Just moving forward step by step.

We made a few interesting demos. One year, Jensen — our CEO — wanted to use a digital human to replace himself to give the keynote. So we helped him make this fake, generated keynote demo. And one after another — that was during the pandemic. During that period, digital humans developed very fast. We also contributed some technology we're very proud of.

DALL·E 冲击与 Picasso 项目

Ten years ago, when I gave my job talk, I wanted to work on the problem of turning a novel into a movie. But back then, I felt this problem might take a very long time to solve. I should say, back then I didn't realize we actually already had the conditions. When your compute — when your data is sufficient, you can make such a big breakthrough. But back then, I was busy working on digital humans, busy with all kinds of interesting applications.

Until one day, OpenAI released the DALL·E work — the earliest text-to-image model. Only then did I realize my ambition wasn't big enough. Only then did I realize my ambition wasn't big enough. I wasn't brave enough — I didn't have the determination to make this thing happen. In the place with the most compute, in the place with the most compute.

Back then, NVIDIA worked like this: if you wanted Jensen to invest compute in you, you had to explain why this matters to the company. I remember when DALL·E came out, I wrote a letter to Jensen, telling him the future is already very clear: it's using deep learning for image generation. Many NVIDIA customers use NVIDIA GPUs with traditional graphics for image generation. We can't fall behind in using deep learning for image generation. We must invest GPUs in our team to help this field grow.

During that period, I also had a lot of collaboration with Getty Images. Because I had been working in this direction, these traditional content companies — they were also very interested in AI, but they were just trying it out; they didn't have enough determination. After seeing DALL·E, I wrote a letter to Jensen asking for GPUs, and wrote a letter to Getty Images saying we should work together — only then would your future be secured. And then we reached a partnership: they provide the data, we have the compute, and we go build a big model to do text-to-image. That was the moment I stepped into large models.

Back then we started a project called Picasso. Our goal was to build an AI foundry. Some companies have data, but they don't have AI talent; they don't have AI infrastructure. But they have data; they have customers. We would help them build a GenAI model, then give the model back to them, letting them serve their own customers, and both sides profit together. Back then it was with Getty Images, and also with Shutterstock, that we did this.

This was still during the Deep Imagination Research team days. We were doing this work. From here, gradually, my research no longer just produced a model; it no longer just produced a paper. We also produced a product that could help customers succeed. It developed step by step like this.

At the time, I thought I was now determined enough — willing to take on the hardest problems. Because I had already asked Jensen for GPUs.

How many GPUs did you ask for back then?

Back then I asked for 1,000 A100 GPUs.

Right — was 1,000 a lot at the time?

Yes, it was a huge amount. That was still in the Ampere era. 1,000 was already a lot. And to string 1,000 GPUs together and do efficient training was not easy either. That's what we tried back then — whenever we hit bottlenecks, we overcame them one by one.

与优秀实习生共事：Tim Brooks 与 Sora

Because I was among the earliest to work on GenAI in computer vision, I was also honored to work with many outstanding partners. Since I was relatively senior, many promising young people back then, while still students, would come to intern with me, including Yu Jiahui, who's now at Meta, and Tim Brooks, who made Sora. They both interned with me.

I still remember when Tim Brooks first joined my team as an intern, he kept wanting to do video generation — he wanted to do what would become his Sora. But back then we didn't have the technology. We collaborated using GANs. Even then, you could see he was full of determination, full of passion. And of course, he's extremely smart, and incredibly fast with his hands. I learned a lot from working with him. We also wrote a pretty good paper together. After he graduated, I wanted to keep him, but he went to OpenAI. I'm also very happy that he got great development opportunities at OpenAI, and later made the Sora work.

After the Sora work came out, I felt very happy, but I also felt my determination really wasn't enough — still not enough, still not enough.

Cosmos 项目的诞生

Back then, a few of us working in this field wrote a letter to Jensen together, saying we had to invest more. This is how the Cosmos project came about.

This group of us scholars — me, and at that time also Sanja Fidler, and Bryan Catanzaro, who leads the NeMo team at our company. Jim Fan was also in that meeting at the time. We discussed together, and we decided to go build a World Model. We felt that for the company — for humanity, this would be an important technology.

Back then Jensen asked me and Sanja Fidler — the two of us — to lead this Cosmos effort together. It wasn't called Cosmos back then. At that time we just knew we wanted to do it. Jensen asked each of us to think about what to call it — what the project should be named. So each of us went back to think about what to call it. I've forgotten how many names were on the table back then, but in the end Jensen said, call it Cosmos. We thought the name Cosmos was very good.

So that's how the Cosmos project came to be. I was still in the Deep Imagination Lab period. In that period, I was originally working on Picasso — AI foundry for this media generation — but at the same time I was also responsible for Cosmos. Later I felt the Cosmos project was more important to the company. And there was no way around it — I was stretched too thin; I couldn't run two major projects at the same time. So I gradually wound down the Picasso project, helped those customers find other tech companies that could keep supporting them, and threw myself fully into Cosmos.

We worked on Cosmos for a while — from 1 to 2 to 3. During this period, more and more customers were using it. You need a certain scale to do the Cosmos project well. You can think of my time in Research as a budding stage. When Cosmos was already relied upon by so many people — whether external customers or internal teams — it reached a stage where it couldn't die; it had to succeed. The resources needed became even more massive.

At the beginning of this year, I left NVIDIA Research. Now I report to our senior VP of software, the most senior leader at our company. Previously you reported to Bill Dally, right? — while leading the Deep Imagination Research team. Now I report to Dwight. He's our company's first software engineer. His story is in Jensen's biography. Right — so now I report to him.

After I left research, we changed the name. I no longer call my team the Deep Imagination Research team. We call ourselves the Cosmos Lab. That's how the whole shift happened.

三、Sora 的遗憾与 OpenAI 的选择

I heard Sora didn't come from your team, which was a regret for you, right?

It wasn't exactly regret. I actually felt really happy. That people I once worked with could make such a big contribution — oh, I felt very happy about that. The regrettable part is that every researcher wants to make a contribution. Seeing how big Sora's contribution was, you naturally feel happy. But on the other hand, you also think, where exactly in my decision-making process, in these processes of my judgment, what were the places where I misjudged, which led me to fail, at the right time, to do the right thing? It must be that — I'm someone who really likes self-reflection. I always try to understand how I can make myself better.

Since we're talking about Sora, I'd like to add one more thing. Why do you think OpenAI later basically shut down this product line?

Because Sora is a significant piece of research. And of course it has many applications of its own. OpenAI is a very ambitious company. They have a huge amount of talent. Sam Altman has always been — from his early days at Y Combinator, he was an investor. So of course he wants to have that investor mindset, hoping that within the company there are all kinds of projects, some of which become very successful, a diverse portfolio.

I think over the past year, they came under enormous pressure from Anthropic — huge competitive pressure. They saw Anthropic, with Coding Agents, generating enormous economic returns. Also, when you're chatting with ChatGPT, the number of tokens you generate takes at most a minute to produce. But with a Coding Agent, it can work for 24 hours, 48 hours. The token volume is huge. So they felt this was a very good direction, and focused the company's energy on going in the coding direction.

As The Art of War says, defend everywhere and your strength thins everywhere. Everyone's resources are limited. So they reallocated resources to go toward coding. I don't think they believed that Sora wasn't good work. It's just that, at this point in time, I think the company had more important things that it had to do, so they had to make a difficult decision.

四、NVIDIA 为什么要做研究？

I'm curious — because for frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, doing research is a given, because that is their product. But for a company like NVIDIA — an infrastructure company, or rather a platform company — couldn't you just sell tokens to these frontier labs? Why do your own research too? What does research itself mean to NVIDIA?

Your infrastructure has to be good, and the definition of "good" is that it suits what these application companies need. But if you don't build these applications yourself, you simply can't understand what they need. So you have to walk the paths they might walk, and through that, come to understand.

Also, designing chips, designing computer architecture — the cycle is very long. You can't just say, "I'll change it right now." It takes a long period to do this kind of planning. So you have to do research in this area, make these investments, to understand what the potentially important problems to solve are. Only then can I design better chips, better infrastructure, to serve these big AI companies.

I've always felt that in this world, if everyone with ambition and ideals had these tools to do what they want to do, the world would be a better place. On one hand, seeing OpenAI, Anthropic, and several big Chinese companies make breakthroughs, makes me very happy. But our society will keep having a steady stream of ambitious young people, and we hope they'll have their opportunities too. We can build these models, share them with them, and they can build great applications, great extended models, or draw inspiration from them to make even better models of their own. All these different ideas can be realized.

I think when so many diverse ideas have the chance to be realized, and can be presented to users, everyone gets more choices, and society progresses better. That's why NVIDIA makes open-source models.

So do your research results create some competition with your customers?

When we do this work — especially when we make these open-source models — we basically put them out for free on the internet, for everyone to use. But actually bringing it to production, truly meeting customer needs — there's still a lot of work to do. Especially in the embodied space, there are many hardware problems, many business problems that must be solved.

I think we're giving the community a signal that we will help you. In this regard, when you see the trend, when you see our commitment — we went from generation 1 to generation 2, to generation 2.5, to generation 3 — going generation by generation like this. You see us, step by step, just trying to make this area better, so that everyone can better anticipate that NVIDIA will keep investing in this and keep improving. Once everyone has this understanding, has this confidence, they can put their resources toward the more critical cutting edges, and make significant contributions.

Because every company — no matter how rich — has limited resources. If you don't find the pain points, find the key points to invest in and make progress, it's hard to stand out. Embodied AI is so hard, with so many problems to solve. I think by making these models and helping share part of the burden, I don't see it as competing. I see it as helping everyone succeed.

五、为什么选择 Physical AI 而非 LLM？

Right. Why did you set up a very important project back then, choosing neither the hottest large language models nor models like Sora, but an embodied world model instead?

Large language models — they were already developing extremely well at the time. Also, my background isn't in large language models. I come from computer vision, a CV background. So naturally I stayed around the media space, hanging around image and video. It's probably my past background that led me onto this path. Of course, because of my background, the partners who work with me have similar backgrounds, so we headed in this direction. That's why we didn't go the large language model route.

Also, NVIDIA has a very strong large language model team. I didn't feel I had much to contribute there. I think Nemotron is getting better and better. On my side, I mainly want to solve problems better suited to me.

When Sora first came out, it was also a world simulator, but its main applications back then were more like creative applications. Creation is very interesting. Everyone hopes to tell stories in better ways, to present what they imagine — to make it tangible — to help everyone understand the world they see. That's a great application.

But at the time we also saw that Digital AI was developing extremely fast — very fast — while many of society's problems need these physical tools — physical tools that can truly change the state of the physical world — to be met.

For example, when people get old, they can't drive anymore. And without driving, one's quality of life drops a lot. If there were self-driving cars, elderly people could still have their mobility. Also, many jobs are very labor-intensive and very dangerous. If Physical AI robots could help do these, that could also improve people's lives. And at home there's always a pile of chores — clearing the dishes, tidying up. Right, these aren't necessarily what you most want to do at home. Having a robot help with these things improves people's quality of life.

We saw the contribution world models could make to Physical AI, so back then we moved in this Physical AI direction, rather than the content creation route.

Jensen 的高标准

Has Jensen made any demands on this team?

Yes, Jensen's demands on the team are very strict. The bar is high. Of course, the first goal is to help customers. That's not an easy thing, because NVIDIA is a computing company, an AI infrastructure company. What we're best at is the entire compute stack, from the underlying infra to CUDA and all the way up. But we're not a solutions company, like providing a robotics solution or solutions for other applications. But our goal is to help the companies building solutions succeed.

Sometimes it feels a bit like scratching an itch through a boot. Right, because you don't really know where the pain points are. When you design a model, when you design a product, if you don't understand your customers, you can't optimize. That's why I often come to China — to understand what problems people are facing and how to help them.

Right, of course that's one of the difficulties, one of Jensen's demands. What we build needs to make impact. Jensen often talks about how he likes zero-billion-dollar businesses — meaning it can be non-profitable, but when this business succeeds, it has to be very influential, something enormous. You can't just be satisfied making $100 million a year. That scale is big for many companies, but for NVIDIA as a company, it's not... a distraction — it's a distraction. You have to solve the most important problems and make the biggest contribution.

We believe Physical AI is a big enough problem to make the biggest contribution. So on this path, you have to be very careful to solve the most important problems, rather than ones that produce short-term results but whose impact isn't that big. That's one of the challenges. Of course, you also have to be the best. That's very hard too.

It sounds like over the past 10 years, Ming-Yu has become more and more ambitious at NVIDIA.

Yes.

六、个人求学之路：从台北到 Maryland

Next, I'd also like to explore you personally — Ming-Yu Liu the researcher — how you explored your research path step by step.

Before answering your question, let me first finish answering the previous one. I think I've always been very ambitious. Because back then I believed you could generate films directly from novels. It's just that my execution wasn't good enough. My sense of timing wasn't good enough. I didn't really understand — back then I hadn't been in the industry long — I didn't yet understand how to gain support within the company, to get huge resources to pursue a direction. I think through the past 10 years of experience, I've come to better understand how to see clearly, at the right time, how to help the company understand it's an important decision for the company, and how to influence how the company invests. That's the change, I think. Always ambitious, just didn't know how to execute.

台北成长与选择留学

Going back to the beginning, because of my upbringing — I grew up in Taipei, (China). When I was in high school, the hottest technology was wireless communications. Cell phones had just come out back then — still those huge cell phones, it was still the Nokia era. I was very curious about this technology. Also, growing up in Taipei, (China), I always wanted to leave Taipei, (China). So I went to National Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, (China), in Hsinchu, to study wireless communications there.

After studying wireless communications there for a while, I came to understand how it worked. My classmates — those studying together at Chiao Tung University back then, the classmates studying wireless communications — many of them stayed in Taiwan, (China), working, for example, at MediaTek, or some went to TSMC, doing the work that Taiwan, (China) is itself very good at. At that time I started to doubt whether this was the path I wanted to choose. Because growing up, I never actually thought about studying abroad in the US. Never thought about it. I never took my English seriously. I thought being good at math and physics was enough.

During that period I began to doubt what path was really right. In my junior year, I got curious and looked at what US graduate schools and PhD programs were working on. I looked at what we had been doing at Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, (China), and then I realized the work was very different. What I was doing then was figuring out how to design a protocol that could make transmission faster. I felt that was an improvement, but not a 0-to-1 change. When I saw what these top universities in the US were doing, I felt that every success there looked like a 0-to-1 change. So at that point I felt I should go out and take a shot.

I remember when I told my parents I was going to study in the US, they were startled, because they'd known me for over twenty years and had never heard me say I wanted to study in the US.

What year of college was this?

My junior year. So they were quite shocked to hear it.

意外遇见 AI

Back then what I wanted to study in the US was quantum communication, because I thought it was magical — using quantum to directly transmit information from A to B. But later, before going to the US, I spent a year at Intel in Taiwan, (China), and met a friend there. We were both interning there. He was working on image recognition there. That was my first exposure to AI, because I'd been studying communications before. And when I saw him doing image recognition, I thought it was magical — he could tell from these pixels what was in there, who it was, what object it was. That's how I first got an impression of AI computer vision.

I got admitted to the University of Maryland in the US, and started my PhD there. The earliest computer vision didn't really work. Most of the research funding came from defense. Maryland is close to Washington, D.C., so back then it gathered some very formidable early pioneers in computer vision AI.

After I got to that school, I was originally going to research quantum communication. Later I found they were doing computer vision there, topics very close to what I'd seen during my Intel internship. And I thought, hmm, this looks more interesting. So I sought out my advisor, Rama Chellappa. He was essentially a pioneer in this field, and I started learning AI computer vision from him. The very first project I worked on was identifying a person from their walking posture in video. Wow, that was a pretty interesting problem back then. That's how I gradually switched tracks into AI.

In the earliest days it was image recognition, video recognition. Later during my PhD I also learned how to use things like shape matching, segmentation — these common understanding-direction AI, computer vision research, gradually stepping into AI.

传统计算机视觉时代与 AlexNet

Back then there was no deep learning. It was the era of traditional computer vision. In traditional computer vision, nothing worked back then. So you had to learn everything. We were doing support vector machines back then. It was a very traditional kind of machine learning approach. Support vector machines are closely tied to optimization. This is something you had to learn, whether continuous or discrete optimization. And I also had to learn some graphical models, energy minimization, and all kinds of 3D calibration, things like that. I learned quite a lot. I'd say my foundation was pretty solid.

But in the year I graduated, ImageNet — AlexNet came out and changed the whole world.

Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab

In the later stage of my PhD, I went to a company called Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab — Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories.

That was a job you took later, right?

Yes, it was my first job — my first job in the United States. It was in Cambridge, in Massachusetts, right next to MIT. This lab was a very strong research institution in the '90s. Back then it was neck and neck with Microsoft Research. It was a leading research institution in graphics. Many professors at MIT used to be researchers at Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab, including Bill Freeman and Ramesh Raskar. They all worked there. By the time I joined, that era had passed, but many excellent researchers were still there.

After I joined that company — well, several things happened. That was the year AlexNet came out. So the things I had learned started to diverge from where the future world was heading.

Did you feel lost at that moment?

No. I actually — I was very interested in these new technologies. Because in computer vision, since nothing worked, I had already developed this habit of learning everything. Nothing worked. Back then nothing worked. Later, when deep learning came out, I found it really interesting.

I remember I was in my final year of the PhD program, sort of the senior student in the lab, and I organized the junior students to actively study deep learning — to do research on it. I remember one junior colleague told me that only a few people knew this stuff and there was no point researching it. I ignored him and kept running the seminar.

Later, my first job was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab. Research labs usually have a fairly free research culture, so I had a lot of time to learn. So that's where I studied deep learning.

生成模型的启蒙

Generative models — my advisor Rama Chellappa really believed in generative models. He believed in Bayesian methods, believed you should treat generation as part of understanding. So while I was learning deep learning back then, I was also keeping an eye on the generation side. Then one year I went to NeurIPS and saw Ian Goodfellow's work on generative adversarial networks. I became very interested in it. After coming back, I started investing heavily in this direction — learning more and more.

It seems you started working on generation quite early.

Yes, I was among the earliest researchers working on generation. Back then, as long as you could generate a 32×32 pixel face that didn't look like a ghost, you felt pretty successful.

So why is generation part of understanding?

Richard Feynman put it this way: "If I cannot create, I cannot understand." It's when you can generate something that you truly, thoroughly understand it. It's a bit like how humans learn. Right. When you can articulate something, it means you've understood it.

Also, in the early days, computer vision had this distinction: discriminative models and generative models. A discriminative model has no generative capability, but it can tell whether this is A or B. A generative model can likewise be used for discrimination, but it also has the ability to reconstruct the signal — it can describe it. When you can describe something clearly, people tend to think you understand it better. So take the earliest AlexNet — it could do ImageNet classification, and we saw it as a discriminative network.

工程师经历的影响

Actually, you spent a year as an engineer early on. Do you think that experience influenced your later research?

Oh, you mean my time as an engineer at Intel?

And what do you think is the essential difference between engineering and research? Which suits you better?

That's a good question. The most important part of doing research is asking the right question. When you ask the right question, you've more or less found the right direction. Engineering, then, helps you demonstrate to everyone that yes, this is the right question. You have to actually build the thing. Engineering's ability to implement lets you get things done. And when engineering is done at a large scale, many other things become important too.

In the year before I went to the U.S., engineering's influence on me — probably the biggest influence was becoming aware of this field called AI, computer vision, and in between, I remember hunting down problems for the company inside a huge software stack. That was a very patience-testing process. I think it was all great training.

So AI was something of an accident for you too?

Right, it wasn't on the predetermined track. Not really. No — I wasn't the kind of kid who said from childhood, "I want to understand why humans — why intelligence can arise." I basically saw this thing step by step, found it fascinating, wanted to understand it, and moved in that direction step by step.

What was it that first struck you?

Why did it strike me? At first? Later on, of course, there could be many reasons. Because I didn't understand it. Right, because I didn't understand it. Didn't understand, yet it was relatively easy to grasp its importance. Some fields of technology — take quantum communication, for example — you have to understand it deeply before you know why it matters. AI is easy to understand: you can recreate intelligence, and some of its behaviors are very much like a human's. That makes you curious.

And also, naturally, everyone feels puzzled about their own existence — the whole species — what exactly is a human? How are we different from other living beings? That's a question you naturally ask. I think it's also for this reason that this field draws so many people to devote themselves to it.

七、研究生涯的三个关键时刻

If you had to pick one moment early on that was crucial to your research career, how would you describe it? Which moment was it? Was it during your time as an engineer, or after you came to the U.S.?

Too many.

Right — so which one mattered most? Or the three most important ones?

关键时刻一：从追求数学之美到接近问题本质

I think the first moment is that early on, I loved elegant mathematics, because in the early stages of computer vision, nothing worked. Computer vision used a lot of optimization algorithms. Optimization — it's about finding the optimal solution. For continuous problems, you often run into nonconvex issues — you can't find the optimal solution. For discrete ones, it's these NP-hard problems — you don't have enough compute to find the optimal solution either. But you still develop algorithms to find an answer, though you don't know how far the answer is from the optimum.

To make sure your answer isn't too far from the optimum, you need some guarantee. You prove what's called a bound. Maybe the answer you find isn't the optimal one, but it's within, say, 4% of the optimum, or within 20% — better than just any random answer. To prove this bound, in a lot of early research you start making assumptions. Assumptions make your math cleaner, so you can find an answer, but assumptions also take you further from reality.

Back then, early on, I leaned a bit toward pursuing mathematical beauty while neglecting the distance from the real world. After a while, I realized this wasn't the right approach, because AI itself is an applied science — intelligence is meant to be applied. I grew more and more fond of getting close to the essence of a problem, rather than being dazzled by fancy mathematics.

关键时刻二：学会让别人理解你的工作

Later there was another phase — probably related to my upbringing — I always focused on getting things built, not on making others understand what I'd built. After I started at NVIDIA, I felt my research was pretty good — quite good. Before others had seen this kind of image translation, I had already built it. But I didn't really understand how to — I wasn't good at presenting what I'd built in a way ordinary people could understand.

I often say that what I built was 100 points, but my explanation was only 10 points, so others only saw 10 points. Back then I started paying more attention to how to make what I built — how to help others understand its importance, to let them understand the process. I think that's a very important lesson. That was when I was doing GANs in the early days.

关键时刻三：团队协作的复杂性

The third one is — I later came to understand, especially once I started working on large models, I began to realize that teamwork is extremely important. Communication between people is actually a high-complexity problem. Say you have — I don't know, call it N squared. Suppose you have N people. Your communication with those other N people is N squared. N squared is a bad complexity in terms of scaling. It just doesn't scale easily. When you have many people and everyone has to communicate point to point, communication gets hard. Something better would be N — or linear or sublinear.

I began to understand that to make a huge contribution, when everyone needs to work together, you have to explain things extremely clearly so everyone understands, so everyone's goals align. It's not enough that you can build the thing yourself — you also want everyone to understand what is being built, so you can all move in the same direction. This still takes a lot of work — helping everyone understand why this matters. That's something I came to see as very important in my later research — especially research at a large scale. You have to build applications, and you have to sell your work, and you have to collaborate as a team.

Right yes. This is actually your own growth trajectory, isn't it?

Yes, that's right. When I made my first — I had a very popular piece of work back then called GauGAN. Everyone was using it at the time. It's the "magic brush of Ma Liang" I mentioned earlier. Seeing the feedback from users filled me with a sense of accomplishment. And I felt that I could influence not just researchers who read papers, but a much larger group of people. That made me feel my life had more value, and I kept moving in that direction.

八、GauGAN 的故事与 GAN 系列工作

Is GauGAN named after Gauguin?

Yes, that's how the name came about. Back then I was working with an intern of mine named Taesung Park. We were researching this direction together, collaborating — also with Jun-Yan Zhu and Ting-Chun Wang. The four of us were working on this problem together. We developed an algorithm back then — we called it SPADE, spatially adaptive normalization. It was an algorithm.

After we built it, I was very happy. I gave a demo inside the company. Jensen saw it and was very excited. He asked me what it was called. I said SPADE, and he didn't like it. The thing is, it's not easy to understand — it's not user language.

Ha — but by then the paper was already written. It had been submitted to CVPR, but hadn't been posted on arXiv yet. When the company saw it, they told me not to post it on arXiv, so that Jensen could, at GTC — that was GTC 2019 — announce it to everyone at his keynote. I was very excited — a great opportunity.

Then they started wondering what to call it. Our company had a marketing genius who thought about what to call it. Back then every algorithm was something-GAN, something-GAN. It was the era of GANs. And that marketing person — his name was Greg Estelle — he proposed calling it GauGAN. Gauguin was French. Once the name was picked, as soon as people heard it, it made sense — a painter, a famous painter. And the application back then was painting, after all.

And so it came out. Originally it was supposed to be at GTC — to be announced at Jensen's keynote. But that year he had too many products to introduce. At the last minute, he — I remember I was still rehearsing with his team on Sunday night, preparing to give a demo on stage. That very evening I got a notice saying there were too many products to cover, and he had decided not to put GauGAN in his keynote. There was still a press release, and we still did demos for media friends, but it wasn't in his keynote.

After many media friends saw it, it turned out to be the most talked-about work at GTC. That year was just like that — lots of things like this happened. We made an online app for everyone to try out. From how people used it, we got a lot of great feedback, and we kept moving further toward applications.

从 CoupledGAN 到 GauGAN 的技术演进

Actually, wasn't GauGAN a step-by-step progression from your earlier research trajectory? It didn't get there on day one. After your PhD, you joined Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab, and computer vision entered the era of GANs. And you did a whole series of work around GANs, including CoGAN, MoCoGAN, and then after joining NVIDIA, things like the GauGAN series of work, right? How did it all evolve?

My very first GAN work was called CoupledGAN. It coupled the generator networks of two GANs together. Coupling them created an information bottleneck. All of deep learning is about learning how to compress information, and a bottleneck gives the network a chance to find the essence. One GAN models one distribution; two GANs model two distributions — one is horses, one is zebras. Once you couple them, there's a constraint, so it looks for commonalities, which lets you do the translation — from horse to zebra. That's the direction it went.

The whole generative network is doing distribution modeling. Distribution modeling means you can sample — produce an image, a mountain, a sea, or a video. But people don't just want to generate — they want to control what they generate. And control requires a signal. There are many kinds of signals. One common signal is using an image as the signal — like, I have a horse here; how do I turn it into a zebra? Another approach is sketch — your own sketch. And another is segmentation — it's like MS Paint: one color means mountain, another color means water. That's a signal. And then there's, say, class labels — this is a mountain, this is a car, this is a motorcycle.

The most sophisticated, the closest to natural human language, is text — text-to-image, text-to-video. That's the most natural form. But the biggest difference between text and something like segmentation is: segmentation is very concrete — it tells you what each pixel is. It aligns everything for you. Text, on the other hand, is quite different. Its structure is very different from image structure, different from video structure. Because the structures are so different, it's harder to learn and requires more data.

So in the course of my work, I understood this problem, and I worked my way up step by step from the easier directions. The easiest were things like segmentation, sketch, or an image. And that's also why I said earlier that DALL·E made me feel my own resolve wasn't strong enough. Because back then I always thought text-to-image was a very hard problem. I felt the field didn't yet have enough data and compute to do it. But actually it did. It was precisely because no one did it that it couldn't be done.

预判语言先于视觉

So you followed the path from image to text, extending bit by bit.

Right. Actually, in the early days, I had a few friends. We attended NeurIPS together every year, and we would discuss. Back then GPT didn't even exist yet. It was all very early days. We were discussing, if AI truly was going to make a real breakthrough, which field would be the first to break through. I told everyone back then that it would be text, language.

What year was this?

It must have been 2016 or 2017. Even though I didn't work on text myself, I knew that image signals have too much noise. There's a lot of stuff in there. It's relatively far from the essence of knowledge. It's more of an observation of this world. Text is already very pure, closer to symbols. So to produce something like intelligence, language would come first. Although I knew the earliest AI would happen in language, and it really turned out that way, back then I just liked visual signals more. So I stayed on the side of visual signal generation.

Mm, would you like to talk about those GAN works that came later?

Back then it was image translation. From A — like turning a horse into a zebra, turning a landscape painting into a real landscape. Later we started working on video. We made something called vid2vid back then. It took a car simulator's very simple cartoonish images and turned them into a realistic driving scene. Very close to things like today's World Model.

Right, this was already at NVIDIA.

Right, all at NVIDIA. Only CoupledGAN wasn't done at NVIDIA. The rest of the GANs were all done at NVIDIA. Doing this work in those early days, also because of that, with Ian Goodfellow, the inventor of GAN, I became good friends. We had lots of discussions.

I was also very lucky that at NVIDIA many excellent researchers — Jiahui Yu, Tim Brooks and many others — came to intern with me. I learned from them. We did a whole series of work, all revolving around image translation, video translation, moving in that direction.

九、从 GAN 到 Diffusion 的范式跃迁

Right, then one year later. During my PhD years what I learned was all traditional computer vision. After I graduated from my PhD, the deep learning era arrived. The thinking back then was you shouldn't do handcrafted algorithm design, you shouldn't do handcrafted feature engineering; it should be data driven.

I also came to understand back then that a more scalable approach, a simple, scalable approach is more likely to succeed. So I often told myself: when you're making choices, look for the more scalable ones. Later on, this is what people call the bitter lesson.

I was very happy working on GAN, but I kept thinking whether GAN was really scalable. Because everyone knows GAN is very hard to train. I worried that this thing might not be scalable in the end.

That year, when Jiahui Yu came to intern with me, the topic he and I researched was how to scale GAN. It was still very early back then. That's when I saw Jiahui Yu's brilliance. He produced so much. Although we didn't end up writing a paper back then, the amount of experiments we ran was astounding. When I saw his ideas — wow, you can even think about it that way.

For example, back then a GAN has a Generator and a Discriminator. I was fortunate to have a huge number of GPUs back then. A whole cluster to train GAN. And he came up with the idea to put a Discriminator on every GPU but with different weights for each. So it was like many people simultaneously playing against this generative network. In that era, being able to implement such a thing was not easy at all.

And then there was another intern back then. His name is Jeremy Bernstein. He's the one who later invented the Muon Optimizer — the Muon Optimizer everyone is using now. He came to intern with me back then. The direction he and I researched was how, at the algorithm level, to use better algorithms to make GAN stable.

But in the end, neither of these two directions succeeded. Yet each of them went on to develop extremely impressive, highly accomplished work. Jeremy started from that time. We wrote a series of papers on how to use the early algorithms behind Muon to stabilize — to make the training more stable. He kept going down that path step by step to develop the Muon algorithm.

It was a very happy period. I learned a lot. Up to a certain year, working really hard, researching with so many smart people on how to make GAN more scalable. But every result led toward — they all reached one conclusion — that GAN is not scalable.

I built this team. Back then, people joined because they wanted to work on GAN. That year I told everyone: we can't do GAN anymore. We have to move on — this direction is not scalable.

Back then we saw diffusion and felt, wow, this method is extremely stable. That must have been 2017. No, it should be 2021. Around 2021. 2017 was when the Transformer was invented.

Right, the Transformer in 2017. After the Transformer was invented, I have to say I wasn't among the early adopters of the Transformer. Its application back then was still LLM. I had been focusing on GAN all along. Early GANs — the ones that trained well all used Convolution Networks. It was Saining. After he brought in the diffusion transformer, we moved into diffusion and gradually shifted toward the Transformer side.

So from an algorithmic perspective, back then we felt GAN was not scalable, and I told the team: something that's not scalable won't go far in the end. Go with diffusion. So we started going down the diffusion path and kept going.

Right, this was a major transition period. So doing diffusion, we started with image, then moved to multi-view image. Multi-view image eventually became 3D generation. We did a series of work in this area. The Edify series — the Edify image generator, Edify 3D, Edify video. And all kinds of generation done with diffusion.

范式转换中的心态

Hearing this, two points come to my mind. Throughout your long exploration in CV, the computing paradigm actually changed several times. From traditional methods to GAN and then to diffusion. Each time such a shift happens, what kind of mindset should a researcher have in the midst of it?

I found that things keep getting simpler. You might feel, oh, all my previous work was for nothing. Jensen often says "suffering leads to greatness". Through all these experiences, I feel I'm increasingly able to grasp the essence of things. I feel it's a bit like traditional scientific research. You keep working until you truly find the essence. Finding the simplest way to describe how the world works.

I think the current approach is making things simpler and simpler. And on the Cosmos side, we also went from several models to the single model we now have in Cosmos 3. It's unified too. Right, we gradually came to understand: OK, so this is the essence of things.

Every direction took 5 to 10 years of investment. I think my future decisions are deeply influenced by these past experiences. And I can't say those were wrong either. You can't say it was wrong — the conditions back then, the compute back then, the data back then, doing those things back then was reasonable. What I learned back then is very helpful for my understanding of many things now.

实习生与思想的流动

Also, I noticed you've mentioned your interns several times. In an AI lab, do ideas often emerge through interns? Is that a very common thing? How do you view young people?

For example, the prosperity of an economy is determined by how fast money flows from one person's pocket to another's. The prosperity of research should be determined by how fast ideas flow from one person's mind to another's. You hear my idea, you have some thoughts and make it better. I hear your new idea. I think, hey, not bad, but this part could be even better. And it keeps flowing, flowing, flowing, and the ideas get better and better.

So because I took the industry path rather than becoming a professor at a university — if you only interact within industry all day, only with your own colleagues, the diversity of ideas is a bit lower. At NVIDIA, we recruit many interns. We collaborate with these people full of ideas, people from different backgrounds, doing research together, learning from each other. I think this helps me grow and also helps them grow. It's a very important development.

十、加入 NVIDIA 的偶然与必然

In 2012 you joined Mitsubishi — after your PhD you joined Mitsubishi Research. Right, then in 2016 I joined NVIDIA. How did that later career change happen? How did you join NVIDIA?

Ever since I started doing deep learning, I've been a strong believer in compute. Mitsubishi Electric was not a company that valued compute. It valued algorithms. Back then, in order to do research — to do good research — I often asked my manager at the time to buy GPUs. In meetings I'd say we need GPUs to get this done.

At Mitsubishi Electric there was a long-term mentor. His name is Oncel Tuzel. He's also a very well-known researcher. He decided to leave back then and join Apple to work on cars. And I suddenly felt the main reason that kept me at Mitsubishi Electric was gone. I started thinking about whether I should change jobs too.

Changing jobs very naturally meant going to Silicon Valley and talking with the big companies. Back then everyone was looking at Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta — those big companies. Later their recruiter found me. I looked, oh, NVIDIA. Right, I wanted to buy their GPUs all the time. I was so short on GPUs and wanted them so badly. Why wouldn't I join a company that makes GPUs? So in the end I decided to join NVIDIA.

My parents couldn't quite understand it back then. Because NVIDIA was a company they had never heard of back then. They said, Apple is great, Google is great. Why would you join this NVIDIA?

What I thought back then was that GPU is the most important thing. Especially back then, when I started working on CoupledGAN, it was an unsupervised approach. An unsupervised approach means data is a bit easier to obtain. You don't need labels. I felt the most important things are compute and data. Since my data didn't need labeling, I'd go where the compute is.

One thing is quite interesting. I later found out that my manager at Mitsubishi Electric back then, every time I argued with him about GPUs, as long as I won the argument, he'd give me some budget to buy GPUs and at the same time he'd buy NVIDIA stock. He retired later.

He didn't tell you at the time, did he?

He told me later.

He didn't tell you then — otherwise you could have bought some too.

Haha yes.

Mm, I saw that during your time at Mitsubishi Electric you already had some collaboration with people at NVIDIA. Right? On some papers.

No, most of those were papers I wrote during that period. Because academic paper review — sometimes you don't get in on the first submission. It might take several submissions before it's accepted. Research done at Mitsubishi might later, after I arrived at NVIDIA, get continued improvements on top of it. That's why some papers have authors from both Mitsubishi and NVIDIA. Right, it wasn't that we collaborated back then. Company-to-company collaboration isn't that easy.

Oh, I thought there was some prior collaboration which is why you joined NVIDIA.

Actually no. It was a normal job-seeking process. Back then I didn't know NVIDIA had a research organization. I thought they mainly sold GPUs. And the colleagues who interviewed me back then — only after talking with them did I learn, oh, they're really doing research — only then did I go over.

NVIDIA Research 的早期风貌

Back then NVIDIA's research organization had no reputation. How many people were there? When I joined, fewer than 100 people. And they weren't purely doing AI research. Most people worked on graphics. The group that later did StyleGAN wasn't working on GAN back then either. They were working on other things.

Something I remember very vividly is that at NVIDIA Research, every year there's something called an offsite. They fly NVIDIA Research colleagues from all over the world to California, to a small town south of Silicon Valley called Monterey. There's an area there where we held two or three days of seminars. That's where I first met Tero Karras, the inventor of StyleGAN. And also Timo Aila, Samuli Laine — these important GAN researchers. None of them were doing GAN back then. I had already been doing it for a while.

When I met them, he told me he was going to solve the GAN problem. And I thought: you probably don't know how hard it is. I very much hoped they would succeed, but I felt they somewhat underestimated its difficulty. Later they really kept investing in StyleGAN. From 1 to 2 to 3, constantly breaking through. I learned a lot from collaborating with them. They kept doing the unconditional kind, not the controllable kind that I was doing. But their pursuit of detail, their pursuit of results greatly influenced the development of my research.

十一、在 NVIDIA 学会争取资源与理解公司

Mm, joining NVIDIA to do research — did you get as many GPUs as you expected?

Well, nowhere in this world has enough GPUs. Right, you always see where it's not enough. But I was very lucky. I was among the earliest inside NVIDIA to build large models, a researcher using massive numbers of GPUs for generative networks. Because early on I did some highly visible work for the company, many people in the company knew me. Jensen also had quite a lot of trust in me. So I was fortunate to have lots of GPU resources to do this research. But every time I saw others had more GPUs, I felt I never had enough.

How do you get more GPUs in a company like NVIDIA? What do you need to learn?

You need to understand what problems the company wants to solve. You need to find a way to explain to the company why what you're doing will have an impact on the company. Every researcher has their own ideas. Everyone wants to solve problems. In a certain sense, researchers are all very high ego. Scholars have always looked down on one another — it's been true since ancient times. Everyone thinks their own idea is better than others'.

But a company's nature is a bit different. A company exists to generate profit for its shareholders. For Jensen, he hopes to take care of family — the whole company, so many people striving together. He built NVIDIA, and he also hopes to help everyone take care of their families. That means the company has to make money.

So one thing I learned is: I deeply believe what I do is very important to the world. This thing will bring about change. And that change will help the company. How do I articulate this clearly so that leadership — so that leaders who don't understand AI — come to understand that this matters to the company. This was a major change.

Mitsubishi 的前车之鉴

This is the second of the three moments you shared earlier. In which specific project did this shift happen?

The second moment I talked about was how to help other researchers better understand the importance of what you're doing. It's an ongoing process of constant change for me. It's hard for me to say exactly when it happened. But I want to say the Mitsubishi Electric case influenced me greatly.

Because Mitsubishi Electric was very important in the 90s. It was an early place where you could do research without any restrictions. Including many famous people in the field. Like, you know, Bill Freeman was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs back then. And Bill Freeman attracted a bunch — Joe Mark, some famous professors, all interned there and produced a lot of major research. So back then it could compete with Microsoft Research.

But at a certain point the company's direction changed. They began to question what impact this blue sky research had on the company. It became harder and harder to justify why they should pay these researchers. And then a very famous thing happened. This is something young people today have never experienced. Back then, a whole group of important scholars at Mitsubishi Electric were fired one after another and left the company. Some joined Microsoft. Some joined universities as professors like MIT, Harvard. Some went to Disney. People left one after another.

Some of the people who stayed were still doing similar research, but it was harder to relate it to the company's direction. For example, Mitsubishi Electric was into cameras. They were very interested in industrial cameras and very interested in robotic arms. So if you did research on those, you could get the company's support and keep going. By the time I joined, all of that had already ended.

But the training I got back then was that blue sky research and the company's interests can also be aligned. And I've often seen — because I've been in the industry for a long time — I've often seen this kind of cycle. Many companies give a lot of freedom at the beginning, and lots of interesting ideas come out. But after a while they start tightening up, and the people who remain are those whose work aligns with the company's interests. You can see it, whether it's Google or Meta, they all go through this process.

I was probably very lucky that early in my career I saw this process happen. So when I was at NVIDIA, I already knew. Back then I always believed first, I knew that what I was doing — using deep learning to generate images — was definitely positively relevant to the company, and I put even more effort into understanding how to explain to the company's decision-makers why what I was doing mattered. This is especially important.

Maybe when the company is on the rise or in an expansion phase, it allows you to do a lot of blue sky exploration. But as soon as it enters a down phase, it contracts. It demands that you answer why the thing you're doing matters. What does it have to do with me? Doing deep learning is very expensive. Right, so you have to focus even more on explaining why this is an important investment for the company.

十二、Research as Product 的哲学

People will also notice that your research often follows the philosophy of "research as product". Does that have a lot to do with that experience? Did it later influence a lot of what you did at NVIDIA in terms of research and products? For example, your GauGAN, the project you just mentioned, the SPADE algorithm was actually turned into a real-time drawing product. And later you also did video conferencing enhancement, an AI-enhanced product. It seems all of your research gets released as a product.

Yes, I consider myself a lucky person. I'm someone who, as I get older, values efficiency more and more. So I very deliberately turned my research into a product. Well, I can't say GauGAN is a product.

模型能力会收敛

There's another thing I learned — an important lesson. AI on its own cannot change everything.

Hmm, what do you mean?

When doing AI, everyone is chasing better and better models. But gradually you realize that model performance is slowly converging. Everyone is about the same. Some people will say there's constant progress, but what you see is: this month Anthropic is better, next month GPT is better, maybe the month after that Gemini catches up. And those strong companies in China — GLM, Kimi, Seed, Alibaba, Hunyuan, DeepSeek, MiniMax — these companies are all constantly making breakthroughs. So gradually everyone's model capabilities become about the same.

When everyone's model capabilities are about the same, you come to understand that relying purely on the model is not enough. I was probably luckier than most. I believed early on that models would converge. I've always emphasized that you can't rely on the model alone. You have to integrate it with the company's other ecosystems. Look at how well Gemini is doing — it's because Gemini, Google has a whole suite — Google Docs, Search, a whole platform combined together.

The more people use your model, the more feedback you get, and the more convenient it is, the easier it is to contribute to the company. When you contribute to the company, the company is willing to invest more in you and you can build even better models. So you can keep pushing the long-term development forward.

So in my early days doing AI, I was like other researchers. The way researchers, PhD students graduate is by writing high-quality papers. What counts as a high-quality paper? Usually it means your benchmark results beat others. You need a killer to defeat other people's methods. So scholars tend to look down on each other, always thinking they're better and keep going that way. So a lot of the time in early research, everyone claims they're better than others.

But later on I gradually came to understand that being better than others is just one way to prove the value of your work. Another way is: you can help others and make everyone better. You'll find my thinking now is increasingly about: what can I build that helps the whole field improve, rather than chasing being better than others.

Is that a high ego or a low ego?

I don't know if it's high ego or low ego. I've been fortunate to meet many smart people over the past 20 years. I always feel there are so many talented people in this world. Many of my interns are better than me. And I think that's a wonderful thing. I feel that what I can build can serve society, but I don't think I'm necessarily better than everyone else. So I wouldn't say high ego nor low ego. I just feel I'm able to make a contribution.

智能是否有天花板？

Hmm, you actually just touched on your approach to building models. You believe models will eventually converge and their capabilities may become homogenized. But as I understand it, those frontier labs believe that intelligence hasn't hit its ceiling yet — that intelligence will keep improving at high speed. You don't agree with their view? They're betting on the scaling of intelligence.

On one hand I'm certainly curious. I use these models myself and I do see them constantly improving. But some people always say there will be exponential growth next. If you don't hurry up and invest in this company or join these companies, you'll miss out the opportunity.

And I think, looking at history, this has never happened in the past — one company holding all the technology with no other company able to catch up. This has never happened in the world. And I don't think AI will be an exception. Right, I think everyone is smart. People move around. You always work at company A for a while and feel your talent isn't recognized, so maybe you jump to company B. And that know-how naturally spreads throughout the field. I just don't think there will be one company that gets massively ahead of all the others. I don't think that's a stable state of society in itself.

大公司与创业公司的竞争位面

Let me extrapolate a bit. If model intelligence reaches a roughly similar level for everyone, what will everyone compete on next?

Integration — integrating with your own ecosystem and with your own products.

That's for big companies. What about startups?

Startups — the advantage of startups is they can take on problems big companies can't. For example, for Nvidia, any business smaller than a billion isn't worth pursuing. But some of those things are genuinely worth doing.

There's a famous book called Innovator's Dilemma. It's often these small companies heading into areas that weren't favored at first, seeing something that can gradually grow. Many companies rose this way. NVIDIA was like this too. Right, that's how NVIDIA rose.

So I think it's still full of opportunities. Right, I don't think you necessarily have to — if you start a company now and try to do the same thing as OpenAI and Anthropic, that's very dangerous. Right, your funding definitely can't match theirs. And you have no customers. How are you going to accumulate? Plus with their massive resources they can make things cheap and it's hard for you to catch up. So you have to solve pain points they can't solve. It's not that they don't want to solve them; it's that they can't. They can't justify why they should solve that problem.

So even if you want to build a large model, in the end you still have to find your own unique niche. Whether it's OpenAI or Anthropic — we can see that Anthropic was considered behind OpenAI early on. Right, but it was the earliest believer in coding. While OpenAI was making diversified investments, not putting all its eggs in one basket, Anthropic made concentrated investments and was the first to build the coding thing. So it saw some opportunities back then and it firmly believed and was determined to make it happen. So I think for entrepreneurs, you should have determination — to see an opportunity, to see your unique opportunity and use your resources to get things done.

But today, whether in Silicon Valley or China, everyone is homogeneously doing coding, agentic coding. How do you see this phenomenon? Do you think it's right?

Every company doing this has a different purpose behind it. I'm not in their position so I can't speak for them. But from my perspective, this is actually a very grueling thing.

You mean homogeneous competition?

Homogeneous competition is a grueling thing. I think — I think they may be forced into doing this. Because this is itself an important technology. No one wants their core technology to be in someone else's hands. But I don't think this is the entirety of their plan. They must have other plans to create some differentiation. Without differentiation, you can't make a distinctive product. In the end you still have to differentiate.

I think so.

十三、从研究者到 VP：不同阶段的挑战

We just went back over a long stretch of your journey. Looking at yourself as a researcher in your first job after arriving in the US, Ming-Yu Liu — and then becoming a tech lead at NVIDIA, and now a VP of Research — do you think the problems you solve in different periods are the same? The scale keeps getting bigger. And this scale doesn't just mean management scale, right?

Not just management scale — whether it's compute or headcount scale. It's also tied to the overall development of AI. AI going from exploration to real-world deployment. That's one change.

These different periods each had different experiences. Sometimes I still miss the old days when nothing worked, no matter what you tried, spending all day thinking about what would work. Why? When there are many possibilities, it's actually quite joyful. Multiple choices — having multiple choices gives you a kind of happiness.

Now there are also many choices. I just feel I'm getting closer and closer. I also quite enjoy going back to the very core of things. Now I find it's very much like the current solutions are all — oh — a heavy sword with no sharp edge; great skill looks effortless. Solidly building the infrastructure step by step and just getting things written. In this process of execution, I also find it a great experience. I've learned a lot from it. How to help the team see the core essence and improve execution. While at the same time, where innovation is possible, enabling the team to make major innovations to keep up with the changes of the era.

I think every period has different challenges, and they're all interesting.

Going from a researcher to a VP at NVIDIA — is that common?

I'm probably the first.

You're the first. Right, why do you think that is? That's what I want to ask you.

In my first few years at NVIDIA I was promoted one level every year. Jump, jump, jump, jump — all the way to VP. And I think it's because in the early days, when NVIDIA had no AI talent yet, I was there, helping the company raise its profile in the AI community and explain how AI would impact the company. And I personally love landing things in practice. Step by step I earned the company's trust, and the company became willing to give me bigger and bigger projects.

Like now — think about it — this whole team with so many people, using so much compute. Every day it's millions of dollars in compute costs, storage costs. I think over the years the company built a certain trust in me and only then did I get the chance to lead such a big project.

研究员本性与管理者角色的张力

Hmm, so aligning with the company is very important, right? The nature of a pure researcher and that of a manager might be somewhat at odds. Right, researchers need to innovate, researchers have high egos, researchers need recognition. And recognition — sometimes the recognition you want is different from what the company wants. So on your path to becoming a manager, was it possible that you had to suppress part of your researcher's nature? Was it like dancing in shackles?

I think I'm still a researcher. I still read papers all the time. And sometimes I do some implementation to understand things. What I worry about most on the road to becoming a manager — the one thing I worry about most is becoming disconnected from the ground level, not understanding where the core of the problem lies.

I force myself to review everyone's code, to read papers, to challenge everyone's ideas, to have debates with people, so to speak, to make sure the direction is right. People who work with me all know I'm probably one of the few VPs who still looks at code and still nitpicks the details. I feel if I didn't do this — of course it's not that I want to become someone great at implementation. It's that I feel if I didn't do these things, I wouldn't understand where the pain points are. And then I'd be even less able to understand each person's contribution to the project. I just hope to always stay grounded and see everything clearly. That way I can help the team grow and also clearly see who contributed what.

Jensen 的影响

Hmm, and what about Jensen? Did he influence you?

A tremendous influence. He's an extremely hard-working person. When I first joined NVIDIA, he would often send me papers to read. He'd send papers and ask me to read them.
