Hmm, if he didn't understand it, why did he dare to invest?

He has his own set of decision-making rules. It's called first principles. He takes the essence of a matter and sorts it out clearly, without being disturbed by outside signals. Then he sees very clearly which direction makes the most sense and heads that way. Early on he dared to go all in on deep learning, giving the company a huge lead. Early on he dared to go all in on CUDA, building a great foundation for the company. Before I got to know Jensen, I feel my decisions tend to be fairly short-term. Watching how he makes these long-term decisions and sticks with them, I think the impact is truly astonishing.

There are other amazing things about him. He gets a huge number of messages every day.

Emails, you mean?

Right, a huge number of emails. But he reads them all very carefully, looking for signals that others can't see and makes major decisions.

He is a very rational person. When you have a lot of things going on, if you can't do prioritization — that is, do the important things — and instead spend your time on unimportant things, you won't get the important things done. So deciding which things are important is a very important thing in itself. That's prioritization.

This is how I reason about it myself. He forces himself to read a huge volume of emails every day, forces himself to decide quickly what is important and what is not. Practicing this every single day, he sees things with great clarity. Okay, once you see clearly what is important and what is not, everything after that is execution.

And when many people execute, they mix in their personal feelings. Like, this isn't that important, but I'm on good terms with that person. Should I let him do it? He doesn't do that. His thinking is simply: my job is to take care of the whole company. I just keep making the most important decisions for the company. As long as you stay with the company, I will take care of you.

Right, I learned from him how to do prioritization. And this left a very deep impression on me. I mean, now — back when I was a researcher, handling two or three projects at the same time felt exhausting, switching between two or three topics a day. And now I switch topics almost every half hour. I couldn't have imagined myself doing this before. But being in this state of constant context switching also helps me better understand what really matters.

Right, and that's a very important thing. And there's another thing. If you've studied Computer Science, the most important thing in Computer Science is laziness. Don't compute what you don't need to compute. What can be computed later, compute later. What can be ignored, ignore entirely. You only have so much time in your life. You only have so much energy. If you can figure out what not to compute and just remove it, your life runs much more efficiently. So I think it's still well worth studying Computer Science. Don't stop studying Computer Science just because of AI.

So what has Jensen excluded from his scope of computation?

It's different in every period. Different at every point in time. Right, it's not fixed forever.

Hmm, for example, right now?

He has way too many things to deal with. It's hard to say what isn't important right now. What I see and what he sees are on completely different levels. What he sees — he's essentially a key driver of AI globally. Right, what he sees far exceeds what I've seen. I'm in no position to comment on what he considers unimportant now.

十五、武术、冰浴与个人自律

Hmm, how do you maintain your energy? Do you have any techniques?

I'm someone who really loves sports. I used to like team sports, playing basketball, playing tennis. Later I — I also have a big passion. I've been devoted to Chinese kung fu for many years, several decades. I've been practicing Chinese kung fu since I was 18.

I heard you practice kung fu, right? You have a kung fu teacher?

I have a kung fu teacher. My martial arts teacher is Xu Ji. He is a very famous martial arts teacher. His teacher was Liu Yunqiao. Liu Yunqiao's teacher was Li Shuwen. Back then he was called "Divine Spear" Li Shuwen, a representative martial artist of Cangzhou. His Bajiquan and Pigua Zhang were a major contribution to martial arts as a whole — the Bajiquan and Pigua Zhang that he systematized.

I was very fortunate, in Taiwan (China). Back then, because of Chiang Kai-shek, a group of martial artists moved to Taiwan (China). My teacher Xu Ji studied under Liu Yunqiao there, and I studied under Xu Ji. That's how I came to learn these Chinese martial arts.

Martial arts are great physical exercise, whether for the mind, for discipline, for physical strength — it's great for both body and mental discipline. Another benefit of martial arts is it's a sport you can do all by yourself. I get up in the morning and do my martial arts training, training on my own, doing some stance work, practicing some punches.

Recently I also picked up a new hobby called ice plunge. You use an ice tub like athletes do after intense exercise, jumping into a pool of ice-cold water to help the body recover. I think this also helps me maintain my energy to face each day's high-intensity challenges.

These are all things you do before work?

Yes.

That's quite different from my impression of you. Because every time I see you, you come across as very gentle and humble. But you still do sports that are relatively a bit intense right? Ice water, martial arts.

Yes. But my goal in learning martial arts was never to fight. At first it was the influence of Jin Yong's novels. And of course I became full of interest in these Chinese martial arts.

After learning, I found it's a kind of self-discipline. Because the essence of Chinese martial arts is controlling your whole body, controlling yourself. Because when you want to exert — when you throw a punch, the maximum power comes from whole-body coordination, channeling the force from your foot all the way to your hand, such a long path. You have to control the whole body's coordination. This force transmission is sequential. Getting it step by step in place is very hard because it all happens in an instant. So you have to keep practicing, constantly correcting yourself. I think this is deeply connected to how I like to constantly self-reflect and keep striving — it had a profound influence on me.

I'm not doing this to show off great destructive power. I feel it later became a kind of pursuit of self-improvement.

Your personality is fairly gentle. Can you even be called gentle? You're probably not like this at the company, right?

Oh, of course not. After doing this for a long time, you get a bit of "wishing iron could become steel". Inside the company I am — I think it's a way of directly pointing out where the problems are. It depends on the listener. If the listener takes me as well-intentioned, they'll be very happy. Because not everyone in this world is willing to tell you where you can improve further. They might be grateful to me for telling them this is where you can do better. But if you hear it as me just being critical, then you'll think I'm fierce.

Hmm, is this quest of yours to win with a single decisive blow — Cosmos?

Our whole group has just one project which is Cosmos. Yes. And I'm extremely focused on building Cosmos. We just hope to make a huge contribution to the world through Cosmos.

Hmm, is this also your most important quest for perhaps the next 10 years? Can we say that?

Why 97 and not 100?

十六、Cosmos 与世界模型：为机器人建造 Matrix

Hmm, let's now focus on Cosmos and world models, which is also your most important topic right now. I saw on your personal homepage that you've been driven by a vision of building a Matrix for robots. Can you elaborate on this vision?

I believe world models can help these embodied intelligences achieve this generalization. I think for any AI problem, the problem to solve is generalization. Can you perform really well beyond the training data you've seen? Generalization right? Like in Coding or in Chat, it's all about training a model so it can solve problems it never saw during training, becoming more like a human, right?

AI for the physical world is no exception. You have to solve generalization. And to solve generalization at Cosmos, here's how we want to help. Three points:

  1. Provide better data.
  2. Provide a better starting point.
  3. Provide a better environment.

For data, you can generate data. Data is the key to making AI models generalize better. You can imagine, in this world, the data you've seen is only so many points. Can you generate some of what you need to see but haven't collected in the real world?

And next: if you can train a good world model, this world model understands how the world works and can predict what will happen in the future. Such a model has a pretty good representation in itself. It can actually provide a physical-world AI, whether it's a policy model or any other model from which you can derive the policy you want. That's a better starting point.

Third — how does a person learn in this physical world? Through experiments, by interacting with the environment. Interacting with the real environment is often expensive. The time you can accumulate experience is limited. That's a limit. If you could use something like The Matrix to generate multiple environments at once, incredibly realistic environments that you can interact with, that give you signals, you could learn very, very fast. That's a better environment.

Better data, better starting point, better environment. The most challenging of these is the better environment. I didn't want to write it out at great length on my webpage like an essay. So I put it as something like The Matrix — it's a better way to help everyone understand what we want to do, how we want to help the Physical AI community.

Right, after Sora. It was exactly that point in time. And everyone felt this was full of resolve — we had to do it. I was honored that Jensen trusted me and let me lead this project.

Right. So he's very disciplined, moving toward the goal slowly, step by step.

Before Sora — well, first movers have a first mover advantage right? And every company has a different positioning. It depends on what problems you want to solve and how you want to profit. By the time Sora came, you felt the timing was right. Right. Did you write him another email?

It was a group of us working on generative models — this group doing media generation — we decided together to write Jensen an email. I guess everyone wrote one.

Everyone wrote one? Not one joint letter?

为什么选 Physical AI 作为目标市场

Why did you choose Physical AI back then? In terms of the market you were targeting.

By then it was gradually becoming clear that Physical AI would be the next revolution. Because it's a rigid demand. Everyone ages. Every place lacks labor. Everyone wants a better quality of life. And on the other hand, Nvidia goes after the developer market, helping these developers build better products. We ourselves wouldn't run a social network nor would we run a creation tool. That's a bit too to C for NVIDIA.

So you decided: I want to build a world model and this world model is for Physical AI to serve the Physical AI community.

十七、什么是"世界模型"？

Today, the definition of a world model is still very unclear. Tell us your definition of a world model.

I'm someone who values practicality. Why do people design a model? Because it can be used. There are many uses.

For example, you design a model to describe this world. Through this model, you can predict what will happen next. So its purpose is prediction. That's one kind of world model, one reason for designing a world model. A use: prediction.

Another is that you want to understand why this thing happened. In a sense all of physics is about building world models to understand how the world works. From Newtonian mechanics all the way to quantum mechanics, it's all about understanding how the world works — also building a model to help us understand how things work. Of course, in deep learning we take this understanding using only some labeled data to teach the model that this thing behaves this way. It's because this thing happened, and then with large-scale data generalization to help when new events happen in the future, you interpret the video signals you see to help people understand what happened. For example, in a factory, why did the production line suddenly get stuck here? Maybe some worker earlier forgot to turn something on. This is also one purpose of building a world model, to understand what happened and find the problem.

Right. And there's another kind of world model whose goal is to reconstruct the 3D world. Reconstructing the 3D world is very useful. You can plan which route your things should take. And you can let people experience it. Even though you're not physically in this real world, you can, in a virtual state, travel around in this world.

So — models for the world. Because your use cases differ, the models take different forms. In the end, we live in the same world. These models, through different observations, describe the same thing. Reconstruction is a very important field. I myself did reconstruction work before. But I no longer do reconstruction now. I now mainly work on understanding the physical world and generation of the physical world — right, things like prediction.

Everyone interprets world models differently. Defining what a World Model is now.

A few years ago, the same thing happened when everyone was defining what AGI is. And after all these years, there's still no shared definition. I think defining the World Model will very likely go down the same path. I don't think it's necessarily a very important thing.

Is that because the term is too big? Too general.

Right, it's too general. Once defined, what impact would that have on humanity?

Then why is LLM a relatively precise term? LLM is large language model. The model is very large, and it works on language. Right. So why does everyone have a consensus on this term, a precise definition, while people keep arguing endlessly about world models?

An LLM is an LLM — a large language model. A language model can predict what word comes next. Right? Large means the model is very big. That's very clear. Right?

A world model is a tool that helps you model the world — a tool for you to model the world. What do you want to use it for? Because the use cases differ, the way you model the world differs. So as long as you have different uses for this model, you get different definitions.

So do you think "world model" can describe Cosmos? Or should another term be used to describe what you're doing?

Yes. At the very beginning, we called Cosmos a world foundation model. Our goal is to build a foundation so that everyone can build the world models that suit their needs. That's why we call ourselves a foundation model, because we hope to be a more fundamental layer that serves everyone. That's how we define it.

Even someone who wants to build a world model can build on top of your foundation model. Yes — you want to provide that base.

Yes, we want to provide this base. Right. Because we believe world models will be an important part of Physical AI. But not every company that wants to work on Physical AI has enough resources to build the world model it needs from scratch — yet they need it. So to help them, we built Cosmos, this world foundation model.

Since you've also invested in LeCun's AMI Labs and Professor Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, are there differences between the world models you each make?

NVIDIA stands from an enabler's perspective. What we hope is, for any company built on our GPU ecosystem, we hope to help them succeed. We hope everyone can succeed together — win-win. Each company sees things a bit differently and wants to solve different problems. So there are all kinds of them. Fei-Fei's World Labs, Yann LeCun's AMI — they're all different, taking different routes. We help all of them, hope they succeed, and invest in them. We also collaborate with them. If they're interested in our Cosmos stuff, they can use it. Other companies need world models but may not be able to, unlike Fei-Fei or Yann LeCun, who are well funded. They may need help even more. They can leverage our Cosmos. Our goal is to help the whole field succeed.

So do you have competitors?

I think NVIDIA's competitors are companies doing the same things as NVIDIA — that is, building this whole AI ecosystem.

You said you have no competitors. But some companies also make compute.

When I'm working on Cosmos now, I don't think about competitors. What I think about is how to help this ecosystem. Within this ecosystem, those within NVIDIA's ecosystem using our GPUs, our computing platform, and our software — if they all succeed, then NVIDIA will succeed. Right? Because it gives people not yet in our ecosystem confidence. I think this is the way to help. I don't really want to compete anymore. I'm past that stage. Like back when, to graduate and get papers published, my algorithm had to be better than others'. Yes. Now my goal is to help this field move forward together.

十八、从 Cosmos 1 到 Cosmos 3 的演化

From the first to the third generation of Cosmos, it actually went through many changes. In the process from generation one to two, did you accumulate any know-how?

Yes. Well, this was last year's work. Right, the pace is very fast. Back when we started working on Cosmos, I emphasized one point: we must iterate fast. At that time I was deeply influenced by DeepSeek. Because DeepSeek is an astonishing company. It can iterate three times within a year and produce DeepSeek V3. So I kept stressing that our iteration speed must be fast. If iteration is fast, you can keep improving continuously, each generation better than the last.

But the problem we were tackling then was physical world models. At that time, especially in '24, it wasn't very clear. Everyone was still groping around for what kind of world model would help people. As I just said, using a world model is nothing more than how you use it — prediction or understanding, making a video model to help predict the future, or making a reasoning model to explain what happened. So at the very beginning, we worked with some partners to understand their needs, had some ideas of our own, and built these models. After iterating with these partners, we gradually converged.

In the process, we slowly converged. After we did predict, being able to predict the future, we thought simulation environments are commonly used, but the video they generate has a certain gap from the real world. Could we use a model to help make it more realistic? So we made Transfer. To explain what happened, we made Reason. At that time there were three.

Later we realized that if I can describe how pixels change, then this pixel change is actually very close to the change in my action. So we made something called Cosmo Policy, a policy model.

Later we gradually realized — as I just said — this is the same world. No matter which angle you look from, you're modeling the same world. Your model is learning an internal representation of the world. That is, this world — in the process of compressing it, what kind of representation you learn. Since it's the same thing, and there's also this thing called foundation model, whose core concept is that it can take in all streams and learn from all kinds of data — a model that learns these patterns. So if you can take the data used to train reasoning, the data used to train predict, the data used to train transfer, the data used to train policy, and combine them all, your model's ceiling is higher. First, you're describing the same world. Second, a foundation model takes in everything, combining things together. So we gradually moved toward this single model.

22 个模型与 LV 的启示

There's also a practical, execution-level issue in between. I remember when I was building the first version of Cosmos, I did the math myself. Because I hoped the models could really help others — working with these partners, I might need models A, B, C, D, E, F, G. I calculated it myself: back then we might need 22 models.

At that time I had a meeting with Jensen, and I told Jensen that I expected to need 22 models. When Jensen heard that, he thought I was working very hard. And he said, "Very good, work very hard." He said, "But you know what? Louis Vuitton — LV, that store — after it reduced the number of items on display, sales actually went up. You don't want too many things confusing your consumers, so they can't make a decision."

That had a big impact on me. I realized that I myself ran into this problem: even I couldn't tell whether to use A or B, let alone other people. Then there's the execution difficulty. Every time you release a model, it's not like we publish a paper and it's done, then move on to the next paper. We have to help users use it. Whenever a model comes out, we have to maintain it and solve problems. When you have many models, it's really hard. Prepare for everything and your strength is spread thin. It affects your iteration speed.

So when working on version one, during the iteration process, we quickly worked on two. While working on two, we realized no — this wouldn't be sustainable. So we decided to make this only model — the World Model, that is, Cosmos 3. First, they describe the same thing, so they can actually be combined. Second, a foundation model absorbs all kinds of data, combined together. It's also much simpler in development. So we went down the path of Cosmos 3.

So 2 to 3 was actually a big change.

Yes. The change from 1 to 2 was basically an improvement in data, plus some others — back in 2 we brought policy in. There were some changes. But I think 2 to 3 is a very big gap.

How long did 3 take?

We started on 3 last October, right after releasing 2. It was October when we released 2, right. Actually, we knew even earlier that we had to do 3. But by then we had already started 2.5. We wrapped up 2.5, and only started 3 after wrapping up 2.5. So maybe around September we knew we needed to do 3. Actual execution was probably October, November. It took nearly half a year. Over half a year.

关于工程 vs 创新的评价

A Chinese founder working on world models said he spent a week reading the Cosmos 3 paper, reading it every day, and there are lots of details in it. He said their view was that Cosmos 3 doesn't have many big technical innovations, but it has engineering-validated many of the details. Do you think their assessment is fair?

Mixture Transformer was proposed by others before, and Policy Model was also proposed before. We are the first to scale this Mixture Transformer to such a large model, combining audio, video, and action together. Conceptually, these things are just combining things together, but actually making it work is not that easy. Actually pulling it off comes down to these details.

All these large language models use the Transformer architecture. You could say nobody innovated, but it's those details that make some models much better than others. I think after all these years, I value more the effects these things can produce, and I care less and less about whether something is a revolutionary original. To me, it's useful and produces impact. Solving the problems people want solved is the point.

Right. With this paper, we hope to help the entire open-source community build open-source models and help all of Physical AI. The phenomenon we've seen these years is that many Frontier Labs have gone closed-source. Even when they write papers, they won't reveal the key parts. We decided to take a different path. We explain everything we can as clearly as possible. We open-sourced the model, and also the framework for how we train it. We also open-sourced part of the synthetic data. We want to stay transparent and let everyone see how it's done. We also hope others can use our open-source materials to build something similar to Cosmos, if they're interested. Our goal is to enable this entire community. Right. I'm not worried that others can make an identical thing.

You just mentioned DeepSeek — is your choice to open-source related to it?

Not exactly related. DeepSeek's work has had a profound impact on all of AI — the first company to open-source MoE. And look at its recent models, the care they put in, pushing it to the extreme. These have all profoundly influenced the field. Right, I think this is very important. From the perspective of impact, I think they're connected. We want to make an impact, laying out all these details. NVIDIA has many Physical AI companies built on the NVIDIA ecosystem. We hope to help them succeed. Our goal may be different from DeepSeek's. We hope to help our users succeed. You are inherently this ecosystem. Right, we just hope to help Physical AI arrive in the world sooner.

十九、多模态设计的深层考量

Why did you choose this time, first at the input layer, to support inputting language, video, audio, and action at the same time? Was this an important decision?

Yes. I think the world isn't only visual. Right? There's also hearing. I'd also like to add touch, but tactile signals aren't good enough yet. Touch sensors and such are still iterating rapidly. This requires dexterous hands. Right, it needs dexterous hands, it needs data.

I think for large models, there are basically two lines of thinking. One treats language as a first-class citizen, like Coding, like Chat. The other treats visual signals — video — as a first-class citizen, like Seedance, like Veo.

We believe the biggest difference between physical world models and digital world models is that physical-world agents take action and change the state of the world. We believe a good physical-world foundation model should also treat action as a first-class citizen. That's why we combined language, video, and action together to build this Cosmos 3.

语言污染视觉？

Right, I remember Yang Zhilin once told me that when they build language models, he treats language as the most important tool for advancing intelligence. They worried a lot that adding vision would affect its intelligence, turning it into a dumb multimodal model. But this year Xie Saining told me he worries about language polluting vision. He thinks language is humanity's scaffolding, not something essential — that's his view. So how do you view these two perspectives of theirs? And when you train all these signals together, do problems arise? Mutual pollution, that is.

Each of these signals is brought in with its own purpose. Language can bring in human knowledge and also help humans communicate with physical AI. Video provides massive visual information, audio provides massive auditory information, describing how the world works. Using video captures the world's physical workings more precisely. With language, that's actually very hard. Right? But between humans and the model — the model is ultimately built to serve people. If it doesn't understand language, you can't communicate with it. Ultimately the model is meant to help machines take action. So if it doesn't understand action, it can't change the world.

I should put it this way: our purposes are different. My goal is for this to become a good foundation model for physical AI. It needs to understand language, needs to know how things change, and then action, and then use this control to bring them together. My goal is not to pursue AGI.

Right, and AGI itself is hard to define. When the AGI you define is purely about understanding the essence of humans, or whatever, doing coding, these visual signals might interfere with you. That's inevitable. Right? Yes, you could say in the distant ancient past there was no language at all, all of this development of human civilization is generated by observing how the world changes. You could argue that after all, language evolved to suit humans, but you don't know whether machines buy into that. Maybe you just, from visual signals, directly learn how the world works and arrive at an intelligence and then develop another civilization. If you look at it from that angle, maybe the language signal is a kind of interference.

I think it depends on what you want. I know very clearly what I want. So I think I need language so that people can communicate with this Physical AI. I need video and audio to describe, from the changes in the physical world, to learn the physical essence. And I need action, because in the end I want it to be able to, for Physical AI, to change the world.

多模态的互补关系

Right, so all modalities are fused together. Do these modalities mutually benefit each other, or do they constrain each other?

Over the past year, even more than a year, we've been continuously researching the fusion of these modalities. And from various different research efforts we got some clues and combined them in Cosmos 3.

For example, in the Cosmos Policy work, we found that combining video and action helps the action side. When you directly predict action — when we were building the world action model, we found that besides predicting what action to take, you also predict what comes next — the state that results after you take this action, that is, the observation — which helps you train it well. So we know that predicting the video helps the action.

This whole family of world action models — sound can also help video generation. When you know there's a "click" sound, the point of contact — you know the moment of contact is that point. So we know these are mutually complementary.

People who work on video generally know that going from text to video is a process where the amount of information increases, the demand grows larger, which means there are many possibilities. A function with many possibilities is harder to learn. One thing might have 10 possibilities. Then there's no fixed target, so it's hard to learn. So in video or image generation, everyone finds that when your text description is very detailed, it's easier to generate a good video. So you can see that a detailed text description also helps the video.

With Cosmos 3, we wanted to bring together the earlier Cosmos Reason, Cosmos Predict, Cosmos Transfer, Cosmos Policy — all these things together. Combining them has its own benefits — the whole thing gets simplified.

How do these signals get combined so that they complement each other rather than working against each other?

This can be achieved through experimental design and by adjusting the proportions of the data. So at the time we firmly believed that these signals all describe the same world and they all contain information about how the world works. There should be a way to combine them so that they help each other. More information helps you understand what the underlying operating principles are. Right, so we had this belief and set out in that direction.

So is there any secret sauce in this, in terms of the mutual benefit?

Actually, there's no secret sauce in building large models. Run rigorous experiments, make hypotheses, run experiments, see the results, accumulate knowledge, then run the next experiment. Just go step by step, do solid work, that's it. There's nothing — I don't think there's any hidden secret. It's just what you pursue: patiently run experiments, validate, and if it checks out, take the next step that way.

二十、双塔架构的设计权衡

Mm. This time you adopted a dual-tower design, one tower processing discrete information and one tower processing continuous information. Why this design?

There are many reasons. In the beginning, Cosmos Reasoning was discrete, starting from a vision language model. Predict, Transfer, Policy were continuous. So we knew discrete works for understanding, and we knew continuous works for generation. Putting them together is a very reasonable choice at this stage.

And another thing, there are many ways to use Cosmos, but the common one is post-training. Maybe you use your video-action pairs to train the generator, or maybe you only want to use the reasoning part and only train it with understanding data from your own domain. When you have two parts that can work together while keeping the gradient influence separated, it makes it easier for customers to use.

If we connected everything together, then generation and understanding would be tied together. Now suppose I want to change the generation distribution. In the process, since everything is connected, your data would also change the performance on the understanding side. If you don't have two towers but just one, then since the understanding side will change, and your data has no understanding data in it, the understanding part can easily get lost. That makes it inconvenient for customers to use.

So splitting it into two definitely helps usability. Although it's relatively less elegant, because you still have to decide the architecture in advance. In terms of dependency, ideally the data decides how it's done, rather than you artificially making the distinction. But at this stage, I think this is the more reasonable choice and better suited for practical use.

Speaking of this, people can probably guess that our next goal is to make it simpler. Why two towers? One tower should be enough. But as we move toward the goal of one tower, we have to consider whether users can easily adopt it. Because our goal is to help everyone win, not to produce a model ourselves that can do many things. We believe every robot is different — the number of cameras, the camera positions — and every autonomous vehicle is different too. We feel we need restraint: even if we merge everything to pursue engineering simplicity and perfection, I still have to consider whether users can actually make use of it. That's a problem we must research.

Mm. But relatively speaking, discrete signals are easier to handle; once you fuse in continuous variables, the processing difficulty increases. How do you combine them and scale it up?

Right. There's now a series of works like Transfusion that can handle both discrete and continuous. When doing next token prediction, it's discrete; when doing diffusion, it's continuous. That's within the same tower. During this period there have been many different variants. Everyone is researching this; it's a problem everyone cares about.

I think these signals can be represented discretely or continuously. I hope that maybe we can develop an architecture that is all discrete, or all continuous, to make things relatively simpler. But that's an ideal; we're not sure it can succeed. We also need to validate step by step with experiments as we go.

Intuitively, which is easier — discrete or continuous?

Ah, each has its own advantages. Discrete is easier to train. Continuous has its own elegance — that is, when doing Influence, the two have very different shapes.

Ultimately, the key point is that customers still have to deploy it. And cost considerations at deployment are very important. So I think in the end it comes down to deployment — what kind of model is best suited for deployment — I think that's what most easily leads to success. So there are many directions, and the discussion should focus there.

A researcher asks you: Since you're now training all modalities into one model, then in theory it could also do Coding very well, it could make robots work, and it could generate creator content like what we have today. So is it possible that in a single dimension, say Coding, it could be even stronger than Claude?

I still like what The Art of War says: "He who defends everywhere defends nowhere". If you want to be good at everything, during training you need to be broadly knowledgeable, you have to cover many different categories to raise your level of knowledge. But if you're sure you only need this single application, then are there some adjustments — since you don't care about the other things — Is there anything you're willing to give up to do it better? Because if you're not willing to give up anything, you'll have a very hard fight. I think strategy is often about deciding what you can afford to give up.

Will the two towers improve each other?

We know that — we have an experiment in this paper showing that when you use a reasoner closer to Physical AI, it can help you do better Physical AI generation. We also know that if you can pass the generator's gradient back to the reasoner, in theory it can help your reasoner learn better representations. In this paper, limited by time, we didn't complete all the experiments we wanted to do. There were already many experiments. But this thing — foundation model development itself is very time-consuming. A decision is made two or three months in advance. It's hard to make quick adjustments. We don't see this 3 as the end point. We'll continue with 3.1, 3.2, improving step by step, adding the capabilities we want to build in and the research we want to do that we didn't get a chance to present this time — we'll keep filling those in.

二十一、未来 Cosmos 与泛化问题

Mm. Besides possibly being simpler — the two towers might become one — what other changes might people see in future models?

What we care a lot about is how this model can help Physical AI builders. After this model was released, as far as I know, everyone has been discussing it. Some partners, some colleagues have given pretty good feedback.

I think generalization is a core problem — a core problem for any AI. And in physical-world AI, I think one kind of generalization we need to achieve is: suppose today I teach a robot that I like my clothes folded this way and placed like this. I show the robot once or twice how I do it — can it then learn it quickly, learn it quickly in real life? If you let the Physical AI read the manual, will it know how to operate the instrument, how to do inspection in a factory? I think these are very important capabilities that Physical AI should be able to achieve.

Of course, there are many considerations when deploying these. What I mean is, in the foundation model part, is there something we can do to help these Physical AI developers? So our improvements will probably all be directed toward improving these generalization capabilities and building these things into the Cosmos model.

For example, what specific optimizations have you made for this?

Optimizations like acceleration will definitely happen. Of course we want the model to run faster and faster. Other optimizations are about capability, optimizations for generalization. Right. That might involve changing some architecture, or changing some training objectives, or using some specially curated data for the training. It's not entirely clear; it needs testing. It's an experimental science.

Right, it's an experimental science. I often feel deep learning is a lot like traditional Chinese medicine — it's figured out through trial and error. Through trial and error, right. And in the process of trying, you keep detailed experimental records and from them you understand the underlying principles. I think this is very interesting. I think these two things are very similar. I think running rigorous experiments, controlling variables, and getting some key results is an important step in model iteration.

Some researchers have also suggested that the model's language rendering — could its weighting be increased a bit more? Because they still believe LLMs are the key to improving intelligence. Do you agree?

I think in early image generation research, including Imagen — Google's Imagen — it was already proposed that the stronger your language understanding, when you use a larger T5 model, the stronger your image generation capability. I do believe that. Using a larger semantic representation should help. I agree with that.

After all, Physical AI applications are different from what people often talk about — Coding or Chat. So experimental validation is still needed. What I want to do is understand the real pain points and from those pain points find the right way to strengthen the model's capabilities.

There are signals everyone has received that a better model — when you have no resource constraints, of course you'd put it in. But the more challenging thing is when your resources are limited, how do you make the trade-offs?

Mm. So maybe for these scenarios, intelligence may not be the most critical variable. Do you need your robot to solve math olympiad problems? Do you need your robot to solve Coding problems? I think you probably care more about whether it can assemble well what your factory needs to assemble, or handle household chores — do these tasks well. Right. So I think the problem you're solving seems somewhat different from what these large language model companies, these Agent companies, are solving. It's a bit different. So since it's a different problem, the cost of solving it is ultimately an important — If you want to commercialize, cost is ultimately an important consideration. So under these conditions, will its architecture really be the same as the existing models built for agents? This is a question I've been thinking about.

Do you have a preliminary answer now? Any intuition?

Looking across human history, the answer is that it should be different. Right? The tools you make for plowing fields are different from the tools you make for weaving. So they're actually different. In the end, "he who defends everywhere defends nowhere", right? The wisdom of our ancestors still works pretty well.

How many GPUs and resources will you invest in Cosmos going forward?

We've been — the GPU count has been increasing. I'm not sure it's appropriate for me to disclose the number of GPUs. But we're already at the tens-of-thousands level, and we hope it can be even more.

NVIDIA 的两大模型矩阵

Will it be NVIDIA's most important model project?

NVIDIA has several model projects. We mainly divide them into two categories:

  1. Agentic AI: doing Coding, Chat — serving customers' needs for agentic, digital-intelligence capabilities. In this category we have the Nemotron model — the Nemotron Ultra their team recently released has achieved pretty good results.

  2. Physical AI: the main one is the Cosmos model.

Cosmos is a base model. NVIDIA also cares a lot about autonomous vehicles, cares a lot about robots, and about factories. For us, these are all Physical AI applications. And for autonomous vehicles — it's a specialization built on top of Cosmos, doing the optimizations specifically needed for autonomous vehicles. GR00T does robot-related optimizations on top of Cosmos, and also includes things like whole body control.

I see the teams working on autonomous vehicles, internally working on autonomous vehicles, and on robots, as my customers too, and I hope to help them succeed. On the Physical AI side, Cosmos is the core, helping these key developers succeed.

So there are mainly two. You ask which is most important — both are very important. Digital AI, how to use agents, how to do Coding is very important. Physical AI is very important too. It's hard to say which is more important.

Right. But the fiercest competition right now is in Agentic AI. Physical AI is the next step. How big a market do you think Physical AI will be?

This should be a huge market. Estimating market size is not my expertise, and it's not appropriate for me to speak for the company on how big. But as the population ages, with the demand for autonomy in manufacturing, and all kinds of applications, we believe this will be a huge market.

二十二、评估、数据与 Ego-Centric 的重要性

Mm-hmm. Since world models currently lack effective evaluation methods, do you have any good explorations?

World models, large language models — everyone is seeking better evaluation and testing methods. Generally speaking, model evaluation has three steps:

  1. Benchmarks — there are some fixed datasets and you test its quality on them.
  2. Arena style — compare A with B and see which is better.
  3. Working with experts — with people who really have this pain point, to solve the problem.

I think all three are important. In Physical AI, the third is especially important. Because every Coding Agent is solving Coding problems, digital-use problems, but for Physical AI, each problem to solve is somewhat different. Right, I think we emphasize more working with customers, with partners who are willing to collaborate. Let's also talk about how to evaluate whether a model is truly useful or not. That's not an easy thing to do. It's an important step in guiding model development. I think in the future of development, this step will become more and more important.

Data is also a difficult problem. How did you do it this time?

Data is a difficult problem, and it's especially hard in Physical AI, because in Physical AI, every form factor is different. To collect data, without a physical setup, there's no way to collect that data. And at NVIDIA it's even harder, because we serve all kinds of Physical AI developers. Every robot is different. So what we can do is find the most common ground.

We think there are mainly two types of Physical AI data: - Navigation data: going from A to B. - Manipulation data: how to use a hand or a tool to manipulate things and complete a given task.

Navigation data is easier to work with. It's just — how a car moves, how a robot moves. These can all be collected. So for robot A and robot B, even if they're different, moving around is just displacement in space, sometimes with some rotation added. So they're relatively similar.

Manipulation is more complex. We've noticed a trend: everyone is increasingly pursuing robot arms that resemble human hands. The argument is that — the human world was built for humans to use, so most tools are designed to be operated by human hands. And AI needs huge amounts of data. The easier your data is to obtain, the faster you can achieve breakthroughs. And most of the data collection is done by people. And people have hands. Okay, so two circumstances — two conditions: hand-based data collection, and the world is largely built for human hands. So that's why you see everyone moving in the direction of human hands.

So with Cosmos 3 this time, we specifically added ego-centric data, which includes how human eyes see things, from a first-person view, and how human hands manipulate objects. Because our goal is not to build a robot ourselves. Our goal is to help everyone build great robots. So we look for the things that are most transferable. I think ego-centric data is very important to everyone.

Given all the current limitations we just talked about, does NVIDIA have any significant advantages?

At NVIDIA, the cost of getting GPU compute is cheaper. After all, we make GPUs. And also, we've been deeply involved in Physical AI for many years. We have the Thor chip, and simulators like Isaac. So I think with all these things combined, we can offer more tools to meet all kinds of needs of Physical AI developers. And one more thing: we genuinely want to help other companies succeed. Because we're very clear about where our own services lie. We don't get caught in constant comparisons. I think customers are often more willing to work with us, because we — we won't go and make exactly the same thing as you and then just — wipe you out. No, that's not our goal.

What's the thing you're most satisfied with about this model (Cosmos 3)? And what might you feel a bit regretful about?

What I'm satisfied about is that — I told everyone back then that we could combine all the past models into one and it would be better than all the previous models. And that actually happened. Our current model performs better than each of the standalone models before. Back then many people didn't believe it. I felt very happy about that.

The second thing is — this was the first time we took the whole team, which had been building several models, and merged them to build one model. Getting such a large organization to come together to build this model — I'm personally very proud that this happened smoothly.

What's the regret? I think our model — because of time constraints — well, I think the model could still keep improving, but because of the time limit, we didn't let it fully converge before we had to release it. There are still many things we wanted to fix that we didn't have time to change before. So that's the place where — after all, you always want to pursue a better result, but time is limited. The good thing is we'll keep making 3.1, 3.2, and we'll take the things we didn't do well and put them back in.

Hmm, have you ever thought about what old Huang said — what it would be like to reach generation 97?

When I heard "97 generations" back then, my understanding was — we have the determination to keep building it all the way, to make it great. That's a very big commitment, because building these models is very resource-intensive. He showed his determination to keep going. The confidence I got from it is that — this thing will keep moving forward. World models, in the end, are about — approaching the real world. Right, approaching the real world. From — through that model, you can learn the things you want to learn in the real world. So I think we're heading in that direction. Actually, the closest thing to it is — you have the ability to create, at any time, the Matrix from The Matrix. I think that's the ultimate form.

I'm not sure whether it needs to go all the way to generation 97. Look, if we do one generation every six months, that's still more than forty years away, right? More than forty years. Right. But I think AI is developing extremely fast now, so maybe it won't take forty-plus years.

二十三、数字 AI 与 Physical AI 的模型差异

Your team works both on models for the digital world and on models for Physical AI. What do you think the difference is in training the two types of models? Is the difference big?

The current state is like this: on the Nemotron side, they use something called a hybrid architecture. Some layers are traditional Transformer, but some layers are Mamba-style, close to an RNN architecture. That kind of architecture has its advantages, because RNN computation is — at inference, RNN computation is cheaper than Transformer. An agent has to generate a pile of tokens. Sometimes you need the agent to do things that take a long time, so there's this compute cost requirement.

On the Physical AI side, our architecture no longer follows that route. We still go with the more traditional Transformer, but we move toward Mamba Transformer, adding action into it. So the development of the models on these two sides is — gradually becoming a bit different. But our two teams work very closely together. You can see in the Cosmos 3 paper that many of the authors came from Nemotron. We collaborate with them, drawing on their experience, building some models together.

In the future, could these two models be unified into one larger model?

It's all possible. Our decision-making is very simple: whatever helps the customer the most — that's what we do. Right, we're very low ego.

二十四、驱动 200+ 人团队的组织哲学

You also mentioned earlier that Cosmos is a very large team. What do you think is the hard part of driving such a large team to work together? The challenge, I mean. I recall the paper had something like 290-plus authors — under 300 people, right?

Right, this team is very big. The way I see it, it's an organizational design challenge. You want everyone's goals to be aligned, but you also want everyone to be able to make decisions autonomously.

When everyone's goals are aligned but nobody can make decisions, progress will be very slow, because only a small number of decision-makers can make decisions. Suppose only I could make the decisions — only I decide how to adjust the data mixture, only I decide how to build the architecture — then our model would not succeed, because my knowledge is limited and my time is limited. What we need is for everyone to be able to make decisions that matter for the organization and the model's development.

And the second thing is, if everyone can make decisions but their goals aren't aligned — I just want to make action great, I don't care at all about how video is doing; I just want to make understanding great, not caring about anything else — then things will diverge. You might end up with different architectures, and it might turn into horse-racing behavior between teams.

I think in running such a big project, the key is to keep everyone's goals aligned while still letting everyone make decisions. In terms of organizational structure, I put a lot of thought into designing how teams operate and collaborate — making information transparent, giving everyone enough information to make the right decisions for the group. Of course, we also provide room for error, because when someone is afraid of making a wrong decision, they won't make any decision at all. So you have to let them make decisions, while accepting that some decisions will be wrong — but when mistakes happen, you have to correct them quickly. All of this takes some time and some training for the whole team to move in the right direction.

How do you get more than 200 people to all make decisions at the same time? That sounds so hard.

Everyone is clear about — the whole key — what the whole project is ultimately trying to achieve. You have to keep sketching out the future clearly, and tell it to every person. Before the Cosmos 3 paper came out, or before the work was done, I had already talked to the main leaders and the major parts of the team, saying, "The model we build will look like this." Did it turn out exactly like that? Maybe 90% similar, 10% not similar. But when everyone sees the same vision, it's easier to converge. It's like when you're a basketball player — before you take a free throw, you always picture the ball swishing through the net. You set that target first, and then everyone moves toward it. Of course, everyone plays a different role, but when everyone sees the same picture, it's easier for each person in their position to make the right decision for the team.

Mm. What management methods did you design to make information more transparent and collaboration better? What management techniques are there?

Put in more thought. Understand how to say something — so that people get it. Focus on communication.

Focus on communication. Do you hold regular meetings, like weekly meetings?

I'm someone who — I care a lot about teamwork and collaboration, so we have a lot of meetings. But not once a week — we probably have ten a week.

Per week?

Probably more than ten.

More than ten. With everyone, or with how many people?

With the main leaders, each — For example, the team doing video — they meet regularly, maybe two or three times a week. The understanding team also meets regularly, two or three times a week. And then for each of the other areas, two or three times as well. So there are quite a lot of meetings.

And you can do a lot of communicating in these meetings. Of course, people often feel meetings are — sometimes very inefficient. One thing I try hard to do is make every meeting more engaging, and let everyone participate. All of this takes some training to get the team to work this way.

It's never going to be maximally efficient. You could have nobody hold any meetings and everyone do their own thing — that won't necessarily succeed either. You could also hold meetings nonstop, do nothing, just talk — that won't succeed either. You have to find a balance. At different points in time, there will be different ways to strike that balance. This all depends on the task and the time. There's no fixed formula for which one is guaranteed to work, which one is best.

You see, in Silicon Valley people say OpenAI's culture is bottom-up and Anthropic is top-down. Which one do you belong to?

We're a bit of both. Any single approach taken to the extreme — you know, "long divided must unite, long united must divide" — things always reverse at their extremes. I think you always have to grasp, at that point in time, what the right thing for the team is, rather than blindly following one direction, operating in one fixed mode.

二十五、Physical AI 的 ChatGPT 时刻

I understand the moment Cosmos takes off might be positively correlated with Physical AI and robotics taking off. Is that right? Correct? When do you think this market will see a so-called ChatGPT moment?

Everyone is chasing this ChatGPT moment for Physical AI. ChatGPT moment — what is a ChatGPT moment? How is a ChatGPT moment different from a GPT moment? The GPT moment told us that things can scale — that after scaling, model capabilities get stronger. The ChatGPT moment was when everyone could clearly see how such scaling, such a good model, would change people's lives. Everyone realized, here's an intelligent agent you can talk to — like asking a very knowledgeable friend.

So what is the ChatGPT moment for Physical AI? I think it means everyone sees an AI-enabled Physical AI application that makes people clearly see this thing is truly useful. When will this happen? That's very hard to predict. But what I see is the whole field's interest in Physical AI growing, more and more capital flowing in, more and more ambitious people starting companies to solve this problem. Physical AI can leverage the success of digital AI. So I think all the conditions are gradually converging. I hope to see the ChatGPT moment as soon as possible. Maybe this year, maybe next year — I don't know. But I think it's bound to happen.

Do you think humanoid robots will become the mainstream in this space?

I think the advantage of humanoid robots is that they can leverage huge amounts of human data as good material for learning, to improve these results. But humanoid robots themselves — the more human-like they are, with legs and hands, the relatively higher their complexity. A lot of people are building wheeled ones, where only the upper body is human-like, but the lower body is a mobile platform. That kind of platform can also solve many problems.

And would you call that a humanoid robot?

I'd say yes — the upper half is human-like, right, even if it's not fully humanoid. Among fully humanoid ones, some are closer to human form, and some humanoids are less close to human form. I think humanoid robots will ultimately be an important key. But exactly how human-like — everyone is still experimenting with that. I think in the very end, fully humanoid may be the best fit for all kinds of manipulation, because the human environment is designed for the fully human form. But in the end, the key still comes down to operating costs — which option delivers the highest economic efficiency. And that's beyond my expertise. I actually don't know. My goal is to help all these different Physical AI builders, so I don't need to make that choice. I just listen to their voices and see what our models can do to help them more.

DeepMind research scientist Jie Tan has a prediction: he thinks 2035 to 2036 might be the tipping point for humanoid robots going mainstream.

Oh, really? I hope it's earlier, but I'm not sure.

Mm. Do you think world models might have a so-called tipping point?

I don't think world models are new. World models have existed for a long time. And I think world models will keep improving in performance. What we've seen with large language models — models getting better and better — right, I think we'll see that with world models too. And this time with Cosmos 3, we've made a rather different kind of world model — this kind of omni-model world model. Right, so I think there are still some changes coming. It will take a bit of time for everyone to absorb and digest it, because after all, this isn't something you can use directly once the model is out. You have to figure out how to deploy it, how to land it in robotics scenarios. I think that takes some time. I think it will keep changing.

The Matrix 的哲学隐喻

Because you said you want to build The Matrix for robots, right? And what The Matrix itself depicts is a world where humans have been reduced to living batteries for machines, living in a virtual world, the Matrix, where an awakened person tries to break free from the fate of this system and end the cycle. So now you're building this Matrix for robots. What if one day the robots awaken and want to break out of this virtual world?

The reason I use The Matrix is to help everyone visualize — that a world model can accelerate learning this fast. Many people worry that when AI becomes too capable, it will take over the world and eliminate us. But I think this society was built by people. These technologies are operated by people behind the scenes. I think as long as everyone shares the consensus, that kind of thing won't happen.

And besides — this gets a bit philosophical. I think pain and suffering is a driver that pushes people to improve — an important key. I'm not so sure whether these silicon-made intelligences experience the same pain and suffering. I have my doubts about that. Of course I know we hope this technology can greatly improve human life, and we also need to build the corresponding guardrails to make sure it doesn't disrupt the normal development of the world.

二十六、竞争观：合作而非零和

Mm, speaking of world models — other teams working on world models see you as a competitor, because everyone thinks you're also building world models. But you keep saying I'm not your competitor. Right? Is there anything you'd like to say to them?

A world model is a tool. Tools are for solving problems. There are many different problems to solve. For the problems you ultimately want to solve, a world model alone isn't enough. It depends on the problem you want to solve. If you say because we want to serve the entire Physical AI system, we build world models for everyone to use. The problem of Physical AI itself is especially hard. There are many other problems to solve. If you can collaborate with us and make use of what we've built, you can go faster and further. Isn't that a great thing?

Right? Everything we do is open source. If you use our work and build a better model than ours, that model is also open source for everyone to use. We're still helping the whole Physical AI system. So you end up better than us, and we think that's a good thing too. I think everyone working together to solve hard problems is something well worth doing. When people push against each other, set high bar and keep climbing higher, that's also a very important part of it.

They'll definitely say oh, NVIDIA just wants to sell me GPUs again. Right, but you do need compute. We — NVIDIA's ecosystem is right here now. There are so many things you can take advantage of. Why not right?

Running any business requires investment. What matters most is how much you earn rather than — Take these cloud companies — they bought huge numbers of GPUs but they made even more money. Right?

Cosmos 会是下一个 CUDA 吗？

Do you discuss internally what the next CUDA will be? Could it be Cosmos?

Software in the past was built on logic. CUDA helped convert the logic these applications needed into GPU computation. Future software will be AI-centric. AI is built on top of other AI. So we think the Nemotron and Cosmos we're building could both be the CUDA of the future.

Because outsiders do a lot of post-mortems on CUDA. From your perspective, how do you think CUDA succeeded? What elements did it need to have? For example, which of them does Cosmos have now? And which does it lack? Is it a replicable path?

I'm not sure whether it's replicable. I think when CUDA was first proposed, it was a very forward-looking idea. It was a very risky idea. Back when it was still uncertain whether accelerated computing would be a big thing, our company made that bold investment. All the large models we build benefit from CUDA and can keep moving forward.

I wouldn't equate Cosmos or Nemotron with CUDA, because I think the whole landscape has become much more complex now. There are many different — The whole industry is many stacks combined together. I think the combination of them might be the new CUDA rather than saying a single model is a CUDA. You still need to do serving. You still have to build all this infrastructure. Many things have to come together.

Mm, so which elements do you think jointly contributed to CUDA's success?

At the beginning, CUDA was searching for applications. At first it was scientific computing. Then later, after deep learning emerged, CUDA found its most important application and kept going. And CUDA keeps providing all kinds of different applications. I think replicating CUDA is a great idea, but I don't think following the original route will take you down the same path. I think the environment is different. Right, I think you need to be adaptive. You have to see clearly what important contributions can be made at which time.

Mm, so you don't go around holding a hammer looking for nails, right? Holding onto "I have to make the next CUDA" just because it was such a successful decision back then to make today's decisions. Just as Jensen often says, his first principle is based on first principles. He goes with what makes sense and then moves in that direction, rather than holding a hammer and looking for nails.

二十七、NVIDIA 10 年：见证一家公司的蜕变

Because you've just hit 10 years at NVIDIA. Yes. Have you changed a lot over these 10 years? How many times has your NVIDIA stock multiplied?

None of this was anticipated. During this period, we witnessed a shift from nobody associating AI with NVIDIA to the whole world associating NVIDIA with AI, to a time when my parents didn't know what NVIDIA was to a time when the whole world knows what NVIDIA is. That's an enormous change.

The journey in between wasn't easy either. If you look at the stock price, the company has had its ups and downs. I remember the year the TPU first came out, the company's stock price dropped by a large chunk. Some colleagues at that time started to think differently about the company's future and left. But later NVIDIA beat the TPU in MLPerf every year, delivering better cost-performance. Eventually we were the only ones left competing.

These things are all very hard to predict. I think these changes are really huge. Over this long period, I've come to better understand what it means to build something slowly. Building slowly means finding a goal you believe in very first-principles and moving forward step by step. You just watch Jensen lead this huge team of the whole company step by step toward today's achievements. I feel honored to be part of it, you know. That's roughly it.

When you joined, you didn't expect any of this. You had other offers back then but didn't take them. Right, right, it was unpredictable.

The reason I joined back then was that I wanted GPUs to support my academic research. It was a very simple reason. In a way, I'm also very first-principles. I thought GPUs are an important tool for doing research. I wanted to go somewhere with lots of GPUs, so why not go to the place that makes GPUs.

Who was the other offer from, back then?

I had several offers. One of them was an investment firm. They told me no matter where I went, no matter how much the other side offered me, we'll give you four times that, and hoped I would join their company to research using deep learning for investing together. I wasn't really that interested in that. I still wanted to do research, so I still chose Nvidia.

At the time Nvidia was probably the lesser-known one, right? Yes, that's right.

Do you think Jensen in 2016 and Jensen now have changed much?

His hair has all gone gray. I think the pressure he carries has grown a lot. But he still really cares about employees. He carefully reads the top 5 emails written by company employees to find signals that help the whole company move forward. There have been huge changes.

The company's scale has changed enormously. When we joined, the company probably had fewer than 20,000 people. Now it's more than double that. Maybe even more. Back then GPUs were still in desktop machines. Now it's all data centers. Right, there was no Physical AI back then. Now Physical AI has become a major focus. Right, the changes are huge.

30 天现金流的忧患意识

Along the way, have you witnessed any of NVIDIA's pain and suffering?

Jensen often says — he says — of course it's not literally true — he says it every time — that every day he feels the company has only 30 days of cash flow left and will go bankrupt in 30 days. He still says it now. He says it every day. He reminds himself of this at every meeting.

Is he scaring the executives?

It's about pushing himself to make the most correct decisions for the company.

And then one year during the pandemic, the whole economic situation was really bad. At that point many companies started laying people off. I remember at that company-wide meeting we decided what to cut. What we cut was travel. Employees just wouldn't travel anymore. Everything went online. That saved a sum of money. We looked into which tools we could drop. For example, in Silicon Valley many companies use Slack for communication. We considered whether to just drop Slack. After all, we have email. We had two or three cloud services. For example, sometimes we used Microsoft, sometimes we used Google. Could we cancel one of them to save money?

You could see the company, in difficult times, making some relatively uncommon decisions. Some companies cut personnel costs through layoffs, but what Nvidia thought about was what unnecessary expenses could be trimmed to take care of employees and get through the hard times together.

为什么不裁员？

Why has Nvidia always insisted on no layoffs? Has it really never laid anyone off?

In all my time at NVIDIA, I haven't heard any news of layoffs.

And no bottom-ranked elimination either, right?

We don't have so-called bottom-ranked elimination. We only have performance reviews. Some people leave because they're unhappy with their performance. Some people leave for other reasons. But we don't let you go just because we changed product direction or because your performance was poor during a certain period we just let you go.

We believe trust between people is very important. When an employee identifies with the company and feels secure, they're willing to speak up about things that in a place where people fear being eliminated, they wouldn't dare to say. When there's no such thing as bottom-ranked elimination, people also don't fight so hard to stand out just out of fear of being eliminated. In a place where everyone is fighting to stand out, it's actually harder to foster teamwork. I think this kind of management approach creates a company culture that's quite different from the culture of companies that do bottom-ranked elimination.

What are its pros and cons?

I think employees dare to speak the truth and are willing to work together. The downside is when a technology gradually matures, these employees need some time to learn new things and transition. Relearning new things takes a bit more time. If you just lay off and hire a new batch of people, you might directly hire people who already know these things. So doing it through transition is a bit slower. But what you gain is the employees' trust and employees who will work together.

Mm, how do you improve organizational efficiency? Is that a problem for you?

As long as everyone is full of passion and feels what they're doing is meaningful, overall efficiency goes up. Everyone has choices. Everyone wants to do things they feel accomplished in. If the company can provide this environment where everyone can shine, then efficiency will improve. Let everyone do what they love most and are best at while these things are also hugely beneficial to the company. As long as you can achieve that, I think that's a great state to be in.

Mm, it sounds like no layoffs has many benefits. But most companies don't do it this way, right? Why is that? And why did Jensen believe from the very beginning that there should be no layoffs?

I think NVIDIA is a company that wants to be around for the long run. I think it's all these years — Jensen has spent so many years in Silicon Valley and seen so many ups and downs. He must have his reasons for choosing this. I don't think it's a random choice. It's a carefully considered decision about the company culture he wants, the operating model he wants for the company.

So does that mean when new technology arrives NVIDIA won't be the fastest one? But it relies on laying the groundwork 10 or 5 years ahead so it doesn't demand so much speed of itself. Nvidia runs a marathon and looks far ahead.

Look, CUDA is exactly such a case. It was laid out 10 years in advance.

Right, ah, so you need very strong vision. Long-term investment. Right, and you don't do internal horse-racing either, do you?

We don't like horse-racing. Because we usually do it this way. You take on this mission and we trust you. But together we set a very high bar for you, hoping you'll complete it. In Jensen's words, it's constantly putting you through pain and suffering — torture you to greatness. Trust in you. Give you trials. Keep tempering you, letting you grow step by step along the way. This is the model we like.

What's the most brutal suffering you've endured at NVIDIA?

Building these large models. These years have all been this hard, pushing forward. The things I just told you about — many of them were learned from mistakes. Many things — at first we didn't realize these were the most important things. To do things well when you get it wrong — how do you slowly improve things. I think this stretch of time, ever since GPT took off, everyone working in AI has felt an inexplicable pressure. During this period with this speed of iteration, everyone has been under tremendous pressure. I think it's all pain and suffering. Especially when you're burning through GPU resources every day, burning through these young people's time, and the results you produce don't reach the outcome you most wanted. I think all of this is an invisible pressure.

Has your lifestyle changed over these past few years?

Highly efficient. Highly efficient. Earlier mornings, later nights. I get up around 4 to 5 a.m.

Oh, that early.

When I get up in the morning, exercise and all that — the time is more continuous. Once I get to the office, it's nonstop meetings. I get to the office around 10 — probably around 9 to 10. Because of the whole industry's iteration speed, the pace of life has gotten faster. There's still a lot to learn, but there are even more things to handle. So you make yourself more efficient.

Mm, what time do you sleep?

Probably around 10 p.m. Sleep around 10. Around 10 to 11. And up at 4 or 5. Right. It's not fixed every day, but that's basically my routine.

二十八、NVIDIA 的独特管理实践

Books about NVIDIA or biographies of Jensen have all talked a lot about his management style. Could you talk about it from a more frontline perspective — some of NVIDIA's distinctive management practices?

We just touched on one: no layoffs.

The second is top 5. Employees tell many people the five most important things they're working on. This lets you see all kinds of signals, big and small, across the company. You can see many cases where two teams are doing exactly the same thing and the top five emails naturally reveal it. Nvidia is a relatively very transparent organization. Apple might be the counterexample. We pursue information transparency. This is also a very different culture.

Some of those Jensen biographies are quite dramatic. But a lot of it you can actually feel when you work at NVIDIA. He knows many employees. We often say mission is the boss, right, so NVIDIA is sometimes like an organism. Without such a rigid framework. When the company wants to move in a certain direction today, teams across different organizations with the relevant skills will automatically align and move in that direction. Like a living organization. Not a fixed framework where if you're in this box, you can't do that thing. It doesn't matter. It doesn't matter where you are in the company. When you're going to move in this direction, if your team can contribute, everyone aligns and it becomes a new direction moving this way. Cosmos is exactly such a case.

Mm, so many people may not belong to this team but they can all come support the team's work. Right, Mission is the boss rather than your boss being your boss.

Mission is the boss. These few are the most distinctive features. These are what make the company so alive. Look at the mission is the boss I just mentioned. It's not a rigid framework. It's an organism. And this top five lets tiny signals from every corner of the company spread out. Unwilling. Not quick to lay off employees. Emphasizing transformation. Emphasizing torture. Building employees' trust in the company. So they can cooperate with each other. I think these are all very unique things about NVIDIA.

S 级人才 vs A 级人才

A group of S-tier people working together versus a group of A plus or A-tier people working together — which one do you think is more likely to achieve greater success?

What everyone pursues is 1+1 being greater than 2. Right — whether people can work together in unity to create a greater effect. That's a very important thing.

When there are many people, there's a communication cost. The communication cost is negative. You need cooperation between people to produce positive returns while reducing this communication cost. When a group of very smart people work together — of course everyone is smart, they understand things quickly and move fast — but if people can't trust each other, it's still hard to achieve 1+1 greater than 2. Everyone is guarding against each other, unwilling to show their best side or trying to prove "I'm smarter than you". That's not necessarily a good state either.

I actually think it's just like playing a game. You don't want the whole team to be all archers. Maybe some people are in charge of defense, some people are in charge of healing. All these different attributes combined together. I think this kind of diversity is a better state.

是低 ego 还是隐藏的自信？

Hmm, you've said a lot today — you have no competitors, you don't compete with anyone. Everyone is a customer. Everyone is a partner. Is this low-ego state something that happened at NVIDIA? Is it truly low ego, or is it a kind of concealment?

I think it's a kind of confidence. A kind of self-confidence. A belief that what we build can help everyone. My goal is to help everyone do well. But I hold myself to very high standards for what I build. I want it to get better. But my goal is not to beat competitors. My goal is to produce great results, to build a better foundation so everyone can move faster.

Did you learn this from Jensen?

Yes, his influence on me runs very deep.

When did you learn this?

If you're a researcher, the way you graduate is by getting your papers accepted at top conferences. Reviewers will question you: is your work state-of-the-art? Being state-of-the-art means you have to beat everyone. So researchers all have this mindset "My work has to be better than yours". So, following this trajectory, I started out as a highly competitive individual. My work had to be better than yours. That's my demand of myself, and that's fine. You want your work to keep getting better and better. But after a while, you know — you're always state-of-the-art for a while, then the next one comes out. This thing keeps progressing nonstop.
