And my position today is different too. After becoming a manager, I hope to cultivate a new generation of talent to help them grow. And from NVIDIA's position in the ecosystem, I also hope the company gradually feels the benefits. Sometimes when my partners tell me that after using one of our models their efficiency in solving problems improved a lot, I feel very happy. I feel that my effort and the whole team's hard work received some recognition in return. This kind of affirmation is also a wonderful thing. You don't necessarily have to beat others to make a contribution. You don't need to defeat your opponents. I don't like treating them as opponents. I like treating them as partners.

Hmm, look at NVIDIA — including you and including Jensen — he often says "take care of others" whether it's employees or external partners. Is this kind of "take care" genuine? Do you think he really thinks this way?

In NVIDIA's early days we were a design house. We didn't really have any consumer product of our own. We relied on other companies to make the GPU cards for us. We've always had this habit of growing together with the whole ecosystem. Everyone makes money together. It can't be that only we make the money. The ones who help make the graphics cards, the servers — everyone has to be able to keep moving forward together.

Because its early graphics cards were used for gaming and we didn't make games. We just kept developing these good libraries to help game companies make games. When we first moved into deep learning, there were several frameworks at the time like PyTorch, TensorFlow, and also MXNet and those. We supported all of them. Right — later there was the Triton Compiler. We supported Triton. When vLLM came out, we supported vLLM.

Right — I think it's genuine. We genuinely want to help the customers building on our GPU platform succeed even more. The more successful they are, the more customers they can serve. And they'll have abundant opportunities to use our GPUs. It's truly a shared interest — a path to success together. I think that's how it is — he ran the company for so many years to put it in such a good position. Helping others while also profiting yourself. I think that's not easy.

二十九、"六边形战士" Jensen

Hmm, you've observed Jensen up close for many years. If you had to describe him in just a few words, how would you describe him?

We call him the "hexagonal warrior". Sometimes in meetings, he can go really deep into registers — registers in computer architecture — extremely fine details. And at the same time he can talk about — even teach everyone how to do marketing. How to do these very high-level things. Handling everything from product pricing to customer relationships. He covers every aspect.

He has enormous passion. He gives everything he has to help the company be successful. It's a truly admirable way of operating. He can contribute in every direction and does his best in every direction. He's a truly remarkable person.

Does he encourage you more, or criticize you more?

Generally both. Back when I didn't yet fully understand how he wanted to run the company, there was more criticism. But the criticism always came with encouragement, hoping you could become better. His goal is to torture everybody to greatness. Through this grinding, you come to better understand what it takes to do extraordinary things.

This is very energy-consuming. Being willing to spend time torturing others — that's not an easy thing. Torturing others — you yourself carry a heavy burden too. Right? And you only have so much time in your life. You could just not bother and maybe still get what you want. But he's willing to spend time torturing others so everyone keeps improving. That's not an easy thing.

What's a phrase of his that left a deep impression on you?

I remember once we were in a meeting. We were comparing two solutions — two things. I was the one who built one of them and the other was built by someone else. I remember at the time I said "I think the setting they used was an unfair setting so our performance on this front didn't meet our expectations" — falling behind the competing product. And he said to me at that moment: "Are you a quiet baby?"

Nothing in this world is fair. When you write papers, you often say "my setting is different from your setting so you can't compare them directly". But if your goal is to solve a problem, then of course you need the conditions required to solve that problem. If you don't have those conditions, find a way to get them.

But that sentence left a very deep impression on me. I became stricter with myself — making excuses is useless. You just have to give everything you have. And I'd heard this saying before. Some famous books from West Point talk about it too. No excuse — no excuse at all. But when he said it to me, it left an even deeper impression on me because after all, he's a famous figure. I think this sentence had quite a big impact on me. After that, I stopped making excuses.

If, as a researcher, your desire to be number one conflicts with NVIDIA's own business — since NVIDIA doesn't want to become a strong competitor. If a conflict arose, which would you choose?

I think the development of science itself is incremental. It keeps progressing. You can propose an improvement anytime, just taking one more step upward. I think "be the absolute number one" — what does number one even mean? It's hard to define number one.

I prefer to look at it this way — train a frontier model. A frontier model, the moment it's built, is number one. That's very fulfilling. But soon after, other models will surpass it. What I hope for is — you possess the ability to build a number-one model but you do the thing that has the greatest impact on society, the most contributive thing.

Right, because you can build a number-one model. Or — it could mean letting power become overly concentrated in a few hands, creating some kind of imbalance. I don't think that's necessarily the right thing. Right — I hope to have the number-one capability but to do the thing that contributes the most to this world.

Yes — so what matters most is the contribution at the end. Right? Not the capability itself.

Right, right — everyone just passes through this life once. Right? What you leave behind is your impact. So you need to live long. Living longer gives you more chances. I just hope to produce some — to make some contributions to prove I didn't come to this world for nothing. That's how it is.

三十、遗憾、期待与中国观察

Hmm, do you have any regrets in your research career? Is there anything you particularly still want to achieve?

I think Physical AI hasn't succeeded yet. The time hasn't come yet to talk about all that. I'm very happy that back then — ten years ago, I was saying deep learning would replace computer graphics and become the most important paradigm for image generation. And that actually happened. I feel pretty happy about it. This thing really happened. I think world models will be an important driving force for the success of Physical AI. That's my next major goal. I hope this can succeed too.

If you compare — you have one best paper award and you think, "I want to win two". Then you find out some people have won a dozen. You can never win them all. Compare paper counts — there are always more papers. Compare citation counts — there are always more citations. Compare money — there's always someone richer. Right? So the point is whether you're proud of your own work. I think a lot of my past work wasn't good enough. But some of my recent work I think is quite good. I accept that. I feel that within the scope of my abilities, I've produced work I'm satisfied with. I think that's enough.

So many of the external metrics — they're gradually becoming less important now, right?

Right — when you're young, they all feel so important. Why? "This person has more best papers than me". Right, and more awards than me. Now I feel — gradually I no longer measure myself by those — my focus has gradually shifted to helping others. Maybe what I care about now is whether I've helped enough people.

Hmm, who do you think you've helped this past year?

The users of Physical AI, the users of Cosmos. I think I've quietly helped all of them. And of course my own team. And some people who've had conversations with me along the way. I think, to some degree, I've had an impact on their lives.

You also come to China often. How do you view the development of this wave of Chinese models?

Very impressive. Very impressive. Starting from DeepSeek, Qwen, Doubao. Let me just name them all. MiniMax. Kimi. MiMo. Hunyuan. Zhipu. They've all done very well.

There's another thing — in the United States, especially at these frontier labs, the current situation is that they rarely take interns anymore. A lot of the know-how, a lot of the research results exist only inside their own labs. What I see in China is these companies all take on a lot of interns, helping to spread this know-how outward. I think for the expansion of humanity's collective knowledge, this diffusion — I think it's a good thing.

Seeing this rapid development, I find it very impressive. And at the same time, they pay attention to this diffusion. Everyone is full of passion for AI, willing to give things a try. I think these are all phenomena I've observed.

Xie Saining (co-founder of AMI) told me Silicon Valley has been hypnotized by LLMs. What do you think of that statement?

I don't think it's purely being hypnotized by LLMs. It's undeniable — the leading companies in AI right now, the companies with the leading models — whether it's OpenAI or Anthropic — they all started from large language models. And these models are indeed — I already don't know how I'd get by without a Coding Agent. I really don't know — they're just too convenient. I think they've brought about enormous change. And that's not a bad thing. LLMs have proven enormously useful, helping to improve our lives.

So I think it's very natural that people start thinking "Since this thing is already here, what's the next step?" I think people naturally want to do the next thing. I know some people in the field turn academia into a faith. But I think most people still start from the pursuit of knowledge and truth. Once something has been fully understood, people will find new things to make breakthroughs on. It's hard to imagine a person — someone so smart — spending their whole life only working on LLMs. I think it will just happen naturally. I don't really think there's any "hypnosis". It's just that for those people at this moment in time, working on LLMs might be the right thing to do.

SpaceX went public yesterday. And OpenAI and Anthropic are about to go public too. Will this year's IPOs of these large-model companies have any impact on the industry?

2026 will be a year of huge change. Everyone has seen the news about these IPOs — they'll create a lot of wealthy people. And I know housing prices in San Francisco are soaring. The people who believed in deep learning early, who believed early in this space mission — it's a recognition of their foresight, of their courage, of their determination. A validation. I think it's all very reasonable. These companies have truly made enormous contributions to the world. I think it's fully deserved.

But I don't think technology will stop here. New things will keep happening one after another. The most powerful companies 100 years ago are completely different from the most powerful companies today. Different from 50 years ago. Different from 20 years ago. I think as long as the organizational structure of society remains in a good, healthy state, innovation will keep happening.

三十一、模型竞赛的终局与创业机会

What might the endgame of this model race look like? So much has changed in just a few short years. What about looking further ahead?

This might be controversial — I think model capabilities will gradually converge. The model itself won't be the differentiator. You'll have to organize some other things together with it. Leading models have more time to find that differentiation. Strong companies can also strengthen their own — build a strong ecosystem to create some change.

I think it's like when software first came out — very few companies could write software. Now everyone can write software. Every software company has its own way of differentiating. Every software company that survives today has its own differentiation. I see no reason models would be any different. I think it'll be the same. So there's no need to mythologize models or model companies.

I treat it like traditional Chinese medicine. It's a black box. So many people making different attempts and eventually it becomes a body of knowledge. And then many people practice medicine. The key is what you use it for. Right — the key is what you do with it. Some people understand it more deeply. Some people just need a bit more time. This is all just my speculation. I think these things will gradually diffuse.

Now suppose a new company says it wants to train a model — does it still have a good chance of catching up? It might be two or three years behind the companies ahead of it. Like Kimi or MiMo — these efforts came relatively late. Kimi is okay; MiMo is later. Right, right — there's still a chance.

I think there will be a period of time when everyone feels compute is insufficient. But I think compute will gradually ramp up, and gradually everyone will find a way to compete. I think there are many people in this world with ambition, determination and the ability to mobilize resources to build a large-model team. And there will be more, right? I think if large models are an absolute differentiator, then of course there will be more of that. But if it's not an absolute differentiator, then a lot of people will probably find ways that are mutually beneficial. Yes, I think it's a natural state of balance. A natural state of balance. Yes.

How long do you think before on-device models take off?

This is very close to Physical AI. As I just mentioned, I think funding is gradually flowing in, and the technology is iterating fast. I can't say exactly how long it will take, but I hope it takes off quickly.

For this year's and next year's model race, what predictions do you have?

On Physical AI it's hard to say. Creation is still moving fast. I still firmly believe that the capability of World Models is a crucial key to helping these physical-world models strengthen their generalization. How to make it land in practice, what modality to use — these are things everyone is still exploring. ChatGPT moment for Physical AI is coming. That's probably a prediction I can make.

As for things like large coding models, I use them myself, but I don't build them myself, so it's hard for me to say. I enjoy using them a lot, but it's hard for me to say what happens next.

中美机器人产业对比

You just talked about China's model companies. What about China's robotics companies? You've probably met many of them too. Do you think they're different from the US in any way?

In the US, very few companies build the robot body itself — just Tesla and Figure AI. In China, many companies are building the robot body. Building the body means they can control more things. They can control the model and the software-hardware integration. There's more room to maneuver.

I think because of China's strong manufacturing industry, it creates a very advantageous condition that lets these companies do things not easy to do in the US. I think it's all well worth watching — what kind of breakthrough this vertical integration will produce. Yes, I find it quite interesting.

Do you think the US might now be, a little, not valuing hardware enough — that could be wrong?

Hard to say. But if software-hardware integration is a trend in robotics, then having no hardware certainly puts you in a passive position. Right? It's a bit hard to say. There are many things to consider, including the financial model. China clearly has the conditions that let everyone do rapid hardware iteration and software-hardware integration.

The ChatGPT moment in Physical AI — where do you think it might break out?

You see an application where everyone obviously knows it will generate huge economic value. And maybe at that point in time, that application hasn't yet generated economic value. When ChatGPT first came out, it was losing money, right? But everyone saw the trend, and I think that's when it happens.

I personally think this kind of thing — where a human simply demonstrates how to do a task, and the robot learns it right there on the spot — I think that's a — If this thing appears, if I see a product like that, I would feel that Physical AI's ChatGPT moment has arrived.

So at its core it's about generalization.

I think it's generalization. It — The core problem of AI is solving generalization.

Mm. When it comes to generalization, what is the single most important problem right now? If you had to name just one?

The problem of generalization — in Physical AI, it's how to learn the required skills from limited signals, and apply them in scenes you've never seen before. This is the main generalization problem to solve in Physical AI: observation to action — the generalization of that pair. You see some — you see this action and observation getting things done. How do you quickly generalize to a new observation with a similar action?

Hey, I'm wondering — if it learns within the Cosmos system, then when it moves into the real world, there's still a sim-to-real gap, right? How do you solve that problem?

That's also a generalization problem. The sim-to-real gap is usually — how we at Cosmos want to help Physical AI builders is through three approaches, as mentioned before: better data, better starting points, and better environments.

I think things like better environments haven't happened yet. Everyone hopes to build this matrix, but it hasn't happened yet. There have been breakthroughs here and there, and we've seen some very good work. What's more effective right now is probably better data and better starting points. You take a model that understands the world's physics and use it to predict physics. Understanding physics lets you — well, you can't say it truly understands physics, but it captures the patterns and can predict what will happen in the future. This can perhaps help you generate a better policy, make a better policy. Because its own prior is better suited for generalization, it can perhaps help you build a policy model that generalizes more easily. Right. I think this is what I see as a contribution the Cosmos model could make to Physical AI builders in the near term.

If I interview you again five years from now, what stage do you hope Cosmos will have reached?

Oh, I hope that five years from now, if we have another interview like this, we can clearly state when the ChatGPT moment happened, yes, and where it happened. I hope we can say it clearly and explicitly — down to the year, month, and day. By then there'll be a concrete date. Yes yes hopefully.

In the history of artificial intelligence, how would you like people to remember you?

Let's not talk about me. I'd say talk about Cosmos. I hope Cosmos can be an important driving force helping several important Physical AI builders reach this ChatGPT moment. I think that would make me very happy.

三十二、快问快答与结语

I have a few more rapid-fire questions. Your favorite food, anywhere in the world?

Beef noodle soup.

Your favorite place, anywhere in the world?

Oh, I like the Bay Area. The weather is just so comfortable.

Any music, books, movies, or games you like?

Quite a lot of books. I don't really listen to music. I don't really play games anymore. The last time I played a game was probably over twenty years ago.

Can you share a book that truly changed you or influenced you?

A book Jensen recommended. It's about Positioning. I forget what the title was. A very interesting psychology book. It helps you better understand the essence of a problem.

When I was young, I read many different books. Right, I especially loved Jin Yong's novels. That was one part of it.

Did Jin Yong's novels help you later in your research or business management?

Not really. It's more that you get to experience Jin Yong's various fantasies, some beautiful imagery. It certainly pushed me onto the path of learning Chinese martial arts, gaining some training and discipline from Chinese martial arts. I think those were all pretty good experiences.

What advice would you have for young researchers?

Don't be nervous.

Why not be nervous?

I think young researchers nowadays often feel like maybe AI will be over next year, that AI will train itself. Don't be nervous. Have confidence in yourself. Calm down. See clearly where it's worth investing your energy. Don't be swayed by everyone's hype into feeling your path is getting narrower and narrower. Right now is a good time for researchers to enter Physical AI.

A good time — is it a blue ocean?

It's a good time — there are all kinds of opportunities, and many areas — I work on Physical AI, so I know that better — but these advances in AI let us make better materials, better drugs, breakthroughs in biology — I think you can gradually see AI's impact across every industry. I think there are many places worth investing in.

Our studio is called "Language Is the World" Studio. When you first heard that name, what were you thinking?

Using language to describe the interesting things happening in this world.

Do you think the large model race is not Squid Game — or the world model race is not Squid Game? Or is it that for you it's not Squid Game, but for others it might be?

I'm not sure. If everyone is trying to solve exactly the same thing, then it's Squid Game, right? So the model race shouldn't be Squid Game. Right, because there are so many problems in the world to solve, so many things that can provide value, and everyone likes different things. Right, I don't think it should be seen as Squid Game.

Have you ever had a period of particularly high ego?

When I was young.

That happens, right?

Yes, I always felt my algorithm was the best and the paper I wrote was the most elegant. You always feel that way. Algorithms matter, but you need very good data and very good infrastructure so you can iterate on algorithms quickly. Because even if there are two possibilities — one is your algorithm is great from the start, OK, that's great. But even if your algorithm isn't good at first, if you have very good data and very good infrastructure, you can iterate. As long as you iterate with strict discipline, following controlled-experiment principles, your algorithm gets better and better.

So I actually think iteration speed is the most important thing. And iteration speed depends on powerful infrastructure to support it. Data is very important, because if a problem can be solved with data, just solve it with data. No need to develop an algorithm, because data is much simpler. Right, so you don't like wasting effort. As long as a problem can be solved with data, go collect data, go create data. And for what truly can't be solved, then use algorithms to solve it.

Does every company need to train its own large model? You don't think it's necessary, right?

If it's a commodity — do you need to build your own power plant? Does every company need to build its own power plant? OK. It comes down to whether it's economically worthwhile, right?

Mm. In the early days, when you were building a car factory, when power plants were scarce, you'd build a power plant, and you could ensure your company ran 24 hours a day. But in this day and age, you probably don't need to, right?

You probably talk to a lot of AI developers, and every one of them feels their AI model is the best. I don't think this has ever happened in history.

I don't think so. Because it's not that easy for people to get along with each other. Look at Dario Amodei and Sam Altman back then — they couldn't get along, right? So he left. And are you sure everyone at Anthropic is exactly the same? I don't think so.

They're all true believers?

What if one day you promote A but not B, and B feels — Hmm right? And then might he take a group of people with him to go build something similar? Right, and everyone has data. They have data, and they can buy compute from you. Compute — as long as you have money, you can still buy it, right? So everyone can do it. If you have the determination and the resources, you can do it. It's just that there's no need to.

Is Cosmos a war you can't afford to lose?

If other companies also build open-source models, then it's not. Right. What do we even mean by "war"? It's not like I intend to kill anyone else. I just have to — Oh no — it's that you all have to grow on top of our ecosystem, and NVIDIA keeps growing.

Physical AI is a major market. Right now no household has a robot, but if there were robots, my family might buy two or three. And every robot needs compute. That means the whole world's demand for compute would grow dramatically. If that happens, it's a huge benefit for NVIDIA.

Our mindset is not about killing anyone else. Our mindset is: how do we create the market? You know what I mean? CUDA created a market. It created today's AI market. What we think about is how to create the next big market.

So you're saying — Yes. Is it a battlefield you can't afford to lose?

I don't think so either. Not really, because it's something entirely new. I'm not competing with anyone, right? Yeah. It's mutual benefit. Bringing everyone along to build that market together. And then — you make money selling this robot, this thing will need some compute to make money. And of course some companies will develop their own chips, and they'll make money too. Then the whole market rises up from what was originally nothing.

Does Jensen share a similar view?

He says it often, right? He says it often: you have to create markets rather than fight over existing ones. Right. If you read his book, you'll find he says we should do this kind of zero-billion-dollar business. What's a zero-billion-dollar business? It's not a business right now, but once it succeeds, it becomes a billion.

Mm. If someone is already doing it now, it's probably not worth doing.

Is this embracing risk, or resisting risk? Is this still a de-risk?

The way we do things is very risky. All of it is — CUDA back then was a very risky thing. It was basically selling at a loss, right? Because we built CUDA in, the price of our entire GPU was higher than others'. For the same FLOPS, we were just more expensive, because we had to support this programmability, right? If you don't do it this way — doing this is very risky, but not doing it is even more risky. Right. If you don't do that thing and someone else does, then for you it becomes very risky. If you don't do it, your stuff gradually becomes a commodity.

Is there anything else you still want to learn from Jensen?

I try hard to learn how he runs other things, and then apply that to running Cosmos.

Why do other companies say the CEO shouldn't be the hardest-working person, but at your company the CEO is the hardest-working person?

Right. Yes. I don't understand that either. Haha. But he — it works. I can not — Right? Nothing in the world is absolute.

What's driving him now?

The drive is to take care families. The drive is to take care of families. Oh. Right.

Doing AI itself is a very interesting thing. You — especially from his vantage point, seeing his contributions change the world — I think it's a very fulfilling thing. Truly worthy of being called the guru. Haha yes.

item.description:
## 一、意外的观察：Ming-Yu Liu 是"反 Sora 的胜者"
表面上看，Sora 出自他曾经的实习生 Tim Brooks，是他"没能做成"的遗憾。但深入观察你会发现一个反直觉的事实——**正是"没做成 Sora"这件事，让他获得了做 Cosmos 的资格**。
如果 Ming-Yu 早两年就做出了 Sora，NVIDIA 会把他锁死在"内容创作"这条路上。因为一旦成功，路径依赖会形成——组织会把资源、叙事、KPI 全部围绕内容生成堆叠。而恰恰是 Sora 在 OpenAI 手里"证明了这条路"之后被战略性放弃，让 NVIDIA 看清了两件事：视频生成的技术可行性 + 消费级内容不是 NVIDIA 该打的战场。Ming-Yu 在这个"真空窗口期"写信给黄仁勋，把整条视频生成的组织能量转向 Physical AI。
**这是一种系统性反讽**：他的"落后"变成了他的"选择权"。在 AI 竞赛里，第二名的隐藏红利是"看清赛道后再下注"。
## 二、跨领域连接：中国武术、CUDA 与 Cosmos 的同构性
Ming-Yu 从 18 岁开始练八极拳。他说八极拳的本质是"

item.title: [Business of Sport] “Infantino is a Symptom of the Problem”: What Really Needs to Change at FIFA
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的"病灶"不是英凡蒂诺，而是"一国一票"的数学结构

大多数评论把矛头对准英凡蒂诺个人的贪婪与傲慢，但节目里最锋利的一句话是："Infantino不是问题本身，他是问题的症状。" 真正的病根在于FIFA的投票算术——211个成员国里，大约90个是非洲和加勒比小型足协，凑够110票就能当选主席。于是任何一位主席，只要想连任，都会被这个数学结构"锁死"在同一条路径上：用小额转移支付（每年5–6百万美元）批发换取选票。这也解释了为什么从阿维兰热到布拉特再到英凡蒂诺，三代主席在完全不同的时代、不同的性格、不同的出身背景下，却都不约而同走向了近乎相同的丑闻剧本——这不是人的败坏，而是制度的引力场。

二、一个跨领域的意外类比：FIFA其实是"资源诅咒"的翻版

这里有个让人意外的连接——FIFA当下的困境，与政治经济学里的"资源诅咒"（Resource Curse）几乎同构。石油国家因为坐拥现金流，统治者不需要向本国纳税人负责，只需要用石油美元维稳精英即可；而FIFA主席因为坐拥世界杯这口"油井"，也不需要向真正贡献收入的欧洲和南美负责，只需用分成"维稳"最贫穷的成员国即可。贡献收入的一方没有话语权，掌握话语权的一方不贡献收入——这套结构在委内瑞拉、在尼日利亚、在很多石油国家反复上演，而FIFA只是把石油换成了转播权。

更耐人寻味的是，这种"倒挂"制度的破裂方式也高度一致：并非来自内部改革，而是来自被剥夺方的"退出威胁"（exit threat）。UEFA这次做的事，在博弈论上其实等价于1992年英超脱离英足联下级联盟的那次分裂——都是"出钱最多的一方"第一次真正拿起"我不玩了"这张牌。

三、被忽略的观察：英凡蒂诺其实是被"提前逼宫"救了

主流叙事是：英凡蒂诺因为提前推出20%世界杯私有化方案而"暴露自己、加速倒台"。但如果反向阅读节目里的时间线，会得到一个更反直觉的结论——如果这套方案没被Ziggler提前泄露、而是在2027年3月他连任成功之后才推出，那么UEFA大概率只会"骂几句然后忍下来"，因为届时他还有四年任期护体，各方会算计"忍他到2031年就好"。真正毁掉他的不是方案本身，而是方案在他"续命之前"就曝光了——他被迫在没有连任背书的裸奔状态下，直面欧洲的核按钮。

这里藏着一个更普适的洞见：权力最脆弱的时刻，往往不是它最弱的时候，而是它自以为最强、还没来得及"锁定"的时候。英凡蒂诺栽在了自己对连任的过度自信上——他先把"必然连任"当成资产提前变现，结果反而把"连任"本身变成了负债。这是典型的"路径依赖式傲慢"：当一个人在体系里赢得太久，他会开始把"体系规则"和"自己的意志"混为一谈，直到体系用它最古老的语言提醒他——你只是一个赛事组织者。

四、给读者的一个反常识收尾

节目结尾那句"如果换成Montigliani当主席，civil servants还是会告诉他：想连任十年，就得继续讨好非洲和加勒比"——这句话本身就是对"换人式改革"最锋利的判词。在一个结构错误的系统里，换一个更好的人，只会让这个系统运行得更"高效地错"。 这也是为什么Charlie最后说"nothing really changes unless the voting system changes"——足球世界这一轮最需要的，不是道德觉醒，而是一次冷酷的、结构性的、带有胁迫色彩的权重重置。

📝 转录文本

开场：一周之内的剧变

Let's talk FIFA. A lot's happened, Charlie.

I mean, I will pat on the back maybe where credit is due. We recorded last week, I think on the Wednesday, a lot happened after the Wednesday before we released on Friday. The main thing being the UEFA stance, which basically led to the UEFA nations saying that they will not participate in FIFA tournaments.

Now, the reason I say credit where it's due is because actually it didn't date the show — considering we'd already suggested that that would be the main way to deal with the situation. And if that did indeed happen, then the plan in essence would be dead in the water, because without the European countries all the value of this scheme kind of fell out at the bottom of it.

So that having happened, and then obviously the very quick withdrawal of the scheme on I think Friday night when Infantino finally realized that this was probably over, um, has kind of brought an end to those four — sorry — days. But of course with this, and I think this is where we're particularly interested to speak as well as what happened, the huge conversation now is what goes on moving forward.

计划已死，那英凡蒂诺本人呢？

Yeah. So the question you're asking is: has this been terminal not just for Infantino's plan to sell off 20% of the World Cup, but is it also terminal for Infantino himself and his presidency?

It kind of looks both, doesn't it?

Well, the plan for sure. The plan, Infantino, as you say, has already accepted is dead in the water. And I will say that, you know, we did predict that. We predicted that UEFA would kill it, torpedo it, and they did.

He was virtually untouchable, right? He was virtually untouchable. I was going to put this out there. He came out of that World Cup. We had all of the stuff that went on with Balagan and Trump, and you had all of this conversation about 64 teams, and some people going, "How can we do that? That's crazy."

But do you know what? We still looked at the voting systems and where the money was going to be going. And we said, "Look, the reality is, unfortunately, until he decides — well, until he sees out his final term in presidency, i.e. 2031 — it's highly unlikely he's going to remove himself. Then he has played an absolute blinder, as the only person that could cause himself any issues, he has done exactly that."

And it is a classic case of even with seemingly unending power and influence, he has found his Achilles heel, and the hubris of the whole situation will be his downfall. And to be honest now, you know, fingers crossed, now is the time where you really need those organizations that we've talked about potentially having power — i.e. the FA, but really it was UEFA as a block — standing up and actually, for the first time, as you said in your memo this week on Substack, for the first time standing up and actually acting with the power that they have to show, in your words, whether the emperor really has any clothes.

And it looks like to me this whole situation has shown now — with UEFA pulling the lever that they did — that the real power in football is not a glorified tournament organizer, really, if I can say it, in FIFA. But it is the people that have the block of countries that they need to participate in these tournaments to make them valuable.

英凡蒂诺不是病，是症状

Yeah, exactly, Charlie. Really the issue now is not so much about, you know, Infantino. We can come to Infantino and the specifics of that. The issue really is more to do with the status of FIFA within the power blocks within the game.

Because don't forget that Infantino — I know it's hard for people to think this way given what a total clown he's made of himself in recent weeks, months — Infantino is not himself the problem. He's a symptom of the problem. Let's not forget Infantino was the secretary general of UEFA, right? Infantino doesn't come from the African, um, you know, conference. He doesn't come from the Oceania conference. He's a UEFA guy, right?

So effectively, you have to ask yourself the question: why does Infantino, and indeed previous presidents of FIFA, end up doing things which either are on the margin sort of corrupt or, as I put in my memo, sort of blackguard? Right? That's one bit of it.

But the other bit of it is becoming very beholden to, in particular, the African nations on the one hand and the Caribbean nations on the other hand, which are the poorest federations in the world in terms of their own revenues. Right?

"一国一票"背后的数学现实

And this is where I get into, you know, roots of problems versus symptoms of problems. Because effectively, to become president of FIFA and then particularly to stay as president of FIFA, what you become aware of quite quickly is that under one member, one vote — where there are 211 member nations, of whom about 90 are either African or Caribbean nations, i.e. federations with very little money — in your aim to get 110-odd votes, you can wrap up pretty much all the support you need simply from the African and Caribbean nations.

And this is something which Blatter did before, and Havelange did before that, etc.

And the reason why that is so corrosive is because those federations, which are constantly struggling for money, they don't have money themselves. So we're talking about federations that have annual revenues of $5 million, $6 million bucks a year, compared to our football association with revenues of £600 million pounds. Right?

So for these small federations, handouts of $5 or $6 million a year are transformational for them. It changes everything. Now, of course, one would love to think that all of that extra $6 million went into football development and lovely schemes overseen by Arsène Wenger, and some of it does. Let's not imagine for a moment that part of this isn't used to prop up those federations, prop up the people who run those federations — who, don't forget, are significant people within their own country's, you know, political ecosystem.

And you know, it's the difference between the president of one of those federations being able to pay himself a $100,000 bucks a year and $200,000 or $300,000 bucks a year. It's the difference between them being able to travel first class to various locations around the world and having to travel in the back of the plane. It's the difference between them being able to look after people within their own football ecosystems with handouts here and there to keep everybody else in line.

买票的最便宜方式

You know that. So Infantino, Blatter, Havelange have been confronted with a mathematical reality, which is that the cheapest and easiest way of keeping your 120-odd votes that you need is by giving enough money on an individual basis to the poorer federations, right, to keep them happy with you, because they're not going to debate you long and hard about the big stuff you're doing.

So when you come up with some scheme to, you know, have hydration breaks or hold the World Cup every two years or whatever it might be, the head of the federation of a small African country is not going to take to the New York Times and give an interview about how this fundamentally undermines the future governance of world football. He just says, "Give me my $5 million bucks and you can do what the hell you want." Right?

That's the underlying reality of how FIFA works.

So whereas he could come to the English FA — I mean, you know, supine and hopeless though it is — and say to them, "Oh, by the way, you know, I'm going to do something here which means I'm going to be able to give you an extra $5 million bucks." And the FA would be like, "Well, that's sort of rounding error for us. Um, Johnny, it doesn't make any difference to us. Like, that doesn't mean that in a year's time we're just going to say yes, yes, yes when you want to go and hold a World Cup every two years and that type of stuff. We'll take the money, sure, but then we reserve the right to debate with you going down the track whether the stuff you think is reasonable and fair."

换个人不解决问题：以Montigliani为例

So effectively, you know, as I said, we in Infantino — we'll get on to a moment whether Infantino himself does survive this. But my point is this: let's just say for a moment that Infantino goes, but he's replaced by Victor Montigliani from Concacaf, right? Let's just say.

So Montigliani comes in, perfectly good guy. I know people who work with him. I know people who know him, etc. You know, he himself has got basically a good reputation, as Infantino did before he became FIFA president. Infantino did not have any stink surrounding him when he was the secretary general of UEFA.

But let's just say that Montigliani is then in power within FIFA, right? And he then wants to get two terms. Doesn't want to be a one-term president. He wants to have his full 10 years. Okay, the civil servants within FIFA tell him, "Well, look, the only way you can do that under one member, one vote is by keeping the African and Caribbean nations happy. Once you start annoying those guys, then you're always going to have problems with the Germans. You're always going to have problems with the Brazilians. You're always going to have problems with the Russians. Just keep the Africans and Caribbeans happy."

And that then drives the relentless short-term desire to increase revenues, because that's how you keep those guys happy. And that's why they come up with all these madcap schemes to try to increase revenue rather than thinking about the medium to long term of the sport.

分水岭时刻：治理必须重写

So, you know, I'll ask you in a moment your view about whether he does or doesn't survive this. But at the same time, the point of my memo was to say that this watershed moment has to be the moment for a fundamental change in FIFA's governance.

And what that really means, right? It doesn't mean some report that takes 6 months. It simply means UEFA saying, "Right, from now on, basically, we are going to run this and you are a competition organizer." As you said, you are a competition organizer for the world, and we're fully on board with there being really good equal distribution of money that comes out of the stuff you do — no problem with that.

But let's be clear: that money that you're distributing is our money. That's our member nations' money. That's our fans' money. And those players are players that are employed by our clubs. So never think for a moment, whoever you are, that you are going to be able to do this from now on by just getting together the support of the African and Caribbean nations. From now on, basically, you need to answer to us. Right?

加权投票：英超的历史类比

Okay, so can I ask you — a weighted system like that would make sense. Like, if they do implement that, what's the danger? Like, what's the cost of doing that? What will people fear? Why would people push back on it and say, "Actually, no, you couldn't do that"?

If you look back to why the Premier League was actually formed, and you read the memoirs of various English football industry people from around that time. What had happened during the late 1980s, mid to late 1980s, where English football also had one club, one vote — so Man United had one vote and Walsall had one vote — is on a continual basis, when the big clubs, who had senior managing directors, more senior people involved, when they would say, "Well, one way in which we think football in this country can progress is this, this, and this," then there would be a block of the lower division clubs who go, "No, I don't fancy it. Don't fancy it. So, um, you know, let's just carry on as we are. Or actually, if you want us to vote for you on that one, you're going to need to give us more money or help us in some other way."

To the point where eventually the big clubs said, "Look, sorry, this isn't working. It's our money. It's our fans mostly. And therefore, we — I'm sad to say — but we're going to need to break away, to be able to do the things that we think need to be done to progress the whole game. And you guys now are going to have to look after yourself."

Now, I don't think it'll be quite as simple as that with FIFA, and I don't think it should be quite as simple as that with FIFA, but I do think that a weighting is required.

加权方案的具体设想

Now, in the memo I suggested, I think something along the lines of you'd have a top council where you had, let's say, four members from UEFA, you had two members from Conmebol — which is a Latin American block — and then you had one member each for the Asian Football Federation, the African Football Federation, Concacaf, Oceania. Right?

So that UEFA couldn't just simply get its way all the time. It would have to persuade somebody else to get on board with them. And it would recognize that the other big power block in world football is Conmebol, which is Argentina, Brazil, and Co., and would give them slightly more weight.

At the moment, Conmebol is even worse treated than UEFA, which is they've only got 11 votes because they've only got 11 countries, because they're all quite big countries in Latin America. So even though they are providing a lot of the revenue and a lot of the fans, they've only got 11 votes. UEFA have got about 50 votes. And then Africa have got about 50 votes, and Concacaf have got about 50 votes.

So effectively, UEFA and Conmebol together are 60-odd votes, 65 votes, whereas the African Federation and Concacaf, who in terms of global revenues are minimal, right, are 100 plus votes.

So this just needs to be — not even looked at — this just needs to be changed by force. Um, and I hope that Čeferin, who is a pretty tough operator, as I noted in last week's show, presses home his advantage now and says to the European member nations, "If you want to stop this happening again, don't imagine that Infantino going is going to be the thing that makes the big difference. We need to change the governance."

Well, it feels — it's that watershed moment, isn't it?

It is. At least it should be. At least it needs to be.

英凡蒂诺会走还是会留？

So let me come on to the question, Charlie, which I'll put over to you. Okay, having said that whether Infantino stays or goes is not quite as significant as some people might think — do you think he does stay or go?

I find it very hard to see how he stays and FIFA retains any sort of credibility.

Look, one thing it certainly does, Charlie, I think, is it means that he will not go into the next election uncontested. So there's going to be an election for the FIFA presidency in 2027 in Rabat, in I think March of next year.

March. Yeah.

Now, previously all the conversation was: no one's going to stand against him. It would mean he does another four years and he goes to 2031, and at 2031 he could no longer take up another term of presidency — which interestingly was where this whole scheme was coming in, because it was assumed he would then go and run the FIFA Enterprise scheme, uh, as, you know, I guess a private entity, um, alongside FIFA, and obviously take a very nice salary in the process.

So he had this very nice plan laid out, I think, in front of him that, as I said at the beginning, was kind of virtually impossible to see how you could change that. This whole situation now, if you're really looking at it — and I noted, Charlie, the some of the commentary that came out internally from FIFA when something like this happens, right — you've got people that are very quick to move away from it and they don't want the association.

And he was very much put forward by some of the top people in FIFA — this was his idea. If you listen to comments on Friday, you know, he actually used these — these are the words, you know, in our quotes — he used the words that they, the staff, had been "deceived", and he said it was "the project of one person". Now, that's your COO of FIFA. You had Arsène Wenger — we were recording on Wednesday — come out last night, all this morning, um, saying that he didn't know about it and was very surprised about the situation.

So you're looking at some very top people in FIFA who are now standing back and disassociating themselves with Infantino and his presidency and this decision. How you maintain the authority that's required to run FIFA and the global game into another cycle is — it's virtually untenable.

罢免主席的三条路径

The interesting question, Charlie, I think is: does he get removed now, or does he go into that election and see whether he gets removed?

Now I just wanted to just touch on this again, because we mentioned it on a previous show, but, you know, I think it's really important to people to understand what has to happen for a FIFA president to be removed or to not be in position. There's three things.

Firstly, he can resign. I mean, still even now, I just can't see that happening.

Um, secondly, the member associations that represent 20% of the membership — which is 43 out of 211 countries — they can formally request what they call an extraordinary FIFA Congress. So if they call that, it basically then goes to a vote, and it will be a vote on whether he does stay or go.

The third way is obviously to lose in an election.

So if you're now looking at this, previously, Charlie, I think we said it's highly unlikely that even number two would happen, because while countries may disagree with his presidency, I don't think they're going to call a special meeting to do it. It does look increasingly like that could happen, particularly with UEFA saying, "You either resign or we will just activate all of our members, i.e. 55. We will call that meeting and we will vote against you."

So taking all those things into account, trying to take all the emotion out of it, I just don't see how anyone in that position who has gone through what he has gone through in a week stays in position and keeps the power that he wields.

Yeah.

I don't know what you think.

傲慢的时间线错误

It was an act of astonishing hubris to start bringing this plan forward before he'd been re-elected. Cuz let's play it a bit differently.

Let's imagine that actually we hadn't heard anything from now until the FIFA elections in March 2027, and that with him having been re-elected — which he would have been. Don't forget, even our own football association in England was formally backing him for it, despite not —

like you would know that now, obviously.

You certainly would not know. There's a very, very funny picture, isn't there, Charlie, um, which I bet she wishes she could take back, of Debbie Hewitt holding the England shirt with her. I mean, you know — anyway, that's a story for another day.

But it was an act of astonishing hubris to start doing this so soon after the World Cup, when there was still a bit of a stench in the air about a few of the things that happened in the World Cup, but also with his re-election still not guaranteed. It was almost as if he banked his re-election up front, right? "I'm definitely going to get re-elected. So on the basis I'm definitely going to get re-elected, I might as well crack on with my massive money-making scheme." Right? Why?

民族国家式的自我幻想 & 泄露的时间点

Two things on that. Two things on that, right?

Firstly, I think you're right, but it plays into what we've discussed again before, which is him genuinely seeing himself in a completely inflated manner as almost the head of a nation state — the power that he wields being equal to those top political leaders.

And look, we joke about — and people have joked about — the relationship with Trump and how close they are. But, you know, you can absolutely see spending the amount of time around him and having him in your ear talking about how powerful you are, saying, "I'm going to put you up for the secretary general of the United Nations" or whatever hogwash that, you know, that this whole stuff was — that, you know, this Gianni brain inside is just getting more and more influenced and convinced of the power that he really wields, versus, as we've just shown, you know, the real power that actually exists within football and who controls it.

The second part, though, I do think, which is important, is: they didn't want this to come out now, right? They didn't want this to come out now.

So this wasn't a FIFA-planned press conference to announce a brand new scheme. This was really from the Times of Martin Ziegler, who everyone — and, you know, quite rightly — has been praising for a lot of very good journalistic work to get this out in the open, has obviously got hold of. And how that's happened and the people privy to this information — you know, someone's leaked it, considering top members of FIFA are even claiming to have had no knowledge of it.

But really, they were caught off guard. They had to react to this. It was going to come out. And, as you said, if he had been able to run this through to next March or so, then it could have been in a far more concerning situation.

Um, but would it really — does it change anything? Because I still think that whether it's now or whatever, the reaction would have been the same. UEFA would have reacted the same. UEFA pull out — and as we've said, UEFA pull out, the whole value of this thing falls out the bottom. There is no $15 to $20 billion valuation on a World Cup commercial enterprise if you don't have the key countries participating in those tournaments. So that if you're looking where the real power is, that's where it is.

时间点为何加速了他的政治死亡

I totally agree with that. My point was simply: if he'd managed to get himself re-elected and was then in for the next four or five years in any case, and this had come out, um, first of all, he would have had a bit more time to buy off some of the support that he needed to buy off to get the thing across the line. He would have known that UEFA were going to be against it, whatever. I mean, that was always going to be clear.

But the problem was he hadn't ticked all the boxes even in terms of his own payroll vote in Africa and Concacaf. So, um, my point was, even if it then got knocked back after his re-election, he probably wouldn't have lost his job as a result of it. They probably would have gone, "Do you know what? You know, he's only here for an extra four years. Just let him hobble on for a bit, and we'll keep him on a bit of a shorter lead" or something like that.

What's added real spice and urgency into this, as you noted, is that there is an election in March, and therefore there is a clean way of getting rid of him by putting up a candidate against him, or more than one candidate against him.

各联合会的态度扫描

Now I think if you look at the federations and their current body language, UEFA are clearly not just against the plan but against Infantino, and very explicitly so — like, this calls into question the whole leadership of FIFA. It's very clear. It's very, very clear that UEFA wants him out.

Concacaf have come out against him. Um, and again, Concacaf is a coming together of the small Caribbean nations and then the larger Concacaf nations of Canada, America, Mexico, um, and some of the other Central American countries that have reasonable football heritages.

Now the head of Concacaf, Victor Montigliani, is a Canadian, and he was already aspiring to replace Infantino. Okay. So that has been in the undergrowth for some time as a likely successor. So from Montigliani's point of view, this is great timing. This is fantastic timing — which is, rather than having to wait an extra four years to challenge Infantino, which is, well, not to challenge — for the FIFA presidency when Infantino leaves — he can now become a sort of, you know, neutral peaceful power broker, you know, sort of, you know, "compromise" guy who comes through the middle. You know: "Me, Victor, everyone knows me, I'm a good guy, I've never, you know, ruffled any feathers, I've always done a sort of, you know, a reasonable job of keeping Concacaf together."

So he is leading Concacaf to come against Infantino's position, and that's problematic for Infantino because a lot of the Concacaf nations are, constitute his power base — the Caribbean nations.

Yeah.

It's pretty clear that the African Federation is going to continue to support Infantino. Right. So conspicuous by its absence has been any clear declaration from the African nations, um, or from CAF itself, against this whole thing.

And then you've got Asia, which looks like it's split. There are some Asian nations who have come out against this. There are some who seem to be either keeping quiet or even somewhat supporting Infantino in general.

And then you have Oceania — people don't — that's not very clear. New Zealand have been very much against it, as you'd expect. Probably Australia will be as well. But the smaller Oceania countries, we don't know. And since they constitute a majority in that confederation, we don't know how they're going to go — but again, they're only 11, they're only 10 or 11 votes as well.

And Conmebol, Latin America, have been, um, fence-sitting, I would say.

So at the moment, you have UEFA and Concacaf that constitute about 100 votes between them — 105, 110 votes — who appear to be coming out against Infantino's presidency. But again, probably in Concacaf's case, not en masse — I imagine there will still be nations within that who don't necessarily back Montigliani in that. And then you've got the other federations who are either fence-sitting or who are still in support of Infantino.

结语：换头没用，除非改结构

So going back to your point, which I think was a point well made earlier — which is, I don't see Infantino resigning here — I think he'll still back himself to try to pick off enough of the individual nations in the meantime to be able to hang on in power. Um, because if he's got all the African nations, he's only 50 away then, isn't he, from having enough to hang on in there.

So anyway, look — watch this space over the next weeks and months. Gradually the politics bit will become apparent.

But in a way, that horse-trading that I've just mentioned — what's this federation saying, what's that federation thinking, all this stuff — in a way, that's all the problem, right? Which is: actually it doesn't matter, because all that really matters is what UEFA think, really. Right?

And — but also, just to leave it on this point — your point really: you can, we can talk about this for days, get blown in the face, nothing really changes unless the voting system, the structural elements of FIFA change. So, you know, it's interesting to look at Infantino, it's interesting to assess the power dynamics, but really, as you said, you're just replacing — it's a different head, right?

And ultimately, as you said, when Infantino came in, Sepp Blatter was the greatest enemy of football. And now he's the spokesperson for integrity and righteous behavior. If you've been following his Twitter feeds — uh, sorry, X feeds — it's been brilliant.

You know, I think you sit this one out, Sepp, I reckon. [laughter]

item.description:
## 一、真正的"病灶"不是英凡蒂诺，而是"一国一票"的数学结构
大多数评论把矛头对准英凡蒂诺个人的贪婪与傲慢，但节目里最锋利的一句话是：**"Infantino不是问题本身，他是问题的症状。"** 真正的病根在于FIFA的投票算术——211个成员国里，大约90个是非洲和加勒比小型足协，凑够110票就能当选主席。于是任何一位主席，只要想连任，都会被这个数学结构"锁死"在同一条路径上：**用小额转移支付（每年5–6百万美元）批发换取选票**。这也解释了为什么从阿维兰热到布拉特再到英凡蒂诺，三代主席在完全不同的时代、不同的性格、不同的出身背景下，却都不约而同走向了近乎相同的丑闻剧本——**这不是人的败坏，而是制度的引力场**。
## 二、一个跨领域的意外类比：FIFA其实是"资源诅咒"的翻版
这里有个让人意外的连接——FIFA当下的困境，与政治经济学里的"资源诅咒"（Resource Curse）几乎同构。石油国家因为坐拥现金流，统治者不需要向本国纳税人负责，只需要用石油美元维稳精英即可；而FIFA主席因为坐拥世界杯这口"油井"，也不需要向真正贡献收入的欧洲和南美负责，只需用分成"维

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Google’s AI Brain Drain, SpaceX's Huge Quarter, Airtable’s 90% Collapse, US Data Fuels China AI
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"人才外流"其实是资本配置的物理定律

Google 失去 Jeff Dean 和 Demis 的降级，表面看是硅谷版的"帝国黄昏"，但真正的驱动力是一个被忽略的会计事实：加速折旧的 Capex 抵税，让基础设施投资的税后回报率碾压了模型研发。当 26% 的企业税率允许你把每一美元资本支出当年全部计入费用，数据中心就变成"高 alpha、低 beta"，而前沿模型是"高 alpha、高 beta"。

这里有个反直觉的洞察：科学家的出走不是 Google 的失败，而是 Google 财务模型的成功。当董事会把钱都投向 GPU 出租业务（因为 ROIC 更可预测），研究员自然会离开去做他们真正想做的事——用 VC 的钱冒险。Google 在无意中把自己变成了"AI 界的中石油"：它不生产最好的智能，但拥有最好的管道。而 Jeff Dean 去创业，本质上是用 LP 的风险预算替代了 Google 股东的风险预算——同一个人做同一件事，只是风险载体换了。

二、SpaceX 的隐藏套利：把火箭工程学套用到数据中心

大家都在算 Elon 每瓦 30-50 美元的算力现货价，但没人注意到一个跨领域的诡异连接：SpaceX 之所以能比 Microsoft、Google 更快地立起 gigawatt 级数据中心，是因为造数据中心比造火箭简单太多。Elon 在电话会上那句"data centers is not rocket science"不是玩笑，是一个残酷的产业事实——硬件制造的"垂直整合肌肉记忆"是无法用软件公司的资本堆出来的。

更让人意外的是 Starlink 与 Starship 的耦合关系：V3 卫星单次发射的带宽是 V2 的 20 倍以上。这意味着 Starship 每成功一次，Starlink 的边际带宽成本就断崖式下降一次。这不是线性改进，而是一个"发射即降价"的通缩螺旋——传统电信运营商 AT&T、Verizon 面对的不是一个新对手，而是一个每次爆炸测试都在变得更强的对手。Huenet、Viaat 的股价已经告诉你结局。

三、Airtable 的死亡与 Vibe Coding 的诞生：SAS 的"熵增诅咒"

Airtable 以 12 亿美元卖身（峰值 117 亿），大部分人解读为 SAS 泡沫破裂。但真正的洞察藏在 Sachs 那句被忽略的话里："only 30% of Airtable's sales team was making quota"。这个数字暴露了 SAS 行业的一个结构性诅咒——当 PLG（产品驱动增长）撞上 VC 期待的曲棍球杆增长时，创始人被迫嫁接一个自己不擅长的 sales-led motion，最终把公司拖入"既非高增长也非高利润"的死亡地带。

跨领域的连接来了：Airtable 的困境和 Google 的 Demis 出走本质是同一件事——当组织的能力曲线与资本方的期待曲线错配时，管理层要么被迫做违反自己 DNA 的事（Airtable 加销售），要么让核心人才出走去做他们本来擅长的事（Demis 去创业）。资本的错配比技术的错配更致命。

而最出乎意料的洞察是关于 AI 与遗留代码的关系：Sachs 指出 AI 让"维护模式"变得极其容易，因为不再需要 institutional memory。这颠覆了软件行业 40 年的一个铁律——过去，代码库的历史知识是一种"人质"，让公司无法轻易裁员。现在，AI 可以瞬间"考古"出任何代码库的意图。这意味着 Bending Spoons 这类"SAS 殡葬公司"将成为未来五年最赚钱的商业模式之一：它们买下的不是产品，是"被 AI 解放出来的现金流"。Airtable 只是第一个，不是最后一个。

Freeberg：资本配置的第三种解释

Maybe it's the third bucket, which is if you're the board and the management, you're having a debate about how to best deploy capital. Google has made a commitment to deploy $200 billion in capex this year in AI infrastructure data center buildout. Because of the capex and accelerated depreciation, making an investment in AI compute in the US right now is hugely tax advantaged. And because of the extreme demand for compute, it's a pretty obvious kind of ROIC model, return on invested capital. So if you make this sort of an investment, you have significant demand for that compute infrastructure. You're very good at running the compute infrastructure. That capital can deliver massive profit returns for you with very high confidence in some forecasted period.

Building the most advanced frontier lab driven model also takes tens of billions of dollars of capital. And the question really is: can you deliver the profits from the model? And in a world where open-source is becoming so good and open weights models are catching up so quickly and all the frontier labs are catching up to each other so quickly, does it really make as much sense to deploy tens of billions of dollars against building a model?

And I think that the scientists that we're seeing transition out are the scientists that have been at the core of model development of making these frontier models. And they were certainly first out the gate. You can look at some of the early interviews with Jeff Dean from a couple years ago where they actually had a ChatGPT equivalent internally a year before ChatGPT came out from OpenAI. Google chose not to release it for fear of cannibalizing search and so on. That's when Sergey stepped in and there was this whole kind of revitalization.

But as time has gone on and as everyone has competed on models, as we've talked about many times on the show, I think it's pretty obvious that it is very hard to get the same sort of return on capital invested in model development as it is in capital invested on compute infrastructure and being model agnostic. What Google has is probably one of the greatest install enterprise bases in the world for compute. So they have the most enterprise customers. They have the most consumers. And in both cases, they don't necessarily need to have the best model to make an incredible business. They can be model agnostic. They can work with Anthropic. They can work with OpenAI. They can work with SpaceX. They have a significant ownership stake in SpaceX and in Anthropic and they can work with all the open weights models. They can host them all.

So now if you're one of the great computer scientists, you're Demis, you're Jeff Dean, you're this whole crew, and you're inside at Google and they're allocating capital not to your models, not to the things that you're most interested in, but they're allocating capital to infrastructure and data centers and supporting the broad ecosystem of models, you start to say, well, given the fact that I can go down the road and visit Brad Gerstner and a couple other people and raise a couple billion dollars at a multi-billion dollar pre-money with a PowerPoint deck because I'm the greatest in the world at doing this, that might be a better path for me. So the way I would frame it is: capex is high alpha, low beta in data center infrastructure — that capital and model development theoretically could be high alpha but it's very high beta, it's a very risky way to deploy capital. So if I'm the board, I'm the management, I'm deploying more capital in computing infrastructure, less capital into model development. That's what I think's going on.
