Well, not a room — it's a conference room with a bunch of big long bench seats that are along the wall. And so we'd have sleeping bags and we'd jump into a sleeping bag and sleep under one of the benches.

Yeah. Just so that we could be there from shift change to shift change. So the first shift starts at roughly 6:30 in the morning. Second shift starts at 4:30 in the afternoon. The next shift is starting at basically midnight.

And so we wanted to be there for shift changes to make sure that we totally could see the problem in every environment. And then we'd work solutions and the solutions would build on themselves from shift to shift.

And so that was part of the reason we were sleeping in the factory — just to be there on the front lines with people who were trying to solve a problem that was existential to the company. These weren't small problems. This is like situations where the company was on the verge of bankruptcy if we didn't solve the problem. So we had to solve the problem.

So when you say "we" — who was "we"?

It's really the entire team at Tesla. So um in that sense, senior leaders are sleeping in the conference room along with engineers and manufacturing engineers and supervisors from the different areas in the factory that might have been involved. Like we're all kind of on this team together trying to first break down the problem and then solve it.

Wow. So it is really not for executive — like senior executives who were very comfortable. These are entrepreneurial stuff.

This is kind of "founder mode" stuff as people describe it. And it doesn't mean — like I wasn't obviously a founder of Tesla, but I started finding myself acting like one because I really cared about the mission.

And I learned in that process that you can have people around that can get into founder mode that weren't founders — but they care about the problem every bit as much as a founder would. And so this really is a different form of executive leadership than you typically see out of non-founders, but you can see out of leaders that step into the problem and really care about it too.

And it's not the type of leadership that is disconnected, that is taking inputs from presentations and PowerPoints. This is leadership that is like diving in, trying to understand: this is an existential problem to our business, therefore we need to be involved — because the business could actually cease to exist and we've got a responsibility to our investors and our people to make sure that doesn't happen.

容忍失败：那块不必要的塑料隔板

This culture sounds like, you know, you guys allow people to make mistakes and you welcome people to innovate, right?

There's no way that bats a thousand with new ideas and innovation. So, you got to put up with mistakes. And the rule is: as long as people aren't repeating the same mistake — which is kind of dumb. If you're not repeating the same mistake, but you're making mistakes out of an earnest effort to try to solve a problem, that's positive. And eventually we're going to find the right answer.

What was one of the problems you were solving?

So, we were introducing the Model 3. There was a part in the Model 3 that was a separator — basically a big sheet of plastic that separated the battery from the cabin. And we're trying to make this separator, this sheet — it just never really fit right. It would delaminate. All kinds of problems.

So Elon took this problem on and he spent several weeks working in the factory trying to figure out how to manufacture this thing, and then finally started to ask the first question of the algorithm about the requirement.

And so he went to the team and said, "Who made the requirement for this piece of plastic? Why is it here?"

And the team he was talking to was a battery team. And they said, "Oh, it's the cabin guys. They wanted a sound dampener between the road and the cabin. So they designed this part and put it into the bill of material."

So he goes to that team and says, "Can you tell me why you feel like this is a requirement for sound dampening to have this kind of plastic sheet that's really difficult to manufacture?"

And they said, "Oh, we didn't do this. This was the battery guys."

He said, "I was just with the battery guys. They told me they didn't come up with this. It's you."

They said, "Well, it wasn't us."

He said, "Give me the name of the person who's on the spec — like the name of the engineer."

And so, they go find the name of the engineer. It turns out it was an intern that didn't even work at Tesla anymore.

So he then realizes he spent three weeks of his life solving a problem that didn't need to exist. The best part is no part. In this example, we shouldn't have had the part.

So that's what the algorithm started — which was: you got to question every requirement, because some of this stuff is just dumb and you don't know where it comes from.

And this particular part — you question the requirement (first step of the algorithm) — you find out it's not necessary. Second step of the algorithm is: you delete it. Get rid of it and make it prove that it needed to be there in the first place. Turned out it didn't.

Now you've got a new manufacturing process where you could skip over this. You can speed up your manufacturing process and then you can automate that last.

And Elon uses that example of: the first thing you got to do diligently every day is question requirements — because otherwise you end up spending 3 weeks in a factory for nothing, and it's a really dumb requirement it turned out at the end of the day which was totally unnecessary and stopped us from shipping cars, which damaged the cash flow of the company. So sometimes these little small decisions can have huge impacts at the end of the day.

提速与自动化：混凝土的比喻

After you delete the unnecessary steps, you accelerate the cycle time.

Yeah. This is key. Like when you add speed to a new process, it reveals all the warts in the process. So you can't get speed without a very clean process that doesn't have quality issues and process issues.

So you add speed to start to help you basically debug the new process that you've just invented. And in this case it's pretty straightforward. You delete that part and you remove that from the manufacturing process, and the process itself starts to speed up because now you don't have this delay from that part.

That's pretty unusual that it's that clean. Most of the time you've deleted a bunch of steps that are proven to be unnecessary because they're not real requirements. And now you got a brand new process that you got to teach humans and machines to do — sometimes software to do. And you add speed to get that process as perfect as possible.

And then once you have it running at speed, which means you've got high quality, high throughput, and now lower cost — so you can get good, fast, and cheap — now you can automate it.

And you should wait to automate it because that automation step, that last step, when you pour automation into any process it's like pouring concrete onto that process, and the only way you get it out is with a jackhammer. So you got to be really careful about when you do that, because you're creating technical debt for yourself if you do it too soon.

AI 如何改变一切（或让烂流程更烂）

Do you see AI changing that because now we can speed up the process?

Yeah, I see AI like making bad process worse and more expensive. So if you pour AI into a process you haven't rethought and optimized, that process is broken. It runs faster to the bad answer and it's more expensive because now you spent tokens to actually get to that answer.

And so what you got to do as a leader is pump the brakes, slow down, and say, "Okay, we got to take a blank sheet of paper and redo this process and make it the most simple and elegant step ever, and then we'll apply AI to it, and then we'll get to the better answer faster."

And I see organizations not taking that step because that step is hard work. It's easier just to take the existing pathway or process and apply AI to that versus really stopping and saying, "Hey, before we do this, we've got one chance to make this a whole lot better." So that AI is actually helping our impact versus hurting our impact.

Is it fair to say that you think human judgment is still better than AI in this case?

I think — well, there are problems where AI is an incredible optimizer and can work way faster than humans. So I don't think that statement is universally true. But I do think you've got to be very cognizant of how AI works, how it can add value to a particular process. It can't add value to every process. And be very very careful that you're working in a way that is leveraging AI to the max and not leveraging AI's flaws.

Is it possible to talk to AI and ask AI how do I simplify this process and use that result?

You can use that as kind of as an input, I would say. But unless you've dumped a bunch of process data about your particular process into a model and trained that model, the answer that you get is probably not going to be all that great because it didn't have much data to go on.

So it's an input, but humans looking at perfecting that process can often have at least the kind of impact an LLM could have, if not greater.

数据主权：为什么不能把 IP 喂给公共模型

You know, Chamath and Alex Karp, they were on CNBC these past couple weeks and they were talking about how companies are not really supposed to spend tokens and feed critical information to AI that doesn't belong to them. And now you are basically being controlled by these platforms.

Well, you're definitely giving very valuable insights to these platforms. 90% of the world's information sits behind a firewall — which means that as an individual company, my information is not out on the web. It's not crawlable by OpenAI or Anthropic. And it often contains trade secrets, IP, other things.

So when you open up your IP and your trade secrets to a general model, it is absorbing that information and essentially sharing that information through inference to the world. So in that sense, Alex and Chamath are right. You want to be running models within a closed environment that are not sharing your trade secrets and your IP with the rest of the world — especially as you're making progress on more elegant, simple processes, innovation breakthroughs, etc.

And there are certainly ways to do that. And that's why you see the world migrating more and more towards open-weight and open-source models that you can run on your own machines in your own environment — so you're protecting your data and your IP, but still leveraging the insights that can come from really powerful AI models.

精益 vs. 算法：增量改进与量子跃迁

After reading your book, I had this question — and I did an MBA and the first class was talking about the Toyota Way, the lean process. I would like to ask you: what's the difference between the lean process and the algorithm five-step framework?

I would say the lean process is amazing for incremental change and the algorithm drives quantum or innovation change.

When I started at Tesla, one of the first problems I was trying to tackle alongside our team was the Model X. And so I immediately came to that problem with my set of lean tools from the Toyota Production System. And what I saw was we could get 5% improvement, 10% improvement, things like that. But if we wanted a real breakthrough, the Toyota Production System wasn't sufficient. The model of lean and constraints and kaizen were incrementally helping but they weren't having quantum breakthroughs.

And as we developed the algorithm as a team — it wasn't just Elon, it was the whole team that developed this framework — the framework was developed to drive big innovations. Like how do you catch a rocket fuselage on its way down back to the earth? How do you build a supercharger network worldwide that will solve range anxiety? How do you build a Starlink internet network — a satellite-based internet network for the world that solves a problem that a lot of big brains were working on for decades?

All those things come from the algorithm framework. They don't come necessarily from a Toyota Production System or a lean framework — because there's a difference between incrementally improving what you already have and then having a breakthrough to something else. And the breakthroughs come in the algorithm from questioning those requirements and then super-simplifying your approach to a potential innovation.

在 DVX Ventures：从零开始创造公司

For people that are watching, they might not be running a huge company. How can they apply this method in their daily lives?

I think we apply it — so what I do on a daily basis at DVX Ventures is we invent companies from scratch. And a lot of these companies come from the original step, the first step in the process, which is you question requirements.

So we have a cyber software business that — we questioned the requirement: does cyber software always have to be penetration testing? In other words, are you trying from the outside in to find leaks?

We said, "What if it could be from the inside out? Wouldn't that be much more effective?" You essentially put a smoke bomb off inside a house and understand where the leaks are and then quickly cover up those leaks. And we said, "Why can't it be that way?" There's a lot of technical challenges why it can't be that way and that's why it hadn't existed. But we worked our way through those technical challenges and now we have a business that is very unique in cyber where we solve cyber risk from the inside out, not the outside in.

We have an ETF business that is now the fastest growing ETF business of all time — where we started with a question: could you build ETFs for emerging super-cycles that weren't based on market cap, instead were based on the build sheet of like an AI data center for an AI data center fund, or the grid for an electrification fund?

So we just ask these questions and new businesses emerge from these questions. They're actually quite sizable. But those new businesses start at zero and then we have to say, "How would we bring this product to market?"

So in the case of the ETF business, we said, "Could we bring this to market in a new way? Could we bring this to market not through the big stock and wealth management organizations, but could we bring it to retail investors through Reddit, through X, etc. at no cost?" And it turned out we built the fastest growing ETF platform with a very different distribution model. Rather than it coming through the large brokerage houses, it came first to the retail investor through Reddit and X.

And so I think if you're an early stage entrepreneur, this applies every bit as much to you as it does to a scaled company like SpaceX or Tesla.

如何验证哪个想法值得追求：五重筛选

There is this saying that, you know, everybody has a lot of great ideas. When you can't sleep, you lie in bed alone — now you have a lot of great ideas, but in the morning you forget about all of them, right? How do you verify which ones are worth pursuing?

Really good question. In our business, we look for five things to be true because we do have a lot of ideas and we want to sort through what the best ideas are. And the five things are:

  1. Do we have a multi-billion dollar TAM here that is provable? Like, will people buy this product into the tune of billions of dollars? That's number one.
  2. Are there 50% gross margins here? Is it a profitable, attractive industry? Part of the reason we have that requirement is we've worked in like automotive with a 13% gross margin and that's a tough way to make a living. It's a lot of fun, but it's a very hard way to make a living. We'd much rather have NVIDIA margins at 80%.
  3. Is there a technical moat here? Is there a really tough software problem that hasn't been solved and that's why this opportunity exists? And if we figured that out, could we have the beginnings of a moat?
  4. Competitive intensity. Is there a lot of competitive intensity in the space? If so, we're probably not going to be all that unique and it's going to be hard to break through.
  5. Liquidity propensity. Do people want to buy companies in this space?

If those five things are true, now you've got an idea that's probably worth working on. And so, we'll pull those ideas up that check those five things off the stack and begin to work on them.

And you find the right people to work on those things.

Yeah, exactly. We start the work initially. We develop the product, put it into market, and we get it post-revenue to prove that we've got the beginnings of product-market fit. And then yeah, we go find people with domain experience who have scaled in those spaces before, and we grab those people.

And you start all these companies.

We do. We do.

That is incredible.

It sounds like — we've got a team of the best of the best. The best people that I have ever worked with alongside at Tesla, at Lyft, at some of my prior companies. And yeah, we are the first entrepreneurs — we start these things. It's a bit of a different model, but it's been highly effective for us.

结语：给年轻自己的一句话

Wow. Before we wrap up this conversation, one piece of advice to your younger self.

I would want to say to myself: don't let fear hold you back. And really pursue opportunities as if there was no downside. Which is really hard to do.

But I've just learned over time that when you're getting signal from a market, listen to that signal and act fast. Don't take inventory of all the things that could go wrong. Take inventory of the signal and go amplify that signal.

And that's probably what I'd say to my younger self — just like, go with more confidence, go with more speed.

That was amazing. Baker's on.

item.description:
## 一、隐藏的洞察：Elon 最大的敌人，是一个已经离职的实习生
整场访谈里最震撼的一幕，其实被轻描淡写地带过：Elon 花了**三周时间**亲自泡在工厂里，试图解决 Model 3 电池与车厢之间那块塑料隔板的制造问题——直到他发现，这个"需求"是一个早已离开特斯拉的实习生写进 BOM 表里的，没有任何工程逻辑、法规或安全依据。
这个故事的真正颠覆性在于：**世界上智商最高的工业家之一，也会被"幽灵需求"劫持三周。** 组织里最危险的东西不是错误的决定，而是**没人记得自己做过的决定**——它们像生物学里的"退化器官"，明明没有功能却世代遗传。Jon 说的"算法第一步：质疑每一个需求"，本质上不是聪明才智问题，而是**组织考古学**：每一条流程规则背后都有一具尸体，你必须把它挖出来问它是怎么死的。
跨界连接：这和心理治疗里的"内摄"（introjection）几乎是同一件事——成年人身上大部分的痛苦，来自小时候不加质疑地吞下的规则。企业不做"质疑需求"，就是集体的心理僵化。
## 二、反直觉观察：McNeill 是靠"越界"被录用的，不是靠简历
注意面试流程的荒诞：他还没

item.title: [Business of Sport] Infantino isn’t the REAL Problem at FIFA, Staveley's West Ham Move Unpacked, & More Racing Drama
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Infantino 不是病，而是症状——FIFA 的"贫困选民陷阱"

节目里最反直觉的洞见不是"Infantino 该下台"，而是：换谁上来都会变成下一个 Infantino。原因是一个纯粹的数学结构——211 个成员国里约 90 个是非洲和加勒比小协会，年收入只有 500–600 万美元，而英足总的年收入是 6 亿英镑。也就是说，FIFA 主席只需要用"英足总的零头"就能锁定连任所需的选票。这意味着任何理性的主席，为了争取第二个任期，都必然会走上"疯狂搞钱—收买小协会—再搞更疯狂的钱"的螺旋。

这里有一个惊人的跨领域连接：这与美国州际参议院制度、欧盟理事会一国一票、甚至 Web3 DAO 中"鲸鱼 vs 长尾"投票的失败案例，是同一种病——当"票权分布"和"价值贡献分布"严重错位时，制度会自动产生腐败激励，而不需要腐败的人。Infantino 只是恰好站在了这个数学结构的输出端。

二、West Ham 的"毒丸条款"揭示了足球俱乐部估值的一个隐秘断层

Kretinsky 用一个绝妙的"卖 2.5% 给朋友"的操作绕开了 drag-along 条款——这本身就足够精彩，但更深的洞见是：这次内斗暴露了英超与英冠之间存在一个隐藏的"估值悬崖"。

600 million 的估值在英超叫"稍贵"，在英冠叫"荒诞"（历史最高英冠估值仅 1.5 亿）。而 Kretinsky 2021 年买入时签下的"如果超过 50% 就必须以 10 亿估值收购 Sullivan"的条款，在英超环境下勉强算商业赌注，在英冠环境下就变成了核弹级毒丸。

跨领域连接来了：这和 2008 年 CDO 里的"触发条款"结构完全一样——在牛市里那些条款看起来只是技术性细节，但一旦资产价格进入某个区间，它们会瞬间从"合同条款"变成"结构性炸弹"。West Ham 董事会现在的僵局，本质上是一个足球界的"合约衍生品爆仓事件"。而降级不是原因，降级只是引爆器。

三、赛马业的启示：为什么"民主"会杀死顶级体育

英国赛马一年 1,500 场比赛、每天 4–6 场——这个数字荒谬到几乎是行为艺术。但更值得警惕的是它背后的机制：同样是"一场地一票"的投票结构，让占行业营收 10–20% 的小马场，用 30 年时间把 80–90% 的价值创造者绑架成人质。

这里最出人意料的观察：赛马的问题、FIFA 的问题、NBA 常规赛"没人看直到季后赛"的问题、甚至 Netflix 内容库过度膨胀导致的"选择疲劳"问题，本质上是同一个问题——注意力经济中的通货膨胀。当供给端无限扩张但需求端（人类注意力）是硬约束时，"更多"会系统性地摧毁"价值"。

更深的一层：Jockey Club 这次退出赛马场协会的意义，与 UEFA 威胁退出 FIFA 计划、与 1992 年英超从英足联脱离出来另立门户，是同一种历史动作的第三次上演——每隔 30 年左右，体育产业中的"价值生产者"就会被迫从"民主协商机制"中撕裂出来，重建一个更集中的治理结构。

这暗示了一个几乎没人明说的规律：现代体育治理不存在稳态。每一次"分权民主化"（1990s 把 FIFA/赛马交给委员会）都会在 25–35 年后被"精英夺权运动"逆转。我们现在正在同时目睹 FIFA、West Ham、英国赛马三条战线的这种逆转——这不是巧合，是周期。

📝 转录文本

开场提要

Has this been terminal not just for Infantino's plan to sell off 20% of the World Cup? Is it also terminal for Infantino himself and his presidency?

I find it very hard to see how he stays and FIFA retains any sort of credibility.

Amanda Staveley and PCP Capital Partners, who formerly were invested in Newcastle, are looking to buy 25% stake in West Ham.

600 million is off the scale — is a huge punt for anyone to pay a £600 million valuation for a club in the Championship. That means if they don't go up this season, they're then staring down the abyss, cuz it means you've only got one season of proper parachute payments left.

Unbelievably, in British racing, there are almost 1 and a half thousand fixtures. Yes, that's right. There are about four race meetings, sometimes five, sometimes six, every single day. The Jockey Club now has stepped forward and said: "Right, that's it. We're out. And we're basically going to start our campaign to off all the small courses." That's what we're going to do.

Substack 提示

Before we start, a quick reminder for those of you that haven't yet joined us on Substack — to get yourselves over there. If you love or even just like this show and want to see bonus segments, written pieces, polls, behind-the-scenes access, and events, there's only one place to go. Come and see what it's all about. It's live now. Check out the link in the bio, and we'll see you there.

开场问候

Good afternoon, Charlie. How are you? As you can see, obviously, I'm back in the studio, but it doesn't look like you are.

I am not. I am, uh, down in Cornwall, Charlie — a place which I know is very, very dear to your heart. Um, I have Cornish family and my family have a place in Cornwall, and here we are, um, in my happy place.

I mean, there's been a fair amount going on in the world of sport while you've been down there anyway. So, there's no shortage of stuff for us to talk through today.

No, it's been an absolute blockbuster of a few days on the sports business front. We need to crack straight on, don't we? We've got a lot to fit in.

FIFA：UEFA 表态与 Infantino 计划的崩塌

Let's talk FIFA. A lot's happened, Charlie. I mean, I will pat on the back maybe where credit is due. We recorded last week, I think on the Wednesday. A lot happened after the Wednesday before we released on Friday. The main thing being the UEFA stance, which basically led to the UEFA nations saying that they will not participate in FIFA tournaments.

Now, the reason I say credit where it's due is because actually it didn't date the show — considering we'd already suggested that that would be the main way to deal with the situation. And if that did indeed happen, then the plan in essence would be dead in the water because without the European countries, all the value of this scheme kind of fell out at the bottom of it.

So that having happened — and then obviously the very quick withdrawal of the scheme on, I think, Friday night when Infantino finally realized that this was probably over — um, has kind of brought an end to those four sorry days. But of course, with this — and I think this is where we're particularly interested to speak as well as what happened — the huge conversation now is what goes on moving forward.

Yeah. So the question you're asking is: has this been terminal not just for Infantino's plan to sell off 20% of the World Cup, but is it also terminal for Infantino himself and his presidency?

It kind of looks both, doesn't it?

Well, the plan for sure. The plan, Infantino, as you say, has already accepted is dead in the water. And I will say that, you know, we did predict that. We predicted that UEFA would kill it, torpedo it, and they did.

Infantino 的"阿喀琉斯之踵"

He was virtually untouchable, right? He was virtually untouchable. I was going to put this out there. He came out of that World Cup. We had all of the stuff that went on with Balagan and Trump, and you had all of this conversation about 64 teams, and some people going, "How can we do that? That's crazy."

But do you know what? We still looked at the voting systems and where the money was going to be going. And we said, "Look, the reality is, unfortunately, until he decides — well, until he sees out his final term in presidency, i.e. 2031, it's highly unlikely he's going to remove himself."

Then he has played an absolute blinder as the only person that could cause himself any issues. He has done exactly that. And it is a classic case of — even with seemingly unending power and influence — he has found his Achilles heel. And the hubris of the whole situation will be his downfall.

And to be honest, now — you know, fingers crossed — now is the time where you really need those organizations that we've talked about potentially having power, i.e. the FA, but really it was UEFA as a block standing up. And actually, for the first time, as you said in your memo this week on Substack, for the first time standing up and actually acting with the power that they have to show — in your words — whether the emperor really has any clothes.

And it looks like to me this whole situation has shown — now with UEFA pulling the lever that they did — that the real power in football is not a tour, a glorified tournament organizer really, if I can say it, in FIFA. But it is the people that have the block of countries that they need to participate in these tournaments to make them valuable.

Infantino 是症状，不是病：FIFA 的结构性问题

Yeah, exactly Charlie. Really the issue now is not so much about Infantino. We can come to Infantino and the specifics of that. The issue really is more to do with the status of FIFA within the power blocks, within the game — because don't forget that Infantino, I know it's hard for people to think this way given what a total clown he's made of himself in recent weeks, months. Infantino is not himself the problem. He's a symptom of the problem.

Let's not forget: Infantino was the secretary general of UEFA, right? Infantino doesn't come from the African conference. He doesn't come from the Oceania conference. He's a UEFA guy, right?

So effectively, you have to ask yourself the question: why does Infantino — and indeed previous presidents of FIFA — end up doing things which either are on the margin sort of corrupt, or, as I put in my memo, sort of blaggard? Right? That's one bit of it. But the other bit of it is becoming very beholden to, in particular, the African nations on the one hand, and the Caribbean nations on the other hand, which are the poorest federations in the world in terms of their own revenues.

And this is where I get into, you know, roots of problems versus symptoms of problems. Because effectively, to become president of FIFA — and then particularly to stay as president of FIFA — what you become aware of quite quickly is that under one-member-one-vote, where there are 211 member nations, of whom about 90 are either African or Caribbean nations (i.e. federations with very little money), in your aim to get 110-odd votes, you can wrap up all pretty much all the support you need simply from the African and Caribbean nations. And this is something which Blatter did before, and Havelange did before that, etc.

为什么"补贴机制"如此腐蚀

And the reason why that is so corrosive is because those federations — which are constantly struggling for money — they don't have money themselves. So we're talking about federations that have annual revenues of 5 million, 6 million bucks a year, compared to our football association with revenues of 600 million pounds, right?

So for these small federations, handouts of 5 or 6 million a year are transformational for them. It changes everything. Now, of course, one would love to think that all of that extra 6 million went into football development and lovely schemes overseen by Wenger — and some of it does. Let's not imagine for a moment that part of this isn't used to prop up those federations, prop up the people who run those federations, who don't forget are significant people within their own country's political ecosystem.

And, you know, it's the difference between the president of one of those federations being able to pay himself 100,000 bucks a year and two or 300,000 bucks a year. It's the difference between them being able to travel first class to various locations around the world and having to travel in the back of the plane. It's the difference between them being able to look after people within their own football ecosystems with handouts here and there to keep everybody else in line.

You know that. So Infantino, Blatter, Havelange have been confronted with a mathematical reality — which is that the cheapest and easiest way of keeping your 120-odd votes that you need is by giving enough money on an individual basis to the poorer federations to keep them happy with you. Because they're not going to debate you long and hard about the big stuff you're doing.

小协会不会挑战大议题

So when you come up with some scheme to, you know, have hydration breaks or hold the World Cup every two years or whatever it might be, the head of the federation of a small African country is not going to take to the New York Times and give an interview about how this fundamentally undermines the future governance of world football. He just says, "Give me my five million bucks and you can do what the hell you want," right? That's the underlying reality of how FIFA works.

So whereas he could come to the English FA — I mean, you know, supine and hopeless though it is — and say to them, "Oh, by the way, you know, I'm going to do something here which means I'm going to be able to give you an extra 5 million bucks." And the FA would be like, "Well, that's sort of rounding error for us, um, Johnny. It doesn't make any difference to us. That doesn't mean that in a year's time we're just going to say yes, yes, yes, when you want to go and hold a World Cup every two years and that type of stuff. We'll take the money, sure, but then we reserve the right to debate with you going down the track whether the stuff you think is reasonable and fair."

与英超诞生的历史类比

If you look back to why the Premier League was actually formed and you read the memoirs of various English football industry people from around that time — what had happened during the late 1980s, mid to late 1980s, where English football also had one-club-one-vote, so Man United had one vote and Walsall had one vote — is on a continual basis, when the big clubs, who had senior managing directors, more senior people involved, when they would say, "Well, one way in which we think football in this country can progress is this, this, and that," there would be a block of the lower division clubs who go, "No, I don't fancy it, don't fancy it. They then got totally blindsided, where instead of executing on that deal, the Gold family then effectively went behind their backs and agreed a deal to sell the entire of their 25% stake to PCP, which is Amanda Staveley and Mehrdad and their backers. Okay.

And the assumption would have been on the basis, from PCP, from Amanda and Mehrdad and Co., the assumption would have been: "Well, Křetínský's had a long time here to buy out these shares and to take a majority. It looks like he doesn't really want to do that. So actually what we can do here is we can probably start to enter into a negotiation with David Sullivan, who's basically no longer even allowed to come to the club, over his shareholding. And we can actually end up leaving Křetínský in there as a 27% shareholder, with us operating the rest of the club with 73%, and that would be absolutely fine, and we could then make an offer to Křetínský at our leisure for those shares."

Křetínský 的"卖 2.5% 给朋友"绝招

So what's Křetínský done? Křetínský's done something really, really interesting. And you know, I was going to say quite sneaky, but I guess he would feel that he's been had — something quite sneaky done on him first. So what he's done is he's worked out that if he gets his 27% down to 24.5%, he could then buy the 25% of the Gold shares and take himself up to 49.5%. And if prior to doing that he'd sold that 2.5% that he needs to sell to get himself down to 24.5% to a mate, effectively he could have 49.5%, a mate of his could have 2.5%, and between him and his mate they would have 52% of the business without him triggering the need to buy Sullivan's shares.

Okay. So that effectively is — and that's using a mechanism that we call pre-emption, right? Which is that effectively what you'll find in any shareholder agreement is that when one of the shareholders agrees a deal to sell their shares to an external party, those shares and that deal gets offered to the existing shareholders, who can gazump it if they want by simply saying, "We'll do that deal, we'll pay you the same amount for that deal."

So in other words: Vanessa Gold says, "Right, I'm going to sell my 25% for whatever it was, £150 million, um, to PCP." And that notification goes out to Křetínský and to Sullivan. Sullivan says, "No thanks very much. I've already got too many shares in this club. I'm not even allowed to come to the stadium. I can't be a director of the club. I need to be thinking at some point divesting myself of my shares. I don't want to be buying more shares particularly. No thanks very much." Křetínský says, "Uh, actually yes, I'm going to buy them. Oh, and by the way, I've just sold 2.5% of my existing shareholding to a mate." Right.

So that is where we are right now. Um, so effectively he has, at least in theory, blocked the PCP offer by making the same offer himself. Now the legal eagles will have to get involved to work out whether Křetínský selling 2.5% to a mate at short notice really does constitute or does not constitute him effectively getting into a control situation and then triggering the entire purchase by Sullivan.

Um, these things will play out, I guess, in the coming weeks and months.

对球队本赛季的影响

What do you reckon, Charlie? I just wanted to ask you a question actually — and for fans as well, because from a business point this is fascinating. We know that what matters most to football fans is obviously how this all translates to on the pitch. And we know that on the pitch has been a big problem for West Ham, and they're going into their first season outside the top flight in many years. How much of a concern is this to the actual operations of the club ahead of this season? Fully appreciating that there are a number of issues that need to get sorted out behind the scenes. There's a huge amount of debt in the club. There's, you know, already challenges with the existing leadership, as we said, even if you don't bring more people in. What do you think about that part of it?

Um, well, it's a totally valid question because at the moment effectively, you got a vacuum of control, right? So, I guess at the moment, in theory at least, the club is being operated by a combination of Sullivan and Křetínský. Um, they've got an interim chief executive in there who I know, who's a really good guy. Um, and, you know, who was at Rangers previously, and I think actually West Ham previously in a less senior position.

Yeah. Commercial, though, wasn't it? Commercial.

They had a commercial. He's a really good guy actually. And I think the general consensus is is that over the summer, for once, they've actually executed a pretty good transfer selling strategy, right? They've actually done a pretty good job of shipping out those big Premier League stars, and they haven't been held over a barrel and sold them cheap. It looks like they've sold them quite expensively. They persuaded Jar—

Matias Fernandez, Crecensio Somerville, just to be clear — both, you know, going for well, I think about 60 to 80 million.

Yeah.

Each.

财政迫使的清仓

And I think we covered on a previous episode that they had to do that. They had to do that because they had this enormous overhang of existing transfer liabilities from the previous seasons that they simply had to clear, right? But what they still then do have, of course, is parachute payments for the next year or two, which enable them to keep together quite a bit of that squad.

And one thing they have been able to do is keep Jarrod Bowen in the club for one extra season. Now the rumor is they've said to Bowen that if they don't get promoted this season that he will then be sold next summer. But Bowen seems to be happy with that scenario.

Um, but there are obvious holes in their squad which they now need to fill. And, um, the rhythms of a Championship season compared to a Premier League season are a little bit different. So, first of all, the Championship or the Football League in general tends to start a week to two weeks before the Premier League. And secondly, I think generally speaking, football league clubs get their squads in place earlier and firmer so they can start the season, particularly if you're looking to get promoted, where you can't afford too many losses. They tend to get their squads together a bit earlier to make sure that they don't go and ship a few early defeats, which can really jeopardize your ultimate promotion.

Whereas in the Premier League, when the aim is simply to try and stay in the Premier League, I almost feel like sometimes Premier League clubs towards the bottom end think, "Well, if we are still putting our squad together towards the back end of August, early September, and if we're not quite in the perfect position, that might not be quite such a bad problem, because, you know, we are going to lose matches on a regular basis anyway. So we're not giving up quite as much."

"混乱"的代价

So I guess my concern would be this — go back to your original question — is that notwithstanding them having operated rather more professionally this summer under Verani than they have done under previous supposed leaderships, um, I guess Karen Brady being the one — nonetheless, they are still a bit of a shambles, right? Um, that they are trying to repair that shambles. They're trying to get the whole thing sorted out, but it is still a bit of a shambles.

And if you then get a slow start, and if after a month of the Championship season you are 7, 8, 9 points off the pace, and there are other well-funded clubs or other parachute payment clubs who are banging away at the top of the table, you're simply making the likelihood of that quick return an awful lot harder.

Now what does that then mean? What that means, if they don't go up this season, they're then staring down the abyss, because it means you've only got one season of proper parachute payments left, which means you then have to start cutting your cloth in terms of your squad size and all that kind of thing. So this is crucial.

And then we come back to this whole valuation piece of — you know, if you pay 600 million for something like this, it just — it's incredibly problematic. And even, you know, Amanda Mehrdad buying in right now, if you're looking at their ability to influence — you know, it's a huge amount of money to put into a club right now where you've got little influence over at least the performance side. At the back end of a window, they haven't made a single signing this summer. They may have sold well, but they haven't made a single signing. And I thought, you know, even some of the decisions — they sold, without getting too technical on the player side, they sold Freddy Potts for 10 million to Club Brugge. This is a player that is Championship-proven. He's actually been carving out a fantastic career at that level, who you'd be looking at as the squad going, "Do you know what, I'm not sure about Jean-Clair Todibo's ability to operate at center back in the Championship." Just that's an area of concern for me. But I am looking at a Freddy Potts, that type of player, to be a real kind of bringer together of that Championship level football requirement. So yeah, I'd be worried. And I'm sure they are very worried, mostly, as you say, if you don't go up on the business.

英冠有多难：Opta 排名的启示

I think you're absolutely right. I mean, there's something that Premier League fans haven't quite got their head around yet is how good the Championship is, right? And I'm saying that on an objective basis.

So I saw the Opta league rankings recently, right? So Opta used data to determine the rankings of the leagues throughout the entire world and how they sit amongst or below each other. The Championship is now the 10th top league in the world.

Wow.

About on a par with the Eredivisie in the Netherlands. So you would expect a top club in the Championship would be about on a par these days with Ajax Amsterdam. That's about where things sit, right?

So any sort of blind assumptions that, "Oh well, it's the Championship, it's all very easy, should be fine, no problem," etc., etc. — I just don't think that's the case anymore. I think it's really, really tough. And the nature of the season when you have many more matches, and where as the big dog you are the cup final every single week, right? So every single week you're playing as a team that ups its game by 5% because they're playing against West Ham United rather than playing against — dare I say from last year — my old club Oxford United. You know, so this is a big sporting challenge that awaits West Ham.

And whilst they have been doing as good a job as they possibly could do during the summer and getting things straight, it still feels to me like they're kind of a month to two months away from having a settled proper Championship squad that's worked out how to play with each other, that Nuno's worked out who fits where, and all this type of stuff. So I'd be very concerned about that going forward.

内斗对球场的辐射

But actually, you know, on a bigger level, the bottom line is that once a club becomes subsumed with this kind of power struggles, internal fighting, and all this type of stuff, you just have problems.

You alluded to earlier on that Amanda and Mehrdad were broadly speaking popular with the Newcastle fan base because they took over a club that had been Bermed and not going in the right direction under Mike Ashley, and they were able to inject that bit of direction, bit of structure, and obviously new capital coming from Saudi Arabia. Without that, I don't think they got very far.

Um, I noticed that the comments from the West Ham fan groups on this proposed takeover are not positive. They felt that under the Křetínský and Sullivan scheme, which basically saw Křetínský taking a bigger role in the club, that that was something which offered stability and a sort of platform to build off going forward. And they are very worried that this whole power struggle is going to basically derail this season, and that that will have significant consequences going forward.

Now that's not obviously something that Amanda and Mehrdad are intending. That's not the point. They want to take over — they would want to be there in charge as quickly as possible. But once Křetínský has pushed back and has said, "I'm going to fight this," then you do have the prospect of, you know, there being wranglings going on over the coming weeks and months.

Exactly. But I mean, less something on Amanda Mehrdad, consortium PCP, more on anyone coming into this and derailing something at this stage. Because as you've highlighted now, you know, whether they like Křetínský and Sullivan or not, it's not really the point. I think sensibly what they'll be looking at is they'll be realizing what the most important elements of West Ham are right now, and it is to navigate the next however many months to try and get back to where they need to be. The last thing they need to be doing is trying to do that on the pitch and in the boardroom with no one actually with the capacity to make decisions. Let's see. It would be really problematic, and it's a great club for them to have problems that put them, you know, further in the mire. I hope that doesn't happen.

赛马业：Jockey Club 出走

Shall we have a quick little look at horse racing? Because —

Yeah. So horse racing —

The big old topic is back.

I'm just going to sit back a little moment here. Right. And it's nice and sunny outside, and I'm going to let a little shaft of sunlight come over and give a little halo over my head here, because Charlie's about to cover me with warm trickle words for having predicted three months ago — or predicted, or encouraged, or said something that I think should happen. Rather like I've just said, I think that UEFA need to now use the moment and take over control of world football.

Back in March, Charlie, we had a look at the political landscape of horse racing in Great Britain and what a mess it was. And what I said was: the Jockey Club need to leave the racecourse association and take charge of horse racing.

And that's exactly what seems to have happened.

And that is what has — the first bit at least — has happened.

Sorry, you meant, so I have to begrudgingly admit that you predicted this and now we must all —

I mean, there's no begrudging about it.

No, Charlie. What happens when I predict something that doesn't come true is you dig up an old clip from two years ago and play it live on a show to try to embarrass me just to give yourself a few kicks along the way. Um, so in this case, um, whilst I'm not expecting you to replay the clip of me predicting that the Jockey Club would resign from the racecourse association and take full leadership of the industry, I am nonetheless grateful that you do at least remember me making this prediction.

Jockey Club 的正式声明

So what's happened? What's happened is this: on Monday — um, that is two days ago as we are recording on Wednesday — um, the Jockey Club put out a statement announcing that it had told the racecourse association that it would leave the RCA by the end of the year.

Now when we did our first survey of British horse racing, I said, "Look, don't get put off by all these three-letter acronyms or TLAs, as I like to call them. Um, that's just how racing rolls."

Okay. The reality about horse racing in the UK is it has been a governance mess and has been ever since the Jockey Club gave up full control of the sport in the mid-1990s and was encouraged by the governments of that time to hand it over to a series of committees. And on those committees sat representatives of all the various different constituent parts of horse racing: a representative of the owners, a representative of the thoroughbred breeders, a representative of the trainers, and so on and so forth.

RCA 的"小马场否决权"

But crucially, the blocking vote was held by the Racecourse Association — the trade body of the racecourses. And because the Racecourse Association has the same voting structure as FIFA — one racecourse, one vote — what that meant was, is that the entirety of British horse racing was held hostage and has been held hostage for 30 years by the small racecourses. Because there are more small racecourses than there are big racecourses. Even though the big racecourses account for 80 to 90% of all of what's good about British racing — revenues, attention, TV, global appeal, all of that kind of stuff.

Nonetheless, the small racecourses, most of which are coagulated into a group called ARC — right, which is a racecourse group owned by the Reuben family — basically had the whip hand over the entire industry, because whenever any proposal came up, the Racecourse Association, which effectively was being driven by the small racecourses, would just say, "No, we're not doing that." Right?

1,500 场比赛的荒谬

And this was particularly relevant in terms of the number of — just to recap what we said in March — in terms of the number of fixtures that there are in British racing. Unbelievably, in British racing, there are almost 1 and a half thousand fixtures. 1,500 fixtures. Yes, that's right. There are about four race meetings, sometimes five, sometimes six, every single day.

And the central funding for fixtures, which comes from a betting tax imposed on the bookmakers, which creates something called a levy, which is then distributed to help fund all those race meetings through prize money, effectively is then spread throughout those 1,500 fixtures — which means that not enough of the funding reaches the bigger fixtures and the bigger courses, which then means that British horse racing is disadvantaged compared to the rest of the world, which then means that large owners and large breeders move their interests away from British racing to Hong Kong, to Australia, to South Africa, to America, even to Latin America, because there ain't enough money going around in UK horse racing.

And this has been well known and well understood for a long while — that the small racecourses, who grab in this funding to fund their irrelevant pathetic fixtures that no one wants to watch, have simply said, "No, we do not want to agree to anything which means that we don't have as many fixtures, because that might mean that we — a small racecourse — cease to exist." Right? So it's existential for them. If you are a small racecourse and you have 20 fixtures a year, and suddenly it's announced instead of having 20 fixtures a year, you're now going to have 10 fixtures a year, basically it means you don't exist anymore. That means as a business, you can't function.

Sorry, Charlie.

So are we looking at a little bit of a FIFA challenge model, in that in the sense where you've just got an imbalance in proportion?

Ascot 出走引发连锁反应

Yes. Yeah. So what happened back in March, which preempted our original discussion on what we call the civil war within racing, was that Ascot Racecourse — the racecourse owned effectively by the King, um, but run for him by a committee that oversees basically — it's run by his majesty's representative at Royal Ascot, Sir Francis Brooke — um, that Ascot had announced suddenly that it was going to leave the racecourse association because it did not believe that the racecourse association was representing the interests of British racing going forward.

Huge row, huge controversy, very brave move, which I absolutely massively applaud to Francis Brooke for overseeing. Fantastic. Well done.

And I speculated, I said the Jockey Club now need to step forward. The Jockey Club now need to get out of their, you know, sort of self-imposed silence of the last 30 to 40 years and they need to step forward.

为什么 Jockey Club 的角色关键

Why? Because — to remind people — the Jockey Club is not just a private members club that used to run British horse racing. It also owns, other than Ascot, a majority of the biggest race courses in the country. It owns Cheltenham. It owns Aintree. It owns Newmarket. It owns Epsom. It owns Sandown Park. It owns Kempton Park. It owns most of the big racetracks in the country. And therefore most of the big races in the country: the Derby, the Guineas, the Grand National, the Cheltenham Gold Cup — all of them, Jockey Club, right?

So effectively they are the ones — and their racecourses and their races — are the ones that are suffering the most from there being too many fixtures, right? Because money that should be being used to give the best possible prize money to the biggest possible races at the biggest possible racecourses is being spread around all of these irrelevant small fixtures that no one cares about.

So —

Okay.

声明本身

The Jockey Club now has stepped forward and said, "Right, that's it. We're out." And I just want to just before we hand over to you — start quizzing me on this — their statement was neither a Belgian Football Federation statement nor a HP HP HP statement. It was a very good statement. It was well thought through in that it was diplomatically put together but carried a punch. Right:

"We have begun discussions with the BHA" — that's the British Horse Racing Authority — "to explore the most appropriate framework for representing the interests of those within the industry who share a commitment to the long-term sustainability and quality of British racing."

Remember that word, quality.

"It is our intention to work with Ascot and other like-minded industry partners to pursue a new vision for racing."

Right. Now this is big. This is really big.

What this really means, when we talk about "like-minded industry partners," what we mean by that are the owners association and the trainers federation and the breeders. That's what we mean, right? So we mean basically the Jockey Club and their racecourses, and Ascot which is overseen by Jockey Club members. So it's the same thing really.

Basically saying: "We're fed up of being chucked in a bucket with the other racecourses. They're a bunch of ass. We're not interested in them. We are now going to basically get together with the big owners, get together with the big trainers, get together with the big breeders, and we're basically going to start our campaign to off all the small courses." That's what we're going to do.

为什么"少即是多"

And is that because in this situation, you talked about 1,500, right, which is an absolutely extraordinary number — as you said, five a day. I mean, that's absolute madness. Is that because this has to be a less-is-more, this has to be a quality-control level at top? You mentioned quality, right? The biggest threat to the industry in this element is having too much crap, too much that doesn't matter. It devalues the broader product. You've got a few key elements here which are hugely valuable, hugely attractive to punters, hugely valuable to the broader industry from a financial perspective of broadcast. I mean, I just try and understand — how big this is, you know, is this shifting power from the top institutions in racing? Are they basically making a stand trying to bring people with them, or are they making a stand going, "No, hang on, we need to be the controlling entity here," and it's like almost more like a land grab for a Jockey Club? Or is it a "We're making our position known and we want you to come with us, but if you don't, we're going to then go and do this anyway"?

交叉重叠的精英网络

Great question. Right.

So behind all these three-letter acronyms — and even just generic things like the Jockey Club and, you know, Ascot and the racehorse owners association and the thoroughbred breeders association and the National Trainers Federation — thing to understand is a lot of people who fundamentally matter in these organizations are the same people, right?

So the biggest owners are also members of the Jockey Club. The biggest breeders are also members of the Jockey Club. Okay. The people who sit on the committee that oversees Ascot on behalf of the King are members of the Jockey Club. So it's all the same people really. All they're saying is: "We're no longer going to be barricaded behind some bloody committee with a bunch of small racecourses telling us what's good for racing. We are now going to work basically amongst ourselves to work out what is best for racing."

BHA 新主席的关键抉择

Now, in the meantime, a new chairman of the British Horse Racing Authority has been appointed. Okay. Now, he's not a well-known person from within the industry. This is not somebody — and it's almost been, it feels to me like he's almost been deliberately chosen because no one really knows who he is, right?

Um, there were other candidates for the job who had been major figures in public life and in racing. So Sir Peter Savill on the one hand — um, famous businessman from the 80s, 90s, and 2000s, who's also a previous head of the British horse racing board. Minette Batters, the former head of the National Farmers Union. You know, these were high-profile candidates for that position. Um, but they chose somebody whose name, I think, is Simon Cox or something like that. His name escapes me because he just doesn't have any kind of profile or background within the industry. Has been chosen to be chairman of the BHA.

Um, now he comes into an interesting situation, which is: does he read the writing on the wall and go and speak with the Jockey Club and Ascot and the various other like-minded — as the Jockey Club puts them — like-minded souls? Or does he try and do the classic thing that happens on committees, which say, "Well, it's very important that we all get in the room together and we all agree — compromise and consensus"? Because if he does that, he's going to fail. Because the Jockey Club have made it very, very clear that that's not where they're headed.

The Jockey Club have basically said, "We've had enough of all that committee stuff. We've had enough of all the consensus. We are now going to lead a conversation with the other groups and entities and people who we think matter in horse racing, and we are going to drive that forward, and that is what is going to happen now."

Um, and it's a long overdue conversation. But fundamentally, what it comes down to is: if at any point, rather like UEFA and FIFA, if at any point the Jockey Club really decided to throw its toys out the pram, right, no one could stop it. Because it controls such a big proportion of the revenues of racing that fundamentally you couldn't really control it. There's no other entity within the sport that can control it because its revenues are so much bigger.

I think we've said before that ARC, which owns all those small courses — that their total revenues, I think, are something like 140 million a year, something like that.

Yeah.

For their entire group, right? But Ascot's revenues as one course are higher than that, right? And that's just Ascot, before you get on to Cheltenham — even bigger, right — even bigger, etc.

两个根本问题：钱和注意力

So what we're talking about here is the big powers within racing saying, "That's enough. These committees don't work. We're not going to be blocked by the RCA anymore. We're not going to work that way. We are now going to work out how many fixtures there should be."

So just to your point, Charlie, is to cap this conversation: there are two problems to having as many fixtures as there currently are.

  1. One of those problems is that the sport cannot afford it. Right? So the total amount of betting levy that we receive in effectively tax from the bookmakers is not sufficient to fund that number of fixtures.
  2. The second problem — which you actually alluded to, which sometimes I think people in racing don't fully understand um perhaps as you do — is you can't expect the sporting public to keep focus and concentration on a narrative surrounding a sport when they're being asked to look at 1,500 fixtures. It's just totally impossible. It's implausible.

Just like — even if you're absolutely devoted to the sport and really care about it and it's your main love in life, you are not going to be able to pay attention to 1,500 fixtures every season. And once you are not paying attention to all of them, then inevitably you start to say, "Well, what's the point of trying at all?" Because if I can't see the whole picture, then there's no point in me really paying attention to the whole lot.

NBA 类比

And I think we see this a little bit sometimes with the basketball season in America, when there just so many fixtures in the main season that a lot of even quite committed basketball fans go, "Do you know what? I'm just going to wait until the playoffs. I'm just not interested. I can't follow this. This is just totally mind-boggling — the amount of matches I'm being expected to watch."

So I think this is a watershed moment. It's a decision that will not have been come to lightly. I'm absolutely delighted that they have come to that decision. And I cannot believe, having come to that decision, that the Jockey Club is now going to agree to some sort of committee structure being put back in again. They're going to want to see a fully independent British Horse Racing Authority board, and they are going to want to control the agenda of that independent British Horse Racing Authority board basically by saying, "This is the direction you need to be going in."

Fantastic. As usual, I sit here and I just sit back and I learn. It's great. I'm sure everyone else does as well. The passion, Charlie. The passion.

And we'll give you the credit, right? You lead the conversation. You brought this up. I was joking before when I, you know, I didn't want to say we'll find the clip and make sure the team play. I can't just play clips of you saying Tottenham will forever be a top six side. I can't just do it. We'll make sure to give you credit where credit's due. Um, but yeah. Yeah. Well, let's see. Maybe they'll get back there.

收尾与预告

Um, but yeah, that's — it's a serious week. There is a huge amount there. We're going to go and talk about even another huge thing that's happened, which was the — should we say what many people believe is a very light punishment that was given to Chelsea for 74 breaches of regulation. And then also look at the more broader challenge of regulation in football and what accurate punishment should really be. So we're going to go and do that on Substack now. If you want to come and join us for that, that'd be fantastic. But otherwise, we will see you next week and I hope there is plenty in there for you to get on board with and speak to us about.

So, huge thank you from Cornwall, Charlie. Appreciate you tapping in for the grind and we'll see you next week.

Let's do more. Let's get over to Substack and keep going, Chaz.

Fantastic. See you next week, guys.

## 一、Infantino 不是病，而是症状——FIFA 的"贫困选民陷阱"
节目里最反直觉的洞见不是"Infantino 该下台"，而是：**换谁上来都会变成下一个 Infantino**。原因是一个纯粹的数学结构——211 个成员国里约 90 个是非洲和加勒比小协会，年收入只有 500–600 万美元，而英足总的年收入是 6 亿英镑。也就是说，**FIFA 主席只需要用"英足总的零头"就能锁定连任所需的选票**。这意味着任何理性的主席，为了争取第二个任期，都必然会走上"疯狂搞钱—收买小协会—再搞更疯狂的钱"的螺旋。
这里有一个惊人的跨领域连接：**这与美国州际参议院制度、欧盟理事会一国一票、甚至 Web3 DAO 中"鲸鱼 vs 长尾"投票的失败案例，是同一种病**——当"票权分布"和"价值贡献分布"严重错位时，制度会自动产生腐败激励，而不需要腐败的人。Infantino 只是恰好站在了这个数学结构的输出端。
## 二、West Ham 的"毒丸条款"揭示了足球俱乐部估值的一个隐秘断层
Kretinsky 用一个绝妙的"卖 2.5% 给朋友"的操作绕开了 drag-alo

item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1466期】软件集体逆袭！大科技的违约风险！大非农展望✨20260806#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"关注度悖论"：涨得最凶的，恰恰是被冷落的

小涛提到亚马逊和微软在上周财报后出现罕见的大幅上涨，条件是"市场仓位不在上面、关注度不在上面"。这其实揭示了一个反直觉的流动性势能定律——在情绪驱动的市场里，被冷落的资产储存着最大的爆发势能。

这与物理学里的"位能"惊人相似：一个物体被抬得越高（关注度越高、仓位越拥挤），它继续上升需要的能量越大；反之，被踩在地上的资产，只需要一个催化剂就能释放巨大动能。大科技今年 YTD 跑输标普500 这个"丢脸"的数据，反而成了它们上周暴涨的燃料。

跨领域连接：这和社会心理学里的"逆向偏好选择"、甚至相亲市场里"太受欢迎反而没人敢追"是同一个机制——共识本身会稀释回报。

二、Memory 的"薛定谔式估值"：投资它，却不信它

这期最出人意料的观察藏在那家机构对 SK Square 的持仓逻辑里——"我买它，但我不认为它能摆脱周期"。这是一种极其罕见的中间态思维：

  • 大多数投资者要么信"这次不一样"（PE 扩张派）
  • 要么信"周期终究会均值回归"（做空派）
  • 而这家机构选择了第三条路：赌 EPS 翻倍，不赌 PE 扩张

这背后其实是一种"降低期待的高级投资学"。跨领域看，这非常像佛家的"无所住而生其心"——持有但不执着于估值重估，反而把结果的确定性大大提升。当你不再期待奇迹，奇迹反而更容易发生，因为你的下行风险被自己的悲观预期锁死了。

更深一层：这也解释了为什么很多"神预测"的机构，其实是靠放弃某一维度的想象力换来另一维度的清晰度。

三、AI 破坏软件的"证伪困境"：一个已经死了两年的故事，为什么还在讲？

小涛点出关键——"AI 会破坏软件"这个叙事已经跑了两年，但从 Figma、Atlassian、Unity 到微软的财报，没有一份实证支持它。为什么市场还在交易一个没被验证的故事？

这里有一个隐藏的系统性真相：叙事的持久性与其被证伪的难度成正比，而与其真实性无关。AI 破坏软件是一个"随时可能发生但永远无法完全证伪"的故事——就像"明天可能地震"，你永远无法反驳它。

跨领域连接：这与流行病学里的"长尾恐慌"、宗教里的"末日预言"、甚至加密货币的"银行崩溃论"是同构的——开放式威胁比封闭式威胁更能长期压制估值。

更意外的观察：Figma 财报里那个"科技公司内部工程师用 Figma 席位超过了设计师"的细节，其实揭示了一个反向叙事——AI 不是在削减软件的用户基数，而是在模糊职业边界，扩大软件的可触达人群。工程师做设计、设计师写代码、产品经理调 prompt——AI 不是杀手，而是"职业穿透剂"，它让软件的 TAM（潜在市场规模）反而变大了。这个观点如果成立，那"AI 破坏软件"这个两年叙事的方向可能从一开始就错了——AI 不是破坏软件，而是让每一款软件都变成"泛用型工具"。

一个额外的连接：CDS 图表的"因果幻觉"

小涛拆解 CDS 上升与股价下跌的"相关而非因果"，这其实是统计学里的经典陷阱在金融社交媒体上的复现。有意思的是，社交媒体的传播机制天然偏爱"因果叙事"（因为好懂、好转发），所以任何相关性都会被算法自动"升级"成因果——这不是投资者的问题，是平台的信息物理学决定的。所以下一次再看到某张"骇人听闻"的图，先问一句：这是因果，还是我们大脑被算法投喂后的幻觉？

📝 转录文本

开场与今日议程

各位观众大家好，欢迎来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。

首先再次恭喜大家，昨天我们一起在留言区里边再次战胜了机器人。你还别说，真的是因为大家的留言，我没有看到机器人。以前每天起码要删50条到60条，甚至于100多条。昨天的视频下面有一条留言非常的有意思，他说：也许这个 AI 机器人感受到了博主的留言区有一些孤单、有一些孤零零的，所以送了一些温暖，给了一些机器人的留言。有可能是这种情况。好吗，今天我就不给大家压力了，有时间的话留个言，这样真的可以对于消灭机器人这一块有些帮助的。

今天我们聊什么？

  • 首先我们看一下市场的一个参与度，因为好像有一段时间没有和大家更新了；
  • 然后我们聊一下周五将要公布的大非农数据，去看一下彭博他们的这个预期；
  • 再接下去一个话题，今天我和一家机构（我最喜欢的一家机构）做了第二季度的这个 review，看一下他们对于当下市场的这个看法；
  • 前两周吧，大家在社交媒体上可能看到 CDS 那张图——信用违约掉期。大科技的信用违约掉期上升的幅度非常的大，在一个非常高的一个位置，是不是代表接下去大科技要出现回调？今天我拿了另外一张非常类似的图出来和大家分享一下，看一下现在这些大科技的那些信用风险到底有多高；
  • 最后我们去看一下这两天发布财报的软件公司都非常的好，基本上再次验证了 AI 对于这些软件公司到底有没有破坏。起码 so far，到现在为止，这个观点或者市场所交易的这个逻辑线一直都没有被证实。

好吗，那我就废话不多说了，直接开始。在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发。

一、市场参与度：中性为主，罗素与标普偏乐观

过去这一段时间，过去一周吧，市场反弹的幅度比较的大，三大指数都走得非常的好，但其实市场的参与度并没有大家想象的那么的乐观。

  • 纳指：20日和50日均线分别在 52% 和 47%，处在一个非常中性的一个位置；包括100日均线、200日均线，43、100日在46，都处在一个非常中性的位置。所以现在纳指的参与度仍然是在一个中性的位置，没有到非常的乐观。
  • 罗素2000：相对是中性偏乐观了一些，20日和50均线分别在 60%。
  • 标普500：也是相对在中性偏乐观的位置，分别在 63% 和 64%。

所以标普和罗素中性偏乐观，纳指还是处在一个非常中性的位置。

二、周五大非农预期

周五的早上 8:30 美东时间将会公布 7 月份的大非农数据。

  • 市场预期：8 万人
  • 彭博 Anna Wang 团队的预期：65,000 人
  • 失业率：市场预期 4.2%，彭博预期 4.3%（比市场稍微要高一些）

那我个人的看法是，现在的美联储其实对于劳动力市场这一块没有那么的担心，无论最终明天的失业率是 4.2 也好，还是 4.3 也好，我并不认为会改变美联储的一些态度。

当然，如果大非农数据好于市场的预期，你说美债的收益率稍微往上涨个两三个基点合不合理？那一定会发生这种情况。那反过来也是一样，如果失业率比市场预期要高，美债的收益率稍微往下跌一些合不合理？也合理。失业率如果比市场的预期要高，那自然 9 月份加息的这个概率就会出现下降。

但总体来说，以当下美联储的这个重心这个角度去看，这组数据相对没有那么的重要，比起这组数据更加重要的一定是 CPI 数据、PPI 数据。

三、机构二季度 Review 的三点 Takeaway

接下去我们来看一下今天我和一家机构做完 review 之后的一些 takeaway。首先这家机构我非常喜欢，是我能接触到的我最喜欢的一家机构，他们对于整个市场节奏上的一个把握，我认为非常的好。虽然它是一个 Fundamental——就是从下到上的这种投资方式，从个股这个角度去出发——但是对于情绪面的把握和掌控，我认为非常的好。

1. 从硬件转仓到大科技

他们在第二季度的时候，从硬件这边转了一些仓位去大科技。因为他们认为就还是停留在 AI 这块，但是相对会保守一些，并且大科技并没有受到市场的这个喜好。

其实和我前段时间和大家分享的一个逻辑是一样的：市场不可能单纯地去喜欢这些硬件公司而不去喜欢这些大科技。因为这些硬件公司，你想在一个月之前我们讨论是什么？讨论的美光的这个 PE 能不能去到 15 倍、能不能去到 20 倍，美光是不是不再是一个周期股？那我说过，如果美光不再是一个周期股，你起码要保证这些大科技它的 AI 这一块的投资是有回报的。大科技这边如果投资没有回报的话，不可能这些硬件板块出现一个 15 倍、20 倍这种 PE，不可能。

那么因为现在这些硬件板块的前金主爸爸是谁？就是这些大科技。所以大科技才是底层落地最重要的一个环节。只要大科技有问题，剩下整个产业链所有的硬件——包括芯片，包括芯片最上端的台积电、阿斯麦——都会有问题。

所以这家基金，他们在第二季度的时候转了一些仓位去大科技，然后在硬件这一块做了一些止盈。那主要是硬件板块走得比较的好。那我个人其实在英特尔上面，在 5 月份和 6 月份也都进行了一个止盈。当然我当时并不知道，因为我和他们做 review 的时候，我们你像八月初才做二季度这个 review，所以他们季度中间的这个操作我们是并不知道的。

所以他们换仓的目的： - 第一点：为了止盈； - 第二点：转去一些市场关注度不高的这些大科技。

其实是这样，到现在为止，YTD 大科技的这个走势都没有标普 500 要好，更别谈和芯片板块去做对比了。所以某种程度也造就了为什么上一周发布完财报之后，亚马逊和微软都出现了那么大的一个涨幅。一般个股出现那么大——大科技出现那么大涨幅是很少见。那一般出现那么大的涨幅，必须要匹配的这个条件什么？条件一定是市场的仓位不在上面，市场的关注度不在上面，才有可能会出现这种结果。这是第一点。

2. SK Square 与 Memory：投资它，但不认为它能摆脱周期

然后第二点，那这家基金本身，他们自己有不少的一些 SK Square。那 SK Square 其实类似于——其实就是投 SK Hynix 三星海力士，只是 SK Square 他们里边百分之二十——三星海力士百分之二十的控股是 SK Square。但 SK Square 和三星海力士的话，中间其实有一个 discount，有一个 discount 在那边。

然后就他们首先持有这个标的本身，就他们也看好整个 memory。但是非常有意思，他们并不认为整个 memory 会走出一个周期行业，他们认为 memory 仍然是一个周期行业。只是这一轮的一个周期比很多人想象的要长，所以他们现在仍然持有 SK Square。同时加上这些公司现在在扩产能上保持这个纪律，那不会去疯狂的扩产能，也使得这个周期会比以前的周期要长，但是他们并不认为整个 Memory 会走出以前的这种周期行业。

所以这背后代表什么？投资了这个标的，却不认为 Memory 能够走出这个周期行情。这背后代表的就是他们不期待有一个 PE 的一个扩张。那现在三星海力士是 PE Forward PE 的话是 6 倍，他们认为持续保持在 6 倍，那未来价格的这个上涨来自于哪里？来自于 EPS 这个增速、EPS 这个上涨。因为他们认为这些公司接下去，他用的词是 print money——print money，印钱。他们认为这些公司接下去还会非常非常的赚钱，但是并不期待它 PE 估值上有一个扩张。

所以就很简单，就如果说明年它 EPS 这个体量可以翻一倍，那即使 PE 不涨的这个情况下，股价也可以翻一倍。一个标的如果一年翻一倍的话，你还不满足吗？

那过去这段时间，市场一直在讨论的是 Memory 到底是不是一个周期行业。你会发现很多问题，它不一定一定非要争出一个黑或者白，有时候会有一个中间那个答案。那中间那个答案就是：我投资 Memory，但是我不认为它能够摆脱一个周期行业，但我的期待就会非常的理性。那么我的期待是 PE 不会扩张，但是它 EPS 的增速、EPS 这个体量的增速还会非常的快。

3. 分散但仍看好 AI：紧盯资本开支与行业动向

然后第三点，也是我前段时间其实和大家分享过——就重仓 AI 的这个同事，他们现在仍然持有很多和 AI 相关的一些标的，只是没有以前那么的激进。那么硬件稍微减了一些，然后就加了一些大科技。那在持有 AI 的这个同时，分散一些标的，去了一些非 AI 的标的。那等于是对自己整体的一个投资组合通过这些非 AI 的标的去控制。

与此同时，就仍然看好 AI，但是仓位的话比以前稍微分散一些。与此同时，非常紧密地去关注大科技的资本开支和整个行业动向。

其实这也是我一直强调的：我们看好 AI，然后你可以投资 AI，但是没有必要像现在，就声音非常的极端——要不就是 AI 有泡沫，要不就是看好未来的 AI 五年十年都非常的好。不可能五年十年都非常的好，在 one point、在未来某个时间点，市场一定会投资过度。

那作为一个投资者，我认为我们需要做的是：就除非我们今天不投 AI，我们不投一些标的，直接去投指数，那没有关系。但只要今天我们投个股，我们去投 AI，那就必须要去关注整个行业发展的这个方向。稍微有任何一些风吹草动，或者我们看到任何的一些风险，就要去思考接下去是不是要进行仓位上的一些调整。所以时刻去关注这一个行业，这是我们必须要做的，而且整个市场现在的一个进展和发展非常的快。那么希望这一类的分享对大家有帮助。

四、大科技 CDS / 利差图：相关不等于因果

然后我们来看下面一张图。这张图是亚马逊债券的一个利差，它是在 21 年发行的一个 10 年期的债券，所以我们看到 21 年发行 10 年期，就是 31 年到期嘛。

那这张图里，白色这条线是利差。利差其实和前段时间社交媒体上聊的比较多的 CDS（信用违约掉期）的这一个指数非常的类似，就基本上你会看到利差出现上升，CDS 一定会出现上升。

在社交媒体上，我们只会看到这一类的图，就是 CDS 上升的幅度非常的快，速度非常的快。所以你基本上会看到图里白色这条线的后半段，从 26 年开始，你看白色这条线一直上升，感觉非常的恐怖——这些大科技是不是会有一些债务上的一些问题？

但其实你把这个时间线放长的话，我只放到 2021 年，你会发现，起码在过去 5 年的时间里边，有三次都比现在要高：

  • 第一次是 2022 年；
  • 第二次是 2024 年 8 月份，那个是那时候什么？Carry trade 的这个平仓。那 Carry trade 的平仓，你想当时和这些大科技基本面有任何的关系吗？和他们的信用有任何的关系吗？其实是没有关系的。只是单纯的日本这些投资者，他们因为 carry trade 的平仓，因为日元的这个涨，因为日元涨然后导致他们 carry trade 的平仓，所以使得科技股的价格下跌，所以使得这些利差出现上升。

所以利差出现上升——这是我一直一再强调的：利差上升、CDS 上升，它并不会因为利差的上升、CDS 的上升导致股价下跌，而是我们看到利差上升的同时、CDS 上升的同时，股价会下跌。这两者之间是一个相关性，不是一个因果关系。

那明显是一个宏观事件所导致利差的上升、CDS 上升，同时股价的下跌，那和它的公司本身的基本面是没有关系的。所以这就是我想把这些东西给区分开来的一个原因。

然后另外一个就是 2025 年，当时是一个关税，那关税导致股价的一个下跌、导致它利差的一个上升。就关税本身对于亚马逊的基本面或者它的债务有任何的影响吗？其实这个影响是不大的。

那再上一次比现在水平还要高的就是整个 2022 年了。2022 年几乎所有的时间都比现在这个利差要高。那如果从债务这个角度去看，其实在 2022 年亚马逊所承担的这个债务体量比现在要低很多了。那为什么当时的这一个利差比现在要高呢？就是因为整个 2022 年是在一个加息周期里面，那在加息周期里面，普遍行业的这些利差都会出现上升，相对整个行业的风险都会出现上升，所以亚马逊的这个利差也出现上升。

所以我不希望接下去如果我们再看到 CDS 这个指数上升或者利差上升，就代表这些大科技有些基本面的一些问题——没有这个问题。你把时间线拉长，24 年、25 年、22 年，当时的一个利差都比现在要高，而且高了很多。

五、软件财报：AI"破坏软件"的叙事还没被证实

最后我们来聊两家软件公司。

1. Figma：客户留存稳定 90%，AI 让软件"出圈"

第一家公司 Figma。那 Figma 先来看一下数据——设计公司，市场认为 AI 会破坏这家公司。

  • 营收比市场预期高了 5%
  • EPS 增速体量比市场预期高了将近 100%（当然，也是因为他们的调整之后的利润相对体量会小一些：1800 万，那最后的数据 3600 万）

所以比市场预期好的幅度非常的大。但是幅度还是归幅度，而且这个 EPS 并没有任何的问题——就确实比市场预期翻了将近一倍。

我们来看一些财报会议里边的内容：

  • 2/3 的客户在续约时都会增加 full seat（seat 就是席位了）；
  • 总体的 retention 稳定在 90%。

那所以即使现在有了 AI，AI 所创的这些工具本身现在还没有——就起码没有看到任何的现象破坏 Figma 现在的客户。因为他们现在客户的 retention 保留率仍然在 90%，和以前稳定在 90%。

另外他们这边举了一个例子，他说一家科技公司的客户，他们现在客户本身内部工程师用 Figma 的这个席位已经超过了设计师。说明什么问题？就说明 Figma 因为现在有了 AI 之后，它出圈了。什么叫出圈了？就是类似于有了 AI 之后，原来做产品的人现在会写 code 了，那原来写 code 的人现在可以去做设计。

类似于以前我和大家举过 Adobe 的这个例子，他们把最简单的功能比如加到 OpenAI 里边，那原本不是设计师，现在用了 OpenAI 然后他们体验了 Adobe 的这些简单的设计功能之后，是有可能从一个以前不是设计师变成了去做设计师的一些事情。那因为现在的 AI 给他们提供了这个场景和工具，也就是因为现在有了这些 AI 平台、有了这些分发渠道之后，使得你的这些 user base、使得你的使用者的这个广度其实比以前要大很多了。那以前只是因为做设计的才会来接触你这些软件，现在即使不做设计的，因为你这些软件也变得非常容易去使用，整个背后的使用人群的这个基数明显扩大。这第二点。

第三点，其实市场最担心的就是收费模式的改变。那从原来的单纯的席位制，现在变成了 AI 额度的一个附加订阅，在这个基础上还会有一个 pay-as-you-go。AI 额度的附加订阅就等于是——和你手机一样的，手机要不就是买个套餐，或者说你是使用了多少流量你就付多少钱，那么两种套餐都有。那这都是和 AI 是相关的，而且这后面的两种收费都是建立在席位制的基础之上。

刚刚过去的这个季度是他们第一次打开了新的这种收费方式，这个季度最后的结果毛利润比上一个季度提高了 2.5%。

而最近这段时间我们所聊到的就开源和闭源的选择——因为我们聊到开源模型，如果接下去能力上去之后（因为开源模型相对会便宜一些嘛），开源模型能力上去之后，有没有可能是利好于这些基建 infrastructure，就像 Hyper Scaler；或者说有没有可能利好这些软件公司？因为软件公司的成本会下降。对软件公司来说，他们调用这些闭源模型的 API 就是他们的成本，那如果开源进来之后成本下降，那对于这些软件公司，他们的成本也下降。

但是到现在，其实在 Figma 身上还不是体现的那么明显，因为他们多数用的都是美国的这些开源模型。所以我认为接下去，从他们内部来说，还有一个降本的空间在那边，就是他们如果使用一些开源模型，有可能可以使得他们在 AI 这一块算力上支出的这个成本还能够进一步地下降，使得他们的毛利润可能还会有扩张的这个空间在那边。

然后接下去一点，在他们给下一个财年做指引的时候，其实并没有把他们现在在测试的一些产品——因为测试的产品上线之后对于营收就会有贡献——这些测试的产品还没有计入到营收的预期里边。所以非常有可能在整个 2027 财年，他们接下去在营收这一块，大概率的情况下会比市场的预期要高。

那是不是一切的东西都变得非常的好，或者完全就是可以去证伪 AI 可以破坏软件的这个故事线呢？还没有到那么的夸张。因为现在 AI 这一块的利润还不是非常的清楚。就举个例子：他们原有在没有 AI 之前，他们的业务利润率、毛利润在 90%，那现在有了 AI 之后，毛利润在 85%。这背后是什么情况？

这背后的情况是：你原本的席位制就很简单，你软件的毛利润可以非常的高。但是现在你加入了 AI 之后，你的成本是什么？你的成本是一些大模型的 API，你的成本是一些算力。但是你的这些算力本身，假设你的成本是 10 块钱，你没有办法卖 100 块钱然后你赚 90 块钱——成本 10 块钱、卖 100 块钱赚 90 块钱，这是他们原有的业务，所以毛利润 90% 嘛。但现在，比如说你额外的成本还是 10 块钱，你没有办法卖 90，你可能只能卖 85、卖 84，那所以你的毛利润就从原来的 90% 降到了现在的 85%，甚至于会更低。等于你新加入了这一部分 AI 的业务，而新加入的这一部分 AI 的业务只要它的毛利润没有达到 90%，就会对你原本的业务的这个毛利润进行一部分的一个冲击，稍微往下拉一些。

但是最终如果稳定下来之后，他们整个的软件毛利润还是可以保持在 80% 至 85% 左右，我认为是完全可以接受的。

那讲到毛利润，我们看一下 2025 年的第二季度，当时的毛利润是 90%，刚刚过去这个季度 85%，那市场预期接下去的两个季度在 81% 左右。其实市场这边是低估了，因为管理层所给出的运营利润率是在 9% 以上了，那现在市场预期是 5.57%。那么所以明显市场是低估了 Figma 他们的毛利润率和他们的运营利润率。

2. Atlassian (TEAM)：AI 反而是加速器

然后另外一家公司，另外一家软件公司 Atlassian，股票代码是 TEAM（T-E-A-M），是周四盘后发布财报。我现在看的话，盘后上涨了 30% 多。

为什么上涨了 30% 多？因为在他们的这一次财报里面，你几乎看不到任何 AI 对于他们的负面影响，反而 AI 对于他们是一个加速。

举一些例子，你看一下他们 Cloud 这一块营收的一个增速：

  • 2025 年的第一季度：31%
  • 接下去：29.6%（同比增速，每一个季度同比增速）
  • 25 点几，反而是 2025 年的 Q3 稍微放缓了一些：25.23%
  • 接下去：25.71%、25.92%、26%、28.62%
  • 刚刚过去这个季度：30.8%

然后在这个基础上，它的毛利润：

  • 2025 年的第一季度：84%
  • 刚刚过去这个季度：89%

的确，AI 对于部分的一些软件公司——相对比较小众的或者针对性非常强的这些软件公司——是会有些影响。那但是这个季度的财报，我们看到现在为止，包括今天盘后还是盘前发布财报的 Unity 也是一样——从微软到 Figma 的财报（虽然 Figma 财报发布完之后出现下跌，但是从财报本身去看的话，你看不出任何的问题，只是就起码是比市场的这个担心要好很多），就是 AI 对于 Figma 的这个破坏或者对于 Figma 的这个负面的影响。然后到了今天周四盘后的 TEAM (Atlassian)，再到 Unity，你可以看到，就市场对于 AI 对于软件所造成的这个破坏，这个观点本身到现在都没有被证实。

已经——这个观点本身已经两年了，我觉得这也说明了一点：就是股价已经下跌了两年，软件板块也被杀跌了两年，市场情绪面也低迷了两年，但是最终我认为市场还是会回归到理智。

什么是理智？就是这些公司：

  • 毛利润有没有受到影响
  • 营收的增速有没有受到影响
  • 最重要的是他们的现金流有没有受到影响

那如果这三样东西都没有受到影响的话，市场不可能把他们的估值打压在一个非常低的位置非常长的时间。

所以这时候作为一个投资者来说，我们要做到两点：

  1. 先不被市场的情绪面或者故事线带着去走；
  2. 有自己独立的思考——我们必须要自己去判断，AI 肯定是不可能造成所有的软件公司都是一个破坏，也不可能对于所有的软件公司都是一个利好。我们就得去区分，找出一些一个或者两个我们认为不会被 AI 受到破坏，甚至于 AI 对于他们来说是一个利好的公司。

六、活动环节

最后是我们今天的活动环节。

  • 富途牛牛美国市场：开户且入金最高可以获得价值 1000 美金英伟达的赠股。最近这段时间英伟达也走得相对会强势一些，那主要是因为 SpaceX 那天财报里面老马说到他接下来要造非常多数据中心，然后只和英伟达合作，那所以英伟达这两天相对会强一些。闲置资金这一块，美国市场最高年化 8.1% 的回报。
  • 加拿大市场：现在正在搞一个我们这个频道的独家活动、独家福利了——开户且入金最高可以获得抽取 100 只免费个股的这个机会，直接抽到手软。闲置资金最高年化 6% 这个回报，然后前 30 天零佣金、免佣金交易。

好吧，大家如果感兴趣的话，在置顶的留言里面可以找到开户的链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。
