item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：核能的失败不是技术问题，而是"产品经理"缺席
大多数人以为核电衰落是因为切尔诺贝利、三里岛这类安全事故，或者是环保运动的政治阻力。但视频里 Radiant 创始人给出了一个近乎商业异端的诊断——**"我们没有听客户的话"**。
这是极其罕见的框架：把核能行业当作一个"失去 PMF（产品市场契合）"的失败产品来看待，而不是一个被政治绞杀的受害者。爱达荷国家实验室 21 年造了 52 座反应堆，1977 年之后归零——不是因为造不出来，而是因为造出来的东西**没人想买**。客户想要的是"像柴油发电机一样插上就用、用完拉走"的东西，而行业给的是"挖个大坑、绑定一辈子的辐射场地"。
这暗示了一个更普遍的规律：**任何一个技术在其"英雄时代"（1950-60 年代）完成规模化后，如果没有经历"消费化转型"，就会被工程师式的自我优化困死。** 航空、大型机、卫星都走过类似的死胡同。
## 二、跨领域连接：Kaleidos 反应堆 = SpaceX 的第二次"可回收"革命
这里藏着一个几乎没人明说的类比线索——Doug 在 SpaceX 干了 12 年。Space

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 黃金教父：美國兆元債務，但政府還在印鈔！各國猛買黃金！那比特幣呢？【邦妮區塊鏈】David Tait
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的黄金牛市：这不是"避险"，而是集体对财政悖论的静默投票

多数人把黄金上涨归因于战争、关税、利率波动——但 David Tait 说了一句极其反直觉的话：这些都是"过场"。真正驱动金价从 1500 涨到 5000 的，是全球对"债务螺旋不可逆"的集体潜意识。

这里有一个被忽视的结构性观察：黄金已经不再是"恐慌指标"，而变成了一种主权信用的做空工具。当亚洲央行悄悄囤金时，他们不是在对冲某场具体危机，而是在对"美元作为记账单位的合法性"投下渐进的不信任票。Liberation Day 那一刻美债收益率曲线整体跳升——不是陡峭化，而是"平行上移"——那才是 Bessant 慌张冲出来喊 calm 的真正原因：市场第一次系统性怀疑美国这个机构本身。

二、跨领域连接：登山者的"零线以下"心智，与他对比特币归零的判断，是同一种认知结构

这段访谈最精妙的地方在于——David 说自己一生活在"情绪零线以下"，因为童年创伤让他对生死漠然，所以在高盛能承担别人不敢承担的风险；而正是这种"看过真正的坏"的心智结构，让他能在瑞信董事会上冷眼看着 20 个投行高管像无头鸡一样乱撞。

这里藏着一个惊人的认知一致性：他判断比特币归零、判断黄金必涨、判断主权债务终将崩溃——用的都是同一种"从最坏情境倒推"的思维模式。他不是在做金融分析，他是在做存续性分析（survivorship analysis）。黄金活了 5000 年，法币活了 50 年，比特币活了 15 年——在他的"生存本能"框架里，时间深度就是价值本身。这解释了为什么他对 CZ 的"你无法验证金条真假"的挑战，回应得如此不慌不忙：可验证性是工程问题，可存续性是本体问题。他更看重后者。

三、最反直觉的一击：World Gold Council 正在悄悄"比特币化"黄金——而这可能是黄金市场未来十年最大的变量

大多数观众听完访谈会记住"金价 5000""比特币归零""登珠峰五次"这些话题——但真正被埋没的核弹是"Gold as a Service"平台。

想想这件事有多讽刺：一个全球黄金采矿业的代言机构，跑到 Consensus 加密大会来，宣布他们要用自己的钱建一个"黄金界的 App Store"，让任何人都能低成本发行黄金稳定币、黄金抵押代币、黄金赎回凭证。这在结构上意味着什么？

跨领域连接：这本质上是把"苹果开放硬件+闭源系统"的商业模式，套用到了物理商品市场。WGC 在做的事，等价于当年 Visa 对信用卡、SWIFT 对跨境支付、ARM 对芯片指令集——它想成为黄金数字化的底层协议层。如果成功，那些今天看似敌对的 Paxos、Tether、JPM 黄金代币，未来都可能变成运行在 WGC 协议上的"应用"。

而更深一层的洞察：David 承认现有的黄金稳定币"是场灾难"——只有几十亿美元 AUM。他没说出口的言外之意是——黄金一直没能真正金融数字化，反倒让比特币抢占了"数字稀缺资产"的心智生态位。现在 WGC 反攻的方式，不是否定加密，而是吸收加密的技术架构来武装黄金。所以他说"如果你持黄金就该持比特币"——这不是外交辞令，这是战略投降与技术收编的混合体。

未来最讽刺的场景可能是：十年后最大的"稳定币"，是一枚运行在区块链上的黄金代币。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个大胆的预言

My personal opinion on Bitcoin is that it's going to go to zero because it—

主持人： What would persuade you to change your mind on the Bitcoin to zero view?

David Tait： It's interesting you ask because people in the know are very scared of that point coming. Those people who think that it is an inert useless piece of metal are valuing it under the terms you would equity or a stock. You are missing the three, four, five billion people out there who think the opposite, and that's why I think it goes up.

黄金上涨的真正驱动力

I don't believe gold has really been driven by wars, interest rates and tariffs and things like that, which have been transitory. There have been small movements when those things have happened. If you look at the most consistent thing that has run through the gold rally, it has been an ever-increasing fear that the US and other governments are adding to the debt, and at some point that will become unsustainable. Even Asian central banks have been buying it.

US is about to go through a trillion dollars worth of annual debt repayment. It's enormous. That cost does reach a point where it runs away, and then it becomes quite a terrifying scenario.

"地堡时刻"：债务危机的终极场景

How do you solve that? It's the bunker moment. Everybody knows there's a crunch day.

主持人： Is it likely to have a run by the bond markets on it?

David Tait： Yes, absolutely. I don't want that to happen. I don't want it to happen anywhere. But there are many countries across Europe that are highly indebted. And frankly, you know, the ECB — there isn't enough money to bail out one or two of the larger bigger countries. They're all in the same situation. They've got lousy demographics, large number of non-producing people. They've got very low levels of growth and productivity. And the only thing they keep resorting to is printing presses.

珠峰五次与"零线以下"的人生

主持人： You've climbed Mount Everest five times.

David Tait： I live below the zero line because of what happened to me as a child. Mentally, shall we say, emotionally, or happiness has always been below the line. And I don't like climbing.

主持人： You don't like climbing?

David Tait： Your past life really does flash in front of your eyes in a few seconds. It does.

人生哲学：跳下去，别担心落点

Don't worry about where you land. Life is short. You can achieve things. You've got to be brave. You've got to have the confidence to take these chances.

When I was at Credit Suisse, I was in a board meeting one day. Suddenly the CEO came charging in and he said, "Uh, we just had our capital cut by 50%, the IB capital, one in one go." And there were 20 people around the table and every one of them were like headless chickens. There was papers going everywhere and there were sweaty existential looks. And I remember sitting there looking at them and thinking: you guys got no idea what bad is.

正式访谈开场

I'm pleased to welcome to the show here at Consensus Miami, David Tait, CEO of the World Gold Council. The World Gold Council is renowned for a number of important facets in the financial markets, among which they are one of the inventors of the GLD ETF, one of the largest ETFs in the world with $200 billion of assets under management and the largest gold ETF.

We'll be getting his view on not just gold but the entire world order — what is next for the global economy and why we should pay attention as investors.

主持人 David Lin： Welcome to the show David. David Tait： Thanks for having me. 主持人 Bonnie Chang： Bonnie Chang.

$1,500 到 $5,000：世界发生了什么？

主持人： How is the world different today at a $5,000 gold regime than it was 5 years ago when it was at $1,500?

David Tait： I think the difference between $1,500 and $5,000 is accounted for by the realization that we're in a situation where our debts keep growing across the world. Public and private debts, sovereign debt continues to grow.

I don't believe gold has really been driven by wars, interest rates, and tariffs — things which have been transitory. There have been small movements when those things have happened, but if you look at the most consistent thing that has run through the gold rally, it has been an ever-increasing fear that the US and other governments are adding to their debt, and at some point that will become unsustainable.

Liberation Day：美元信任的裂缝

You may remember that when Mr. Trump announced his Liberation Day tariffs, all markets declined at the same time. There was this point at which the US yield curve, instead of steepening which it normally does, it jumped as a whole. And that's the point I believe Mr. Bessent stepped in and said "calm, calm, calm" — because if the US yield curve does jump as a whole because of lack of trust in the US dollar, US would find it very very difficult to fund its debts going forward.

That was when everything had to calm down a bit. I believe that's the main driver of the gold price because people are far more savvier than they were. Even Asian central banks have been buying it for those reasons. That's what I believe. The rest comes and goes — wars come, wars go — and it sounds crass but it's true.

我们为什么还没进入"地堡"？

主持人： Three or four or five years ago when I first started covering the commodity space, I remember asking analysts and economists what the world would look like if gold were to reach $5,000 within 3 to 5 years. The answer was almost unanimously that we would be probably talking about this in the context of some catastrophe, with the extreme example being we would be in a bunker having this conversation. To what extent is this analysis right and to what extent is it wrong?

David Tait： We're not in a bunker today because — very much personal view — the fact that we haven't reached the point at which that spiral occurs when the interest cannot be afforded.

US is about to go through a trillion dollars worth of annual debt repayment. It's enormous. If that yield curve shifts and interest rates go up — let's say you have an enormous inflation spike that forces everything up — that cost does reach a point where it runs away and then it becomes quite a terrifying scenario.

How do you solve that? It's the bunker moment. Because what do you do? Do you all sit around a table and debt-forgive each other? The wealth destruction across the world is immense.

So I think people in the know are very scared of that point coming. And when you see various governments spending on even defense which is necessary as an example, you're seeing longer-dated yield curves keep tipping up, keep ticking up, keep ticking up. Some countries are better than others, and you keep seeing the gold price continue to accumulate.

央行的沉默购金潮

Will it be found in a war? No. Will it be a tariff? No. Will it be another tweet? No. But the one thing that runs all the way through it, bit like managing your own finances, my own finances, is: everybody knows how to run something correctly. Everybody knows you can't keep running up debt. Everybody knows there's a crunch day. It just is. And that is what I think has been driving the gold price.

I will say that I believe central banks who have been the main driver over the last three years — particularly Asian developing central banks, or shall I say developing banks — have looked upon it the same way. Their currencies are very vulnerable. Their economies are quite vulnerable. They're the ones who have seen bond defaults and currencies having runs on them. So they've been accumulating gold to stabilize their economies because they look around the world and they see the incredible amounts of debts that have been accumulated.

That's what I believe is the main driver, and I believe it's been borne out in all the evidence that we've seen so far. Tariffs — how often, as an example, do we hear the comment "nuclear this, nuclear that" with Mr. Putin? Markets don't budge. Tariffs barely budge.

西方主权违约的可能性

主持人： One final follow-up and I'll pass it to Bonnie. Do you believe that a sovereign debt default would occur in the West, particularly the US or other G7 countries? You mentioned developing countries within Asia. Could it happen here?

David Tait： I think that the US is in a rather unique situation of $39 trillion that it can sort of get away with — but it can only get away with it if interest rates are relatively low. It can fund itself. It can fund its debt burden.

It is a deficit — a current account deficit — of seven and a half, eight percent. That's too high. It can't. It will keep adding one to two trillion every single year, and at some point that interest rate, if growth falls, won't be sustainable. They'll have to do something.

And do I see them defaulting? No. Does the US default? Will they try and inflate their way out of it? Perhaps that's what we're trying to see here.

But do I think other countries could default? My own for instance, which has got its back to the wall financially, has no spare cash, needs to reconstitute its defenses, and can't find its way to stem fiscally, to restrain itself fiscally — is it likely to have a run by the bond markets on it? Yes, absolutely.

I don't want that to happen. I don't want it to happen anywhere. But there are many countries across Europe that are highly indebted. And frankly, the ECB — there isn't enough money to bail out one or two of the larger bigger countries. They're all in the same situation: high lousy demographics, large number of non-producing people, very low levels of growth and productivity. And the only thing they keep resorting to is printing presses.

黄金作为"生存者"的价值

And that is why your gold bugs of the world — and I don't want to be pejorative — rational human beings in many respects are resorting to putting a portion of their portfolio at least in gold because of its longevity. It proves it's a survivor. And it's hard to see where the world growth is going to come from that will allow people to start reducing their debts.

That's the thing. And with these conflicts where we're having to spend more money we don't have, you can see where the bunker mentality does come from — simply because you can't come up with an answer.

"黄金是真钱，其他都是欠条"

主持人： I've heard the statement that gold is the true money, everything else is I owe you. Is that true?

David Tait： I see why they would say that. Fiat currencies have been wonderful over the years but have been depreciating endlessly because you can keep printing them, as you know. It relies on that faith that you have in its divisibility, its transferability. But of course, the fear is — I don't know if it'll ever materialize — the fear is that that loses that trust.

That moment when Liberation Day was announced, there was a ripple through the market of loss of trust in the US dollar, loss of trust in the US as an institution. It was discussed for the first time. Credible or uncredible doesn't matter, but it was there for a moment and it scared everybody senseless.

So does a physically backed product appear attractive in scenarios like that? Absolutely.

The one thing with gold is there's not enough gold in the world to reverse Bretton Woods, as an example. So couldn't happen. But as long as you have a physical — a digital gold product that is physically backed and can be redeemed in a physical form, whatever that form might be — you end up with something quite solid that doesn't devalue. And that's where the comparison comes from.

比特币归零论

主持人： What is your thought on Bitcoin being called digital gold?

David Tait： My personal opinion on Bitcoin is that it's going to go to zero.

主持人： Wow. Tell us more. Ouch. Tell me more.

David Tait： It's not because it's an anti-gold thing. I think if you have gold in your portfolio, you should have Bitcoin, and vice versa. If you have Bitcoin in your portfolio, you should have gold.

It's because — you've noticed in most of the crises that Bitcoin has been very correlated with risk assets in general. I don't think it's meant to be that way. I think it was meant to be an offset — something that you could compensate for having exposure to risky assets. It's meant to disassociate itself from risk assets. And it didn't really do that to that extent.

So if you have gold in a portfolio — which I think everybody should because it does the opposite of everything, simple as that — then if you have Bitcoin and you're a Bitcoin lover, it makes sense to have gold, and vice versa, because they offset each other.

稳定币的例外

My personal opinion is that I see a use for stablecoins. I see them at an institutional level very much so — whether they're asset-backed or real-world-asset-backed or otherwise, or fiat-backed, for their various uses. But I can't see how it's going to be sustained in the very very long term.

主持人： You're talking about stablecoin or Bitcoin?

David Tait： Bitcoin.

主持人： What would persuade you to change your mind on the Bitcoin to zero view?

David Tait： I don't know. I don't know really. I don't know if there is anything.

主持人： Would there be a use case that one would have to demonstrate to you?

David Tait： No, because — it's interesting you ask — you could make the case for fiat currencies. They rely on inherent trust. And they also rely on the fact that there is a central bank that's going to come to the rescue. Big institutions will bail it out at some point in the future. They just will support it.

"黄金也只是块闪亮的石头"

主持人： Not to belabor the point — I had an economist on recently and I'm paraphrasing, I don't remember his exact words but he said "gold is a shiny rock." Those were his exact words. There is no intrinsic value to gold. The value that we've assigned to gold, 46 or 47 whatever the price is, is because somebody else is willing to pay that price for gold. That's all it is. And that's the same argument the anti-Bitcoiners use. I just find that very applicable to the yellow metal itself. How would you respond to that?

David Tait： I see why you say that. Except — I know that most people who look at discounted cash flows for equities as an example and can price these things perfectly — how they would very likely say that. And I think I know the same people who have said those things.

But I would say that they're missing a large portion of the world who do think of gold as an intrinsic store of value. They see in and of itself — China, India — there's billions of people out there who wear it as their only source of value.

I accept that you could look at a piece of metal and say it doesn't have anything. You could look at a dollar bill and say the same thing. You could a dime the same thing. So I would say that those people who think that it is an inert useless piece of metal are valuing it under the terms you would an equity or a stock. You can't produce a discounted cash flow. You can't create an inherent value.

But as I said on a podcast recently, you are missing the three, four, five billion people out there who think the opposite. And that's why I think it goes up.

CZ vs. Peter Schiff：可验证性之辩

Bonnie： This reminded me of something. So last year I was at the Binance Blockchain Week and — gold supporter Peter Schiff versus Bitcoin supporter CZ.

David Tait： I know Peter Schiff.

Bonnie： CZ is the founder of Binance. What he did was he pulled out a gold bar and he asked Peter, "Is this real gold?" Peter said, "I don't know." And CZ said, "If it was a Bitcoin, you can verify it right away. But with gold you don't know — you have to test that." So is that not a flaw?

David Tait： Can you test gold instantly side by side? It would take longer to prove that gold is okay. But in the ecosystem that we are creating, the provenance of the gold and the integrity of the gold right back to the mine site can be proven. Yes, it is a bit Heath Robinson compared to Bitcoin and coding — I accept that. But that mechanism is there now, and we can prove where it's come from. Once it's in this ecosystem, it can be relied upon and can be proven that it is what it is, and being sourced responsibly and all those.

But it is a real world physical asset, and there's only so much you can actually do to that point. But it can be proven to be four nines, 59 gold at some point. Right now, if you were holding a gold bar and I couldn't touch it, I wouldn't be able to tell. But it can be proven.

为什么 World Gold Council 出现在加密大会？

主持人： We'd like to learn a little bit about you. But before we do that, just one question: why are you here at a crypto conference?

David Tait： Exactly. That's the question I'm waiting for. Thank you.

The World Gold Council, let me explain, is a body that represents the large-scale gold mining industry. I have 31 CEOs on my board, and my job, through virtue of GLD and GLDM — the funds that it gives me — is to improve the gold market sustainability for gold and also instill it with trust.

As part of that process, and because I came from a world where I shut down commodities trading and Credit Suisse and all that sort of stuff, my role is to try and make gold usable to the institutional world and everywhere else. And as part of that, I've got to try and lower the barriers to entry to the market and make it more like other asset classes.

Gold as a Service：黄金的 App Store

The way in which we're doing that, largely speaking, to begin with, a few years ago was to digitalize the ecosystem — improve the ecosystem in London from copper wire to fiber optic, literally the functioning of the market.

And most recently, we're trying to address the situation as to why don't gold crypto assets, gold stablecoins, gold tokens depending on your phraseology — why have they been a disaster? Why have they not worked? If you look at the AUM included in those asset classes compared with other AUM, they haven't worked. A couple of billion, 4 billion dollars — in the world to you and I it's a lot, but not to the financial world.

We spend a lot of work trying to figure out why that is. What we are creating is a system called Gold as a Service. It's going to be a platform that will allow the complexities of the physical gold market to be accessible, or to be overridden by a digital layer that this community and others will be able to back into to create gold products of any shape and size.

For instance, it's very difficult to start your own stablecoin. You've got custody issues. You've got compliance issues. You've got a variety of different things that are very expensive and complicated to do. You will have seen the Paxoses, the Tethers, the JP Morgans, the HSBCs have all got their own little silos, but they essentially don't communicate. They don't function. If you want to buy a JP Morgan, you can go and do it — no problem. And it tracks the gold price. What do you do with that? Nothing much else.

What we're going to create is this platform, and we are creating it with our own money, such that all the noise and difficulty that you would have setting up your own product is taken away. Think of the Apple Store. You create your own. Apple's done most of the hardware and all the worry, all the difficult bits, but the rest is up to you to create your products.

This is not just for tokens as stablecoins — they're for any other forms of product that anybody in this institution could lend themselves to thinking about. Redemption tokens, collateralized tokens, lending tokens, anything. But it will back into a gold market that is very simple, standardized, non-complex, one single price, simple, cheap, low capital — such that it'll be on a par with other asset classes, but in a digital way, a digital use, a crypto use.

That's why we're here. We're trying to popularize — obviously socialize — this. We're going to be doing it during the course of the year. We should have proof of concept produced by the end of this year. It's ambitious, but we should have it done. We've issued a white paper over the course of the last month which I can give you access to — it's online. And we're trying to invite this community to come and play with us and use this platform to build products.

珠峰五次：一段不情愿的攀登史

Bonnie： You've climbed Mount Everest five times. I don't think any of us could have done that. Can you tell us the story?

David Tait： Basically, I've been raising money for a charity in the UK I've been closely affiliated with. It's called the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. It's an anti-sexual abuse charity. The reason I have been is because my childhood was awful — it's public knowledge. I've used it for that reason.

I eventually found that I'd exhausted every other way of raising money — jumping out of planes, all this, crashing cars. And I decided I would try and use that mountain. So I rocked up in 2005, climbed it, went back every other year subsequent and raised just short of £10 million, 15 million bucks for this charity by climbing.

And I don't like climbing.

主持人： You don't like climbing? Wow. I thought you were going to say "I'm passionate."

攀登世界最高峰的心理机制

主持人： What is the mental fortitude one has to have to force himself to climb the world's tallest mountain if one does not enjoy the activity — not once, but five times? What is the conversation like?

David Tait： I did it because the very first time — there was a part of it, without too much detail — I lived below the zero line because of what happened to me as a child. Mentally, shall we say, emotionally, or happiness has always been below the line.

Then in 2005, when I decided to use that as a vehicle to raise money, when I succeeded — not only did I raise 10 times as much money as I thought (instead of 20 grand I raised 270,000) — I also felt brilliant for literally the first time in my life. Literally.

And I wanted more of that. So I decided to go back in '07, raise 300,000, '09, etc., accumulating this money for the charity. But I also felt semi-trapped because it's cold, miserable, you poo into barrels, it's horrible. I didn't much enjoy that. I enjoyed the kudos, but it became less about me climbing the mountain and more about the benefits I was bringing to children, without sounding holier than thou. That sustained me.

Then in 2015, I tried to climb K2. I got to within that far the top, but the weather killed us. When I decided to go back in 2017 to climb Everest, no one gave me any money. It was all sponsorship money. They'd got bored of me, and that gave me a chance to stop, which was quite a relief. And then I just speak on behalf of the charity now, and I find myself getting above the line by doing it that way as opposed to climbing a dumb lump of rock.

濒死体验的教训

主持人： My final question to you before I pass to Bonnie: what has a near-death experience on Everest taught you about appreciating life?

David Tait： That's a good question. Until I experienced my near-death experience on Everest, I was ambivalent about living, without getting too heavy. But I was.

And then I got caught in an avalanche. As it slammed into me and I was underneath the snow and rock really, I was so scared — it's hard to describe. If you've never been terrified, you really don't know what that's like.

I was carrying a flag from the Queen to the summit that year. And I remember being under the snow and thinking, "Wow, ow, I've broken my leg." Because my leg was killing me. "The Queen's going to be really pissed. I'm not going to get her flag to the summit."

The second thing I thought is — your past life really does flash in front of your eyes in a few seconds. It does. It's strange, but it's like a collage.

And the third thing I thought was: I don't want to die.

Until that moment, I hadn't been tested. I used my other arm, which — this one was broken — and I pushed myself out of the snow. From that point on, I decided that I was going to throw everything at life and make sure that I enjoy what was left of it because my childhood had left me subdued for too long. And so all this work and these projects and stuff I now treat as my new Everests. I put myself thoroughly at the front of — and yeah, strange story. Thousands of Everest stories, I'm afraid, quite interesting ones.

从濒死到重生：一次重病与新视角

Bonnie： I've actually binge-watched a lot of your documentaries and interviews, and I want to know what changed after that. You said you appreciate life more, you don't want to die — but how does that change your everyday life?

David Tait： It changes in strange ways. Most recently, I found out I was ill, very ill, three years ago, and I have now come out the other side of it 100% clear, which is wonderful. But much like that, it gives you a new perspective on life.

I've said to many young people: jump. Don't worry about where you land. Life is short. You can achieve things. You've got to be brave. You've got to have the confidence to take these chances. I spend a lot of my time talking to kids and young people, trying to get them to not be fearful, to understand that life is too short to be worried. You've got to take chances.

高盛年代：不怕死带来的优势

Bonnie： You are extremely successful, and I want to know what drove you.

David Tait： Funny people said when I entered Goldman Sachs back when I was a 20-year-old, 21-year-old, I was perfectly suited to that environment at the time (early 80s) because I didn't care if I lived or died, without sounding dramatic. I didn't care. So I was able to take risks and gambles — considered risks and gambles — that others were not, and they couldn't understand how I could do it.

But when you don't care, it's easy. It's not bravery. It's just — you don't care. And it suited me. I was perfectly made for that.

Then I reached a point where I've been questioned throughout my life: "Do you think what happened to me as a child has helped you in any way?" And looking back, I can say yes. It created a single-mindedness, an almost can-do attitude that perhaps seems irrational to some others, but it also made me realize that it's given me the ability — and I keep using this phrase — to jump and enjoy the ride.

Credit Suisse 的董事会时刻

I remember when I was at Credit Suisse, I was in a board meeting one day — the investment banking board meeting — and suddenly the CEO came charging in. He won't mind me saying, and said that — well, Credit Suisse doesn't exist anymore, it doesn't matter, does it? — he said, "We've just had our capital cut by 50%, the IB capital, one in one go."

And there were 20 people around the table and every one of them were like headless chickens. There was papers going everywhere and there were sweaty existential looks. And I remember sitting there looking at them and thinking: you guys got no idea what bad is.

Because if you've been somewhere really awful, you find yourself capable of doing rather extreme things without having the same reticence as others. So I think it helped me in a strange way. I'd much prefer not to have gone through it, but I think it helped me.

结束

主持人： We appreciate your contributions, and I thank you for your time today.

David Tait： Thank you for having me.

主持人： Thank you so much. That was — thank you for watching.

## 一、被误读的黄金牛市：这不是"避险"，而是集体对财政悖论的静默投票
多数人把黄金上涨归因于战争、关税、利率波动——但 David Tait 说了一句极其反直觉的话：**这些都是"过场"**。真正驱动金价从 1500 涨到 5000 的，是全球对"债务螺旋不可逆"的集体潜意识。
这里有一个被忽视的**结构性观察**：黄金已经不再是"恐慌指标"，而变成了一种**主权信用的做空工具**。当亚洲央行悄悄囤金时，他们不是在对冲某场具体危机，而是在对"美元作为记账单位的合法性"投下渐进的不信任票。Liberation Day 那一刻美债收益率曲线整体跳升——不是陡峭化，而是"平行上移"——那才是 Bessant 慌张冲出来喊 calm 的真正原因：市场第一次系统性怀疑美国这个机构本身。
## 二、跨领域连接：登山者的"零线以下"心智，与他对比特币归零的判断，是同一种认知结构
这段访谈最精妙的地方在于——David 说自己一生活在"情绪零线以下"，因为童年创伤让他对生死漠然，所以在高盛能承担别人不敢承担的风险；而正是这种"看过真正的坏"的心智结构，让他能在瑞信董事会上冷眼看着 20 个

item.title: [Mercatus Center] Sympathy, Justice, and the Impartial Spectator with Kristen Collins
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"自我克制"：不是压抑，而是共情的前置条件

大多数读者把 Smith 的 self-command 理解为斯多葛式的情感压抑——一种"男性化的坚忍"。但 Collins 在这场对话里揭示了一个反直觉的结构：self-command 不是切断情感，而是让情感变得"可翻译"。你之所以要节制自己被冒犯时的怒火，恰恰是因为你要保留识别他人被冒犯的感官带宽。压抑得太彻底，你就丧失了共情的语法。

这里有个几乎没人指出的隐藏对称：Smith 笔下的"公正旁观者"其实和现代心理治疗中的 mentalization（心智化）惊人地同构——都是让主体在情绪高峰时保留一个"可观测的自我"，以便同时看见自己与他者。也就是说，Smith 早在 1759 年就描述了当代依恋理论直到 21 世纪才命名的能力。Nussbaum 批评他冷酷，但被她指为"冷酷"的那个动作，恰恰是"温情得以稳定传导"的必要机械装置。

二、正义的起源不在契约，而在"戏剧"：一个被忽视的美学转向

对话中最锋利的一刻，是 Collins 指出：Smith 的正义感不来自"己所不欲勿施于人"这样的规则推理，而来自我们替一个已经死去、无法再愤怒的受害者去愤怒的能力。这是一个几乎带有宗教献祭色彩的姿态——我们把亡者"复活"到自己的想象剧场中，让 ta 借我们的身体重新感受被冒犯。

这里出现了一个跨领域的意外连接：Smith 的正义理论在结构上其实更接近悲剧美学，而非契约论。契约论要求生者之间的对称谈判，而 Smith 的正义要求生者对亡者的非对称代言。这让 Smith 意外地和本雅明的"历史天使"、以及当代转型正义（truth and reconciliation）中的"代位见证"同属一条思想血脉——即：正义的社会心理基础是替失语者说话的戏剧能力，而不是理性推导的规则。经济学家把 Smith 简化为"自利+看不见的手"，恰恰漏掉了他理论中最戏剧化、最不"经济"的那一层。

三、Bentham 的隐秘反转：从"全景监狱"到"反全景庇护所"——一个被历史遗忘的女性主义乌托邦

最令人震撼的洞察藏在对话末尾：同一个设计出 panopticon 的 Bentham，在同一时期还偷偷设计了它的镜像反面——sotimion。panopticon 让囚犯永远暴露给隐形的权力之眼；sotimion 却让未婚孕妇反过来隐形于访客，由她们决定谁能看见自己、以何种方式被看见。看的权力被翻转、被下放。

这里的跨领域连接非常锋利：sotimion 在结构上预演了 200 年后互联网时代的"隐私架构"核心难题——如何在不切断社会连接的前提下保护脆弱者不被公开审判？Bentham 的答案是"由被观察者控制观察条件"，这几乎就是当代差分隐私（differential privacy）、端到端加密、以及 Signal 式威胁模型的哲学祖型。

而更 aha 的是：panopticon 和 sotimion 表面对立，深层其实共享同一个 Bentham 式直觉——"可见性"本身是可以被制度设计的原材料。他不是"支持监视"或"反对监视"，他真正的立场是：谁掌握可见性的开关，谁就掌握尊严。这一点把 Bentham 从功利主义漫画中解放了出来，也让 Foucault 那个著名的"panopticism"叙事显得单薄——Foucault 只读了 Bentham 抽屉里一半的手稿。

四、一条串起全篇的暗线：孤立才是现代性的真正敌人

如果把 Smith 的 sympathy、Bentham 的 sotimion、Shklar 的 legal standing 三个概念并置，会浮现一条罕有人指出的暗线：这三位思想家都在对抗同一种现代病——"被看见但不被承认"的孤立。监视 ≠ 承认；曝光 ≠ 连接。真正的自由不是"没人看你"，而是"你决定谁看你、以及看到什么"。这个观点在算法推送、社交媒体羞辱、AI 人脸识别泛滥的今天，比 1776 年更迫切。Collins 在无意中给出的，其实是一份 18 世纪的数字时代生存指南。

📝 转录文本

开场与介绍

You're listening to the Hayek program podcast. This podcast includes audio from lectures, interviews, and discussions from scholars and visitors of the FA Hayek program for advanced study in philosophy, politics, and economics at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University. To learn more about the Hayek program, visit hayek.mercatus.org. To learn about graduate student fellowship opportunities with the Mercatus Center at George Mason University for students at Mason as well as at universities across the globe, please visit students.mercatus.org.

All right, today is Tuesday, June 2nd, 2026, and I'm here with my colleague Kristen Collins here at the Hayek program, and we're going to be talking about Adam Smith. So, Kristen, thank you very much for joining me here.

Thank you so much for having me, Pete. I'm so excited. The Hayek Program podcast was the first podcast I was ever on. So, it's nice to be back after a lot more practice.

Well now you're a seasoned podcaster, you know. And maybe you can bring up some of the sessions or programs that you've done related to this. But I'm really thrilled to talk to you because we're doing this series of talks on Adam Smith's Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, but more in general just Adam Smith. We Smith scholars — you and myself and others — have had a very fortunate boom period because we had a 300th birthday and then the 250th anniversary all within a very short period of time.

对 Nussbaum 的挑战：自我克制与感受性

And I was rereading an article of yours on Smith and self-command, and in reading it I was quite jarred about the connection to — or your challenge maybe to — Martha Nussbaum. I'd like to ask you about two challenges maybe while we're here: to Martha Nussbaum on the one hand and Judith Shklar on the other hand, if we could talk about those things.

In this one, you have this article on sensibility and self-command. And when Martha Nussbaum writes her book The Cosmopolitan Tradition, which she argues is a failed ideal, she has two chapters on Adam Smith. In some sense she ends up by arguing that no matter how great Adam Smith is, his theory leads us to a kind of stoic machismo — which I see you as directly challenging — in his moral philosophy, because it normalizes an indifference to misfortune. She thinks he disregards the material conditions required for the vulnerable to develop the necessary capabilities to live a meaningful life. And ultimately, since Smith elevates self-command over justice, he therefore misses or divorces the right to justice from the material conditions necessary to achieve it.

All right, that's Martha Nussbaum. Now, Kristen Collins is sort of challenging — and it's not directly a challenge to her in some sense, it's actually just more in general teasing through Adam Smith's text. So if you could just react to that and pursue it, I'd like to hear that.

Yeah, no, I'd love to. And I'm so grateful for us to talk about this, and I know we've had many conversations about Smith, including on some of these topics, so it's nice to hash this out now.

It's not a direct challenge to her, in the sense that I love and admire Martha's work. So much of her work on emotions, the politics of emotions — those were formative for me in grad school and is very much what I see my research agenda engaging with as well. That's also why I turned to Smith: I find Smith to be, of a lot of the canonical thinkers especially in the modern period and also the broader liberal tradition, one of the most uniquely balanced in terms of thinking about this more co-productive or relational dynamic between reason and emotions and passions. We don't need to see these as antagonistic and oppositional. Good political and social moral judgment comes from this proper negotiation of one's emotions, and doing so not just alone but in concert with others — being shaped by others while also being quite sensitive to how often we get all this wrong.

男性化理想的女性主义批评

To what you were talking about specifically, this idea of whether or not Smith privileges self-command — especially a lot of feminist thinkers engaging with Smith will focus on the fact that he seems to be portraying this masculine ideal. One thing to keep in mind with the Moral Sentiments is to think about the audience that he had in mind specifically and the conditions of that time. So I want to, you know, maybe the focus on men as figures in public life — that aspect of the feminist critique.

And yet there's also a lot of feminist scholars, and other scholars as well, who will emphasize: look, he was inspired to some degree and engaging with stoic thought, right — ancient stoics. But he also was very much engaged with sentimental novels, with more of the language and ideas around sensibility. And in fact, the way that he cultivates the system in the Moral Sentiments is that he's not just privileging the virtues of self-denial that we associate self-command with, but also the virtues of sympathizing with other people, of sensibility, of empathy, and of the notion of humanity — this idea of being sensitive to the needs and desires and feelings of other people.

In fact, I think self-command is not just this idea of suppressing your needs or suppressing your feelings, but being in touch with those such that you can recognize those in others. So when you have your sense of injustice that you've been wronged, you also extend that to knowing that that's what other people experience and feel — and then negotiating that in terms of both having the self-command to prevent yourself from being unjust to other people, from exercising what he talks about in Wealth of Nations, which is the love for domination that people have. And so, in fact, I think self-command itself is not just about kind of emotional modulation or moderation — which is often what we think of it as — but it's also about the ability to live in concert with others peacefully and to act justly as well.

So I don't think that these are necessarily incompatible. And just like I don't think self-command — this idea of it's again not just suppressing the emotions but learning from them and expressing them in a way that other people can better understand — and again taking that into our lives as spectators of each other's lives.

同情、想象与旁观者

So I want to ask a little bit more about that. You know, Hayek — who we read a lot and talk about — he's not really a snarky writer, but he has a snarky line in his Individualism True and False where he says all the great tomes of social psychology that have evolved in the 20th century pale in comparison basically to Adam Smith. While that's snarky, it's also in some sense true, in the sense that Smith has this sense of humanity that when you read him — and I think that's in both books, so I don't think there's a divide —

There's no divide.

— but I was wondering if you could talk a little bit about the difference between say Smith and Hume, and this discussion of the relationship of sympathy being a product of our moral imagination to project ourself into the shoes of another as opposed to our proximity. Right? So I sit next to a child who's crying and I might feel sympathy for them, but at the same time my moral projection doesn't require me to have proximity. It requires me to have a moral imagination. And to a large extent it's developing that moral imagination, I think, that the spectator plays a role.

That question really brings to mind for me somebody who had a huge impact on how I think about these as well now — Michelle Schwarze and her book Recognizing Resentment: Sympathy, Injustice, and Liberal Political Thought. She goes into much more detail than I'll be able to go here, and I would just reference that in terms of the differences between Hume and Smith.

正义作为消极美德的再解读

But I want to focus more on agreeing with you and that importance of the projection of the act of moral imagination. And I'm going to try to bring this more to the question of justice that we were just talking about. I don't know for sure what you're going to be flagging about, but I know I think about this a lot: there is of course this very famous passage in Smith where he describes justice as a negative virtue, and he describes it as something that we can accomplish just by sitting and doing nothing. But then I think in context it's quite clear that he's aware also we live — we are social beings. We live as members of community. So in practice that isn't quite how justice could always be done. I wouldn't go too far in terms of what he's articulating here.

But what I love about Michelle's work is that she really focuses on this other passage where he's talking about the act of sympathizing with a victim of oppression, of domination, of violence. In that act, we actually get a lot more of this emotional basis or social psychological account of the emergence of ideas of justice. We form this sense of justice not just by this idea of "oh just don't bother people," you know, "do as the golden rule" — which is valuable, do as you'd like others to do unto you — but also because we witness injustice in the world, and that gives us a sense of right and wrong and resentment on behalf of the victim.

That sympathetic resentment that Michelle talks about is so essential in this passage. And that again showcases how rich his theory is here, and it has this inherently almost theatrical component to it. So it's more than just kind of a social contagion of "oh we feel the feelings of somebody else around us." I think this is what's always tricky with Smith: he's acknowledging the fact that we have these kind of almost immediate and visceral responses of empathy, of empathetic emotion, and yet there is often — even if it's quick — a more deliberative component or imaginative component.

I actually will be talking about this a little bit just later this month in Glasgow at the International Adam Smith Society conference and the British Academy proceedings there for the celebration of the anniversary of Wealth of Nations. What is striking to me about this passage is that this really is an imaginative practice, an interpersonal practice of representation — of representing to ourselves the experience of the victim, and in sympathizing gaining a sense of what's right or wrong. Even when that victim especially — and this is what he — there's almost this like proto-Gothic imagery where we bring back to life the dead victim. So even if they can no longer feel that resentment, we feel it on their behalf. And in doing so, we gain this sense of understanding of justice.

We have all these systems of justice — all these rules, both social norms, practices, even institutions. But he's arguing that a lot of these things that we now see are useful, we now see they're beneficial — that's not where their origins lie. Their origins are in this emergent process that is a part of our emotional lives with each other.

"It is not true that the newer school of Sozialpolitik in Germany stands in substantive contrast to classical political economy. In every conflict of interest between the rich and the poor, the strong and the weak, Smith sides without exception with the latter. I use the term 'without exception' with proper consideration, as one cannot find a single instance in the works of Smith in which he represents the interests of the rich and the powerful against the poor and the weak. The reason why I wanted to read that out is because many years ago, Jim Otteson, who's a Smith scholar, went to University of Chicago, and his dissertation was on Adam Smith and The Marketplace of Life, I think is the title. But he always used to tell the story that the very first question he got at his dissertation defense was one that was basically arguing that Smith is in favor of the powerful and the strong. So why — one, could you address that concern with Smith as you do in your article, but then also why do you think there's a persistence? That's a really great question. The way I would maybe quickly answer what mistake was made — I don't think that this is necessarily so much of a mistake, but there is this problem that we always have maybe as a part of liberalism: this emphasis on neutrality and impartiality. So when you focus on a language of Smith articulating this natural system of liberty and a — I don't want to say minimalist state because that's kind of imposing our own language onto it — but this sort of, as you know the line better than I do, the "easy taxes and administration…"

Peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice.

So much of that language, when it's used too simply and too quickly and as almost like a slogan or the motto to others, will read as though a validation of the status quo. When you look at when you have that language and you see how deeply plagued the world is by various injustices — by various forms of relations of power, not only between the state and private actors, the state and corporations, but also within the private realm, within families, within private organizations like churches and schools, and of course within companies — people will read that as somehow to say impartiality, to say neutrality, to say something simple and easy in the face of all that differences of power, is going to come across as though actually just affirming the powerful, is actually just legitimating the powerful.

And I don't think — like I said, I actually think you know, often the Chicago school thinkers will sometimes be kind of oversimplified as doing that. And then you read a little bit more and you'll see, or for example James Buchanan quite clearly — and Maria Pia Paganelli, who I had on the podcast, so recommend that episode for sure, has great work on Buchanan as well and Smith and this idea of Smith kind of being an early public choice theorist — and the way that Smith's doing it, and maybe this wasn't done clearly enough for various reasons. Maybe it's also thinkers being impacted by the politics of their own time, their own partisan beliefs or other things, and we do that as well.

Smith was not only concerned from a public choice perspective — and in writing Wealth of Nations as a project that's engaged with ideas of justice and power — he also was extremely aware that the way the political system functioned was very much in favor of both the aristocrats and also the manufacturers, the merchants, the capitalists as we would call them, or the employers of the workers. And also there's all sorts of important infrastructure there too, that further enriched or entrenched a certain class and special interest groups of his time — that is distinct from ours. But maybe we haven't done a good enough job — because that history is also so complicated — articulating all of that texture and all of that context within the book.

Like, that to me is so obvious — I just thought we all know that. He has all these incredible passages on the plight of the poor, including the poor without jobs, including the working poor. So I thought all that was obvious. So to the degree that my article focused on Theory of Moral Sentiments, I was going the direction where I felt like we didn't adequately attend to all this rich argumentation in Theory of Moral Sentiments, where he's not just talking about economics, he's not just talking about political institutions, political economic institutions and relationships and contracts affecting employment — but he's talking about the actual psychological experiences of being judged by the public.

I think the idea here is that people will read Theory of Moral Sentiments and they'll say: look, this model of spectatorship he has, and this idea that we internalize this idea of spectatorship, is almost panoptic. It's almost what Michel Foucault would ascribe to the Enlightenment and kind of the liberal tradition, as "oh, if people just internalize judgments, we'll be able to have a peaceful orderly society, avoid any kind of unrest without necessarily using the violence of the state." And so there's this sort of pernicious element of that where it's people internalizing power relations as well and learning to be obedient.

Whereas in fact Smith paired all that political economy in Wealth of Nations that was concerned with power and oppression with a sensitivity to the different experiences that maybe the average observer or the middle class observer would have of admiring the rich versus disdaining, neglecting, or ignoring the poor. All those are slightly different, but in the end was extremely sensitive to both the psychological and also what that meant morally and ethically for how people understood and attributed blame and praise, and what that would feel like in society.

"The leader of the successful party, if he has authority enough to prevail upon his own friends to act with proper temper and moderation (which he frequently has not), may sometimes render to his country a service much more essential and important than the greatest victories in the most extensive conquest. And so this is all about civil violence, civil conflict, of fanaticism, of partisanship, of party. And he's suggesting: if there is such a thing as an ideal leader, it's someone who's able to manage all this while negotiating all the different interests and affections within the society, and being motivated by the well-being of the fellow citizens, by the public spirit of humanity, of sensitivity to individuals and the community and its traditions and what inspires and shapes people, right?

That's distinct from the spirit of system, which is the idea of kind of acting politically, trying to establish a certain kind of politics on the basis of what's almost a more aesthetic approach. And that kind of imposition — that's a really dangerous motivation.

And it's something that — you know, it's not only one side of the political spectrum that does that. It's something that I would even say perhaps — like we say with the physiocrats — I mean, that kind of system can also be its own… even somebody who's motivated by something like the invisible hand, something that should be about emergence, should be about institutions that enable people to pursue their interests in ways that benefit everyone in a positive-sum way rather than a zero-sum way — that can also become its own kind of aesthetic system that might inspire more reckless or ruthless, to use Joshua Cherniss's, a political theorist that I know you're familiar with, his liberalism book recently, kind of understanding liberals as trying to guard against this ruthlessness. And the question is how do you then move from the here and now off of that position towards this other one without imposing violence.

But the point I want to make with this is that the risk that we have is that if you don't — what you need to at least do is show that sort of sensitivity to what's wrong with the world, and that in that way, whatever your proposals are, they won't be taken as just an attempt to justify or just an attempt to cool down the temperature, but as one that's much more keen — mean with a "we see things that are wrong, we are just sensitive to the fact that it's so hard to correct them, and in knowing that we're going to be inter—" there's a reflexive process here. So maybe you can explain that.

索蒂米昂的构想

No, thank you. And it's funny because this institution — and I am always asked how to pronounce this, and I always worry because I pronounce so many things wrong, that I'm sure I can't possibly be pronouncing it right.

That's why I avoided saying it — because I'm afraid I'll say it.

I also believe in — like, people should be able to say — I don't love — I'm the opposite of a grammar Nazi. I'm like a grammar anti-fascist or anarchist or something. I just feel like everybody should be able to say what they want to say, and we should try to just make sure we can understand each other. Maybe use more words if required.

But anyway, so he had these other designs. And what's so fascinating is he's working on these after the initial panopticon designs, but in the same time period where he's working with the government to try to create what would have been this panopticon prison that then becomes this huge influence on Foucault and still influences the way people talk about surveillance today.

But at the same time, he had these notes on something that he referred to as a sotimion, or we could also say sotimian would be the maybe other way to say it. I like saying sotimion mostly because it rhymes with panopticon — it just seems like we should lean into that kind of what people are already used to saying.

边沁对性道德的批判

What this institution — what's so fascinating about this is he has all these other writings at this time too that we should read these notes in context with. These were writings that were very critical of the criminalization of sodomy, the social censure as well, the Christian aesthetic norms around sexuality. So he's both defending homosexuality, but he's also defending other marginalized sexual practices, including prostitution, including unmarried pregnant women — the idea of illegitimate pregnancies and childbearing outside of marriage.

And in all of these writings, he has such an institutional approach to these questions. So in terms of institutions at the time that were similar to what he ends up designing in the sotimion — which the sotimion never existed. It's all hypothetical. It's all notes. It's all in his archival manuscripts. But it's such a provocative — I mean, it's similar to the panopticon. The panopticon was this project he was really enthusiastic about, but it wasn't created in his time, and by him, not in the way that he was envisioning.

And so, we have less material on the sotimion, but he had these writings about criticizing the way society would stigmatize and socially punish women who had children outside of marriage. And he makes it quite clear that from his point of view, this was really not a problem for people to do this. And often, to the degree that this was happening, it was maybe because of poor marriage laws. Similarly with prostitution itself, or sex work, that it was difficult to have marriage — marriage laws — it was difficult to get divorced.

抹大拉医院与短期婚约

He also talks about the institution that did exist at the time — there were the Magdalene hospitals for penitent prostitutes. If you're familiar with the book Small Things Like These by Claire Keegan, she talks about what is essentially Magdalene laundries in Ireland later. But the Magdalene Hospital for Penitent Prostitutes was an institution to try to reform young women who were sexually promiscuous and potentially prostitutes. And it required this kind of "oh, I repent, I regret what I did." Bentham talks about how some of these women — their fundamental problem here was poverty, was a lack of opportunities.

Also all these hospitals were so focused on the problem of these women, and not the idea that men who were in the armed forces, military, and the navy — they were unable to create the relationships required to have marriages. So you couldn't have people having short-term marriage contracts. What Bentham argues in all that literature is talking about you having short-term marriage contracts, so that you would ensure that a man would be responsible for any offspring, and enabling these more — these couplings — this idea of like, why are we punishing people for these activities when our institutions make it more likely that they will do this?

索蒂米昂的设计细节

So the sotimion is something he designs in — or he imagines — in this period for how do you deal with this problem that women are punished for their pregnancies outside of marriage. And he has this really moving writing in some of these pieces about describing what it's like to be a woman who is punished by society for this. She's essentially opened up to the center of the world. It has this language that we would say panoptic — of the idea of being an object of surveillance, of being judged, and then being encouraged to internalize that public shame and stigma. But it's an isolating experience.

And that is what I think is interesting about surveillance. I mean, talk about atomism. What surveillance can do is force you to be exposed to the public and exposed to total social judgment and observation, while isolating you as well. So he talks about how the women then are isolated from their friends, they're treated as dangerous, right? And so how can you deal with a situation where you want to protect women from that social judgment, maybe give them measures of privacy, but you also don't want to actually isolate them from their friends, their family, because from Bentham's perspective, they didn't do anything wrong. There's no reason for them to be punished for this.

So he imagines this institution called the sotimion, which was not a panopticon in design. The panopticon is this central inspection tower with cells circling around it — or spaces, because it could be applied to various things — but in a prison, all the prisoner cells around it, such that the inspector at the top, hidden by blinds, wouldn't be seen by any of the prisoners at any time, but the prisoners would know and internalize that they could be under surveillance at any moment. So this is this disciplinary — and I think, to say that Bentham has all this other stuff doesn't deny how disturbing and strange this is, although there's more we could say here too where he was attempting to create a system that would actually also protect prisoners from themselves. It would also make the prisons more hygienic, would also subject the inspector, the guards, the management to the public as a whole system of public oversight as well.

But setting that aside, the sotimion was very much not that. It would have been a part of the same — he was imagining as part of the same grounds — he was trying to get the government to set up in the center of London, so it could all be under public oversight to some degree, not be kind of set aside and on the fringes of society.

There would be a bunch of cabins for each woman to live in — very well equipped. A common room that the women would govern themselves. It was basically like a gentleman's club at the time. A blackball system where if they disagreed with each other in terms of their behavior — any kind of offensive behavior or something like that — they might be able to exclude one another at least temporarily, or from various parts of the grounds, from that common room. But it was still managed by the residents themselves, not the management. And it was very much a social environment. He also envisioned all these very fun, nice things. It made it seem very idyllic, almost utopian really.

检查室：可见性的翻转

But all that — so a mix of common spaces, of these private spaces — but then the entrance. This was, I think, the special crowning for me, like such striking element of this design: there would have been an entrance and a porter at the door to welcome any visitors to this space. Again, very unique, very different from the other institutions at the time like the Magdalene hospital. Not only could these women be pregnant and give birth and maintain their privacy, but also they could allow visitors, friends, lovers, family members to come.

But they would have what he called an examination room in this entrance, such that the woman could be hidden and they could observe whoever the visitor was that came. They would give to the porter their name, the visitor would give their own name. The porter would go back, check with the resident: is this the person that they say they are, and do you mind that they know you're here and they want to see you? Is that okay? And they can say yes or no.

They could be actually in total control over the terms of their public appearances. They could conceal the fact that they were pregnant. They could maintain their social reputation, which mattered so much in this time — would help them maintain things like domestic servant roles, various jobs, but also of course a time — I mean, this is the era of Bridgerton really, after all — the ability to get married. All those things. While also still not being isolated, not being atomized.

被咨询的女性novelists

And it is this extremely — he writes about women that he would consult for this project. In fact, it seems like he probably was maybe influenced by Mary Ford, who was his sister-in-law — I have to remember the timing — she, I think, had not quite gotten married yet to his brother. And potentially Maria Gisborne may have been — that's something that Eileen Hunt, who's also one of the guests on my podcast, talks a little bit about this possibility that maybe she was also an influence, although that's very speculative. But in these circles in his life are women like that. And he writes about these novelists, these female novelists, that he thought maybe they would be people he could consult for this project, who were writing sentimental novels.

So this is all to say, it doesn't deny his utilitarian arguments, his conceptions of utility, but there has always been this oversimplification of Bentham as not concerned with individual rights or not concerned with the individual and autonomy, or not concerned with this more emotional, complex social experience that in fact he was very much motivated about.

And again, to go back to what I was saying about Smith, the fact that these thinkers — they were not just envisioning these simplified projects of how to make the world adhere to a system. Like it wasn't just this system thinking of the man of the system or something. It was also a social criticism. It was also a keen sensitivity to the relations of power, the entrenched institutions and interests that shaped the status quo.

被看见：斯密、边沁与尊严

When I was reading your piece and a couple other things that I've read, I kept on thinking to myself: there's this relationship that these people have — Smith and Bentham — to the essentialness of being seen as connected to the cultivation and practice of the moral sentiments. And so that's such a crucial thing for them, to make sure that you spread out who is seen, more and more. I was quite struck by that, and I thought that this example that you gave of this thing that Bentham envisioned, given the time in which he's writing, is pretty amazing.

It's also the case, I see it also when Adam Smith talks about slavery — he refers to the slavers as the refuge of the prisons of Europe, but refers to the slaves as nation of heroes.

Yeah.

He wants you to see them, right, in a way. And so it gets all lost when we just pigeonhole these thinkers in different ways.

无法忽视的可见性欲望

100%. And I want to add to that. Because that is a part of this larger book project that I've been working on. What I think is so striking about this notion of being seen is that there is this pernicious surveillance that we can feel. We can feel as though — especially when we are not in control and we don't have the discretion over how we're observed and judged by other people — we're exposed in this way. There's also a way in which people can subject people to public shame, can bring them out in society in order to humiliate and punish them, and to serve as an example for others, to kind of make others afraid and control them, right?

But the issue with this is that we can't just then avoid visibility entirely. There isn't this way that we could just ignore, or we could say, "well, just don't think about what other people think of you." I mean, that's — I think also to get to the opening stuff we were talking about — even though there is a way in which you could say Smith's answer to us would be something stoic of "don't worry about what the public thinks or what the average person thinks, or this idea of vanity, or all these public performances we have in our lives — just try to cultivate that inner sense of integrity and self-esteem, and imagine that impartial spectator that you're trying to imagine."

I think he's quite so sensitive that this is not something we can just wish away. It's very hard for any one person to form the total security of self absent — you know — validation, but also in the face of such stark social opprobrium or judgment, or even more severe legal prohibitions and punishment as well.

In fact, it is a political and social problem that we must face. And I think we have to acknowledge — to get to the sort of "how do we manage our emotions?" — you don't just suppress the desire to be seen and understood. You figure out a way to find these fulfilling experiences, and how can we create a society, both through more emergent or bottom-up, or what is available to us, where people really do feel seen and acknowledged and recognized on equal terms — as opposed to in that kind of punitive, disciplinary surveillance way.

结语与推广

Well, Kristen, I greatly appreciate you taking the time today. I'm so grateful that you are here as my colleague, because I constantly learn so much from you about the liberal project and how we need to restate it for the current generation and build on it and improve on it. So thank you so much for that as well. And I wish you all the best this summer and be a big hit in Glasgow.

Thank you so much, Pete. No, I'm really grateful. And again, I'm always so grateful when we get to talk. It definitely is one of the privileges of my job that we get to be at so many tables together chatting and thinking and arguing too — but in a way that is always productive and always makes me feel seen and respected. So thank you so much, Pete, for creating that environment, for giving me the opportunity to come on the podcast.

Virtual Sentiments 播客与新书预告

Thanks Pete for having me on the Hayek Program podcast, and to you for listening. If you want to hear more from me, Kristen Collins, check out my podcast, Virtual Sentiments, a series on the ethics and politics of digital technologies today with an eye to the past. I talk to scholars, practitioners, journalists, and other experts in political science, history, philosophy, computer science, and all sorts of other fields, with the aim of bridging the gap between expertise and public discourse. My goal is that you come away from every episode feeling like you learned something new and are more confident to contribute your own voice to the public debates about major technological, political, and economic changes our societies are undergoing today.

Currently releasing our fourth season, we have a truly varied and interdisciplinary slate of guests from over the years that you can choose from. Our latest episode was with AI scientist Katherine Gormley on her work on data privacy and open-source or open-weight large language models. Past guests include international political economist Henry Farrell on AI as a social technology, political theorist Deva Woodly on social movements, journalist Samantha Cole on how sex changed the internet, and political theorist Eileen Hunt on Mary Shelley and the ethics of AI.

If you're interested in my work, I'm currently finishing up my first book, Spectatorship and Surveillance in Liberal Democracies: Seeing and Being Seen. Drawing on canonical figures, including Thomas Hobbes, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Adam Smith, and Jeremy Bentham, I reinterpret the liberal tradition and illustrate its continued relevance for criticizing the impact of surveillance and inequality on freedom and democracy today. I also write a Substack newsletter, Theory of Virtual Sentiments, and my handle is Kristen Rosec on Twitter and Blue Sky. I also share news about my latest research, including my book at my website, kristenrcollins.com.

Thank you for listening to the Hayek Program podcast. To learn more about the research, scholars, and work of the Hayek program, visit hayek.mercatus.org. For more information about graduate student fellowship opportunities for students at Mason as well as at universities across the globe, please visit students.mercatus.org. We hope you recommend students to our programs or consider applying yourself.
