item.description:
## 一、被误读的"自我克制"：不是压抑，而是共情的前置条件
大多数读者把 Smith 的 self-command 理解为斯多葛式的情感压抑——一种"男性化的坚忍"。但 Collins 在这场对话里揭示了一个反直觉的结构：**self-command 不是切断情感，而是让情感变得"可翻译"**。你之所以要节制自己被冒犯时的怒火，恰恰是因为你要保留识别他人被冒犯的感官带宽。压抑得太彻底，你就丧失了共情的语法。
这里有个几乎没人指出的隐藏对称：Smith 笔下的"公正旁观者"其实和现代**心理治疗中的 mentalization（心智化）**惊人地同构——都是让主体在情绪高峰时保留一个"可观测的自我"，以便同时看见自己与他者。也就是说，Smith 早在 1759 年就描述了当代依恋理论直到 21 世纪才命名的能力。Nussbaum 批评他冷酷，但被她指为"冷酷"的那个动作，恰恰是"温情得以稳定传导"的必要机械装置。
## 二、正义的起源不在契约，而在"戏剧"：一个被忽视的美学转向
对话中最锋利的一刻，是 Collins 指出：Smith 的正义感不来自"己所不欲勿施于人"这样的规

item.title: [投资TALK君] ✨【投资TALK君1464期】马斯克ALL IN 数据中心！AMD暴雷？看看估值✨20260804#CPI #nvda #美股 #投资 #英伟达 #ai #特斯拉
item.dc:creator: 投资TALK君
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"估值锚点漂移"：市场正在悄悄重写 AI 公司的估值语法

小涛这期最反常识的一点埋在他对比 Oracle、Broadcom、英伟达、AMD 时的一句话里——"现在市场对纯 GPU 公司给了非常低的估值，而对 CPU、ASIC、Inference 相关公司给了溢价"。

这其实是一次估值语法的静默政变。过去两年市场用"训练算力增速"给英伟达定价，但当英伟达 29 财年 forward P/E 只有 13 倍、而博通 28 财年还有 16 倍时，市场实际上已经把英伟达重新分类为"周期性硬件"，而把 ASIC 玩家重新分类为"软件式复利资产"。

这里有一个跨领域的类比：这跟 2010 年代智能手机产业链的估值迁移一模一样——最初市场给高通（芯片王者）最高估值，但当 iPhone 生态成型后，估值溢价迁移到了做"定制化最后一公里"的博通、Skyworks、村田身上。GPU 正在经历它的"高通时刻"：越通用、越强大，反而越像"电力公司"而不是"AI 公司"。

二、马斯克的"数据中心 ROI 一年论"是一次高风险的会计叙事错配

老马说 SpaceX 数据中心回报周期"小于一年"，而亚马逊 Andy Jassy 说的是"两到三年"。小涛敏锐地指出这是长租/短租的差异，但更深一层的洞察是：老马正在用短租 On-Demand 的现金流曲线，去讲一个需要长租折旧节奏的资本开支故事。

这是一种典型的"期限错配叙事"——就像 2007 年前的次贷机构用短期票据滚动融资去持有长期 MBS。逻辑上短期数据都成立，但一旦短租价格下行（而这在 15GW 供给上线后几乎必然发生），估值模型会瞬间从"一年回本的黄金印钞机"翻转成"十年折旧的电力资产"。

一个跨领域的意外连接：这和电影行业首周末票房与长尾流媒体收入的关系高度相似——你可以用《复联4》的首周末数据说服投资人"电影公司回本快"，但你不能用它来给整个片单估值。老马正在做的，就是拿"首周末"给"整个片单"定价。

三、真正的隐藏赢家不是英伟达也不是 SpaceX，而是 HBM 供应链的"隐形税收官"

财报会议里那个关于 HBM 涨价的问答，小涛点到了但没有拆完。AMD 承认 HBM 涨价成本无法加价转嫁，只能通过"减少 HBM 用量的产品重设计"来应对——英伟达的 Rubin 也在做同样的事。

这透露一个惊人的结构性事实：HBM 厂商（SK Hynix、三星、美光）实际上对 GPU 巨头拥有"税收权"——它们的涨价直接吞噬下游毛利，而下游巨头只能通过牺牲产品性能（减少 HBM 数量）来"避税"。

这个模式的跨领域镜像是中世纪的"莱茵河关税城堡"：河流上下游都是大公国，但真正稳定收租的是控制关键渡口的小主教国。在 AI 产业链里，HBM 就是那个渡口。

一个让人意外的推论：如果 SpaceX 真的要在 27 年前上线 15GW（哪怕打对折 8GW），加上英伟达、Meta、谷歌、Oracle 的扩张，HBM 的结构性短缺会持续到 2028 年之后——这意味着市场目前对存储周期股仍在用"周期股 P/E"定价，是一个和"给博通打推理溢价"完全对称的错误。当估值语法在 GPU 端已经改写，它在 memory 端的改写只是时间问题。

四、一个元洞察：小涛的方法论本身正在成为市场信号

值得注意的是——他反复强调"估值是模糊的正确"、"不需要天天看"，但观众"尝到甜头后想天天看"。这实际上暴露了一个反身性陷阱：当越来越多散户用同一套 forward P/E + PEG 框架时，这个框架本身会失效，因为估值折价的窗口会被更快消化。

3 月和 7 月的两次低估值窗口能被抓住，恰恰是因为大多数人还没转向这套思维。方法的普及是方法失效的开始——这是每一个价值投资者最终都要面对的悖论。

📝 转录文本

开场：为什么今天不聊市场

各位观众大家好，欢迎来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。今天我就不多聊市场了，不像往常的一样，主要是因为：一，市场走得非常的好；第二点，我在上……该聊的我在上周都已经聊完了，估值在一个相对的低位，无论是纳指也好、SOX 也好，对吧。

那在昨天的视频里面，有不少观众已经反映了，就感谢我分享的那些数据，然后他们在上周进行了加仓。那恭喜大家。因为我个人，我一直说我作为一个市场分析员，那么我给大家带来数据、带来我的这个观点，最终会不会加仓、会不会减仓，完全取决于大家。那么能不能避开一个相对比较高估值的一个区间，或者在高估值区间进行减仓、在低估值区间进行加仓，完全取决于大家自己。

那今年起码经过了 3 月份的一个低估值，包括 7 月份的这个低估值，两个时间段，两次和大家这样的一个分享，包括个股标的上对于估值上的一个判断。我希望今年最终结束之后的一个 key takeaway，最重要的一个 takeaway 就是：估值对于我们在做价值投资时候的一个重要性，也是我在过去这段时间一直强调的——美股的一个基本面、估值，才是整个美股的一个核心。

在低估值的时候，很多市场里边那些宏观因素也好、技术指标也好，我个人认为都是偏向于噪音，好吗？

关于"估值"的使用方法提醒

那因为我知道部分的观众在估值上面确实尝到了甜头，对吗？诶，估值高的时候我减仓，诶，估值低的时候我去加仓。但是我在这边强调一下：就不需要天天去看估值。这不是因为你在这个标的身上尝到了一个甜头之后，你会发现我天天要去关注这个，没有必要。

估值本身它是一个模糊的正确，我强调过很多次，它没有办法帮助你每天去做这个交易。并且今天即使涨了 2%、涨了 3%，也不代表这个估值就会去到非常高的这个位置，不会。所以估值是一个模糊的正确，且估值我们用来判断高估还是低估，它是要有时间的这个跨度的。没有时间的这个跨度或者涨幅，你短期之内涨了 3%、跌了 3% 再去看估值的话，没有什么意义，好吗？

那今天我就市场的话，我就稍微聊这些，然后主要和大家聊两家公司财报：盘后发布财报的 SpaceX 和 AMD。

互动提醒

那在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发。昨天我和大家说，我说如果你们在留言区里面留言比较的积极，一些机器人比较不容易出现。我没有说错。我今天特地回过头去看了一下，整个从昨天视频上传到现在为止，留言区的机器人留言可能就 20 多条，我全部手动删了。但是如果大家留言不积极的话，上百条机器人，我删都删不过来。所以大家再接再厉，继续努力，让我们一起努力，通过留言把机器人给赶出我们的留言区，好吗？看一下我们能不能做到。

一、SpaceX 财报解读

1. 财报数据总览

OK，来来，先来看一下 SpaceX 这次的一个财报。首先先来看一下数据：

  • 营收本身大幅超出市场的这个预期
  • EPS 的这个增速或者体量也大幅超出市场的预期
  • 营收超出了 15%
  • EPS 超出了 62%
  • 如果你去看它的 adjusted operating income，调整之后的一个运营利润超出市场预期 91%

所以是和市场预期去做对比的话是非常好的这个财报。但是因为是刚刚上市，且里边的业务的波动本身非常的大，所以现在其实市场几乎没有办法对于未来 SpaceX 所有的业务去进行一个比较准确的一个预估。经过几次财报之后，包括管理层给出指引之后，市场会有这个更好的一个把握。

2. 市场对 SpaceX 的估值预期

但没办法，即使在这种情况下，我们还是要去先看一下市场对于 SpaceX 的一个估值。先来看一下整个 26 年，你看一下 26 年市场预计运营利润是多少，0 点……就一个 billion 都不到。那从这个角度去看，而且是 forward、是向前去看的嘛，如果你 2026 年一个 billion 都不到的话，现在多少？一个 T 的一个估值、一个 T 的一个市值，你自然就会觉得现在 SpaceX 贵到非常的夸张。

但实际上呢，没有那么的夸张。你看一下 2028 年市场预期多少？Operating Income 运营利润 38 个 billion。三年不到的时间里边，将会从一个 billion 上升到 38 个 billion，翻 38 倍。那么，如果假设现在市场预期是正确的话，那到 2028 年，它的 EV（Enterprise Value）除以 Operating Income 估值是在 44 倍。看起来就没有那么的夸张。

3. 三大业务分部拆解

然后我们来看一下具体它三家业务或者三个业务。那这三个业务我之后再给大家做估值更新的时候，一定要把这三个业务分开去看，对吧。你如果不分开去看的话，就像我前面和大家看的，你一年的 operating income 才一个 billion，你合在一起去看的话，一个 T 的一个估值，你的估值是上天了的嘛。所以没办法这么去看，一定要把三个业务分开去看。

第一个业务：Space（火箭业务）

那市场预计，我这边看的是 26 年、27 年和 28 年整个我看的全年： - 27 年营收增速是 44%，还是比较的高，6.2 个 billion - 28 年营收增速将会放缓，到 7.2 个 billion - 从盈利这一个角度去看，基本上 27 年的话还没有盈利 - 到 28 年才开始出现盈利，Operating Income 27 年的时候是 2000 多万，然后到 28 年的时候是 0.2 个 billion，两亿美金左右

所以我们大致要有个概念：他 Space 这一块的业务，26 年不赚钱，27 年可能刚刚 break even，然后从 28 年开始进行赚钱。这是它第一块业务。

第二个业务：Connectivity / Starlink

然后第二块业务也是它最赚钱的这一块业务，叫做 Connectivity，就是和 Starlink 有关。那这一块的业务市场的预期其实非常的 bullish： - 整个 25 年你看下它的营收是 11 个 billion - 26 年同比增速 50%，来到 17 个 billion - 27 年继续增速 50%，来到 25 个 billion - 28 年增速在提速，增速 61%，来到 41 个 billion

那从它利润这一块，Starlink 是赚钱的： - 26 年的话 6.6 个 billion - 27 年几乎要翻倍，到 11.5 - 28 年几乎再翻一倍，20.2 个 billion

所以 Starlink 这一块的业务是非常的赚钱，而且增速非常的高。如果去按它利润上的这一个增速，26 年是 60%，然后到 27 年和 28 年都是在 70% 以上。这样的一个增速比 Palantir 的增速还要快。这是它第二块业务。

第三个业务：AI

第三块业务：AI。那 AI 这一块的业务也是不确定性最高的这一块业务。你看一下 25 年它的营收才多少？3.2 个 billion。市场预期 28 年到多少？84 个 billion。三年的时间要翻 20 多倍。

而实际上，如果我们听完财报会议的话，你会发现 28 年市场做的这一个预期，如果在财报会议里面老马说的是正确的话，28 年的这个营收非常有可能在 27 年就可以做到。

那我稍微给大家一个概念，就是 84 个 billion 的这个营收、22.3 个 billion 的这个 Operating Income 到底是什么样的一个概念：市场预期 SpaceX 将会在 28 年的时候能够做到，但其实 Oracle 在 27 财年（也就是他们下一个财年）马上就可以做到。市场现在预期 Oracle 27 财年营收正好是 90 个 billion，比 SpaceX 里边的 AI 稍微高一些，然后运营利润这一块 35.8 个 billion、36 个 billion 也比 SpaceX 稍微高一些。

所以这差不多给大家一个概念：27 财年 Oracle 在整个 AI 这一块、数据中心这一块的营收，包括它的利润，和 SpaceX AI 这一块现在市场的这个预期，差不多两年半之后会达到同样的水平。

另外一点我们也需要有一个概念：就现在市场预期 Oracle 他们在 29 年（也就是三年之后了），29 年它的营收将会达到 128 个 billion。就三年之后的营收体量大概有多少。那现在市场给 Oracle 多少的估值？差不多在 400 个 billion 稍微多一些吧。就你可以假设：OK，我三年之后的营收 182 个 billion，然后现在的估值是 400 个 billion，那你往未来去看，三年之后的一个 Price to Sales Ratio 多少？两倍左右。

4. 我的分部估值方法

那带着这样的一个概念，我们来对 SpaceX 的估值去做一个更新。我前面说过了，要把它的业务分开去看，拆成三个业务去看。

火箭业务 → 0.2T（200 billion）

第一个业务就前面说的火箭业务这一块。我给了他 0.2 个 T，就是 200 个 billion。我怎么去算？我是算现在市场里面另外……我们叫大火箭小火箭的那种，起码在社交面上大家喜欢怎么去称：大火箭就是 SpaceX，小火箭就是 Rocket Lab。Rocket Lab，我们如果去看营收的话，SpaceX 的营收差不多是 Rocket Lab 的四倍，但是增速的话其实比 Rocket Lab 要稍微慢一些。所以我现在按照 Rocket Lab 的一个市值 50 个 billion 去算的话，那你可以假设 Rocket Lab 现在是低估的或者高估的都可以，那我只是按照 Rocket Lab 这个估值去算：市值 50 个 billion，4 倍的这个营收，那 SpaceX 火箭业务这一块就是 200 个 billion，或者 0.2 个 T。

Starlink → 1.12T

第二块业务 Starlink。我如果按照它 2026 年上半年的这个运营利润去算的话，把它年化——运营利润上半年是 2.8 个 billion，年化之后是 5.6 个 billion。如果你去看过去 12 个月的话，会比这个数据还低一些，所以这一个算法本身相对是乐观一些的，并不是一个保守的一个算法。

5.6 个 billion，我给它按照 200 倍的这个估值去算。为什么给 200 倍？因为如果市场假设是正确的话，其实它未来的两年 Operating Income 的这个增速还是比较高的，每年平均如果在 70% 以上的话，就像我前面说的比 Palantir 的这个估值还要高。所以你给 200 倍的估值，你说贵吧，一定是贵，但是没有到非常的夸张，对吗？

再说的简单一点：就 200，如果真的是 200 倍的这个估值，然后你平均每年 EPS 的增速可以有 70% 的话，那你 PEG 是多少？PEG 就是 3 倍，好吗？但是还是一个比较慷慨的一个估值啊，200 倍的这个估值。你算下来就是 1.12 个 T。所以这是他们第二块业务。

AI → 0.2T

然后第三块业务就是 AI。那 AI 这一块，现在 SpaceX 他们拥有 1.4 GW 的这个算力。我按照 CoreWeave 现在只有一个算力，CoreWeave 一个算力对上 50 个 billion 的一个市值。那因为基本上 AI 这一块它就是卖算力的。老马在这次财报里边也聊了，因为他看到现在这个市场非常的好，所以会去布局很多数据中心这一块的建造，然后去卖算力这一块的业务。

那 1.4 GW 嘛，他这边是 CoreWeave 一个 GW 对标 50 个 billion 的市值，那 1.4 GW 就是对标 70 个 billion。再加上 Cursor 收购的价格是 60 个 billion，剩下乱七八糟的广告业务全部加在一起，凑一个整数吧，0.2 个 T 或者 200 个 billion。

那很多人说：哎，三年之后 AI 这一块的营收可以达到 80 个 billion 呢，你现在估值只给他 200 个 billion 是不是合理呢？其实一样。我前面为什么带大家看 Oracle 他们在三年之后的营收是多少，包括现在的估值是多少，那么未来三年之后 Price to Sales Ratio 两倍的这个估值呢，你就假设 OK，SpaceX 两三年之后也是 80 个 billion 的一个营收，那两倍的估值 160 个 billion，那你再加上 Cursor 的话就是 220 个 billion，你再加上乱七八糟的业务，可能就是 250 个 billion 左右。那么就是 200 至 250 个 billion，就取决于我们怎么去算。

那如果按照 0.2 个 T 的话，那全部加在一起就三个业务，那么全部加在一起总共是 1.52 个 T。

5. 结论：SpaceX 仍不便宜

就我说了，1.52 个 T 里边包括了给了 200 倍 Starlink 的这个估值。我给了，是因为它的增速比 Palantir 还高嘛，那如果能够做到的话，这个估值也没有非常的夸张了。

那 1.52 个 T 市值啊，对应的就是 113 块钱的这个价格。所以我现在认为——而且我这边是给了一些比较乐观的假设嘛——所以我认为现在的 SpaceX 仍然是不便宜的。

那而且接下去会有非常大的一些解禁。几乎我能够接触到的一些一级市场的投资者，SpaceX 的投资者没有一个不等着解禁之后卖出的。所以接下去 SpaceX 这一块的抛压，我仍然认为会非常非常的强。那所以我的看法是：等解禁全部结束之后，市场找到这个共识、找到这个估值上的一个共识，或者说等 90 以下才开始去考虑 SpaceX 这个股票本身、这家公司本身有没有投资的这个价值，有没有性价比在这边。

完了，最后我想提醒一下的是，估值本身它只是一个模糊正确的，所以没有必要和我去争我是对的还是错的。我只是给大家分享方法本身，包括我自己主观的看法。

6. 财报会议：老马的宏大叙事 vs. 华尔街预期

最后我们聊一下财报会议。如果去听财报会议的话，你会发现前面我们分享的华尔街的一些数据，基本是狗屎了，就是老马所分享的这些数据远远是高于华尔街现在所做的这些预期。但它到底能不能做到呢？不一定。

关于 15GW 数据中心

那么，首先，老马说到他在 27 年之前，他要上线 15 GW 的这个数据中心。15 GW 什么概念？非常非常……体量非常夸张。你不算 GPU，如果你算上 GPU 的话，现在一个 GW 100 个 billion。你算上 GPU 的话，15 个 GW 起码在 1.3 个 T 到 1.5 个 T。也就是说，你一家 SpaceX 在资本开支上的这个花费，抵上了整个全部市场全部加在一起——现在全部市场加在一起才 0.7 个 T。在 0.7T，他一个人要建 15 个 GW。他又说 20 个 GW，他说 20 个 GW 假设其中 1/4 是会被延后的，所以我们就按 15 个 GW 去算。

即使是 15 个 GW 也是非常非常的夸张。我觉得是做不到的。也没有那么大、也没有那么多的钱。如果说 SpaceX 真的要这么去做的话，接下去的融资体量会非常非常的大，他们没有这个现金流去支撑，好吗？

然后行业里边的一些调研机构，比如说方德 AI，最近他们的观点也被 Gavin Baker 所引用了。方德 AI 认为 SpaceX 从今年到 27 年底能够上线 8 个 GW 的算力。如果真能够上线 8 个 GW 的这个算力的话，那他们上线算力的这个速度其实也已经超过了这些 HyperScale——比 HyperScale 都要快了。好吧，所以老马在财报会里面所讲的这些数据，我认为是有待验证的，我这边打一个非常大的一个问号。

因为首先你现在建数据中心的话，最难的点是什么？你本身大多数的成本来自于哪里？来自于 GPU 和 memory 的这个价格。第二点就是你的电到底哪里来？没有那么容易去拿到这个电。

看好 SpaceX = 看好英伟达

然后我们继续看下去。第二点，就如果说我们看好 SpaceX 的话，你必须要看好英伟达。为什么？是因为老马接下去他所要建的这些数据中心全部是和英伟达去合作，起码现在他表达的是全部是和英伟达去合作。并且他说到期待明年英伟达有很大一部分的 GPU 会安排给 SpaceX。

1000 亿美金 ARR 到底可不可能？

第三点，老马说到认为今年年底 ARR 的营收就可以达到 1000 亿美金、100 个 billion。我去算了一下 1000 亿美金，而且他在财报会议里面特别强，他说我们什么事情都不用干，就可以达到 1000 亿美金 ARR。我还是打上一个问号。因为我去算了一笔账：

  • 1000 亿美金的话，代表一个季度的营收达到 25 个 billion，年化就是 1000 亿美金
  • 谷歌：差不多从 10 月份开始每一个月给他们一个 billion，那四季度谷歌可以贡献 3 个 billion 的营收
  • Anthropic：差不多一个季度给 1.25 个 billion，四季度贡献 4 个 billion；再加上最近新签的这个订单——6.7 个 billion 的订单，10 月份开始持续 6 个月，那四季度总共还可以贡献 3 个 billion
  • Cursor：因为现在 6 月份 Cursor 的 ARR 是在 2 个 billion，我假设 Cursor 到年底的 ARR 是 12 个 billion，那就是 12 月份单单一个月的营收就是一个 billion，我把它乘以 3，也就是四季度会贡献 3 个 billion
  • 这些东西全部加在一起 13 个 billion
  • 再加上 Connectivity / Starlink 这一块 5.4 个 billion，Space 这一块 1.5 个 billion
  • 全部加在一起也只有 20 个 billion

和老马所说的 25 个 billion 还差了 50 亿美金，我不知道哪里可以获得。

回报周期 <1 年的疑问

最后另外一点，老马提到了，就包括他们的 CFO 也有提到，他说现在他们整个数据中心的一个回报周期是多少？小于一年。小于一年。

然后你会发现，如果大家有仔细去听的话，在亚马逊的财报里边，Andy 有说到——安迪，亚马逊它的一个回报周期是两到三年，基本上通常是三年，那但是他们可以做到小于三年。但是这边 SpaceX 却告诉我们，他们的回报周期是一年。

为什么会出现这种情况？那这就是取决于你签的这个订单到底是长期订单还是短期订单。长期的这个订单，首先你订单的时间会长，那你的价格一定会低。那这就是现在在租算力的时候，租算力有一个长租价格和一个短租价格。短租价格叫做 On Demand。所以短时间之内，如果市场对于算力的这个需求非常的高，短租的这个价格就会非常的贵。

这也是为什么我们看到了谷歌和 OpenAI 都向 SpaceX 去购买这个算力，然后我们看到了 SpaceX 开始出租这个算力，然后我们看到了 Meta 开始去卖自己的这个算力。之所以他们会选择去卖自己的这个算力，就是因为短期的这个回报 ROI 非常非常的高。

但是像老马这样，如果说我要建 15 个 GW 的数据中心，然后我的期待是每一次的回报都是在一年以内的话，都是非常非常不合理的。为什么？你要建那么大的这个数据中心，不可能所有的数据中心几个 GW 的、10 个 GW 的数据中心全部是用于短租，你不可能这么去做。因为短租的这个价格波动非常的高、非常的大。

两点结论

所以 SpaceX 大举进军 AI 市场或者算力市场，其实是对于 NeoCloud 整个运营模式的一个验证，这是第一点。第二点绝对利好英伟达，因为他们现在 exclusive 这个合作伙伴就是英伟达。

二、AMD 财报解读

1. 财报"没有惊喜"是常态

OK，然后我们来聊一下 AMD 的财报。那首先 AMD 的财报和我昨天视频里面聊的一样：他们财报出来，每一次的财报结果出来，你都很难会发现他们超出市场预期非常的多。

我这边举了他们过去 8 个季度财报出来之后 EPS 好于市场预期的这个幅度。我们可以看到，只有一个季度——2025 年的第四季度超出市场预期 15.62%——其他所有的季度几乎都和市场的预期一样，其中有一个季度还比市场预期稍微低了那么一些。就基本上每一次华尔街的这个摸底，或者说 AMD 给予下一个季度这个指引，都非常的准确，完全不给自己留任何的空间在那边。

所以 AMD 有这样的一个历史。这也是为什么在昨天的视频里面，我会给大家聊到：就你不会发现 AMD 的财报出来之后会给你有非常大的这个冲击，不会的。因为他们历史上的财报出来这个结果就是这样，好吗？

2. 财报会议要点

然后我们来看一下财报会议。那基本面我不用太多聊，AMD 的基本面还是非常的好。

要点 1：27 年服务器 CPU 增速 70%

财报会议里边，27 年服务器 CPU 增速 70%，速度非常的快。那这一块的服务器的一个 CPU，你也可以理解为接下去 27 年英特尔的一个增速。那么我在上一次分析英特尔估值的时候，我说你得把英特尔的 product 和他们的方矩这一块分开去看。product 这一块我假设 27 年是多少？我给了 50% 的这个假设。

很多人问我：你凭什么能够给 50%？如果营收增速在 70%，你的 bottom line、你的 EPS 增速那绝对不止 70%。那如果你有一个运营效率在那边的话——而当时我只给了 50% 的这个增速。所以你会发现，而当时我在下面我说其实我给的这一个预期已经非常的保守了，好吧。

要点 2：GPU 总增速 100%+，一个 GW ≈ 15B 营收

所以 CPU 的这个增速 70%，然后总增速是 100%。为什么？因为他们 GPU 的这一块的增速会非常的快。那主要 GPU 这一块的客户——MI 系列嘛——GPU 这个客户来自于哪里？OpenAI、Meta 和 Anthropic。

那当时分析师问的一个问题是：一个 GW 是不是代表对你来说是 15 个 billion 的营收？然后你们 27 年可以卖 3 个 GW 的这个芯片？这是一个概念性的一个问题，就你起码和"一个 GW 约等于多少营收"可以去画上这个等号。这是第一点。

要点 3：HBM 涨价压力与产品重设计

第二点，分析师有问到，他说你们 GPU 里边 HBM 比你们的这一个竞争者（谁？英伟达嘛）多用了 50%，那你们怎么去管理这一个毛利？因为他们在卖芯片的时候，他们的芯片本身和 HBM 是捆绑在一起去卖的。那如果 HBM memory 这一块的涨价，涨完价之后对你来说是直接的这个成本的一个上涨。而你成本的这个上涨，你是不可能在这个成本上面再去加这个溢价的，不可能的。你就只能把 HBM 的这个成本完全转移到消费者身上。但是你统一的价格绑定在一起，将会因为 HBM 的这个涨价，将会使得一个毛利润出现下降。

所以这个问题问得非常的好。那 Su 妈有聊到，她说我们可以对自己的产品去做出这个调整。如果说模型本身不需要那么多的 HBM，我们可以去减。其实是类似于现在市场里面所聊到的下一代英伟达这个产品——Rubin 有可能会把 HBM 的这一个数量给往下降一半。也就是因为现在市场里边 HBM memory 这一块的一个短缺，从产品端这一块，英伟达和 AMD 正在做一个产品上的一个优化，为了去应对不同的场景，你使用不同的产品，那而这不同的产品对应的是不同数量的 HBM。这是第二点。

要点 4 & 5：CPU 量价齐涨 + GPU 27 年增速远超 100%

第三点，CPU 27 年将会出现一个量价齐涨，就是出货量也会上升，然后价格也会上涨。然后第四点，GPU 在 27 年的这个增速将会远超 100%。

要点 6：EPS 指引"significantly 高于 20 美金"

最后一点，其实在他们上一次这个投资者大会里面有给过这一个指引——他们给出了未来三年之内他们 EPS 的这个体量可以达到 20 美元，就每股收益可以达到 20 美元。然后在这一次财报会里边 CFO 有聊到，这个数据将会 significantly 远远高于 20 美元。那我的一个假设就是 25 美元每股收益。

3. AMD 估值测算

那我们先把这 25 美元放在身后，我们先不聊这个数据，因为这个 25 美元呢是非常的重要，大家先记在那边。

这一个季度数据出来之后，看一下总共过去四个季度（Trailing Twelve Months）静态的一个 EPS 是多少？5.76。一年赚了 5.76。按照盘后的这个价格 472÷5.76，得出来静态市盈率是在 82 倍。

那你看，现在原本在发这一季度财报之前是多少？113 倍。因为这个季度数量体量非常的高，144，同比增速要超多少？246。那所以他们一下子 PE 静态的市盈率的 PE 就从 113 跌到了 82。这就是当财报的增速非常高的时候，你 PE 下降的速度也会非常的快。那所以直接从 113 倍降到了 82 倍。

那未来三年 EPS 这个增速——假设你看现在 78、86 和 37——我假设它平均 60% 的话，那你 82 倍的一个静态市盈率对应的就是 1.4 至 1.5 倍的一个 PEG。那讲到这边 1.4 至 1.5 的话，贵吗？其实不贵。我认为就是在处在一个非常合理的一个阶段，甚至于你可以说它是相对便宜的。

这是我在根据市场预期的这种情况下所得出的这个结论和结果。然后我们回到前面管理层所给的这个指引：25 美金，就 25 美金的一个每股收益。现在市场预期 28 年 EPS 是多少？19 美金。而管理层给的这个指引是在三年之内能够达到 25 美金。那如果我把 25 美金给带进去的话，带入现在 472 块钱的这个价格，得出来 28 年它的 forward P 是多少？19 倍。那现在市场预期是多少？27.34 倍。

也就是说，现在如果管理层给的这个指引完全能够做到——当然他们只给了 20 块钱，那他们给了高于 20 块钱、远远高于 20 块钱，假设 25 块钱——他们如果能够做到的话，28 年的 forward P 19 倍。那这样看起来贵不贵？其实 AMD 现在一点都不贵。

4. 但英伟达更便宜——市场估值语法的错位

但是，对吧，没有对比没有伤害。我们来看一下英伟达的估值。根据现在市场的这个预期，且不算英伟达能够做得比市场还要好，英伟达的预期： - 28 财年（两年不到之后）能够做到多少？16.4 倍 - 这个 forward P 远远低于 AMD 的这个 forward P - 29 年差不多三年之后的话是多少？13 倍，非常的低

再来看一家公司 Broadcom 博通： - 27 年一年半之后是多少？21.7 倍，明显比英伟达要高 - 28 年的话是多少？16 倍

那博通和英伟达，它的增速也都非常的高。所以其实如果我们把这三家公司放在一起去看的话，我们可以得出一个结论：现在市场其实对于纯 GPU 这类的公司，像英伟达这类的公司，给了一个非常低的这个估值。而相反，对于未来在 ASIC 这一块、定制 ASIC 这一块，包括 CPU 这一块，都给了一个相对比较高的这个估值。 为什么？是因为现在市场给了 Inference（推理）这一块的一些公司——就只要和推理相关的一些公司——给了一个估值上的一个溢价。

5. 综合结论

所以听完 AMD 的财报之后，我认为 AMD 的估值非常的合理，且 AMD 的估值是便宜的。

然后你听完 SpaceX 的一个财报之后，如果你看好 SpaceX 接下去在数据中心这一块建造非常大的体量的话，你应该是看好英伟达，因为英伟达接下去将会非常获益于 SpaceX 数据中心这一块的上线。

那最终可能很多人会问我，他说："Topc，那我到底应该是去买英伟达，还是应该去买 AMD？" 我觉得这是见仁见智的，就取决于你：

  • 从估值本身去看：英伟达绝对是便宜的，比 AMD 的话还便宜
  • 从故事线这个角度去看：似乎英伟达现在缺少了一个故事线，就是你缺少了一个现在市场聊的比较多的 Inference 这一块、推理这一块，CPU 这一块或者定制 ASIC 这一块

两家公司都是好公司，基本面也都非常的好，估值来说都便宜的。你从一个绝对的 risk reward 这个角度去看，两家公司都可以去布局。你从一个相对的 risk reward 两家公司去做对比的话，英伟达会比 AMD 要稍微好一些，因为毕竟相对便宜些嘛。而如果我们从故事线的这个角度去看，AMD 的这个故事线会比英伟达暂时来说会比英伟达要稍微好一些，好吧。

结尾：活动信息

那最后是今天的活动。富途牛牛美国市场这边，开户且入金，最高可以获得价值 1000 美金英伟达的赠股和闲置资金最高年化 8.1% 的回报。加拿大这边现在有一个我们这个频道的独家福利，通过开户且入金，最高可以获得 100 只免费股票的一个抽取，直接抽到手软，闲置资金最高年化 6% 的这个回报，和前 30 天零佣金交易。那大家感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里面找到开户的链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，我们下期见。

## 一、被忽略的"估值锚点漂移"：市场正在悄悄重写 AI 公司的估值语法
小涛这期最反常识的一点埋在他对比 Oracle、Broadcom、英伟达、AMD 时的一句话里——**"现在市场对纯 GPU 公司给了非常低的估值，而对 CPU、ASIC、Inference 相关公司给了溢价"**。
这其实是一次**估值语法的静默政变**。过去两年市场用"训练算力增速"给英伟达定价，但当英伟达 29 财年 forward P/E 只有 13 倍、而博通 28 财年还有 16 倍时，市场实际上已经**把英伟达重新分类为"周期性硬件"，而把 ASIC 玩家重新分类为"软件式复利资产"**。
这里有一个跨领域的类比：这跟 2010 年代智能手机产业链的估值迁移一模一样——最初市场给高通（芯片王者）最高估值，但当 iPhone 生态成型后，估值溢价迁移到了做"定制化最后一公里"的博通、Skyworks、村田身上。**GPU 正在经历它的"高通时刻"**：越通用、越强大，反而越像"电力公司"而不是"AI 公司"。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Cold Card 事件与 Leopold 爆仓，其实是同一种"熵坍缩"

表面上，一个是硬件钱包的密码学漏洞，一个是 24 岁天才的 AI 基金爆仓，风马牛不相及。但把两者叠在一张图上，会发现它们共享同一个致命机制——"熵源退化"。

Cold Card 的 bug 是：本应流经真随机数发生器的密钥生成，因为一根"线接错了"，静默地退回到低熵源，于是数十亿种可能坍缩成攻击者可暴力枚举的空间。Leopold 的组合是：本应分散在多个不相关因子上的风险，因为都押在 AI 叙事这一个"变量"上，同样静默地退回到单一熵源——一个 Micron 财报的坏消息就足以让整个组合坍缩。

真正的教训不是"要用好钱包"或"要做风控"，而是：任何声称"我很随机 / 我很分散"的系统，都要问一句——你的熵到底从哪里来？谁在审计这个熵源？ 五年没人发现 Cold Card 的问题，因为大家假设"它当然是随机的"；LPs 五个月里给 Leopold 加杠杆，因为大家假设"这些股票当然是不同的赌注"。假设，就是熵的敌人。

二、跨领域连接：Ken Griffin 是 21 世纪的"最后贷款人"，而这重塑了金融的物理学

节目里 Rahm 顺口讲了一件被低估的事：1998 年 LTCM 爆掉时，是纽约联储把投行召集起来"传帽子"接盘；2026 年 Leopold 爆掉时，接盘的电话直接打给了 Citadel、Jane Street 和 Millennium。

这不是"华尔街换了个门牌"，这是最后贷款人角色的私有化。在物理学上，这类似于把一个由政府维持的公共"引力场"，替换成了几个由私人做市商维持的"局部势能井"。后果是深远的：

  • 危机不再走"银行 → 央行 → 财政"这条监管链，而是走"基金 → 私人做市商 → 市场"这条不透明的链。
  • 信息不对称被制度化：Citadel 不仅是接盘者，还是做市商、还是数据的第一手观察者。它在几乎无摩擦地把危机转化为利润。
  • 反脆弱性集中化：整个市场的抗震能力，正在寄生于三四家私人机构的资产负债表和风险胃口。

有意思的联想：这跟 Cold Card 事件里"self-custody 的信任最终又流回 Coinbase / Fidelity"是同一种拓扑塌陷——去中心化的理想在压力下会自发收敛到少数节点，因为"可以起诉的对手"本身就是一种流动性。Austin 引用的那句话堪称本集金句："I want a throat to choke."——机构不是在买托管服务，是在买"可诉性"这种衍生品。

三、隐藏的系统真相：AI 安全的"防御-进攻不对称"，正被美国自己的护栏放大

这一段最值得停下来的信号是 Alex 的一句抱怨：负责审计 Bitcoin 硬件钱包代码库的美国红队工程师，不得不使用中国开源模型 Kimi 和 GLM，因为 Claude、GPT 的安全护栏会拒绝这类"看起来像攻击"的任务。

这里面藏着一个反常识但很严重的系统性事实：

当前 AI 安全策略在无意间创造了一个"防御者征税、进攻者免税"的市场结构。

  • 攻击者本来就在灰色地带，用越狱模型、开源模型、自训模型毫无心理负担。
  • 防御者反而被合规、TOS、护栏三重征税，甚至连"分析自己本地数据库"都要被 refuse。
  • 结果：护栏越强，边际上受影响最大的是善意使用者，而不是恶意使用者。

跨领域连接一下：这跟 1990 年代美国的加密出口管制（Crypto Wars）几乎是同一个错误的第二季。当时限制强加密出口，结果是全世界的加密标准反而绕开美国发展，最终美国不得不放开。今天限制 frontier 模型的攻防用途，很可能重演——中国开源模型正在成为全球网络安全的默认工具链，这不是意识形态问题，是纯粹的可用性梯度决定的。

再往深走一层：Cold Card 的漏洞五年没被发现，可能不是因为没人有能力，而是因为有能力的人被护栏拦在门外。 如果这个假设成立，那么"AI 安全护栏"本身就正在成为一种系统性金融风险来源——一个几乎没有人在讨论的、隐藏在合规叙事之下的负外部性。

一个留给你思考的问题：如果熵源退化（观察一）、最后贷款人私有化（观察二）、防御者被护栏征税（观察三）都是同一个更大结构的三个切面——那这个结构是什么？我的猜测是："信任的重新集中化"正在以三种伪装出现——技术假象里的分散、监管缺席下的私人兜底、合规叙事下的能力垄断。 这三条线，可能在未来 5 年会汇合成一次我们尚未命名的危机。

📝 转录文本

开场：机构时代的核心心态

"We're in this institutional age of crypto and when you unpack the institutional mindset, it really comes down to one thing. I want a throat to choke. I want to be able to sue somebody. That's what they'll tell you over and over again. I don't care. Like, I need somebody who's capitalized that I can sue. And I think there's value in that for many institutions."

Hey everyone, welcome to Bits and Bips, where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time. We're here to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto and macro.

And as a quick heads up before we dive in, remember Bits and Bips has its own channel now separate from Unchained. So if you're not subscribed here, you're going to stop seeing the episodes. Don't lose your dose of the sharpest takes in crypto. We're on X, YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, really wherever you're watching. And before we begin, a quick commercial break.

广告：Cape

This episode is brought to you by Cape, America's privacy first mobile carrier. Same premium service you'd expect from any other carrier, but designed so your number, your location, and your data actually stay yours. Get 33% off 6 months at cape.co/chained.

Not listening to Bits and Bips yet? It's our weekly crypto and macro market show with Rahm Alawalia, Austin Campbell, and Chris Perkins. Search Bits and Bips and subscribe.

市场快照与嘉宾介绍

All right, everybody. Welcome back. So, a quick market snapshot. Bitcoin has been trading around the 63K-ish level today. ETH around the 18,850s. 10-year is still hanging around like 4.72 to 4.75. Not ideal. Um, the FOMC hike odds are elevated above 50% right now.

And here to discuss all of this today, I'm your host Austin Campbell as always with my co-hosts Rahm Alawalia, Maester of Wealth, Leader of Lumida, Chris Perkins, the golden hand of Franklin Crypto. And joining us today is Alex Thorne, head of research at Galaxy Digital, uh, who has been tracking the cold card exploit in real time. And by the way, if you're not listening to Galaxy Brains with Alex, you need to be. Galaxy Brains is a leading indicator of quality crypto content.

第一段：Aschenbrenner 基金爆仓事件

事件概况

Um, all right, let's start with one of the two big stories of the day, which is the Aschenbrenner blowup. So, the biggest AI fund of this cycle blew up in basically a single month. Uh, the situational awareness fell from about 45 billion to roughly 10 billion after steep July losses. All numbers approximate according to Bloomberg.

Margin calls from prime brokers forced a distressed sale of its public stock portfolio to Ken Griffin Citadel and what remains is the Anthropic stake and private vehicle instruments for the fund according to TechCrunch. Um, this is a 67% drop in AUM, drop is 35 billion. Again, hard to know how much of that is allocated where thanks to the deleveraging.

But what happened is both legs of this trade broke at once. The AI infrastructure trade — SanDisk way down, Nebius way down, Micron way down, CoreWeave way down. If you're forex levered, you don't need a crash. You need a bad month according to chart.

Citadel 阴谋论 vs. 杠杆解释

Um, there's a spicy claim that Citadel timed it. Uh, that Sha Balour said Ken Griffin Citadel was pushing surprise rate hike fears just days before the AI trade collapsed and forced the forex levered situational awareness to unload its book near the lows.

On the other hand, Scott Milker said it's leverage, not conspiracy. "If you believe that Citadel intentionally crashed the market, that I have a bridge to sell you on Mars. Citadel had the dry power to take advantage of the situation. That's it."

So I kind of want to start here before we go further into this. Rahm, you've talked a lot about momentum. You've talked a lot about the current dynamics of the stock market. This has played into some of your previous themes. So what do you think happened?

Rahm 的分析：动量、风控与硅谷回声室

Yeah, I don't think Citadel did anything uh nefarious here. Uh, when Micron reported the stock sold off double digit percentage points. That same thing happened last quarter when Micron reported momentum was three standard deviations uh bid that came undone. We saw tremendous volatility in the South Korean stock market. Uh and Leopold the PM was just drinking his Kool-Aid way too much.

It actually reminds me of the blowup of Asymmetric which is long Solana and short ETH. Those are like the same trade on leverage. Very similar kind of concept. Um, he's a young 24 year old kid. I don't think people should uh um I don't think people should exclude him from the industry. I mean he's learned and he's accomplished quite a bit here.

Uh, but that kind of positioning is reckless though. Like that's not a good portfolio. Basic stress testing capabilities would have identified this — like where were the adults in the room? Where was the AI based stress testing and scenario analysis?

Um, I think he's also just too close to Silicon Valley. You know, his now new wife uh was the chief of staff or is the chief of staff at Anthropic. So he's so close to he can't see outside the AI bubble.

LPs 的损失结构

Um, the LPs in this got hurt a lot. It seems to be the case that the year-to-date gain comes almost exclusively from the Anthropic position. If you mark that to market, that's not much of a gain. You know, publicly listed closed-end funds that contain Anthropic or trade at discounts to par value of double digits.

So a major blowup and a lot of the new money I would speculate here came in in the last three months because that's what happens — people subscribed when the money goes up. Uh and those liquid positions were novated to Citadel on a margin call on a distress basis. So they probably lost their principle on that liquid book and that new money didn't get the benefit from Anthropic.

So imagine this. Imagine in June you get a month-end statement saying you're up a gazillion %. I guess it was like 200%, some large number. Um, you're looking forward to the wedding invitation and of course he's invited all his LPs to the wedding. It's a big celebratory moment and now everyone shows up a week before — they got a liquidation notice and they're saying "can you please contribute to our next fund and we're going to have a breakout session to talk about the future of AI."

There's so many angles to the story too. By the way, the seed investors were the Stripe, the Collison brothers — $200 million they put into this — Daniel Gross and others. Uh, so just a fascinating story, lessons learned all around.

Alex Thorne：技术性 vs 基本面 — AI 基建仍在早期

So one of the things that I have looked at in these situations is you've got to look at the price dynamics and the underlying market fundamentals differently from each other to figure out where things go from here.

Right. One move, we saw this with Archegos in the past, is you have something levered that blows up and it still continues functioning. The market is fine. It's just somebody levered got carried out on a stretcher. These things happen. On the other hand, you could have situations where the underlying market itself is breaking down. I don't need to tell anybody here stories about 2008 and where leverage collapsing ended up there.

So Alex, I know you guys have some involvement in this space. Can I ask you — among things you're allowed to talk about — what are you fundamentally seeing in AI world right now, data center land, all of those sorts of things?

Alex: Yeah, I would call this 80% technical and 20% fundamental. Um, you have to think — some of the, it's not just the recent you know unwind or you know whatever you want to call it, what's happening in the memory and and data center trade the last month or so, also what happened on the run-up was probably a lot to do with situational awareness as well. The percentages of like every major public equity involved in this.

Um, but if you look at the big four hyperscalers they're still guiding big capex spend growth. Um, even if the growth operator is monitoring, I think we still see substantial demand for new AI buildout which is you know important for everyone and all of our uh portfolios. But also um I think very clearly now especially with the increase in cyber um needs for AI, I really don't think we're close to the to the you know supply hitting the demand for compute and for data centers.

Um, we may be sort of in the end of the second or so and so a little bit of a pause and uh you know a brief repric — I think makes some sense. I mean if you recall just think about how uh how far we've come since just last December. You know I think a lot of people left and and went on sort of holiday vacation, found out about coding agents literally like the last week of December. I know I basically did although I'd been using ChatGPT and Claude for you know research and writing a little bit for at least a year before that.

Um, came back in January, by February you know people are coding, by you know the spring we're in a full-on panic slash euphoria about the impact that AI will have. Now you've got frontier models like Methos that are blocked by the government, but you've also got open-source models like Kimi and GLM that are almost as good and everyone is using.

So um I think we've still just scratched the surface. And from the from the energy and um you know compute buildout side, you know, it's hard to know. You're going to see — it reminds me of the internet bubble. It also reminds me of um some of crypto like from 2016, right? People said 2017 was blow-off top. You know, today we're you know 3-plus-x higher than the 2017 top in Bitcoin. And you know the internet — well, like, that exuberance was real earlier this year on AI, but um we haven't actually gotten to a steady state uh that we think is coming. I think there's a lot more demand and again if you look at the big hyperscalers, like they're not blinking an eye here on the demand that they see and the money they need to spend on this buildout.

Chris Perkins：早期市场 + 杠杆 = 剧烈波动

100%. I'll chime in. Um, this is a young market. We're not entirely sure where how things are going to level out. It's super early and when you have something so early um volatility is very much to be expected. And when you pour leverage on top of volatility, which works in both directions — I don't want to say it's not surprising, but it's kind of not surprising that you have the outcome here with situational awareness.

And all of us have gray hair because we spent years on Wall Street and and like blowup after blowup. You know, what do you do? You go back to your stresses, you go back to your VaRs, you calibrate your risk. You know, if you come into this as a 24 year old with a background in tech, you know, you hope that you surround yourself with some of those gray hairs who have that experience in risk management — maybe that was a gap that will be expected.

Uh, I think the thesis is directionally correct, but it's early and super volatile. I think it's going to get more volatile. I mean, experts are projecting that we're going to have AGI as early as 2030. Do you not think there's going to be massive volatility leading up to that and after that? It's going to happen. So, um, lesson learned. Not the first, not the last. Um, it'll happen again and again.

群体讨论：Halo 效应、AI 与投资、风控

Austin: How wild is it that he took on leverage like a den and everyone had this halo effect around him and were just shoveling money to subscribe. They thought he was the oracle and it like he was doing what the South Koreans are doing. Actually, even more so.

That means that attackers with compute that know this vulnerability can go and use that random number generator that it did end up using and compute billions of public keys — then go and private keys, seeds, seed phrases and then derive the public keys across the whole derivation space and then go and see if any of them have coins, and if they do — bam, submit transactions to move those coins to new locations.

And, you know, they might not be as much a Bitcoiner as you if you're rolling a hundred dice to introduce your own entropy into your Cold Card, you know, MK5. Um, but that's okay. That is okay. You know, this is your money. If you don't feel strong that you have the uh education and training to do self-custody, um don't and don't feel bad about that.

I think it's totally fine. You know, I use River.com all the time as a Bitcoin uh exchange. It's a great Bitcoin brokerage. Um, I've got accounts at most of the big exchanges and custodians. I bought and held Bitcoin at Fidelity Digital Assets. You know, I own ETFs, right? So, like, all of that is fine.

I think in the near and medium term you absolutely are going to continue to see uh people move towards those, and I agree. Look, they have a checkered history — crypto exchanges — of catastrophic failure. Um, but again, it's sort of like the nuclear uh power plant thing. You know, was Chernobyl a nuclear power plant thing or was that Soviet mismanagement? Was FTX fundamentally like a crypto exchange thing or was that a criminal named Sam Bankman-Fried? Right. I do think with strong regulation and oversight and industry standards, centralized intermediaries can be very safe and are demonstrably very safe.

监管过的中介 vs 无中介理想

Rahm: I have to pile in on the regulated front — the one area where FTX had a truly regulated subsidiary, which is FTX Japan, they didn't lose any money, right?

Chris: US2 or LedgerX. Do you name any US?

Rahm: Yeah, LedgerX. That's a great call. And by the way, on the ETF front, like Chris, I'm just shooting from the hip here, but EZBC, do you know anything about that thing? But I was going to make the point — like, have you lost any Bitcoin to this hack?

Chris: Personally, no.

Rahm: No. Well, no. Franklin, right? Like, no. No. No. So, like I think the point is, and I think Eric Balchunas has made it, um, look, we've said this over and over again, um, you shouldn't be forced to use an intermediary. I think we all agree on that.

Alex: Yes.

Chris: But I think we also agree that intermediaries do deliver certain value and there's going to continue to be a desire to use intermediaries by certain parts — probably the preponderance of the population — because you get value added services. Um, and so like you know DeFi maxis can be DeFi maxis but remember, like, what did we learn? You're still placing trust in something or somebody even if you're trying to be, you know, self-custody. You're trusting that software. You're trusting that provider. You know, I tend to hope that Alex is right and these MPC players are secure, but you're trusting them.

So, um, you know, you have to choose at the end of the day: who do you want to trust? Do you want to trust an intermediary that's well capitalized? Do you want to choose an intermediary that's insured or not? And I think we all agree on this, you know, because we've been in this space for so long — the government shouldn't tell you what to do. You should make that choice and it should be an informed choice.

多重签名与信任分层

Alex: Yeah, I totally agree. And it's not just like the random number generator in this hardware wallet. Like you are trusting — making different trust assumptions depending on how and where you store your coins, right? Like it's true that at a centralized intermediary, they could have a catastrophic failure. It's also true that even if the random number generation and key generation in a hardware wallet's great, they could have a different error, right?

So, I mean, this is one reason why — if you — one reason why me personally, I'm not in the business of recommending uh ways to store Bitcoin, but um I like the multi-sig collaborative custody where I hold some keys, a vendor that I pay uh holds some other keys and that gives me some peace of mind. I can lose a key or two of mine or they can go away and I can restore — they can't. Right? To me, and by the way this is I think as we know, this uh fundamentally is the way that regulated custodians basically also store, which is with multi-distributed multi-sig setups. Um, that they — those are available to individuals — they still may be too difficult for you, and that's okay.

机构心态：想要"一个可以起诉的人"

Rahm: Yeah, last point if I just make one more point. So we're in this institutional age of crypto. And when you unpack the institutional mindset, it really comes down to one thing. I want a throat to choke. I want to be able to sue somebody. That's what they'll tell you over and over again. "I don't care. Like I need somebody who's capitalized that I can sue." And I think there's value in that for many institutions. Um, so that's my last point about this segment.

Austin: Yeah. There are not institutions that are single-sig Cold Card. Well, that is not a thing. We hope.

Alex: And very few — I would say Fidelity and Coinbase I think are the — and maybe uh I guess Bitco doesn't have an ETF. Fidelity and Coinbase I think are the only two ETF uh — because well, Coinbase doesn't have one either.

Austin: Gemini —

Alex: Well, they don't have an ETF though. I guess Fidelity is I think maybe the only ETF that is self-custodying, but of course they themselves are an institutional custodian using all the sort of same principles as Coin. So most are — and I think at this point many if not most of the major Bitcoin ETFs in the US are using multiple custodians um for this reason again. So everyone's sort of making that same point.

And I think you know again, we — I typically do not go to you know defined contribution or defined benefit plans or high-net-worth individuals or liquid funds or family offices and suggest even that they self custody coins. Right? We're all suggesting qualified institutional custodians.

Austin：多元化是唯一的免费午餐

Austin: So another point that I would like to make here — because I've given this advice to my students actually about US regular way bank accounts — is the only free lunch in finance is diversification. And what I mean by that is always have multiply redundant options. Don't leave your stuff in one place because things that have nothing to do with you can break your [ __ ] if you do that.

If you only have one bank account and your bank goes bankrupt or something gets hacked or there's some sort of fraud that you had nothing to do with, which totally happens due to things like account compromise, all your money can get bricked until that gets fixed. You should always have a backup plan.

It's probably not a bad idea to extend that thinking into crypto, right? Like everybody, you're going to need to decide on your own personal situation, but I do not have all my Bitcoin in like one single ETF. I have it spread out amongst — for exactly this reason.

Alex: Yeah, I think Giannis — uh not going to try his last name — the NBA superstar Giannis from Greece, right?

Austin: Thank you.

Alex: Uh, he said in an interview once that he has his literal cash in American banks spread across like 50 banks. Yeah. He comes from a unique, you know — Greece has a unique history with banking and haircuts, right? Like, you know, the Cypress haircuts are literally why like the Winklevoss twins got excited about Bitcoin. Um, so I mean that's an extreme example, right? But I agree. I think it's great advice, Austin.

第三段：FOMC 与利率环境

会议结果与市场反应

All right, so final point on something that requires trust before we run out of time. The Fed.

So FOMC kept rates at 3.5 to 3.75. The vote was 9 to 3 uh with three people dissenting. Um, Kashkari spoke publicly about his — saying data center investments have added a new demand element to inflation. "I would rather tighten policy incrementally as we gather more data."

Uh, the long end's not thrilled here. It's pushed up into the 4.7s at the 10-year point as I talked about. We're going to pretend the 30-year is not looking even worse.

Um, and Lyn Alden said "bond bulls don't make arguments for why deflation is coming anymore. They just look at WSH like this now" and included the amazing meme from The Whale.

Alex：不确定的利率环境，没有 Fed put

So, Alex, while we've got you here — I know you talked to your friends at Galaxy about this frequently on your own podcast — but what are you making of the rates environment?

Alex: Oh man, it's the market. They're letting the market uh try to do it for them. Um, I think that's — there is no more Fed put, right? I mean, that's sort of the obvious empirical consensus. And are we in an era now of — I mean I'm starting to feel like this is a parliament at the Fed voting uh you know with many different ideas.

I think it's a very uncertain rate environment um is the simplest way to say it. You know, I declined not just for this reason at the end of last year — I said I was refusing to make a Bitcoin price call for this year. I'm quite happy I did refuse. I have to say I said it was a very uncertain investing environment. Not just because of AI or macro or the Bitcoin drawdown and the crypto bear market, but also because of rates. And to me, you know, I'm an observer but a relatively novice one, but um I don't know what to say here exactly.

And did you see um Scott Bessent's photo of the uh buying JPY — and Trump said on Air Force One that "why are we doing — we really love the Japanese, they've been really great to us except for that one time about Pearl Harbor-y." How to throw —

Austin: Yeah. And we're selling the euro, too, right?

Alex: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I think it's a very tricky environment and so far uh it looks like we're kind of getting less information from Powell as now is pretty clearly expected um than what we're used to and so the market has to react on its own.

Chris：市场自主定价可能是健康的

Chris: It may be healthy. I mean, it ultimately that may be a healthy option here. You know, I tend to lean free market and you know, I am a Bitcoiner. I am — I would say my sort of base position is to be a critic of the Federal Reserve.

Um, I think that this is in some ways although not necessarily the ones that matter to your pocketbook right now, you know, a little bit healthy to have the market sort of drive the rates a little bit more than the Fed. But um again, I'm not an expert in that. That's just my sort of sense.

And for years, the yen carry trade like really was one of the foundational parts of markets. We saw it, you know, we saw it get shocked um some months back. We saw markets puke because of it. I'm just hopeful now that traders are realizing that that's not here to stay forever. Uh and that they'll adjust.

That said, the Secretary of the Treasury wants to keep rates low. It's very much on his mind. We're also seeing more power move from the Fed to the Treasury. We've known this. And um look, if there's anyone who understands currency markets and uh it's our current Secretary of the Treasury. Um, you know, he was on board when they broke Bank of England. So I think he knows what he's doing.

Let's see how he plays it out. But um yeah, it's — how do you keep rates low? How do you stabilize and not shock markets through an abrupt uh unwind of the carry trade? And uh how do we stay uh onwards and upwards?

Rahm：Fed 问责、前瞻指引与"茶叶叙事"回归

Rahm: I like Kevin's message creating accountability for the Fed. He's right to point out that the Fed has missed its aim. We've been well above 2% for over five years. So, he's saying the right — but he's not really cutting rates. The bond market is doing the work itself on the long end of the curve.

Um, on forward guidance, we'll have to see how this plays out. This element, I'm not sure, right? Because you may have other Fed members that do in — if Kevin Warsh uh provide less feedback, right? The market's going to make a reaction function for the Fed anyway, even if it's imperfect.

What used to happen before forward guidance — I remember this distinctly — go to these conferences, there'd be some connected party that knows someone at the Fed or in the FOMC, and everyone would gather around the fireplace and they would tell the story about how they're reading the tea leaves. It's kind of similar to the world before Reg FD — buy-side investors who have access to sell-side analysts and could front run research and exploit — take advantage. The is that people have privileged access have an advantage over other investors.

收尾

Austin: All right, so Rahm thank you for closing us out. I've got to stop us here because we have a couple of hard halts at 5:30 today.

So, for everybody listening, remember to subscribe to the new channels. Thanks for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. Special thanks to Alex for joining us to discuss these topics today. We appreciate it, man. And for everybody else, we'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding.

Until then, thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

Hey, hey,

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Cold Card 事件与 Leopold 爆仓，其实是同一种"熵坍缩"
表面上，一个是硬件钱包的密码学漏洞，一个是 24 岁天才的 AI 基金爆仓，风马牛不相及。但把两者叠在一张图上，会发现它们共享同一个致命机制——**"熵源退化"**。
Cold Card 的 bug 是：本应流经真随机数发生器的密钥生成，因为一根"线接错了"，静默地退回到低熵源，于是数十亿种可能坍缩成攻击者可暴力枚举的空间。Leopold 的组合是：本应分散在多个不相关因子上的风险，因为都押在 AI 叙事这一个"变量"上，同样静默地退回到单一熵源——一个 Micron 财报的坏消息就足以让整个组合坍缩。
**真正的教训不是"要用好钱包"或"要做风控"，而是：任何声称"我很随机 / 我很分散"的系统，都要问一句——你的熵到底从哪里来？谁在审计这个熵源？** 五年没人发现 Cold Card 的问题，因为大家假设"它当然是随机的"；LPs 五个月里给 Leopold 加杠杆，因为大家假设"这些股票当然是不同的赌注"。假设，就是熵的敌人。

item.title: [Lex Clips] How the Civil War ended | Gary Gallagher and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正结束战争的不是军事胜利，而是一个"谢林点"

请注意转录里一个被轻描淡写、但极其反常的事实：李将军投降时，南方仍有数万人处于武装状态。按纯军事逻辑，战争根本没结束。但"virtually on both sides"都认定它结束了。

这不是军事事件，而是博弈论里最经典的焦点均衡（Schelling point）：当所有参与者都在寻找一个"大家都会认为对方也会认同"的信号来停止行动，李的投降就成了那个共同注视的坐标。Jefferson Davis 是唯一没读懂这个信号的人——不是因为他更有战斗力，而是因为他在协调博弈中掉队了。

这里藏着一个反直觉的教训：战争的物理终结和心理终结从来不是同一件事。同样的模式在软件系统崩溃、婚姻破裂、公司倒闭中反复出现——真正的"死亡时刻"是所有相关方在心里同时勾选的那个瞬间，而不是最后一行代码 / 最后一份文件 / 最后一颗子弹。

二、Grant 让南军带马回家——这其实是 19 世纪版的"马歇尔计划"

大多数人记住 Appomattox 会想到剑、旗、正式仪式。但 Gallagher 反复强调的那个细节——让骑兵带马回家去春耕——才是这场谈判的真正天才之处。

跨领域连接：这在经济学上是一个生产要素保全（factor preservation）决策。Grant 直觉性地明白：如果你彻底剥夺战败者的资本存量（马 = 当时最重要的农业资本），你就制造了一个结构性绝望阶级，而结构性绝望是叛乱的种子。80 年后马歇尔计划做的是完全一样的事，只不过资本变成了工厂和港口。

更妙的是，这个决定在逻辑上违反了"无条件投降"的字面含义——你怎么能"无条件投降"却带走战争资产？Grant 用一个非常小的动作，把"惩罚性和平"重新定义成了"重建性和平"，而且他做得如此低调，以至于连宪法级的原则冲突都被绕过了。

这是一堂关于"制度性妥协的艺术"的大师课：真正会协商的人不改变规则的名字，只重写规则的内容。

三、被埋没的第三方主角：抗拒"胜利者的自然冲动"的那个人

转录后半段真正炸裂的部分不是 Grant 对 Lee 的宽容，而是——Grant 事后威胁辞职，来阻止自己的总统（Andrew Johnson）追杀 Lee。

想想这个画面：一个刚刚赢得战争的将军，把辞呈当作武器对准自己国家的最高领袖，只为保护昨天的敌人。

这里有一个让人意外的心理学观察：胜利后 6-12 个月，才是复仇冲动的高峰，不是战争期间。战争进行时，你忙着活下来；战争结束后，多巴胺退潮、代价开始清算、幸存者内疚翻涌成愤怒——Thaddeus Stevens 和激进共和党人的"惩罚还不够"叙事，就是这种时间差的完美症状。

跨领域连接：这和离婚后的诉讼周期、政权更替后的清算浪潮、创业公司被收购后的"胜利者内战"是同一个曲线。人类系统在从"战斗模式"切换到"共处模式"时，会经历一个反常的愤怒延迟爆发窗口。

所以 Appomattox 真正的英雄不是握手的两个人，而是那个愿意用自己的职业生涯去对冲"胜利者延迟愤怒"的中间制度。Lincoln 死后 Grant 单人扛住了这个窗口——如果他动摇一次，整个 Reconstruction 的可能性就会不同。

一个悖论：南北战争没有变成永久性的种族/地区宿仇，靠的不是伟大的和平条约，而是几个人在几个关键早晨拒绝做人性告诉他们做的事。这比任何宪法修正案都更脆弱，也更值得敬畏。

📝 转录文本

战争的终局：Atlanta、大选与不可逆的推进

Lex： How does the war end?

Gary： So clearly there's the turning point with Atlanta and Sherman's March, and the election of '64 is the — that drives the dagger in. I mean, there's no question but that the war will be pushed to the end, because Lincoln and Grant are in charge and they are not going to take their foot off the pedal. They're going to push it. So it's a question of time.

It drags on — still drags on another six months. Lee surrenders on April 9th. They lay down their arms on April 12th. There are still tens of thousands of Confederate soldiers under arms in different places. But it's a measure of how important Lee and his army were, that for everybody virtually on both sides, that's the end of the war.

Lee surrendered. There's no reason to push this any farther. And other surrenders came pretty quickly. Jefferson Davis was one of the few people who didn't figure that out. He thought something was still possible, but it wasn't. That was the end of the war. The final surrenders are over in June, and that's it. And everybody gets the same terms that Grant offered to Lee. His friend Sherman tried to do more, and they had to rein Sherman in and say, "You can't. No, you're a general, not a politician. You can't do this."

4月9日：Grant 如何对待战败的对手

Lex： So, can we talk about April 9th? I mean, this is a really important moment — of what Grant did in terms of how he treated the opposing army.

Gary： As I said earlier, he treated him the way that he knew that Lincoln wanted them treated. And it may be that Grant thought exactly the same thing. But I think this is a measure of how Grant was — a very — he's a soldier who knew his place. He has civilian superiors. Other generals didn't act that way. I know I'm beating up on McClellan — he's one. Joseph Johnston on the Confederate side is one. They didn't really defer to their civilian superiors. US Grant did.

And in this — this is one of those cases — he sent the rations. He didn't know that Confederates supplied their own horses. If you're a Confederate cavalryman, the government didn't buy a horse for you. You had to supply your horse. And if a horse got killed, you had to buy another one, or they'd make you an infantryman. When Grant found that out, he let them take their horses home with them. He said they'll need them for the planting and so forth.

He did everything in a generous way that you could reasonably think might happen in a situation like — it's still an unconditional surrender. You are surrendering. You're going home. You're not an army anymore. But nobody's going to prisoner-of-war camps. Nobody's doing those things. You lay your arms down. You lay your flags down. You lay your ammunition down. But that's it.

象征性举动与长期和平的地基

Lex： Yeah. But there's certain symbolic actions like this that can lay the groundwork for long-term peace.

Gary： Yes. He didn't demand that Lee give him his sword. He didn't do that. None of those kinds of things that you could have done.

Lex： Sorry to linger on it, but there's certain elements of humiliation that prevent long-term peace. I have to go back to Hitler and what Germany experienced at the end of World War I.

Gary： You mean Versailles — the terms from Versailles. No question about it.

Lex： Some of it is economics, some of it is geopolitics, but some of it is just on a basic human level — humiliation. And people are just not good with humiliation. They remember.

Gary： No. And they can turn that around into something you don't want it to be, to get back national pride.

But Lincoln's bottom line was: the point is to put the nation back together. And the good way to start that is not by imprisoning tens of thousands of Confederate soldiers. That's not the way to do it. Send them home. Make them accept the terms, but then send them home and leave them alone.

Grant 捍卫投降条款：宁愿辞职

The president wanted to go — after Lincoln's death, Andrew Johnson wanted to go after Lee — and Grant said, "I'll resign if you —" because his term — we extended the terms. He's abiding by the terms. You can't change the rules here.

But — like, it should be said — that's not easy to do. You have just fought an extremely bloody battle. There's hatred. There were lots of people who wanted Davis to swing and Lee to swing. Kill them. Execute the rebels. They're rebels and traitors who almost destroyed the nation. "Why are you being so easy on them?"

Thaddeus Stevens was on board that train. Lots of radical Republicans — "you need to punish them." "For what? You haven't punished them enough. You're not punishing them. Yes, you took slavery away from them, but that's not enough. They should be punished more for what they did."

Lex： Confiscate their lands. Take their wealth away from them.

item.title: [Business of Sport] “The Next 50m fans will come from outside the US” | Brett Gosper
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏在“扩张”背后的悖论：NFL不是在出海，而是在“出口稀缺性”

大多数人以为NFL国际化是在把美国产品卖给世界——错了。仔细看Brett的话：一年只在一个市场投一场“大石头入水”的比赛。这不是扩张，这是刻意的稀缺工程。

有意思的对照——奢侈品行业的爱马仕从不打折、限量发售铂金包，反而拉高品牌溢价。NFL在做同样的事：用地理上的稀缺替代时间上的稀缺。橄榄球本身17场常规赛已经是"稀缺产品"，现在他们把这种稀缺切成地理切片，让墨尔本、马德里、慕尼黑各自成为"一年一度的圣殿时刻"。

真正让我震惊的是：NFL宁可放弃在伦敦设立第五队的机会（那意味着立即增加大量收入），也要保住这种"一年一次的仪式感"。因为他们算得清——一场稀缺的比赛，创造的品牌溢价大于50场常规供应。这是极少数敢于"不最大化短期收入"的体育联盟。

二、意外发现：NFL其实是在偷偷学Formula One，而不是相反

Brett自己提了一句"Formula One is in that model in many ways"——这句话被访谈匆匆带过，但它揭示了一个惊人的方向颠倒。

传统叙事里，F1一直被视为在向美国体育（尤其NFL）取经，学习娱乐化包装、学习Netflix《Drive to Survive》式的叙事经济。但仔细看NFL的国际战略——每年一站、每站变成城市级事件、大石头入水的涟漪效应、把比赛变成"一整个周末的城市庆典"——这不就是F1大奖赛的模板吗？

跨领域连接：这其实是"巡回赛制"（tour circuit）逻辑对"主客场制"（home-and-away league）逻辑的悄然入侵。歌剧、马戏团、TED大会、Coachella音乐节——所有这些"稀缺-巡回-仪式化"的商业模型，在数字时代反而击败了"密集-常规-流量化"的模型。NFL国际化的深层含义是：当供给可以无限复制时，稀缺+在场感成了唯一的护城河。

三、最反直觉的洞察：他们改造的不是市场，是浴室

这个访谈里最耐人寻味的细节，藏在一段几乎被当作笑话的对话里——为了让NFL球队打客场，他们要拆掉伯纳乌和安联球场的更衣室重新布管、加淋浴、砸墙。

这看起来是段趣闻。但停下来想想它的符号学意义：世界上最伟大的足球圣殿——皇马的伯纳乌、拜仁的主场——为了迎接一场一年一度的NFL比赛，愿意让美国人重新给他们的球队更衣室通水管。

这不是租赁，这是基础设施殖民的软性版本。而且是被邀请的殖民。

跨领域连接：这和苹果早期做零售店时的策略惊人相似——乔布斯坚持苹果店必须自建，因为"店铺本身就是产品的延伸"。NFL发现了一个类似真理——体育产品不止是场上90分钟，而是从更衣室水管到观众席infinity screen的整个物理空间。他们不是把"比赛"运到欧洲，而是把"NFL体验"这个物理系统整体空投过来。

更深的隐藏系统真相：Brett说的"我们不设神圣不可侵犯的传统"（fewer sacred cows），配上"欧洲球迷更保守更纯粹主义"的评论，其实指向一个体育产业的根本裂变——欧洲卖的是历史，美国卖的是体验。而在一个注意力越来越稀缺的时代，可复制、可升级、可娱乐化的"体验"，正在慢慢吞噬不可复制、不可扩容的"历史"。

那些愿意让NFL来砸墙加淋浴的欧洲豪门，其实已经在无意识中承认了这一点。

It's kind of back to the scarcity piece on games — if you're not selling absolutely everything that's potentially available to you, you create more value when the opportunities do arise.

That's it. That's it.

It's hugely important for us. And in the social media area, we're working with our athletes all of the time, giving them materials, teaching them how to use social media in the right way, and so on. Do they do it independently?

从 World Rugby 到 NFL

You came for as Chief Executive of World Rugby, right? It must have been a fascinating transition — the different types of sporting environments and how these organizations work, particularly as we've said with the American model at the center of this.

Yeah, it was very different. A federation is very different to a league to begin with. So it's hard to compare them.

In what way, just for people?

A federation is very oriented towards participation, because a lot of their local federations get funding from governments because of how many people are competing in or participating in that sport in their country. It's very regulatory. Almost most of these federations began as legal entities to regulate the game. So they don't really think about the fan aspect or the fan engagement aspect. And I think World Rugby transitioned during the period I was there — not saying I was the only one driving it, but very much transitioned from regulation as a priority to inspiration a lot more.

It's a much more fragmented sport, because you've got different entities managing — you've got Six Nations, you've got leagues, you've got — so you can't do everything that you want to do. Whereas the NFL is a hermetically sealed business operation, laser-focused on fan growth.

And to be fair, in all the meetings, there's rarely conversations about money. It's all about fans. What can we do to please them? What can we do to engage them? What can we do to bring them in? And people know that that's going to show up as revenue at some point.

It's a very different environment. And I said to you before: in many ways, I'd have done a better job, I think, as CEO of World Rugby had I done this job before. Because I think the understanding and the sophistication with which they go about fan acquisition and pleasing their fans is second to none. And it's been a great school for me, even at my late age.

球迷参与

Every football team, sport, speaks about fan engagement, saying they haven't cracked it, because they don't know their fan. Has the NFL cracked fan engagement — that relationship — in a way that football teams haven't?

I don't know if even the NFL would say we've cracked it, but they are cracking it. It's an ongoing process. You never feel that you've quite got it. Have you got enough fans in your database? Are you talking to them in the right way? Are they transacting with you? Where's the bridge between those fans that you're collecting data for and the ones actually watching and viewing who are actually generating 70 to 80% of your revenue? So, no, I don't think the NFL's got everything worked out, but they certainly know where they're headed and know what they're looking for. And I think that's probably where they've got to advance on maybe a lot of other entities.

可以复制到其他运动的部分

Having had the experience that you had outside of the NFL — I've talked about the obsession that we often have in transition, trying to take out the bits — what bits do you think you could lift from seeing how successful this business has been into a sport like rugby, into a sport like football, to bring in some of that value? Recognizing that it is a very different environment to how this American system is operating.

I just think it's having a fan-first view of everything. Every time you suggest an idea or generate one, it's with the fan in mind. And it's that obsession on making sure — sort of like in a consumer business being client-centric or customer-centric or consumer-centric or whatever. Everything we do at the NFL is about: what's that going to mean for the fan? How's that going to translate as the fan enjoying that, liking it, wanting to pay more for it, wanting to pay something for it, and being involved with it? It's more the prisms through which you look, and then that generates the ideas and the thinking.

举例：定价与文化差异

What's an example in another sport where a fan is not put first for the benefit of a business, just for people listening — for me genuinely?

Ticket pricing. Ticket pricing is the thing that comes up a lot, particularly in football. But the flip side of that — which is where the US-size supply and demand — you have a huge demand for a lot of these matches live in attendance. Could you raise the price? Yeah, of course you could. But at the same time you're likely then to get far more people coming in for a game from, let's say, a tourism perspective than you are from getting the hardcore fans who have been there for 30 years. That is a trade-off that you have to make a decision on.

You also have a different sort of fan in America as well though.

And what do you mean by that?

I think there's a fan in America that wants to be sold to, that wants those opportunities, wants those choices. But I think sometimes the fan in Europe is a little bit more conservative and a little bit more purist — I'm exaggerating to make a point — "this is about the sport, this is about, why are they selling me this?" So you're dealing with a conservatism to a certain extent in the landscape in Europe that aren't used to the commerciality that perhaps an American fan demands — not just sees but actually expects. That's a different environment.

Yeah. A perfect — sorry, you asked for an example — I guess you could say a really good example of that question, "where was the fan first?" — the halftime show at the World Cup. Is that for a football fan? Football is just built so differently to the concept of maybe halftime shows.

Well, I'd love to ask the American audience what they thought of the halftime, because it definitely rubs up — a halftime show as a concept almost in football ruffles feathers a bit. Generally in sport, we hate change, right? People just don't enjoy change in these — but it's particularly change in the pure. So I have this argument all the time with the 100 with cricket. Cricket fans will come to me and go, "oh I hate the 100 and it's not cricket." So have you been? "No, I've refused." It's like, well, genuinely — how can you comment? I saw last night on the TV you had pretty full Oval for a 100 game on a Sunday night. I'm thinking, wow, that's incredible. So they're finding their own register of entertainment and sport and getting that balance right — but for each audience.

You've got to get the balance right. If you go too far one way, then you'll lose your audience.

美国色彩 vs 本地化

But that's what I'm saying: you in a way have the hardest job because does the non-US audience automatically buy into all of that because it's from the US?

Yes, is the answer. We're given a license that's broader than the traditional European sports to do something which is not as traditional. So in many ways this is a bit of an experiment area for the NFL as well in what they can do and what they can put on in other markets. But there's a license to do as you do in America here, and people come for that. If you turned up to an NFL game in London or Paris and it wasn't like an NFL game in nature like the US, you'd feel, "I've missed out. This is not what I came for. I'm short changed."

But at the same time we try and also create some local personality around what we do, and acknowledge some things which link us and make us more culturally relevant in that market.

场馆基础设施

It pains me to say it as a Chelsea fan, but the Tottenham stadium is incredible, right? For lots of different reasons, but the NFL element planning for the hosting of games was such a huge part of what this stadium offers. Do you think tying in and integrating the opportunities to host these games starts to influence infrastructure plays across Europe? So Spurs now — they have a fantastic NFL-suitable, ready stadium.

It's an NFL stadium. It's the only NFL stadium purpose-built in Europe. Therefore, I'm looking at the value of Spurs total collective — that's significantly gone up because I am capable of hosting. I'm now associated with the biggest sporting league in the world. And I think that's why it's a good partnership with Tottenham. They get something out of it, we get something out of it. And it's a very, very strong partnership. And it's a fabulous stadium for us to perform our games in.

And across Europe? Well, you have to — each city you have to go to where you feel the experience is going to be best for our consumers.

Have you ever walked up to one and thought, "oh no"?

We've walked up to a lot of those, well, we've usually not chosen them though for that reason. We're very careful. We have a football operations group that go in and work out viability, we work out the attractiveness of playing in that stadium. We also work out what's a good relationship to have with the people who occupy. So Real Madrid is probably the biggest club in football worldwide in terms of its fan base. You play at the Bernabéu. We play at the Bernabéu. So we played the Bernabéu for the first time last year, we'll play again this year. We play in the Bayern Munich stadium — it was the first time a non-football event was held; had to be voted by the Munich parliament.

So these have got to be steady, because we do quite a bit of work on them to make sure the changing rooms are big enough, because you've got 53 —

What needs to change?

Mainly changing rooms. You've got 53 — the non-playing elements of the touring party don't fit into a normal football dressing room, let alone the players themselves. So you've normally got to re-plumb, knock down a few walls, put in more showers.

Are you serious?

Yeah, you've got to re-plumb.

You've got to re-plumb?

You re-plumb to put more showers in. But you do that, you hope you come back the next year and you amortise that.

And they're okay with you doing that?

Not at first, but then they generally come. Yeah, we do ask. We're very polite.

Can you imagine a football team coming back in and going, "where are some showers?"

Exactly. We see it as helping them improve their infrastructure. "Mel the kit man — I was here for 20 years and the NFL came." That's right. Well, no, the good thing about it is it's only expanding it. It's not taking anything away from the club, right? It's not taking anything away from the culture. That's extraordinary. And also, it's a little bit of a promise we'll be back.

And anything else? The changing rooms get bigger — anything else?

Changing rooms get bigger. You've usually got to extend the field a few metres at each end. Playing surfaces are all a big discussion point and so on.

未来的基础建设逻辑

Which was really — sorry, I mean, I guess poorly asked, but that was part of the previous question of: now when you have big new infrastructure builds, a core part of the business plans of major sporting powers in Europe, these stadiums will start to incorporate this in the hope of being able to host these.

Totally, because it gives you the option. And you also need a certain sized spectator bowl because you want to pass the break-even and start to make it —

What's the pass-the-break-even?

You probably need 60,000-plus, really.

60,000?

Yeah, you probably need that sort of audience.

Oh, poor Stamford Bridge.

So that's probably the kind of — we've done it in less, but generally you want to be around the 60. Also for the fan experience — you want to be in a big stadium as well.

What stadium have you never done it in that you would love to do it in?

The MCG. But it's going to happen. Yeah, that'll be — MCG is going to happen in September.

So that must be a special moment for you?

Well, I'm from Melbourne, so it actually is quite a special moment. But it's also again — quite in that town, it's the heartbeat of the city, and it's just a big — 100,000 people.

You won't need to expand the pitch much on there, will you? That's a nice thing.

It's a different footprint, completely different footprint. But they play rugby tests and FIFA qualifications there and stuff. So it'll be brilliant. But that would have been my wish had it not already been granted, but it hasn't happened, so that's the one.

But suddenly now you can go, "okay, Italy — that could be a challenge now," just because the infrastructure in Italy famously has been challenging.

They're renovating some stadiums and all of that, so that's all possible in the future. Exactly. Oh yeah. But it's pretty big — you can tie that in now as you look at this, be ambitious with some of those stadia. Going, "well, Real Madrid, they were in renovation when they contacted us about, you know, we'd like to make this NFL-fit." And so, although things needed to be done after they finished, they were kind of swimming in the right direction when they did their renovations on that. It's an incredible stadium, the Bernabéu.

Oh, the new one? Someone landed a spaceship right in the middle of Madrid. Have you seen it?

橄榄球球迷 vs NFL 球迷

I was thinking then just about rugby stadiums and experience. Have you seen — is it too simple to say that just the nature of the sports maybe (being like that high contact, high intensity, heavy) — have you seen a crossover of fan bases being a slightly easier one for you to capture, of those fans really keen to engage with the NFL having some form of rugby?

Yeah, look, I mean we often get that. Because you don't have that in Germany, for example — you've just got football, and then there's — and actually probably top three handball. But probably NFL's probably the next in broadcast views. It's in the top three in that market, which is not in many other markets outside of the US, other than Canada, Mexico perhaps.

And people ask the question about France, for example. They say, "but actually find it hard to get, because rugby's so big there." We say, "yeah, but it's big in England too — it's not a problem in England." So there's no — in a way, it's not "if there's rugby, you're more likely to do well." If there's not rugby, I don't think there's a real difference. I tend to think it helps because I think rugby people who are into rugby are interested and curious. They may not be a major fan, but they're willing to look, because you can't not look at someone tackling and being tackled if you like rugby. But maybe it scratches the itch already, that you don't need American football to scratch. But it's a hard one. We don't have data on that, but I think that the barriers aren't there either way, whether there is or isn't rugby.

Brett 的个人球队与所有权结构

Did you come in as a fan of the sports when you started working, or was this quite a casual fan?

Yeah, I would have said I was a casual fan. I had a team, I watched it a bit, but I was that ensconced in rugby, that didn't have that much room for other sports in winter anyway, even football to a certain extent.

And have you found yourself from a professional, now going like, "wow"?

I'll always be an avid — if I left the NFL this week, I'd continue to be an avid fan of NFL.

Do you support one in NFL? Can't say?

No, I actually can. Unless you're the commissioner, he can't. But everyone in the mix has one. I'm actually, unfortunately, a Jets — a New York Jets — supporter. I say unfortunately because they haven't won a lot recently.

Who owns the Jets?

Woody Johnson owns the Jets — Johnson and Johnson. So he was an ambassador — US ambassador — to the UK for a period. And it's the Johnson family that own the Jets. But I was a rugby player and we toured America — I was playing with the Racing in Paris, and we toured America, and they did a big article in the New York Times on the Racing coming to New York, and they said they're like the Jets. Don't know why, but I thought, "I'm going to support the Jets."

私募股权与所有权

The ownership structure around it — I don't know how much you get exposed to it or you expose a lot to it — a fascinating side of it, right? Especially in one sport where, for example, private equity was only allowed to invest in it for the first time a few years ago. You've got all 32 owners are US owners traditionally. It's been families that have had these organizations. What's strong about that?

Stability, longevity of decision-making. And that shared revenue also means we're all in the same bath and we're going to row in the — it's a bad analogy, "I'm rowing in the bath." In some extended change rooms.

But they make their decisions, as you say, in that group. They come together in committees about four times a year — twice a year all 32 in the same room. And you go and you present in front of that audience. It's quite nerve-wracking. In front of all of them? There's not a room like it. So each club in those meetings bring in three people usually, two owners, one CEO or whatever. But when you present to that group, and I've presented over the years to a lot of different groups, you do have your heart in your throat, because it's an impressive bunch of very successful people.

How do you prepare for that?

Just with anxiety and trepidation. But you prepare — that's the point. You prepare, and the league office is managing those meetings, and they're running the show, and who's presenting what, and what are we selling and what are we telling. It's quite a production of all the presentations, the speeches.

All of that that you've had to do as a top executive — what was the one that you generally felt the most —

Oh, the worst I had to do was to sell a leasing agreement that the Jags had done with Wembley. And I kept saying, "I'm not a leasing guy, I'm not a leasing guy." "No, no, you're the man, you're going to go in and tell them exactly what this leasing agreement was all about," because all of the leasing agreements of all the clubs had to pass through the league office. So that was one that I prepared every inch, that anyone was going to ask me any questions about the leasing agreement between the Jags and Wembley. But no one asked the question, unfortunately.

私募股权是否好事

Do you think opening up to private equity is good for the NFL?

It must be, because they voted for it, and that's what the collective wanted and that's what they voted for — because these things are voted upon.

You've got a timeline which is very different. Suddenly you've got a six or seven year timeline rather than a generational timeline for a family and so on. But these are small percentages of the ownership — ensuring that basically you could never lose any of the control. Exactly, control and management is retained and the influence retained.

Well, we have a 20 billion dollar team in 10 years' time — very possible.

Yeah, I just thought that was possible. But again, I'm not a financial expert. If you go to the revenue right — again, how do you value these entities in the first place? You highlighted the opportunities that continue to exist both in a domestic market — and being lazy saying "oh it's saturated domestically," it's not at all. You're making — maybe from a fan but not commercially. Not commercially. Then that price can keep going up.

Because, hey, at the moment sports teams on the whole, whether rightly or wrongly, and a lot of people have opinions on this, are generally valued on multiples of revenue. So the Cowboys — I think the Cowboys generate the most of any sports team, just ahead of Real Madrid, revenue-wise. But it's interesting on that side — I mean, I always think on sport it's fascinating because you have these massive global brands, but as revenue businesses they're actually nowhere near the size of their brand. I mean, the Cowboys did just over a billion last year, Real Madrid the same. But you think about the brand — the brand seems like it's much more influential.

It's incredible. Scarcity value has to keep coming back into it. Now you get a chance to own part of an NFL franchise — it's part of the attraction.

快问快答

Quick fire.

Yeah, go for it.

What's the single best experience you've had in the stadium?

I think the opening/closing — you know I'm going back in time here — opening and closing ceremony of the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics.

Wow. There you go. Why?

Just because it was creative, directed by Steven Spielberg for a start, so you know it's going to be good. But it was just the most incredibly creative and entertaining opening and closing of Olympic Games I've seen — quite a few of those.

Sporting?

I think — I'm going to entertainment more than sporting here — but the London opening ceremony was fabulous too. The London Olympic ceremony in 2012 was extraordinary.

如何向欧洲初学者介绍 NFL

So you're taking NFL, you're talking about NFL to someone in Europe that's never seen it before, that doesn't know what it is. If you're trying to say the reason why someone should watch it or be engaged with it, what would you say?

I think the athletes mainly. I don't think there are better athletes in the world — every aspect of athleticism you're going to see in a game of American football that you might not see in other sports is the first thing I'd say.

I'd also say it is an acquired taste, and you have to understand a certain amount. So if you're not allowing yourself to understand the mere basic of it, you're never going to get fully into it. But just allow yourself to get into that first step: you've got four attempts to get 10 metres — it's yards in America, 10 yards.

But yeah, so I wouldn't lead with a halftime show, because I think that's the cherry on the cake.

Did the NFL, with expansion in mind, put any like additional budget or whatever to creating a content series — like YouTube videos etc — around explaining the NFL?

We do all of that. Whether it be on the big screen in those games that are played internationally, whether it be on YouTube, there are all sorts of — not titled the Dummies Guide, but the Beginners Guide or whatever — to getting into America. We do a lot of that, and it's important. And flag football is going to help that a lot too, because that's going to become far more ubiquitous, and that will help people just see, "oh I see — every time they throw it and they gain yards, they get another chance to do that," and so on. It's very simple in that sense. Once you get past that gate, everything else becomes interesting learning.

橄榄球 vs NFL：谁能跨界？

Who would do better: an American football player playing rugby, or a rugby player playing American football?

Probably the American footballer playing rugby is my view, because we've seen a lot of rugby players try to break into the NFL and have not succeeded in doing that. It's very difficult. It's very technical. It doesn't look it maybe to the outside of it.

No, it doesn't.

It's very complicated. Christian Wade, lots of these players who are magnificent athletes — they did well, but they didn't break into it at the level that they did with rugby. You don't see it happening the other way so much because the money's too big. Which schmuck's leaving there? The river flows more that way — that's your daily salary, yearly. Oh my god. So your changing room's so small.

You can see so many American athletes, whether it be wide receivers, running backs, offensive linemen, whatever. They all find their spot in rugby in a significant way, I think.

So do you think those core skills — a Louis Rees-Zammit, let's say, for the technical, physically incredible speed, obviously has to have the strength to play certain positions — but if you're looking at that technicality piece, it's very hard —

You never say impossible. It's very hard to pick up that technicality if you haven't grown up with it. Exactly. These kids are baked through high school, through college, and then into the NFL. And just turn up — and we've got an international player pathway, we're trying to create these athletes, and some of them do make it through. They tend to be the less technical positions and they do break through, and they spike interest in the countries where those people come from, and so on — which is why we do it.

And we have an academy in the UK for European young athletes to become European NFL players. Which over time some of them will. But generally it's not an easy task for that transfer to happen. And as a former rugby player and as a guy out of the rugby community, I thought it would be a much easier thing of "he's good, he'll do well there." It's not as easy as that.

Is having more international players come into the NFL a metric of success?

Yes, for us it is. We're trying to create more international — like the Premier League, like the NBA — it breeds interest in those markets those players come from. We've got a player, Jordan Mailata, who's with the Eagles, won Super Bowl a couple of years ago. He's one of the biggest stars in Australian sport. Everywhere he goes — we were with him in Australia a little while back — signing autographs, people coming to him in the street. He's huge as well, you can't miss him. But the effect he's had on fandom in Australia has been phenomenal.

So yes, we're looking for those international athletes, and not just to spike interest in those countries, because the NFL wants the best athletes in the world to be at the NFL. And so whether they come from the African region, the European region, Asia, whatever, we're on the lookout for those top athletes.

五年后的展望

Five years' time, what are going to be the top three countries for the NFL outside of US? And I say excluding Canada.

Germany for sure. Germany is on a huge growth spurt. We have incredible partners, media partners. Our office there is high-performing. But that market is quite obsessive about American football.

I think the UK will be the other market. And I think in European terms, probably France. It could be France or Spain, but I think France will embrace American football a lot more. They love their NBA, they love American sports. I think the rugby will probably on balance help them get into American football — to look at it and be interested by it. So I think that'll be the third market.

It tends to help when those markets are on time zones. Asia's more challenging for us because it's on a far more challenging time zone to watch American sport from American broadcast. The day will come, I think, when international is significant enough that we can move some of those windows in America to more favorable viewing times for other markets. That'll be the sign that international is really really growing in terms of its interest and revenue.

But as you said, for now, I mean, the power of just having the NFL means people will hopefully turn up, whether you put it on at 10:30am or 8pm.

Certainly in Australia, that's the case.

Well, to be honest, Australia lives on such strange time zones for most of their sport anyway that they're used to it, aren't they?

结束语

Brett, I've absolutely loved it. Thank you so much for giving us some of that insight into this world. It is amazing to actually have a proper chat about this rather than just referencing it all the time. So thank you for coming in.

Thanks for having me. Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、隐藏在“扩张”背后的悖论：NFL不是在出海，而是在“出口稀缺性”
大多数人以为NFL国际化是在把美国产品卖给世界——错了。仔细看Brett的话：一年只在一个市场投一场“大石头入水”的比赛。这不是扩张，这是**刻意的稀缺工程**。
有意思的对照——奢侈品行业的爱马仕从不打折、限量发售铂金包，反而拉高品牌溢价。NFL在做同样的事：**用地理上的稀缺替代时间上的稀缺**。橄榄球本身17场常规赛已经是"稀缺产品"，现在他们把这种稀缺切成地理切片，让墨尔本、马德里、慕尼黑各自成为"一年一度的圣殿时刻"。
真正让我震惊的是：NFL宁可放弃在伦敦设立第五队的机会（那意味着立即增加大量收入），也要保住这种"一年一次的仪式感"。因为他们算得清——**一场稀缺的比赛，创造的品牌溢价大于50场常规供应**。这是极少数敢于"不最大化短期收入"的体育联盟。
## 二、意外发现：NFL其实是在偷偷学Formula One，而不是相反
Brett自己提了一句"Formula One is in that model in many ways"——这句话被访谈匆匆带过，但它揭示了一个惊人的**方向
